The ongoing protests by members of the Indian Youth Congress (IYC) against Meta's content moderation practices in India have again put the tech major's practices questions about political bias, algorithmic transparency and the extent of government influence over online speech. The demonstrations by IYC workers in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram come amid an allegedly sharp increase in the volume of content restricted by Meta in India under local laws. The company restricted access to more than 5.44 Mn items on Facebook and Instagram between January and June 2026, compared with around 41,400 in the preceding six months, as per Meta's latest transparency disclosures. The surge represents a roughly 131-fold increase over the preceding six-month period, placing India among Meta's largest markets for government-mandated content restrictions. The restrictions covered several categories, including content relating to online gaming, synthetically generated material depicting prominent figures, threats to India's sovereignty and integrity, gender-based harassment and the promotion of enmity between groups. The data has put the spotlight on India's evolving regulatory framework for social media platforms, particularly the tightening of timelines for content removal and the growing use of automated systems to enforce government directions. The Controversy Protesters have alleged that Meta is selectively enforcing its content moderation policies and removing posts and accounts critical of the central government. The primary accusation against the US-based company is its bias towards Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Case in point was the removal or restriction of Instagram accounts linked to opposition figures. Congress has demanded an explanation for these actions as well as restoration of affected accounts. The opposition has also questioned the role of Meta's recommendation and moderation algorithms and sought clarity on identification and flagging of said political content. As per Meta, its content moderation framework combines automated detection systems, human review and enforcement of local legal requirements. However, when restrictions are imposed following government requests, users may not always have sufficient information about the authority behind a takedown or the specific legal provision invoked. This creates a transparency challenge. Meta has declined to comment on the protests and Congress' allegations of politically motivated restrictions. The company has maintained that it restricts content in India to comply with applicable local laws. Nevertheless, the scale of restrictions has intensified concerns about the potential for overblocking, where legitimate content could also become inaccessible because of automated enforcement. India's Laws Governing Social Media Takedowns India's social media content moderation framework is primarily governed by the Information Technology Act, 2000, and the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021. Under Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, intermediaries are required to remove or disable access to unlawful information after receiving a valid court order or a reasoned intimation from an authorised government officer. The provisions cover content that threatens India's sovereignty and integrity, national security, public order, friendly relations with foreign countries, or relates to defamation, contempt of court, decency and morality, among other grounds. The framework allows the government to direct platforms to restrict specific posts, URLs or other online content. Platforms are required to comply with these directions to retain the legal protections available to intermediaries under Section 79 of the IT Act. However, the government has also introduced additional safeguards and compliance obligations over the past year. In October 2025, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) notified amendments to Rule 3(1)(d), which came into effect on November 15, 2025. The amendments mandated that government takedown notices be issued by senior authorised officials and clearly specify the legal provision invoked, the nature of the alleged unlawful act and the exact URL or electronic identifier of the content to be restricted. They also introduced periodic reviews of government directions by senior officials to assess whether the restrictions remain necessary and proportionate. In February 2026, the government tightened the compliance timeline further. An amendment effective February 20 reduced the deadline for intermediaries to remove or disable access to specified unlawful content from 36 hours to just three hours after receiving a valid court order or reasoned government intimation. The shorter deadline has increased the pressure on platforms to maintain automated content detection and enforcement systems capable of responding to government directions within a narrow window.

'Our Super Bowl moment' - what can WSL learn from booming US league?
- Published
"It's turning into our Super Bowl moment."
Sarah Jones Simmer, chief operating officer of the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL), could not wait for the championship game between Washington Spirit and Kansas City Current on Saturday night.
The NWSL showpiece was played out in front of a sellout crowd of more than 19,000 at Audi Field in Washington DC, with tickets retailing at more than $300 (£229).
Ultimately, the Current triumphed 2-1 to clinch their first title, condemning Spirit to an unwanted record of three lost finals in a row.
Just a few hours earlier on this side of the Atlantic, Alexia Putellas, who last month was crowned the best player in the world for the third time at the Ballon d'Or ceremony, was scoring twice for London City against Crystal Palace in front of 4,000 people in Bromley.
It is a totally unfair comparison. After all, a championship final is the type of jamboree the USA does particularly well.
Nevertheless, women's football is booming in America at the moment, with attendance figures at record highs, more franchises joining the league and club retail sales double those of 2025.
So what is behind the explosion in popularity?
And what can the Women's Super League learn from it?
A unique history of popularity
The US is the most successful nation in women's international football.
The four-time World Cup winners (1991, 1999, 2015 and 2019) and five-time Olympic gold medallists, the nation of Mia Hamm, Alex Morgan and Megan Rapinoe, has a history of winning - and the domestic game is key.
"If anything, soccer is more seen as a women's sport [in the USA]," says broadcaster Jacqui Oatley, who currently commentates on the NWSL for ESPN.
"Women have won World Cups and Olympic Games - and the men have been nowhere near as successful."
While teams in the United States became professional in 2001 - for WSL teams it was 2018 - the top flight has taken several different guises over the years.
The current NWSL kicked off in 2013 as an eight-team competition, and has since expanded to 16 franchises, with two more joining from 2028.
There is no relegation and Kansas City's victory on Saturday means the league has had eight different winners since its iteration.
As the below graph shows, the ownership picture for these sides is far more varied than in the UK, with American sides much less dependent on their male counterparts.
Indeed, Kansas City are blazing a trail. Established in December 2020, unaffiliated to a men's side and backed by ambitious owners that include Brittany Mahomes - the wife of NFL quarterback Patrick Mahomes.
Winning the championship is the crowning achievement for an ambitious franchise and such success is something independent London City hope to emulate in the UK. They are four points from the WSL summit nearly halfway through the 2026-27 season.
Kansas City were also the first club to build a bespoke stadium solely for women's football and the demand for seats at their 11,500-seater CPKC Stadium is huge. Earlier this year, Brighton announced their own purpose-built venue, planned for 2030-31.
"I think our independence is a hallmark of the league," says the NWSL's Jones Simmer.
"It is something we are very proud of. It allows us to invest in our own growth, prioritise the women's game and ensure resources are flowing to it."
It is markedly different from the UK set-up, where all WSL teams bar London City are, at least, affiliated and more often financially reliant on the men's side.
But that presents just as much of an opportunity, according to Jones Simmer.
"I know Nikki [Doucet, chief executive of the WSL] and I admire what she is building," she says.
"There's a really unique opportunity to build on the legacy of these 100-year-old men's clubs that are household names, to build women's brands that embrace the legacy but also have their own identity."
- Bespoke women's football stadiums? Why US sides are making the move 
  - Published15 March
- Brighton plan Europe's first purpose-built £80m women's stadium 
  - Published28 April
An on-pitch product that delivers
Fans of both the NWSL and the WSL are spoiled when it comes to talent.
Most of the US national team play their club football at home, with the likes of Trinity Rodman, Mallory Swanson and Rose Lavelle household names.
International stars such as Malawi's Temwa Chawinga at Kansas City, who came 10th in the 2026 Ballon d'Or rankings, and former Chelsea striker Sam Kerr further enhance the league's quality.
"Where it starts is the product on the pitch," says Jones Simmer. "The quality of football has to be incredible and we have the best players in the world.
"And they are incredibly engaging with our fans. For so many supporters, their entry point to the league is they care about a particular player."
Provided the standard of competition is present, Jones Simmer says fans will return - and her confidence is backed up by the numbers.
In 2026, the average gate for an NWSL match has been more than 11,000 - only Arsenal in the WSL consistently receive a higher attendance than that, albeit the US is almost five times more populous than the UK.
On Thursday, the final few tickets for the NWSL's showpiece were retailing at $300 on ticket site Viagogo, with Jones Simmer suggesting resale tickets could be purchased at six times market value in advance of the match.
As London City and Washington Spirit owner Michele Kang put it: "The answer could not be clearer that there is an audience for the women's game."
"It's our job to hook fans by making sure they have a great experience watching a game in a venue and that's about the quality of the product," Jones Simmer adds.
"Once folks have that experience, it's a really easy yes to tune in again."
- Families v loyal fans - women's football's attendance dilemma 
  - Published30 October
Not that quality is an issue in the WSL where high-class footballers abound. Take Putellas, goal machine Khadija Shaw and most of England's double European Championship-winning squad for example.
American stars such as Alyssa Thompson and Naomi Girma at Chelsea, and Manchester City's Sam Coffey, have also swapped the US for the WSL in the past two years.
Broadcaster Oatley, who has been covering women's football since the 2005 World Cup, is keen for such players to be more visible off the pitch.
"I would love to see WSL players on mainstream TV shows, podcasts, social media platforms, not just on women's football programmes where the audience already knows everything about them," she says.
"It would not be for everyone, but for those who are comfortable, who have the biggest personalities, I think we could use that much more to grow our audience."
A matchday experience that matters
Oatley has been covering NWSL games for the past four seasons and she believes US clubs have mastered putting on events.
"When you're trying to promote a product in sport, you can't guarantee the team is going to play well and win," she says.
"But you can ensure the people who come to the game have a great experience.
"I love the enthusiasm, the positivity, the vibe of 'let's make this big'. It's a brilliant experience."
It is a balance the WSL wrestles with. With attendances plateauing this season, questions have arisen around its target audience and whether to market matches such as the north London derby between Tottenham and Arsenal as a rivalry or a family-friendly event.
Oatley's perspective is that it ought to be both, while recognising the different challenges in this country.
"I didn't understand that criticism," she says, "because they weren't saying: 'Only come to this game if you're a family'. It was being promoted all round.
"I don't think it's one size fits all marketing wise - the main thing is awareness."
It is a challenge the NWSL has embraced, and seen attendances rise accordingly.
"We want to ensure that we provided a big enough tent where everyone can feel welcome and included, whether they're there for the rivalries and the competitive tactics, or they're experiencing it for the first time," says Jones Simmer.
"To grow the sport, all fans need to be able to come to an NWSL game and have a great experience."
This season, league finalists Current and Spirit played at a remarkable 17 different times between them, reflecting the four timezones and vast nature of the USA.
It is all part of the country's sporting landscape, but given the WSL's continued conundrum about fixture scheduling, it is interesting that NWSL supporters manage to find the matches regardless.
"I have a lot of sympathy with schedulers because men's football got there first," Oatley says.
"Maybe the solution is deciding certain time slots are for women's football and sticking with them."
It does not appear the growth in the NWSL will slow down any time soon.
The Women's World Cup in Brazil next summer will feature the USA as one of the favourites and women's soccer will feature at the Olympic Games in Los Angeles in 2028.
The US will also host the 2031 Women's World Cup.
"It is amazing how the NWSL is cracking into culture," Jones Simmer says.
"We get excited about these catalytic opportunities to expand the community engagement, awareness and relevance of the NWSL."

In November, a claim circulated that U.S. banks warned customers they could be liable for money lost to mistakes made by artificial intelligence agents acting on their behalf.
An AI agent is a tool that can act as a digital assistant and carry out tasks such as writing and sending emails or planning and booking travel. In October, Axios reported that major U.S. banks had found "unauthorized third-party AI agents" logging into banking services using details that belonged to real customers.
Some AI agents, such as X's Grok Bot and Meta's Muse, advertise their reported ability to manage a person's money. Bank executives who spoke to Axios reportedly feared the risks of giving such agents permission to move or manage real people's funds.
By November, social media users claimed banks had taken action to discourage customers from using AI agents to manage their finances. For example, one X user wrote (archived):
BREAKING:
🇺🇸 If an AI agent empties your account, your bank won't refund your money anymore
U.S. banks like Citi, PNC and Citizens changed their terms this week.
If you give your credentials to an external AI agent, everything it does counts as if you had done it yourself, even if it gets hacked or ignores your instructions.
Similar claims also circulated on Facebook and Reddit (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim.
The claims appeared to come from reporting by Tech Crunch and Business Insider that claimed major banks, including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citi, Wells Fargo, Ally, PNC and Citizens (which included five of the Federal Reserve Board's 10 largest banks in the U.S.) had warned their customers they could be held liable for mistakes third-party AI agents made on their accounts if they gave them permission to use their log in details.
Based on Tech Crunch and Business Insider's reporting and our own verification, we find claims that major banks like the ones listed above warned customers they could be liable for money lost to mistakes made by AI agents acting on their behalf to be true.
Emails sent to customers and the various banks' own terms and conditions suggested that they either advised against or outright prohibited users from allowing third-party AI agents to access their accounts. If users did allow third-party agents to access their accounts, several of the banks listed above said they would treat any transactions that agent carried out as if it were approved by the customer themselves, meaning it might not always be possible to recover funds an AI agent had mistakenly spent on a customer's behalf.
What major US banks say about AI agents
JPMorgan Chase
Jamie Dimon, chief executive officer of JPMorgan Chase & Co., said on a company earnings call on Oct. 13 that the bank was "not going to allow just any … outside agent to come in inside the company," describing fears of "rogue" agents causing a threat to customers.
The bank was reportedly developing tools to find and defend against outside AI agents acting on behalf of its customers.
Business Insider reported that Chase bank warned customers in an email that, "authorized transactions may not be reversible if your information is misused," where AI agents were involved.
One Snopes reporter who is also a Chase customer received this email, which asked customers to "Keep your sign-in information private, including when using AI tools." The email continued (emphasis ours):
As AI tools evolve, it's important to understand how your financial information is being used. Always verify who you're sharing with, as authorized transactions may not be reversible if your information is misused.
The bank's "Digital Services Agreement," updated in October, outright prohibits sharing login credentials with third parties "including External AI, automated tools, or data aggregators" (Page 14).
Bank of America
At least three Snopes reporters recieved an email that also circulated online (archived) in October about Bank of America's stance on third-party AI agents. It read (emphasis ours):
Please remember that your username and password should never be shared with another person or provided to an outside service, including an Al-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on your behalf. If you do share your credentials, keep in mind that you're responsible for activity resulting from that access.
Citi
The bank updated its "Online User Agreement" in November to include a policy on third-party AI agents. It wrote:
You are cautioned against using any third-party AI Agent to access your accounts or use any digital services including, but not limited to, use of such agent to provide any information or instruction to Citi or perform any transaction through Citi Online or Citi Mobile.
It continued (emphasis ours):
If you disregard this caution and provide your Online Credentials to any third-party AI Agent or otherwise permit such agent access to your accounts or allow such agent to use any digital service and to perform any transactions on your behalf, Citi will consider any access and actions taken by the agent as authorized by You.
Wells Fargo
The bank updated its "Online Access Agreement," effective Nov. 24, to outline the customer's responsibilities if they allowed a third-party AI agent to access their account. It wrote (emphasis ours):
Unless otherwise provided by law or regulation, if you provide an AI Agent with access to the Service or any Eligible Account using your login credentials, or otherwise authorize an AI Agent to act on your behalf, you agree that:
- Any instructions, actions, or transactions initiated by the AI Agent are deemed to have been initiated and authorized directly by you, without further verification, and we have no obligation to investigate the validity or scope of such authority;
- We may rely on any such instructions, actions, or transactions as valid and binding and as evidence of your authorization; and
- We have no obligation to investigate, verify, or confirm the authority, authenticity, or validity of any instruction or action taken by an AI Agent.
Ally
Business Insider reported that Ally emailed its customers in November to warn against the dangers of using an AI agent for managing accounts. One Snopes reporter received this email, which read (emphasis ours):
When you use an Al service, you're responsible for any actions that the Al takes. Al can make mistakes, hallucinate, misunderstand your instructions, or follow them in ways you didn't intend, which could lead to significant loss.
PNC
The bank's "Digital Services Agreement," which becomes effective in December, included the following language on third-party AI agents (Page 9):
Unless PNC expressly permits otherwise for a particular Service, you may not authorize or permit a Third-Party AI Agent to initiate, request, submit, or complete a payment, transfer, or other transaction on your behalf.
It added:
To the extent permitted by applicable law, you are responsible for access and activities you authorize or permit in violation of these restrictions, including unintended activities or activities exceeding the authority you intended to provide.
Citizens
Tech Crunch reported that the Citizens bank sent an email to customers warning that they were "on the hook" for any actions a third-party AI agent might take on their behalf. Snopes contacted Citizens to verify the authenticity of this reported email and await a reply.
Industry group calls banks' precautions 'reasonable'
Though the major banks we investigated expressed in emails or policies that they did not approve of customers using AI agents, some banks were simultaneously developing their own alternatives.
Dimon's statement to investors that he would not allow "just any" AI agents access to the company suggested that some might still be allowed. CNBC reported in November that JPMorgan, which Dimon heads, was working on AI agents that could carry out foreign exchange transactions and aimed to test these in the first half of 2027.
Similarly, PNC said in its "Digital Services Agreement" (Page 9) that customers could "sometimes" be permitted to connect an AI agent to their account if the bank approved of the agent and its use.
Sucharita Kodali, a financial analyst whose specialisms include e-commerce and consumer behavior, reportedly told the technology publication Wired that banks were "fundamentally risk-averse," suggesting that any hesitation they had about AI agents at this early stage in their development might not remain forever.
The Bank Policy Institute, an industry trade group where Dimon sits on the board, predicted in November that "eventually, externally developed agents will be conducting financial transactions at banks and other financial institutions" but that, until the agents had shown they could safely manage people's money, banks that were disallowing their use were engaging in "reasonable risk management practices designed to protect their customers from fraud or mistaken transactions."

In Brazil, they rallied online by the millions, sharing videos and spreading memes. In Serbia, they cycled across Europe and ran ultramarathons to make their voices heard.
Both movements burst into international public view last month as they became central during election campaigns to the pushback against authoritarianism. What they also offered, however, was a window into a wider phenomenon playing out across the globe, as youth-led movements reshape political landscapes.
“Gen Z is rising,” said Erica Chenoweth, a political scientist at Harvard Kennedy School. “It is abundantly clear that a significant proportion of gen Z is tired of sitting on the sidelines while their political systems fail them.”
Researchers have documented at least 25 protests around the world in which this age group – roughly those between the ages of 14 and 29 – has played a role.
From Bangladesh to Belgium and Italy to India, it seems gen Z, who account for about a third of the world’s population, have found their voice. “Gen Z may be experiencing a global political awakening,” Chenoweth wrote in a recent essay.
Their reasons for taking to the streets have varied widely, from protesting against corruption and an unequal playing field to calling for more investment in education, affordable housing and action on the climate crisis.
Many of the first protests to make waves were in Asia and Africa. In 2024, students in Dhaka, Bangladesh, made global headlines after they pulled off what was described as the world’s first successful gen Z-led revolution.
The protests began over a quota law but swiftly snowballed into a wider show of discontent against the increasingly autocratic rule of the prime minister, Sheikh Hasina. Two months later, Hasina resigned and fled the country by helicopter after being, as the Associated Press reported, “chased out by young protesters”.
Two years later and 4,000 miles away, students were at the helm of another revolution in Serbia, pushing back against a government that had steadily tightened its grip on the media and stuffed institutions with party loyalists.
Late last month, Serbia’s students’ movement was catapulted from the streets to the halls of power as they ousted Aleksandar Vučić in elections, bringing an end to his party’s 14 years in power.
Students and young people have long been at the forefront of the push for change, the analysts Cait Dallaire and Sebastian Dittgen wrote recently, citing the US civil rights movement and the 2011 Arab spring.
“What is unique about the current movement is the infrastructure of mobilisation: TikTok and X amplify and accelerate grievances; Discord servers and group chats enable decentralised planning; virtual private networks and mirrored content help organisers circumvent internet shutdowns,” they said.
It was this potent combination – young people in the streets and social media – that helped drive Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s comeback to win Brazil’s presidential election last month. After a bruising loss in the first round to the rightwing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, there was dismay in the country’s political left.
That was until students from the Fluminense Federal University mobilised in a pro-Lula march, setting off a wave of similar actions across the country. Soon after, the congressman and Lula ally André Janones, 42, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army” that attracted millions of people looking to help boost pro-Lula content on social media.
On the night of his victory, Lula recognised their power. “I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” he said.
Some politicians have sought to engage gen Z from the start. In the US, Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for New York mayor combined a canny use of social media with a legion of about 50,000 volunteers that had young people at its heart. The New York Times wrote that “volunteering for Mr Mamdani’s campaign became a salve” for young New Yorkers as the campaign became not just about “mobilising, but socialising”.
It was a nod to the global context in which many gen Zers have come of age; one riven by conflicts such as the Israel-Gaza war, the escalating climate crisis and the rise of nationalism, while the rules that have shaped the international order since the second world war are fraying.
In recent weeks, youth-led protests have begun to sweep Europe, from school students in France demanding better conditions in which to work to those in Spain who pitched tents to rally for affordable housing. In Germany, thousands of people took to the streets to protest against the cost of living and call for more investment in education, health and climate action in a movement organised by a group calling itself Gen Z regelt!, or Gen Z will sort this.
Analysts have been swift to point to the link between the protests. “The reasons are different, but they share the same spark: the breakdown of the social contract,” Arancha González, the dean of the Paris School of International Affairs, told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. “In Europe, the idea that economies generate wellbeing and social equality has been shattered.”
A similar note of disillusionment threads through India’s Cockroach movement, which began as an online satire and has since swelled into a show of force against the strongman government of Narendra Modi. Fuelled by social media and rooted in democratic ideals, the power of the movement was laid bare this summer after Cockroach-led protests forced the resignation of the country’s education minister.
Equally visible is the pushback by India’s security forces against the movement, detaining thousands, unleashing teargas and beating people with lathis, or wooden clubs. Authorities went to extreme lengths in October to keep them from gathering in central Delhi, barricading roads and shutting down the internet and public transport.
It was a window into another facet that has defined youth-led protests, as research suggests they tend to be met with higher levels of repression, despite the fact that they are no more likely to use violence than others.
In France, lawyers and rights groups say several teenagers have suffered war-like injuries from police weapons. After the 2024 protests in Bangladesh, UN human rights experts said as many as 1,400 people had been killed, mostly by security forces, while thousands more suffered severe, often life-altering injuries.
In a recent analysis, Civicus, a non-profit that monitors global civic freedoms, said: “Because they question the distribution of economic and political power, gen Z-led protests have invariably been met with state violence,” linking the violence meted out to young protesters with their focus on systems and institutions that have long been generally accepted.
In Morocco, more than 2,000 people were charged and many received harsh prison sentences after a 2025 movement known as Gen Z 212 targeted officials over corruption, neglected public services and the lack of opportunities. Weeks later, in Mexico, youth-led protests over corruption and crime led to clashes with police in which dozens of people were arrested.
The outcomes of both of these movements show the varying success of gen Z protests. But at times, the foundations laid in one protest have given rise to others. In the US, much of today’s youth organising was shaped by the pro-Palestine student movement, in which there were thousands of arrests, expulsions and suspensions. Many schools instated anti-protest policies amid a broader rollback of educational freedom on campus.
Students, however, have continued to push for change. Last month hundreds in North Carolina marched in the heat to the polls after their historically Black university was denied a polling site, while thousands across the country have responded to the Cornell 7 case by skipping class, protesting and launching occupations.
As Chenoweth of the Harvard Kennedy School noted, the wave of recent youth-led protests may mark the beginning of a “profound generational transformation in world affairs” – one that could be capable of countering the global trend of democratic backsliding.
Ultimately, however, as Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris recently told the Associated Press, the explosion of youth movements across Europe hints at a wider truth that has long been overlooked across the globe.
“We all agree on one point,” he said. “That young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren’t listened to enough.”

Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules
- Published
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.
Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.
A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The case brought by The Gambia centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.
After fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) launched deadly attacks on more than 30 police posts there, Myanmar troops, backed by local Buddhist mobs, launched a wave of violence, prompting a mass exodus of Rohingya.
Refugees recounted entire villages being burned down and the mass killing of civilians, while numerous survivors and eyewitnesses provided testimony that the Myanmar military had also raped and abused Rohingya women and girls.
The ICJ determined that around 10,000 Rohingya were "violently killed" during the clearance operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.
Iwasawa said Myanmar's military engaged in "indiscriminate" killings, the execution of men, "widespread" sexual violence, "extreme violence" against children and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes.
He said the military had also attacked Rohingya as they were fleeing to Bangladesh.
Myanmar, he added, had engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" by burning or disposing of bodies, burned and bulldozed sites that were cleared and failed to prosecute those who had perpetrated the acts of violence.
While the ICJ recognised the role Arsa played, it found there had been "overlap" between an "anti-Rohingya hate speech campaign" - which portrayed the Rohingya as "sub-human" and "a violent threat" - and the clearance operations that made violence against the population more likely.
Myanmar consistently denied genocide against the Rohingya, saying its operations had targeted militant or insurgent threats in response to the Arsa attacks.
In January, its representative Ko Ko Hlaing told the ICJ that the country "was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free reign". He said he had "no comment" following Thursday's verdict.
The ICJ also looked at the wider treatment of Rohingya leading up to the clearance operation and found that policies like limiting married couples to two children were discriminatory and aimed to erode their rights.
It said Myanmar had an obligation to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure could be determined at a later date.
'Recognition of our suffering'
The court's decision was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups.
"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of Rakhine in 2017 and now lives in Canada. "The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades."
Human Rights Watch said the ruling was "long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured".
Meanwhile, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the "suffering, misery and humiliation" inflicted on the Rohingya people was a "stain on the conscience of humanity". He added that the court's decision "must now translate into real action".
To implicate the Myanmar government in genocide, the court had to determine not just that terrible acts had been committed, but that there was an intent on the part of officials or arms of the state to partially or completely destroy the group.
Thursday's ruling is without precedent. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first nation to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The ICJ has only twice before ruled on claims of state-backed genocide in the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in the aftermath of the Holocaust, in both cases finding there was insufficient evidence to attribute the actions to the state.
Dozens of individuals have been found guilty of genocide, but finding their actions were at the direct behest of the state requires a higher evidential bar to prove genocide, the gravest crime under international law.
Philippe Sands KC, a top human rights lawyer who helped bring the case, described it as an "historic judgment".
He told BBC Radio 4's World at One programme that it was "right up there with the great moments of international justice: Nuremberg, Pinochet, and others", referring to the trials of Nazi leaders following World War Two and that of the Chilean dictator, respectively.
However, the ICJ is not a criminal court and its powers of enforcement are limited. It cannot send military officials to prison, while it relies on the UN Security Council and political pressure to impose its rulings.
The verdict will have implications for other genocide cases pending with the ICJ, though, including one brought by South Africa against Israel over its war in Gaza.
Sands said that pending case had been the "elephant in the room" during the Myanmar hearings.
He added that, while ruling against Myanmar did not mean the court would find similarly with Gaza, if it had not found Myanmar responsible, the case against Israel "would, in effect, be over". Israel says the case against it is "wholly unfounded".
Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, told the BBC that the court had not accepted Myanmar's counter-terrorism defence and had found for the first time that rape and sexual violence was an act of genocide, positions it would bear in mind for future cases.
A US State Department spokesperson said "the proper interpretation" of the Genocide Convention was of "paramount importance", as was "preventing politicisation" of the International Criminal Court.
Noting that the US was the "leading donor for the Rohingya refugee humanitarian response", they said they shared the "grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights" against Rohingyas and other minorities, adding: "We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications."
Following Thursday's ruling, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the government was ordering Myanmar's defence attaché be expelled and that he was summoning its charge d'affaires.
He pledged to set out "further action in the coming days to ensure those responsible are held to account" after a cross-party group of MPs called for the government to resume sanctions against Myanmar's military.

The Mexican military captured one of the FBI’s top 10 most wanted fugitives during a special forces raid in the Mexican state of Sinaloa on Friday night.
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro”, was arrested along with two other alleged leaders of his gang after a gun battle that triggered widespread panic in the city of Guasave.
The alleged leader of a major drug-trafficking cartel, the Meza Flores Transnational Criminal Organization (TCO), he had managed to evade arrest for more than a decade, even though there was a reward of up to $5m (£3.8m) on his head.
His FBI “most wanted” poster states his organisation “is allegedly responsible for the possession, distribution, and importation of large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl and marijuana into the United States, and has predominately controlled drug production, transportation and distribution in several locations throughout Mexico”.
Mexico’s defence ministry also alleged he is the leader of the Beltrán Leyva criminal organisation, which is allied to the Mayos, one of two rival factions in the powerful Sinaloa cartel.
Meza Flores’s alleged second-in-command, Germán N, whose alias is “Serafín”, and José N, an alleged financial operator for the Beltrán Leyva group, were also arrested.
The operation to capture the men was carried out by “elite military forces” with help from US intelligence, according to Mexico’s defence ministry.
After arriving in the “target area … using stealth and surprise”, the ministry said the arresting force came under attack “with gunfire and explosives” but managed to enter a house and make the arrests.
The men were then evacuated to Mexico City on a Mexican air force plane to be handed over to prosecutors.
Videos and photos show civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game at Kuroda Park stadium in Guasave, as well as burnt-out cars.
A barrage of rapid fire from what appeared to be Mexican security force helicopters fired at the ground, according to CNN, and players from the Venados de Mazatlán and Algodoneros de Guasave teams abandoned the field mid-game.
Meza Flores was originally indicted in 2012, and in 2013 the US Treasury placed sanctions on him under the Kingpin Act, freezing his assets.
In 2017, the US Department of State’s Narcotics Rewards Program began offering up to $5m as a reward for information leading directly to his arrest or conviction.
He has been charged with multiple counts of drug-trafficking violations, and use and possession of a firearm in the US, and was wanted in Mexico for organised crime and offences against public health.

The 'Magic Six': How to strengthen your marriage in midlife
Ever argued with your spouse in the car? NPR's Nina Totenberg can relate.
She and her husband, David Reines, have been married for 26 years, and it's on the road where they're most likely to have a spat. "The car is awful," Totenberg told me, laughing. It comes down partly to the brakes. She taps them "way before" Reines does. And when another driver cuts him off, he sometimes wants to return the favor. Totenberg's advice from the passenger seat: "Don't take the bait."
It's so relatable. And as Reines put it, "You can't not have some conflict after 26 years. I think the secret is how you deal with it." (They began our interview for this episode of Your Turn by giving each other a kiss!)
As we ask "What comes next?" in midlife, who's standing beside us matters a lot. Kids leave home, careers shift, and relationships can change, too. So what does a good partnership look like at this stage?
David and Nina's Four L's
When people ask Reines why their marriage works, he points to four L's:
Love. "You gotta love each other."
Like. Do you actually like each other? For Reines, respect is part of this. He says he has total respect for her work, and she respects his career, too. He is a retired trauma surgeon and now keeps busy as a volunteer at the Library of Congress and serves on boards. Each of them also keeps a strong sense of self. "Although we meld," Reines says. "I still have me, and she still has her."
Lust. Physical intimacy matters. They kiss every day, hold hands, "all the time," and have held off on buying a king-size bed. In hotel beds, they joke, they can't find each other if the bed is too big.
Laugh. He says she has one of the best senses of humor he knows. They laugh together every day.
The Magic Six
I also talked with clinical psychologist Julie Schwartz Gottman who I interviewed for my book, Your Turn. She and her husband, John Gottman, co-founded the Gottman Institute and are two of the best-known names in relationship science, and co-authors of Fight Right: How Successful Couples Turn Conflict Into Connection, where they describe the "Four Horseman" which are four destructive communication patterns that can help predict the breakdown of a relationship.
Gottman points to research that shows many dual-career couples spend little time together and much of the communication can be transactional. Did you call the plumber? Did you walk the dog?
The Gottmans found that couples can improve their relationships by intentionally carving out about six hours a week together, and making changes to small, daily and weekly habits. They call it the Magic Six.
Some of these things may sound obvious, yet oftentimes these are the very things that can fall away when couples are too busy or distracted. And she says it's illuminating when couples actually track progress.
Partings (a few minutes each day). Before you leave in the morning, spend a few minutes communicating about what's happening in your partner's day.
Reunions (about 20 minutes a day). At the end of the workday, share a kiss or physical affection. Then have a 20-minute stress-reducing conversation about your day.
Admiration and appreciation (35 minutes a week). Spend about five minutes a day expressing genuine gratitude or naming a trait you admire in your partner. Or tell a story to remind each other.
Affection (35 minutes a week). That works out to about five minutes a day on physical touch, such as holding hands or cuddling before sleep.
Date night (2 hours a week). Have distraction-free time together to enjoy being together. It doesn't need to be dinner and a show. It can be a low-key hike, a museum visit or any activity you enjoy.
State of the union meeting (1 hour a week). Review what's going well as well as concerns or things that are not working, and then talk things out.
Listen. Don't Fix.
Many partners fall into the trap of trying to "fix" the other person's problems or tell them how to proceed. But the point of the daily conversation is to step away from this mentality.
"Most of us just wanna be seen," Gottman told me. "We wanna be witnessed." Jumping in with advice can cut off the conversation before your partner gets the chance to describe what's bothering them.
Instead, she suggests three simple words: "Tell me more."
It's an invitation, Gottman says. It tells your partner, "I really am interested in what you're saying." It shows them that you care.
Nina Totenberg and David Reines have their own version. Every night at dinner, they sit down and ask, "How'd your day go?" He calls Nina a good listener and she says she enjoys connecting this way and spending time together. They keep each other in check and serve as each other's confidant.
Find Your Rhythm
Gottman also had good news for couples who don't share every hobby. You can pursue different passions as long as you bring them back to the table and stay curious about each other. Some couples want lots of independence, and others want to do everything together. The key is to keep asking: Are you missing me? Do we need more time together, or less?
Totenberg and Reins have found their balance. They agree on watching British murder mysteries together. And when he wants a shoot-'em-up, she heads upstairs for Law & Order. Summer vacations on Cape Cod are friends-only, where they spend days doing what they each enjoy. Winter holidays are for her sisters and family.
As Totenberg put it: "If you find somebody that you really love who loves you back, you should grab that and run for all the world because it's ... an enormous gift."
So, if you'd like: give this a try: Ask your partner one open-ended question. Then say, "Tell me more."

A video showing a white airbag emerging from the helmet of a biker who appears to crash is being widely shared on social media (here, here). The video claims that China has developed helmets equipped with airbags to prevent head injuries in the event of a motorcycle accident. The video has also been shared by several prominent media outlets (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the viral post.
Claim: A video shows a helmet equipped with airbags developed in China.
Fact: The viral video is AI-generated. While some companies are developing airbag helmets, the airbags shown in the video are exaggerated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
First, upon examining the viral video, we noticed that the bike and the biker are not visible in the phone recording of the fall for a few moments. After the airbags deploy, the biker suddenly disappears. Moreover, the way the bike loses control and the biker falls onto the road appears unnatural. Such visual inconsistencies are commonly seen in AI-generated videos.
Further, we verified the viral video using AI content detection tools Hive Moderation and Sightengine. Both tools indicated that the video was AI-generated, confirming that it is not a genuine video.
Moreover, a reverse image search of the viral video led us to the original video, which was uploaded on Facebook (archived) by a page named Zero Gravity Gang. We found that this page regularly uploads AI-generated videos depicting various vehicle-related experiments.
While it is true that a few companies are experimenting with airbag technology for helmets (here, here, here). However, these designs are not as large as the airbag shown in the viral video. They are designed to provide protection to the head and neck rather than inflate into a large structure around the rider.
To sum up, this viral video of the airbag helmet developed in China is AI-generated, not real.

Rosemary Nyirumbe became a nun when she was just in her mid-teens – and she felt her true vocation lay in rehabilitating children who had been through some of the worst trauma imaginable. So that’s what she did. In this episode Mike Wooldridge hears Sr Rosemary’s astonishing story. The feared rebel group, the Lord’s Resistance Army, started to terrorise the north of Uganda in the 1980s. Many children, girls as well as boys, were abducted and forced to become child soldiers. In many cases, the LRA forced them to commit atrocities, leaving them deeply traumatised. Many of the girls also bore the children of rebel leaders. As they started to return home, these children were often rejected by their families and communities, says Sr Rosemary. So she set about giving them a future and a hope: through enabling them to acquire skills like sewing, and by helping them see that God had not rejected them for the atrocities they had been forced to commit. More than once, Sr Rosemary put herself in enormous danger in order to fulfil her mission. But, she says, she also learnt that small acts of kindness can touch the hearts of even battle-hardened rebels.

Researchers have identified changes in the metabolic activity of the gut microbiome associated with exceptional longevity in humans, and found that amplifying the same activity in aged mice using engineered bacteria improved metabolic health.
Published in the journal Cell Metabolism, the team's study suggests that specific age-related changes in the gut microbiome may be protective adaptations rather than signs of decline, and could potentially be harnessed to support healthier aging.
Senior author Amir Zarrinpar, chair in circadian biology and medicine, and professor of medicine at the University of California San Diego, said while many studies on aging focus on what goes wrong as one grows old, the findings suggest "some changes in the gut microbiome may actually represent the body's attempt to preserve metabolic health".
"If we can identify those beneficial functions and safely strengthen them, we may eventually be able to develop new ways to promote healthier aging," Zarrinpar said.
The gut microbiome, the community of bacteria and other microbes living in the digestive tract, is known to change throughout life and plays an important role in metabolism and inflammation, among other aspects of health.
Studies have also found distinctive microbiome features among people who age exceptionally well.
The researchers focused on how gut microbes modify bile acids, substances produced by the liver that help digest fats but also act as signalling molecules in the body.
Studying young and aged mice, they found that aging was associated with an increased microbial activity linked to enzymes called bile salt hydrolases. These enzymes chemically modify bile acids, allowing them to influence pathways involved in metabolism, inflammation and the body's internal clock.
The team also found greater bile acid modification in the mice.
To determine patterns in humans, they reanalysed publicly available data from a human ageing cohort, analysing bile acid measurements from 48 young adults, 107 older adults and 125 centenarians.
The centenarian group showed higher ratios of modified bile acids than both younger groups. An analysis of microbiome data also revealed a greater abundance of a gene associated with bile salt hydrolase activity among centenarians compared with the older adult group.
Further, aged mice -- 82-week-old mice -- were introduced with a strain of bacteria native to the gut engineered to continuously produce bile salt hydrolases.
About 20 weeks after treatment, mice receiving the enzyme-producing bacteria had a significantly improved insulin sensitivity and modestly improved glucose tolerance, compared with mice receiving a non-enzyme-producing bacterium.
By 32 weeks, the treated mice also showed changes consistent with a lower body weight and fat mass and a greater lean mass. Other findings pointed to an increased use of fat for energy, improved mitochondrial function and changes in gene activity related to inflammation and the body's internal clock.

Okinawa celebrates restored Shuri Castle hall 7 years after fire
Officials and residents in Okinawa have celebrated the restoration of Shuri Castle's main hall, marking a significant return of the island's cultural symbol
TOKYO -- Officials and residents in Okinawa celebrated the restoration of Shuri Castle's main hall on Sunday, its deep red exterior and dragon ornaments marking the return of a symbol of the island's heritage seven years after it was destroyed in a fire.
The fire on Oct. 31, 2019, destroyed several buildings at the castle complex in Naha, Okinawa’s prefectural capital, as it was hosting a festival. Firefighters struggled for nearly 12 hours to contain the blaze as it spread from building to building in strong winds. Investigators could not determine the cause but considered an electrical fault the likeliest explanation.
“The fire was a tremendous shock to the Okinawan people," Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja said at Sunday’s ceremony in the courtyard outside the main hall. "Seven years after the major loss, as we mark this milestone of the main hall restoration, I am deeply moved and delighted.”
The castle is a symbol of Okinawa’s cultural heritage dating to the Ryukyu Kingdom, which lasted about 450 years from 1429 until 1879, when Japan annexed the island.
It also represents Okinawa’s recovery from World War II. The castle burned down in 1945 during the Battle of Okinawa, which killed about 200,000 people, many of them civilians.
Koja thanked historians, artisans and other experts from across Japan who contributed to the restoration, as well as donors at home and abroad. He called for rebuilding the rest of the castle, saying the opening of the main hall, known as Seiden, is "not the end.”
The 2019 fire destroyed Seiden and two adjacent halls, as well as four nearby structures, while two other structures were heavily damaged.
Shuri Castle's main hall opens to the public Monday. The other parts of the castle are being restored in stages in a process experts say could take more than a decade.
After its earlier loss 80 years ago, the castle was largely restored in 1992 for the 20th anniversary of Okinawa's reversion to Japan to mark the end of the island's 27-year U.S. occupation. The island still hosts a large U.S. military presence. Work on other parts was still underway when the 2019 fire struck.
Kurayoshi Takara, a historian who also helped with the previous restoration, said the main hall was reproduced to more closely resemble the original building, based on new findings including the ingredients of the red pigment and other details from historical documents.
Experts traced the pigment to iron bacteria found in northern Okinawa. After lengthy experiments, artisans recreated the deeper red by blending the bacteria-derived pigment with a commercial product, Takara said in an interview with Japan’s NHK public television.
“We still have a long way to go,” said Takara, who led the latest restoration effort. “I hope Shuri Castle will remain for a long time so that many people come visit and learn rich history and culture on this island ... as a symbol of peace."
Shuri Castle is a major tourist attraction and reconstruction raises hopes for more visitors to the island, whose economy has long lagged behind the rest of Japan.
Koja, who took office at the end of September, has pledged to double Okinawa’s per capita income and tourism revenue within the next decade and make the prefecture a more attractive place for young people.

Trump claims credit as Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia
Sign up for alerts on breaking news and exclusive reporting from NPR.
Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO of the world's largest chipmaker on Monday, sending the company's stock soaring as President Trump claimed credit for brokering his close ally's return.
It was a stunning reversal of fortune for Huang. He resigned less than two weeks ago, following news reports of extramarital affairs, including with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of being a Chinese spy.
In a statement put out just before the market opened, Nvidia said its board voted unanimously in favor of bringing back Huang after a series of conversations and meetings, as well as input from people at "senior levels" of the U.S. government. "Based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk," the board said.
Nvidia's stock price shot up more than 30% on Monday, helping buoy stock indexes after last week's losses, which were driven by the tech sector.
Trump endorsed the move, calling it the "correct and proper decision" in a social media post. He said Huang's leadership was needed "in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy."
The president had repeatedly urged Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang as CEO in public comments and on social media. In a lengthy interview with CNBC Monday morning, Trump claimed his influence helped Huang get his job back.
"I don't want to say, but basically I was represented at the board," the president said, in response to a question about a report in Semafor that he had called directly into the Nvidia board meeting.
"I spoke to them. Let me just put it that way. And I convinced them," Trump told CNBC. "And I must tell you, it was a lot easier to convince them yesterday than it was a week and a half ago."
He later added: "When the stock starts dropping forty, fifty percent, it was a lot easier for me to do it yesterday than it would have been."
Huang stepped down amid a growing scandal
Nvidia, which Huang co-founded and has run for the past 33 years, dominates the market for the chips used to train and run artificial intelligence. Trump and Huang have grown close during the president's second term in office, with Huang becoming one of the most influential business leaders with the president's ear on AI policy. He has successfully lobbied the U.S. government to allow chipmakers to sell some chips to China, although Nvidia's most advanced chips are subject to export controls.
Huang resigned from Nvidia on Nov. 12 after news reports that he had affairs with multiple women, including an Nvidia executive who reported to him. But the most explosive allegation was that he'd engaged in a relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that was buying Nvidia chips, whom U.S. officials believed had ties to Chinese intelligence.
The Justice Department has said it is conducting a criminal investigation of Megaspeed for potential chip smuggling.
On Monday, the Commerce Department said it is adding Megaspeed to a list of companies barred from buying advanced technology, including some AI chips, without a U.S. government license.
Megaspeed didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. The company previously denied wrongdoing and said that Alice Huang left the company in 2025 and that it is conducting an internal investigation.
Nvidia's board said as recently as Nov. 17 that it did not intend to reinstate Huang, though Huang publicly said he would return if the board allowed it. On Monday, board chair Harvey Jones said in a statement: "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers."
The board said its turnaround followed a series of meetings with Huang that left them satisfied with his "candor and ability to lead" the company. It said its investigation into Huang and the reports he had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort continues and that Huang is "committed to cooperating with it."
In a statement on Monday, Huang said he was "honored" to return. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment," he said.
Silicon Valley cheers as questions about Nvidia's governance linger
The board's abrupt reversal was cheered by many Silicon Valley leaders and investors who had joined calls for Huang to return.
"The mistake has been corrected," SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on his social media site X. Gavin Baker, whose firm Atreides Management invests in Nvidia, posted a video of employees applauding Huang as he returned to the chipmaker's headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif. on Monday.
"The idea that this company can only be successful and continue to do what it's doing with that person at the helm ... is the argument made by a lot in Silicon Valley last week and by the president — that Nvidia's success depends on Jensen running it," said Margaret O'Mara, a historian who studies Silicon Valley at the University of Washington.
Some women who have advocated for the tech industry to tackle gender inequality and abuses of power say that for the board to reinstate Huang after previously saying his behavior was "inconsistent" with the company's code of conduct sends a signal to Silicon Valley.
"It is a resounding message that all that matters is money," said Freada Kapor Klein, a social impact investor who's advocated for women and people of color in tech.
Nvidia did not respond to NPR's questions about those concerns.
Huang's reinstatement also raises questions about Nvidia's corporate governance and how the board is weighing short-term considerations against the company's policies, said Rob Lalka, a professor at Tulane University's Freeman School of Business.
"It really was sort of an eye-opening moment to think about how this board, just a few days ago, had said they would not bring Jensen Huang back and that they had voted unanimously for that. There's still an investigation open in their company" into Huang's behavior, Lalka said. "And the board basically went around its entire process that it had set in place for that investigation to put him back into power."
Trump dismisses national security concerns
On Monday, Trump wrote on Truth Social that the government has "no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security," and that Attorney General Todd Blanche says the U.S. "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."
Last week Nvidia's board said it had formed a committee to oversee the company's national security policies, compliance with U.S. export controls, and risk management of global trade.
Huang is expected to testify before multiple congressional committees next week.
To explain why it was so important that Huang remain at Nvidia's helm, Trump told CNBC he feared China attempting to bring his expertise to their country.
"I could see China coming in and saying to Jensen, 'Hey, how would you like to come to China?' He's got a little blood in him, you know. He's got a little blood there. 'How would you like to come to China and head up Huawei, okay, and head up one of our companies?'" Trump said. "And you know what? If Jensen was angry enough, if he was treated badly, maybe he could do that."
When CNBC asked Trump if he wasn't worried after he was alerted that Huang was in a relationship with a potential spy, Trump demurred, saying, "I won't get into it."
Following the CNBC interview, Trump celebrated Huang's reinstatement on Truth Social by posting a doctored image invoking a famous photo of the president after the assassination attempt in Butler, Penn., in 2024. In the posted image, Huang is in President Trump's place with blood spattered on his face, raising his fist — holding a red bra — as a flag bearing Nvidia's logo waves in the background.
NPR's Andrea Hsu contributed to this report.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has sanctioned prosecution against packaged drinking water manufacturer Bisleri International after one of its water samples was declared "unsafe" in laboratory testing. The company, however, has disputed the findings, triggering a row over the presence of bromate and polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in the sample. According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), prolonged exposure to certain chemical contaminants in drinking water, including bromate and some PAHs, may pose health risks, including potential kidney damage and an increased risk of cancer. The two substances have different sources and potential health effects. Bromate is a chemical compound that can form during drinking-water disinfection, particularly when ozone reacts with naturally occurring bromide ions in water, according to the WHO. The WHO has set a provisional guideline value of 10 micrograms per litre (µg/l) for bromate in drinking water, primarily because of concerns about its potential carcinogenic effects. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has classified bromate as a Group 2B substance, meaning it is "possibly carcinogenic to humans". According to the WHO, while evidence of carcinogenicity in humans is inadequate, animal studies have shown sufficient evidence of cancer-causing potential. Bromate has also demonstrated mutagenic properties in laboratory studies, meaning it can cause changes in genetic material, or DNA. The WHO's assessment discusses oxidative DNA damage as one possible mechanism behind its carcinogenic effects. Animal studies have linked prolonged exposure to bromate with tumours in the kidneys and thyroid, among other tissues. These findings raise concerns about long-term exposure, although they do not mean that consuming water with a slightly elevated bromate concentration will immediately cause cancer. The potential health risk depends on the concentration consumed, the frequency of exposure and its duration. The WHO's guideline is intended to limit long-term exposure and reduce associated health risks. Polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons, commonly called PAHs, are a group of organic chemical compounds containing two or more fused aromatic rings. According to the WHO, PAHs are formed primarily through the incomplete combustion of organic materials. They can enter the environment through industrial emissions, vehicle exhaust and other sources of atmospheric pollution. They may also contaminate drinking water through coal-tar coatings used in water distribution pipes. PAHs can enter the human body through food, air and drinking water. The WHO notes that these compounds may be present in food following exposure to airborne pollution and in fish from contaminated waters. They can also form during cooking methods such as grilling, roasting, frying and baking. Some PAHs are particularly concerning because of their carcinogenic potential. The WHO identifies benzo[a]pyrene as an important indicator of PAH contamination and has prescribed a guideline value of 0.7 micrograms per litre in drinking water. The WHO's assessment says evidence linking PAH mixtures to cancer in humans comes primarily from occupational studies involving inhalation and skin exposure. It also notes that human data on cancer risks from oral exposure are unavailable. The health effects vary depending on the specific PAH, the amount of exposure and its duration. Prolonged exposure to certain compounds, particularly benzo[a]pyrene, is a concern because of their cancer-causing potential. The dispute relates to a sample collected by FSSAI from Bisleri's Goa manufacturing facility on September 30, 2025. According to the company, the regulator collected six samples, of which five initially met the applicable standards. The sixth recorded bromate at 12 micrograms per litre, against the prescribed limit of 10 micrograms per litre, it mentioned, as per PTI. Following Bisleri's appeal dated November 22, 2025, FSSAI sent the sample to a referral laboratory for retesting. The company said the laboratory found bromate within the prescribed limit but separately flagged the presence of PAHs. Bisleri subsequently arranged an independent test at an FSSAI-approved laboratory, which also found bromate within the prescribed limit, it said. The company submitted the results to FSSAI's Western Regional Office through a formal letter dated February 2 this year. Bisleri said it received no further communication from FSSAI and understood the matter to be closed. It also maintained that it had not received any formal notice by email or in hard copy. However, FSSAI announced on Sunday, November 22, that it had sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd after finding its packaged drinking water sample "unsafe". In its statement on Monday, Bisleri said it would cooperate with the regulator to address the issue and reiterated that its packaged drinking water was safe for consumption. "Drinking water safety is a priority for Bisleri. We maintain stringent quality controls of over 90 tests across our 10-step manufacturing process," the company said. Charlie Cox wanted the opportunity to audition for the role of James Bond in the upcoming Denis Villeneuve-directed film.

Police authorities in Bengaluru’s Electronic City have reportedly registered an FIR against Karnataka Chalakara Okkuta’s president G Narayana Swamy, among others, for destroying recruitment posters of Green SM. Swamy and his group of unidentified cab drivers allegedly barged into a private hotel in Hosa Road and vandalised the property by tearing up banners, abusing company representatives, in a bid to impede the Vietnamese ride-hailing firm’s recruitment drive. As per a report by the Deccan Herald, the FIR was registered suo motu under five sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) relating to property damage, unlawful assembly, intentional insult, breach of peace and criminal intimidation. Inc42 has not been able to source the FIR so far. We have reached out to Green SM for comments on this development. The story will be updated based on their response. This comes about a week after the state government directed transport department officials to stop registering new Green SM taxis until further orders, even as around 100 vehicles operated by the company have already been registered to ply on Karnataka roads. The e-taxi operator, part of Vietnam’s Vingroup, which also operates electric car OEM Vinfast, received an aggregator licence from the Karnataka Transport Department earlier this month. The issuance of the same triggered protests across the state. Bengaluru-based private transport associations such as Karnataka Rajya Chalakara Parishath and Peace Auto Union demand protection citing interests of local taxi owners and drivers. Yet, the state government is yet to take a final call on whether Green SM will be allowed to continue its operations in Karnataka. However, the transport department is said to be planning to make fare meters compulsory for all cabs, including those operating through ride-hailing platforms such as Uber and Rapido. Green SM started India operations in June this year. It is already operational in Delhi NCR and Hyderabad and touched the 15 Lakh rides milestone earlier this month. The issues in Karnataka come at a time when it is preparing to expand across six new geographies. The firm has also secured aggregator licences in Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh.

My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive
- Published
When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified.
They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there.
"Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him.
But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive.
This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded.
Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry.
Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community.
After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience.
"As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works.
The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate.
The first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team.
After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve.
Butembo does not have the equipment to quickly test for Ebola - samples need to be sent to the city of Beni, 54km (33 miles) north.
This delays diagnosis as the condition of roads in this war-torn and underdeveloped part of DR Congo means it can take between 48 and 72 hours to travel even this relatively short distance.
After three days at home, Kamwanga felt extremely weak and experienced muscle pain. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea.
This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre.
"She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says.
Around 18:00, he set off on foot to the nearby centre but refused to use the main entrance.
He called his colleagues and asked them to put on their protective gear before they approached him and isolated him. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids.
The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment.
"The treatment given to Ebola patients is symptomatic - meaning that doctors treat the symptoms the patient presents," says Kamwanga, explaining that in his case it was severe vomiting and diarrhoea.
In some patients these symptoms can lead to organ failure and then some develop internal and external bleeding.
Kamwanga lost a lot of fluid and struggled to stay hydrated - he was terrified.
"I was afraid for myself. Every day, patients were dying right before my eyes. But I stayed positive," he explains.
Over 13 days lying in his hospital bed, he tried to keep his spirits up by watching movies and TV shows on his phone, reading and scrolling through TikTok.
The day he learned he had recovered, Kamwanga felt immense relief. He thanked the healthcare workers who had cared for him.
However, even a certificate showing he was Ebola-free did not initially dispel the unease those around him felt after he was discharged.
"We welcomed him home warmly. But because of our fear, we didn't get close to him any more," Ndungo, his mother, tells the BBC.
For 21 days - the incubation period of the virus - the doctor lived separately in another part of the family home, which was crowded at the time with at least 18 people living there, including several children and people displaced by recent fighting in the region.
He would only see them from afar when he went to pick up his meal, while other family members kept their distance.
Neighbour Kavugho Sifa shared these concerns.
"We were really afraid, but we prayed to God to protect him at the treatment centre. With God's help and the doctors' efforts, we saw him return in good health," she tells the BBC.
They all agree the experience changed their perception of Ebola.
Some do not believe the disease even exists - Ndungo says that witnessing Ebola first-hand helped to dispel some of that misinformation.
After his recovery, Kamwanga threw himself into community outreach - sharing his story as a way of combatting rumours and mistrust.
"I started writing my book - The Price of Saving Lives - one week after recovering and leaving the hospital," he says. "However, it is not finished yet. What I currently use during my awareness-raising activities is the draft, and it is already making a significant impact."
During these sessions, he also distributes photos taken while he was sick to help convince residents that Ebola is real.
But in Butembo, this mission remains difficult. Kamwanga explains that some people view awareness campaigns as a way for humanitarian organisations to profit from donor funding.
Such mistrust, which is also levelled at healthcare professionals, is often fuelled by poverty and trauma related to years of armed conflict, he says.
"Ebola has come alongside the war," he says, explaining that some even interpret it as a way for those in authority to threaten a vulnerable population "to finish off those whom the war failed to exterminate".
He also believes that the number of deaths observed during epidemics - compared to recoveries, which are sometimes less visible - reinforce fear and suspicion.
But putting himself on the front line also comes with risks - and Kamwanga says he receives death threats on his phone.
Some residents accuse him of being paid to spread information about Ebola. He also reports that outreach workers have been attacked by members of the community.
He feels the authorities do not work effectively to address all these problems: "Our government is taking things lightly."
He agrees too with the recent report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) that Ebola funds are going missing.
"The money allocated to the Ebola response is being misappropriated by the government. We do not have enough protective equipment," the medic says.
The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.
Despite the intimidation and the obstacles he and other medics face, he remains determined - his goal is to help put an end to the disease.
"Should we give up the fight against Ebola? No. We continue to do what we can with the resources available to us, which are unfortunately very limited."
