Between the pages of a logbook recording Dakshina’s treatment are ₹100, ₹50, ₹20, and ₹10 notes. Dakshina’s mother, Minnal Rani, had filed them away for her daughter’s medical expenses. The child is gone, but the money remains untouched. “We will never spend it,” she says, fighting back tears.
Dakshina was five months old when doctors detected a hole in her heart. Born on June 13, 2025, she was taken to many hospitals, including one in Thiruvananthapuram, Keralam’s capital. With surgery ruled out, she was eventually referred to a cooperative hospital at Perinthalmanna, in Malappuram district, a two-and-a-half-hour drive away from home. She died here, on April 13, 2026.
Rani and her husband Chandra Sekhar say the hospital refused to release their daughter’s body until they paid a bill of ₹10,000. They managed to raise the money with the help of a ward councillor.
“We buried her under that tree,” says Rani, pointing to a coconut tree near their house at Vechapathi hamlet in Sholayur panchayat of Attappadi, Palakkad district.
Dakshina’s death is among a series of 10 infant deaths reported this year from Attappadi, a predominantly tribal settlement. There have been four back-to-back deaths in October. Of the 10 infant deaths, six involved congenital anomalies, with heart defects among the commonly reported conditions. An expert committee of doctors and researchers is examining the deaths.

WASHINGTON — The Trump administration on Monday said that the federal government will save $9.2 billion on drugs purchased through Medicare next year as a result of price negotiations, a net savings of 45% compared to what it would’ve paid last year had the negotiated prices been in effect.
This is the third time the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has negotiated drug prices following the passage of the Inflation Reduction Act, but it’s the first time those drugs have included treatments administered in doctors’ offices, which are covered by Part B. Only retail drugs covered by Part D were eligible during the first two years.
The estimated $9.2 billion in savings does not account for discounts the drugmakers pay to the Part D Manufacturer Discount Program. That program was created by the same law that created the price negotiation program. If those discounts were included, the estimated savings would be about $5.5 billion, or 33% in lower net aggregate spending.

Flights grounded in Belgium due to strike against austerity measures
- Published
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and train services have been severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.
All air traffic has been halted in Zaventem airport in the capital, Brussels, as well as Charlerois, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.
Trains and underground services have also been halted in Brussels where large numbers of people are expected to join a protest march.
The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever has so far failed to agree a budget to cut costs with his coalition allies. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.
No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers. More than 50,000 travellers' plans were being disrupted - with more expected to be affected overnight and on Tuesday.
A similar situation has affected Charlerois, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure of arrival.
"Without air traffic control, no flights can take off or land," the airport said on Saturday when the strike action was announced, warning of "disastrous consequences".
As thousands descended on Brussels for the protest march, the leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".
"A genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes," Bert Engelaar, head of FGBT, said.
"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," Engelaar said, praising the left-wing Vooruit party - the only member of the five-party governing coalition reported to have stalled efforts to agree the budget.
Vooruit wants to raise taxes on the rich, and fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.
Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.
Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.

China said it sentenced an official to death for spying for a foreign intelligence service, publicizing the case as a warning against leaking state secrets.
The official, identified only by the surname Ma, was given the penalty after being found guilty of espionage, according to a Monday post on a social media account linked to the National Administration of State Secret Protection. In an intensive care unit, every second matters. A critically ill patient may be connected to several devices, including patient monitors, ventilators and infusion pumps, while laboratory systems and electronic health records continuously generate additional information. Together, these systems create a large and rapidly-changing picture of the patient’s condition. However, when the information remains fragmented across devices and platforms, clinicians may spend valuable time locating, verifying and reconciling data before they can act.
This makes interoperability a clinical priority in critical care, not simply an information technology requirement. Integration enables systems to exchange data, but true interoperability ensures that the information being exchanged is accurate, interpretable and clinically relevant. This can help care teams coordinate and prioritise interventions more effectively while reducing the need to move between multiple systems to assemble a clinical picture.

Thirty-four-year-old Sundar lives in Tappal village in Khair tehsil of Aligarh district, Uttar Pradesh. His name was absent from the state’s draft voter list published on January 6, 2026. However, in the final list published on April 10, his name appears four times, at serial numbers 730, 738, 739 and 757 in booth 19. Each entry carries a different Elector Photo Identity Card (EPIC) number.
The official list of Form 6 applications, used for voter registration, records only two applications from Sundar, dated January 9 and 14. The office of the Uttar Pradesh chief electoral officer (CEO), however, said that he had filed four. The discrepancy aside, the CEO’s office’s response confirms a crucial point: Multiple applications by the same person resulted in the issuance of multiple voter IDs.
The Election Commission launched the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Uttar Pradesh in November 2025, with the removal of duplicate and incorrect entries among its stated objectives. Alt News compared the draft and final electoral rolls across 69 booths in 20 districts, covering 60,558 voters, and cross-checked newly added names against the corresponding Form 6 application lists. The analysis found 230 people whose names appeared at least twice in the final rolls, with some listed three or four times, each against a separate voter ID. Such duplicate entries were found in booths across the political spectrum.
On October 27, 2025, the Election Commission announced the second phase of the SIR across 12 states and Union Territories, including Uttar Pradesh. The exercise, covering approximately 51 crore voters, began on November 4.
The schedule for Uttar Pradesh was subsequently extended four times. The draft electoral roll was published on January 6, 2026. Those whose names were missing from the draft had to submit Form 6 to seek inclusion. Following the fourth extension, the deadline for filing claims and objections was March 6, while the final electoral roll was published on April 10.
At present a special summary revision (SSR) of electoral rolls is going on in the state. The draft roll was published on November 17.
The Methodology
For each of 69 booths in UP, Alt News read the draft list (January 6, 2026) and the final list (April 10, 2026) entry by entry, and matched the count with the totals on each list’s cover page. We treated two entries as the same person only if the name, father’s or husband’s name, age and house number all matched.
We checked every case against the scanned entry. We then looked up Form 6 applications in the Form 9 lists. The latter is a public list of every Form 6 application an election office received, with the applicant’s name, relative and address. The lists we examined cover 13 assembly constituencies. The 69 booths that we chose fall into the three following groups:
One Form, Several Voter IDs
Listed below are 11 voters (chosen randomly from the 230 to explain the nature of the anomalies) whose names did not appear on the January 6 draft list but were all added to the final list. In each of these cases, the entries share the same name, relative, age and house number, but carry different EPIC numbers. We use first names because they are private citizens.
Our findings revealed two patterns: For Ishlok, Najmeen, Himanshu, Pinki, Saurabh and Aakash, every form became a voter ID, and the entries sit next to each other on the list. Saurabh’s are serial numbers 1004 and 1005.
From Sundar to Sunita, the list has more entries than the published Form 6 list has forms. Married couple Vijay Lakshmi and Dharmendra have a cumulative total of five voter IDs. Vijay Lakshmi has three, while her husband has two.
Anushree Verma, whose husband is Akshay Verma, had filled Form 6 twice and received three voter IDs.
Sundar, mentioned at the beginning, had filled the form twice (According to Form 9) and in return got four voter IDs.
The biggest single cluster of duplicate voters is booth 449 in Chachoi, Sikandrabad (Bulandshahr), where the BJP won 94% of the votes in 2022. The final list adds 69 names to this booth.
Of these, 34 entries are for 17 people, each listed twice with a new EPIC. None of the 17 names are on the January 6 draft list. Fifteen of the 17 filed one Form 6 each on the published lists. For two, Hasmuddin and Heema Devi, we found none. Six of the 17 live at house 91. One of them, Vikas, is listed once as female and once as male.
Some duplicates were already there before the revision and were not removed. In booth 330 of Husainganj (Fatehpur), two brothers appear twice each, at serials 108 and 109 and at 110 and 111 respectively, on both the draft and final lists.
In booth 1044 of Sahibabad, a father and son already on the list at house number 306 were added again with new IDs at house number 840. We found no Form 6 for either.
The published Form 9 lists for Khair village show one applicant, Bhuvnesh, son of Sanjeev Kumar of Simrauthi village, ten times between January 31 and March 6, 2026.
Across the Form 9 lists of the 13 constituencies, 3,369 people were found to have filed Form 6 between two to 10 times.
Missing Addresses, Renamed IDs, Suspicious Deletions
In booth 330 of Husainganj (Fatehpur), 20 of the 64 new voters have no house number. The field holds a place name, Oramha, for unrelated families.
Across the 37 city booths, 62 new voters were added with house “0” or a blank. In booth 354 of Kairana (Shamli), 48 voters were already listed at “house 3” on the draft list, and eight more were added from at least seven different families.
In Khair constituency, house number 658, under which all four of Sundar’s entries are listed, is associated with 36 voters from approximately 19 families.
A shared or missing house number is not, in itself, evidence of electoral irregularity, as most villages do not have a system of house numbering. The concern, however, is how entries without a verifiable address could be physically checked during field visits.
Moreover, in booth 351 of Sidhauli (Sitapur), three women’s names appeared changed between the draft and final lists, while the EPIC number, husband’s name, house number and age stayed the same. Rekharani became Lakshmi Devi, Gayashri became Meena Devi and Shivrani became Neelam.
We found 15 such cases across 20 rural booths. These changes could be legitimate corrections. However, only the corresponding Form 8 applications, used to request corrections to electoral roll entries, can establish the basis for the changes.
The most striking example of renamed entries is in booth 327 of Gorakhpur Rural. Serial 799 was Bhathwa, male, 53, house 156, on the draft list. On the final list, the same EPIC belongs to Rusha Devi, female, 50, house 56. Rusha Devi, husband Parmeshwar, also appears at serial numbers 924 and 930 of the addition list under two new EPICs. We found no Form 6 for her among the 23,136 applications in the Gorakhpur Rural lists.
In booth 943 of Sahibabad, 298 entries from one part of the 2025 electoral roll were deleted, 280 of them marked as “absent”. The deletions occurred in consecutive chunks of 23, 17, 14 and 10 names (shown in the plot below). Since electoral rolls are arranged by house and lane, such clusters could simply indicate that an entire building or group of homes had been vacated. A door-to-door verification would establish this. Whether such visits were conducted is something the Election Commission can clarify.
It is worth noting how many voters in every 1,000 appear twice or more on the final roll. See the chart below:
Questions for the Poll Panel
The analysis above poses several significant questions for the election commission vis-a-vis the SIR exercise in Uttar Pradesh. Some of them are the following:
- How did one Form 6 become two or three voter IDs – and how many times did this happen across UP?
- Why are repeat applications from the same person, at the same address, not merged before an ID is issued?
- How did officials verify new voters at house ‘0’, blank addresses and catch-all house numbers?
- How to explain the long runs of consecutive ‘Absent’ deletions – were these homes actually visited?
UP CEO’s Response
The Uttar Pradesh CEO initially denied findings by Alt News co-founder Mohammed Zubair, who flagged Sundar’s case of four different EPIC IDs on X. The office responded with the following post:
Mr Fact-checker please fact-check your own facts.
There is no such scheme as “Buy one Get one free” scheme by Election Commission.
As per your post, the voter had submitted only two applications and he got 4 EPIC cards.
This statement is false.
The voter had submitted 4 applications.
If you want to dispute our facts then you post the reference numbers of two applications that you claim he had submitted and we will post the reference number of the remaining two.
The problem of generation of multiple EPICs on submission of multiple forms of an individual is a long standing one. We do deduplication through ECINET periodically. We are on path to achieving the objective of catching multiple forms submitted by an individual at the submission stage only. We will achieve our objective very soon.
Please do not incite people by making patently false statements about ECI and thereby trying to create disaffection among the citizens towards a Constitutional Body.
You are advised to rectify your mistake by amending or deleting your post after completing your own due diligence now that you have been informed by us about your wrong information.
— CEO Uttar Pradesh (@ceoup) October 17, 2026
The CEO claimed that Sundar had submitted four Form 6 applications, resulting in four separate entries on the final electoral roll. This contradicted the official Form 6 application list, which recorded only two applications from Sundar. However, the CEO’s response also acknowledged that “the problem of generation of multiple EPICs on submission of multiple forms of an individual is a long-standing one”.
The discrepancy over whether Sundar submitted two or four applications does not alter the central issue: the Commission itself acknowledges that multiple applications by the same voter can result in the generation of multiple EPIC numbers. Its response also indicates that the system does not consistently prevent such duplication at the application stage, necessitating periodic deduplication through ECINET.
On October 19, the CEO directed election officials to expedite the removal of duplicate entries ahead of the 2027 Assembly elections and identify cases in which individual voters had submitted multiple applications during the SIR.
Readers should note that some of the errors documented in this article were rectified by the Election Commission in the intervening period between our initial identification of these anomalies and the publication of this report.

The sandpaper plot - who was there, who said what?
- Published
The sandpaper scandal, one of the biggest controversies in the history of Test cricket, continues to engulf Australian sport.
Fresh evidence from Cameron Bancroft - the culprit of the ball-tampering in South Africa in 2018 - has heaped pressure on Australia captain Pat Cummins, former coach Darren Lehmann and Cricket Australia.
In a detailed account of more than 4,000 words published in the West Australian newspaper, Bancroft alleges all the Australia players and coaches present in Cape Town eight years ago knew of the plot.
Bancroft's explosive testimony supports claims made by Usman Khawaja, David Warner and Chadd Sayers.
However, Cummins denied Khawaja's version of events in his own extraordinary news conference in Sydney last week. Cummins spoke to the media for 68 minutes in an address broadcast on live television.
Here, BBC Sport collects the most recent accounts of players and coaches involved in the saga that became widely known as sandpapergate.
Usman Khawaja
Batter Khawaja played all four Tests in South Africa and a total of 88 for Australia before retiring from international cricket earlier this year.
Revelations in his autobiography reignited debate around the sandpaper scandal and made headlines across the globe.
"It was all of us," Khawaja said. "Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us.
"In an ideal world, I don't want to do this. I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now.
"Even in the change rooms when I was talking to them after the game. I said, 'Take this as a team'.
"We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team, and so I was always of that stance."
- Whole Australia team knew of sandpaper use - Khawaja 
  - Published6 November
David Warner
Warner was Australia's opening batter and vice-captain during the 2018 series. He, along with captain Steve Smith and Bancroft, were the three players punished for the ball-tampering.
The Cricket Australia (CA) investigation in 2018 found Warner developed the plan and that he instructed Bancroft to carry out the cheating.
After serving his ban, Warner returned to play a further 133 times for Australia across formats, including three Ashes series and the 2023 World Cup win. He retired from international cricket in 2024.
In response to Khawaja's book, Warner said: "I thank you for what you've done. It's 100% accurate what you've said. Now everyone knows the truth."
He also accused Cricket Australia of a cover-up, describing the CA investigation as "rushed" and botched".
"As far as l am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," Warner said.
"If that's correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?"
- Warner accuses Cricket Australia of 'cover-up' 
  - Published4 days ago
Pat Cummins
The Cape Town Test was the 13th of Cummins' Test career. A key bowler, he would go on to be named Australia's Test captain in 2021. It is a position he still holds.
Prior to Khawaja's book, Cummins and the other bowlers from Cape Town - Hazlewood, Starc and Lyon - had always denied knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper.
In an extraordinary news conference last week, Cummins called Khawaja's claims that the whole team knew about the plan "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense".
"I said that consistently for the last eight years," Cummins said. "I did not know that was happening.
"He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball-tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense."
Asked if he knew of any plans at any stage to tamper with the ball during the series against South Africa, Cummins said: "No."
Cummins also said he did not remember a meeting where Khawaja had called on the team to take collective responsibility - something his former team-mate claimed.
Cameron Bancroft
Opening batter Bancroft was playing his eighth Test in Cape Town, aged 25. He was the player caught using sandpaper on the field.
He played another two Tests after serving his ban and is still playing for Western Australia. He turns 34 this week.
In 2021, Bancroft said it was "self-explanatory" whether the bowlers knew of the plan, and on Wednesday he backed Khawaja's account, saying Cummins' news conference made him "feel angry, betrayed and alone".
Like Khawaja, Bancroft said sandpaper was first used during the second Test against South Africa – the match before he was caught - and also said he had conversations with the Australia seamers about whether the ball was "swinging enough".
He said the entire playing group and staff had "celebrations" about the effect of the sandpaper. He also claimed that coach Lehmann and bowling coach David Saker were present in the initial discussions and that Bancroft's role was also discussed in a team meeting before day three.
In an account published by the West Australian on Wednesday, Bancroft wrote: "All the bowlers gave me feedback if my work on the ball was working. It was helpful.
"Is it going yet? It's not going yet, it needs more. So I would use the sandpaper more on the ball.
"There was even a time I was told to stop out of fear what I was doing was becoming too obvious."
- Bancroft sandpaper claims heap pressure on Cummins 
  - Published9 hours ago
Darren Lehmann
Lehmann was Australia coach at the time of the scandal. He was cleared by the CA investigation and said he had "no prior knowledge" of the plan to ball-tamper.
He resigned after the series and has been Northamptonshire coach since the start of the 2025 English season.
After Khawaja's revelations, Lehmann said: "I don't think everyone would have known [about the use of sandpaper]. You do know ball-tampering is going on because it's been happening for 150 years."
After Cricket Australia said it would hold an open forum, Lehmann said he has "nothing to hide".
Speaking on radio coverage of the third one-day international against England after Bancroft's account was published, Lehmann said: "I need to sit back, process it and work through each allegation.
"That's what I'll be doing over the next few days.
"I need to have a really good read of it. I need to make sure I'm saying what I want to say."
Steve Smith
Smith, one of the greatest batters of his generation, was Australia's captain at the time of the scandal.
After serving a 12-month ban, he returned for the World Cup and Ashes the following year and has stood in as captain at times since.
He was found to have been aware of the plan to cheat and to mislead the public and match officials.
Smith, who broke down in tears when apologising at a subsequent news conference, as cameras captured the emotional toll of the moment, has not spoken publicly since Khawaja's book was published.
Speaking about the episode in September this year, he said: "That was a traumatic experience in my life and when I hear the flash of a camera it makes me revisit that in a way.
"I've tried to kind of erase a lot of 2018 and what happened. I can't remember a lot about the series. I've tried to block most of it out of my memory bank."
Mitchell Marsh
Marsh was bowling when Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball in Cape Town. As an all-rounder, he was not part of the 2021 bowlers' statement.
Marsh was captain during Australia's recent ODI series against England and refused to answer questions on the topic before the series opener.
"I am not here to share mine [story] today," he said.
"I respect Uzzie [Khawaja] has told his story; my focus is on tomorrow. I am not here to go back on South Africa."
Following the conclusion of the series, Marsh did not take part in his post-match news conference, with 26-year-old bowler Jack Edwards taking his place.
Tim Paine
Paine was Australia's wicketkeeper during the South Africa series and was made captain when Smith was banned.
He served in the role until he stood down in 2021 over a historical investigation into sexually explicit text messages sent to a female colleague.
In his autobiography, Paine said the suggestion everyone in the Australia dressing room must have known about the sandpaper use is "rubbish" and claimed he first found out when images appeared on the big screen in Cape Town.
"Everyone out there was shocked when they looked up on the big screen and saw Cameron Bancroft with a piece of sandpaper in his hand," Paine wrote. "I was stunned. We all were.
"My heart sank, I was thinking, 'What the f***?' A sense of dread came over us all."
Bancroft said he discussed whether the ball was reversing with Paine during the second Test.
David Saker
Saker was Australia's bowling coach during the South Africa series.
Bancroft alleged Saker was present for discussions about the use of sandpaper and told the batter he needed to do more to the ball.
Saker was also England bowling coach as recently as last month's tri-series in Pakistan. He was an influential part of England's 2010-11 Ashes win.
In 2021, reflecting on the sandpaper saga, Saker said: "Obviously a lot of things went wrong at that time. There was a lot of people to blame. It could have been me to blame, it could have been someone else. It could have been stopped and it wasn't, which is unfortunate.
"Cameron's a very nice guy. He's just doing it to get something off his chest… He's not going to be the last. You could point your finger at me, you could point your finger at Boof [Lehmann]. Could you point it at other people? Of course you could.
"The disappointing thing is it's never going to go away. Regardless of what's said. We all know that we made a monumental mistake. The gravity wasn't as plain until it all came out."
Mitchell Starc
Starc was an integral part of the vaunted Australia attack in Cape Town and remains so in the present day. He is ranked as the number one bowler in Test cricket by the International Cricket Council.
Left-armer Starc repeatedly denied knowledge of the sandpaper plot, including in the statement released with Cummins, Hazlewood and Lyon in 2021, and in a news conference in the days after Khawaja's claims emerged.
Speaking on 10 November, Starc said: "Obviously, there's differing opinions of eight years ago. We were heavily grilled through the process at the time, and since, and I guess I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers, but where I stand, my opinion hasn't changed. My recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021.
"I'll stick to what I said five years ago, what I said at the time, eight years ago. Clearly, there's different versions from different people, and I'll leave it where I left it back then."
Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon
Along with Cummins and Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon have remained part of Australia's first-choice bowling unit in the eight years since the sandpaper scandal, forming one of the greatest four-man attacks in Test history.
Seamer Hazlewood and off-spinner Lyon joined Cummins and Starc in releasing a statement in 2021, responding to an interview given by Bancroft to the Guardian newspaper when he said the bowlers' involvement in the sandpaper plot was "self-explanatory".
Neither Hazlewood nor Lyon has spoken publicly since the fresh claims from Khawaja, Warner and Bancroft emerged.
Their statement released with Cummins and Starc in 2021 said: "We pride ourselves on our honesty. So it's been disappointing to see that our integrity has been questioned by some journalists and past players in recent days in regard to the Cape Town Test of 2018.
"We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands.
"We respectfully request an end to the rumour-mongering and innuendo. It has gone on too long and it is time to move on."
Chadd Sayers and Jon Holland
A swing bowler, Sayers played his only Test for Australia after the sandpaper controversy erupted – the fourth and final match of the series against South Africa in Johannesburg.
Sayers, who retired from first-class cricket in 2021, spoke to Australian radio station SEN in the aftermath of Khawaja's claims, to corroborate the former batter's account.
Sayers claimed to have removed sandpaper from the field in the second Test against South Africa, the match before Bancroft was caught. He also backed up Khawaja's assertion that the entire Australia squad discussed the sandpaper issue after it was revealed in Cape Town.

"After the occurrence in Cape Town, we all sat in the changing rooms after that day's play and, probably for 60 to 90 minutes, we talked about what had happened and I guess where to next."

Centre to launch fifth edition of Nayi Chetna gender campaign on Nov 25
New Delhi, The Centre will launch the fifth edition of its national gender campaign, 'Nayi Chetna, Pahal Badlav Ki', on November 25, with a focus on strengthening women's economic empowerment, access to assets, safe mobility and equal opportunities, an official statement said.
The month-long campaign, spearheaded by the Ministry of Rural Development under the Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana-National Rural Livelihoods Mission , will run from November 25 to December 23 across the country.
Union Rural Development Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan will inaugurate the campaign in the presence of Women and Child Development Minister Annpurna Devi and Minister of State for Rural Development Kamlesh Paswan.
The fifth edition, themed "From Access to Agency: Empowering Women through Livelihoods and Equal Opportunities for a Viksit Bharat", seeks to move beyond awareness generation towards coordinated action to improve women's economic participation, independence and decision-making, the Rural Development Ministry said.
It will focus on recognising women as economic contributors, strengthening their access to and control over assets, promoting safe mobility and ensuring a more equitable distribution of unpaid care work.
The campaign will also seek to address barriers restricting women's access to livelihood opportunities, markets, financial services, public spaces and essential services.
A key highlight of the launch will be the release of a joint inter-ministerial advisory involving 15 ministries and departments to promote coordinated action on the campaign's objectives.
The advisory will provide a framework for aligning government schemes, programmes and institutional mechanisms to improve women's access to livelihoods, assets, financial services, safe mobility and support systems at the national, state, district and community levels.
A quadripartite memorandum of understanding among the Ministries of Rural Development and Women and Child Development, the Department of Justice and the National Legal Services Authority will also be released.
The agreement seeks to strengthen institutional coordination for preventing and responding to gender-based violence at the community level, including through greater awareness of legal rights, access to justice and support mechanisms.
Community institutions set up under DAY-NRLM, including Self-Help Groups , Village Organisations, Cluster Level Federations and Gender Resource Centres, will play a central role in implementing the campaign.
New Gender Resource Centres will be inaugurated as community-level platforms to facilitate women's access to services, entitlements, support systems and grievance redressal mechanisms.
The Nayi Chetna 4.0 Assessment Report, documenting the findings and learnings from the previous edition, will also be released. State-level videos showcasing good practices and community-led initiatives, along with campaign video resources, will be unveiled.
Launched in 2022, Nayi Chetna has evolved into a nationwide campaign to address gender-based violence, challenge discriminatory social norms and promote gender equality.
The fifth edition will also seek to involve men, boys and young people in challenging discriminatory practices and promoting equality and shared responsibility.

It used to be called "pulling a Steve Jobs." Then it became "pulling a Sam Altman."
Moving forward, don't be surprised if it's referred to as "pulling a Jensen."
Jensen Huang just became the latest founder to return to lead their company after being pushed aside. On Monday, Nvidia reinstated Huang as CEO, 11 days after his November 12 resignation amid reports of extramarital affairs.
Here are other founders who, like Huang, made their comeback after being pushed out.
Sam Altman
Sam Altman's ouster as OpenAI CEO didn't last long.
The ChatGPT maker's board abruptly fired Altman on November 17, 2023, saying he had not been consistently candid in his communications with directors, hampering their ability to oversee him.
The decision set off a corporate crisis. OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman, whom the board had removed as chairman, resigned from the company before also returning. Microsoft, OpenAI's largest investor and commercial partner, offered Altman a job leading a new AI research team.
OpenAI chief scientist Ilya Sutskever, who had voted to fire Altman, publicly reversed course three days later. On November 20, Sutskever posted that he deeply regretted his participation in the board's decision and would do everything he could to reunite the company.
On the same day, more than 700 OpenAI employees signed an open letter demanding that the board resign and reinstate Altman, threatening to join him at Microsoft if it didn't.
On November 21, four days after firing Altman, OpenAI announced an agreement in principle for him to return as CEO under a reconstituted board. Altman officially resumed the job on November 29, with Brockman also returning as president.
Steve Jobs
Steve Jobs, Apple's cofounder and chairman, was first pushed out by the person he had recruited to run the company.
In 1985, then-CEO John Sculley and Apple's board stripped Jobs of his operational responsibilities after a power struggle over the company's strategy, amid slowing Macintosh sales. Jobs remained chairman but soon resigned, leaving to start the computer company NeXT.
More than a decade later, Apple came calling. The company announced a roughly $400 million deal to buy NeXT in December 1996 and completed the acquisition in February 1997, bringing Jobs back as an advisor.
Jobs became Apple's de facto leader after Gil Amelio's departure in July 1997. Apple announced his appointment as interim CEO that September, setting the stage for a monumental turnaround.
The colorful iMac, launched in 1998, helped sustain the company's profitability. He then took the company beyond computers, introducing the iPod in 2001 and the iTunes Music Store in 2003, before unveiling the iPhone in 2007 and the iPad in 2010.
Jobs resigned as CEO in 2011 amid long-standing health problems, including a rare form of pancreatic cancer. By then, Apple had grown from a roughly $2 billion company when Jobs returned to one worth about $350 billion.
Jack Dorsey
Jack Dorsey's stint as Twitter's first CEO lasted less than two years.
Dorsey, who co-founded the company in 2006, was pushed out of the CEO role in October 2008 as the company grew and directors questioned his management approach. Dorsey stayed on as chairman of the board, while cofounder Evan Williams took over as CEO.
Dorsey went on to cofound payments company Square, now known as Block, and remained a major Twitter shareholder and board member.
He regained the position roughly seven years after being pushed out, returning as interim CEO in July 2015 before being confirmed permanently that autumn.
Dorsey then led Twitter and Square simultaneously until he stepped down from Twitter in 2021; the board appointed then-CTO Parag Agrawal as his successor. Less than a year later, Elon Musk completed his $44 billion acquisition of Twitter and fired Agrawal.
Matt Mullenweg
Matt Mullenweg's brief ouster as CEO of Automattic, the company behind WordPress.com, lasted 33 hours and 20 minutes.
In September 2026, Automattic's board voted to put Mullenweg on a paid leave of absence, naming CFO Mark Davies as interim CEO. Mullenweg said board members conspired against him in messages to employees.
The board's attempt to sideline the founder quickly unraveled after Mullenweg challenged the move and leveraged his controlling voting stake to regain authority. Mullenweg told employees he was back in control, and the company confirmed his reinstatement on September 12.
Mullenweg had said at TechCrunch Disrupt in 2024 that he controlled 84% of the company's voting power.
After the reversal, the board was reconstituted, and Davies and Automattic's chief legal officer departed.

The 20th annual LA Skins Fest concluded on Sunday following the five-day celebration of Native American cinema and special screenings at the TCL Chinese Theatre.
Since its founding, the festival has become a platform for Indigenous filmmakers to showcase their work, connect with entertainment industry professionals and reach new audiences. It also extends its mission outside the annual festival through its partnership with the Native American Media Alliance, supporting year-round professional development initiatives that includes writing labs, animation programs, showrunner training, development workshops and youth media education.
This year’s LA Skins Fest featured a line-up of narrative features, documentaries, short films and special screenings that recognize Indigenous artists. This year’s festival opened with films presented by Amazon MGM Studios and also included a Netflix screening of “North of North” with actress Anna Lambe and a Cherokee-language screening of “The Rings of Power” followed by a discussion with the actors and Cherokee Film’s language revitalization team.
The festival also began with a Native Youth Studio Tour at Sony Pictures Studios, providing students from Sherman Indian High School an introduction to career opportunities in media, which further reflects the festival’s dedication to supporting future generations of Native American entertainment professionals.
Presented by Paramount Television Studios, the 15th Annual Native American Media Awards hosted by Q’orianka Kilcher and Kiowa Gordon concluded the festival with a celebration of Indigenous filmmakers, writers, actors and creative professionals. Among this year’s winners were Orlando Skidmore for achievement in filmmaking and Sophia Lindholm for achievement in student filmmaking. The emerging filmmaker award was given to Gina East for the narrative film category and Elissa Simons for the documentary category.
The ceremony also recognized the 6th Annual Native American Writer Accelerator Grantees. Sponsored by Netflix, the program selects 12 Indigenous writers to receive financial assistance and opportunities to advance their careers in media. This year’s grantees are Doane Avery, Rachel Baldwin, Ripley Barnes, Sonny Brava, C.J. Caughman, Bryson Chun, Kelly Lynne D’Angelo, Yelyna DeLeon, Marleah Makpiaq LaBelle, Desiree Leiahloha, Jason Marcus and Vlad Perez.

The FAA fired several hundred employees in February 2025. However …
DOGE itself did not have the authority to make the firings. In all, 352 probationary employees — meaning those in their first year — were let go; 132 were reinstated the following month. According to the FAA, no airway transportation systems specialists, who maintain critical navigation systems, were among those dismissed.
In mid-November, following a nationwide ground stop ordered by the Federal Aviation Administration, social media users shared claims that the Department of Government Efficiency, a Trump administration initiative to cut government spending and jobs, laid off hundreds of technicians responsible for maintaining and upgrading critical air navigation systems.
"DOGE laid off 400 technicians in charge of maintaining and upgrading critical FAA navigational systems," one Facebook post (archived) read.
(Facebook user Tom Riley)
Versions of the rumor spread on multiple social media platforms, including X and Facebook. Some posts suggested the alleged layoffs contributed to the Nov. 13 ground stop. Snopes readers also asked about a possible connection between the layoffs and the disruption.
In short, the FAA fired 352 probationary employees in February 2025, but they were not 400 technicians maintaining critical navigation systems, as the posts claimed. According to the FAA, no airway transportation systems specialists, who maintain such equipment, were among those dismissed. The firings did affect employees in other aviation safety and support roles, and some were later reinstated. There was no evidence that the job cuts directly contributed to the Nov. 13 ground stop. As such, we have rated this claim as mostly false.
We have reached out to the FAA with questions about the firings and whether they affected FAA operations. We will update this article if we receive a response.
FAA fired fewer than 400 employees in February 2025
The job cuts mentioned in social media posts did happen, although the number of employees was slightly lower than social media users claimed. In February 2025, the Trump administration fired 352 probationary FAA employees, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. Of those, 132 were represented by the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union.
Although social media posts attributed the firings to DOGE, the initiative itself did not have authority to fire FAA employees. The FAA fired the employees as part of Trump administration's broader cuts to the federal workforce.
DOGE was, however, involved in discussions about the cuts. In a May 2025 interview with NBC's "Meet the Press," Duffy acknowledged discussing with Elon Musk — who led the DOGE initiative — which FAA positions should be protected from the cuts.
"We went back and forth, and Elon agreed, the president agreed," Duffy said. He also claimed the agency retained all positions considered critical to aviation safety, saying: "The FAA has 46,000 employees. And if you lost 350, is this affecting our safety mission? There's a lot of things the FAA does. But for us, safety is key. So, no, we've retained all those safety positions."
In response to our questions, the Transportation Department directed us to a Nov. 16 statement on X, which read:
MYTH: DOGE got rid of essential employees that made FAA less safe and effective.
TRUTH: The FAA has around 45,000 employees. Less than 400 were let go via DOGE, and they were all probationary, meaning they had been hired less than a year ago. Zero air traffic controllers or critical safety personnel were let go.
(X account @USDOTRapid)
The department also told us that the dismissals "did not negatively affect the Department in any way."
Who was affected by the FAA firings?
Contrary to social media posts, the dismissed employees were not 400 technicians responsible for maintaining and upgrading critical navigational systems.
According to the FAA's May 2026 workforce plan, no airway transportation systems specialists were terminated as probationary employees. Such employees are specialized technicians responsible for maintaining and repairing "radar, communications, navigational aids, airport lighting, backup power, heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) equipment."
The Transportation Department also confirmed this in an email to Snopes, stating, "No ATSS were terminated as probationary employees in February 2025 and the FAA has continued to hire and onboard ATSS since the start of this administration."
However, the firings did affect employees in other positions, including some supporting aviation safety and technical operations. According to the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists, 59 of the dismissed employees represented by the union worked in technical operations, 39 in flight standards, 19 in mission support services and 15 in air traffic services.
In an email to Snopes, the union provided the following breakdown of the affected positions and their responsibilities:
Aeronautical information specialists – evaluation, selection and preparation of navigation
maps, routes, chart, procedures and flight paths.
Maintenance mechanics maintain and repair the grounds and buildings where controllers and systems
specialists work. This requires detailed knowledge of specific trades such as carpentry, plumbing, and electrical.
Management & Program Assistants and Aviation Safety Assistants – maintain office records, office supplies, updates, logistics support and maintain data reports.
Environmental Protection Specialists – manage, supervise, or perform administrative or program work relating to environmental protection programs. They ensure compliance with environmental laws and regulations.
The union also clarified that the employees dismissed from the FAA's Technical Operations division worked as maintenance mechanics, environmental protection specialists and management and program assistants. "So no, none of them worked directly on navigation or communications equipment," the union told Snopes — referring to all 132 dismissed employees it represented.
Still, the fact that no airway transportation systems specialists were fired does not mean the other positions were completely unrelated to aviation safety. In March 2025 testimony to Congress, PASS President David Spero warned that the job cuts would increase workloads for employees already working in an understaffed agency, saying, "This action will increase the workload for frontline aviation safety workers and place new responsibilities on a workforce that is already stretched thin."
Another complication is the lack of a consistent definition of safety-critical positions. A September 2026 audit by the Transportation Department's Office of Inspector General found the criteria for classifying such positions varied across FAA offices.
Some employees were later reinstated
On March 17, 2025, the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists announced that the FAA was reinstating all 132 dismissed employees represented by the union, following a federal court ruling. According to the union, the employees were expected to return to work on March 20 and receive back pay.
In an email to Snopes in November, the union said that approximately 40 of those 132 employees were no longer represented by the union. "They could have found other employment before or after the court order, been reassigned to another FAA bargaining unit or taken a detail or promotion at the agency," spokesperson Liz Doherty told us.
Therefore, it remains unclear how many of the dismissed employees were still working for the FAA at the time of the Nov. 13 nationwide ground stop. We also asked the Transportation Department for updated figures on the reinstatements and the employees' current status. We will update this article if we receive a response.
No evidence firings caused the ground stop
As for the nationwide ground stop, there is no evidence that the February 2025 FAA firings contributed to the disruption. As we previously reported, the FAA said the problem involved its older communications network. In a Nov. 15 statement, the agency identified two possible locations connected to the disruption, including a site in Arkansas where contractor L3Harris was installing a new router. As of Nov. 19, the exact cause of the shutdown remained under investigation.
In a statement shared after the incident, the union said its represented technicians "were not involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop." The union also told us via email that it found no direct connection between the firings and the incident:
PASS sees no direct connection between the February 2025 terminations and Friday's ground stop. All the probationary employees are essential to the aviation ecosystem that keeps the National Airspace System functioning safely and efficiently. However, none would have been involved directly with the router upgrades that appear to have caused the ground stop.
Still, the FAA had broader staffing problems. In its May workforce plan (Page 8), the agency said it did not have enough employees to cover all shifts at 67 facilities. The report also found that airway transportation systems specialists worked an average of 115 hours of overtime in fiscal year 2025.
The union also stressed the need for more technicians, telling us:
PASS fully supports the modernization efforts undertaken by the DOT and FAA. However, the FAA agrees that the airway transportation systems specialist workforce is understaffed and earlier this year released that workforce plan calling for the hiring of 750 more technicians. The workforce needs to be fully staffed, funded and provided the resources need to continue performing their safety critical work.
However, there is no evidence that the February 2025 firings contributed to the November ground stop despite these broader staffing problems.

There is an uncanny similarity between Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), the virus responsible for the COVID-19 pandemic, and air pollution. During the pandemic, the virus entered our bodies through the air we breathed; harmful particulate matter and toxic gases enter through the same respiratory route. Additionally, both damage multiple organs, including the lungs, heart and brain. Yet, while COVID-19 prompted an unprecedented emergency national response, air pollution continues to be treated largely as a seasonal inconvenience.
The harmful effects of air pollution are well-established. An adult takes approximately 20,000–25,000 breaths daily, meaning that even a relatively miniscule worsening of air quality can have substantial health consequences over time. This alone should make improving the quality of air an urgent public health priority.

AI-native data security platform Matters.AI (formerly OptiQ.AI) has raised ₹115 Cr ($12.0 Mn) in a pre-Series A funding round led by Tanglin Venture Partners. IIFL Fintech Fund, Piper Serica’s Bharat Tech Fund, Foster Ventures, and Tetration Ventures also joined the startup’s cap table, while existing investors Kalaari Capital and Endiya Partners doubled down on their earlier bet on the Bengaluru-based AI startup. The startup will utilise the capital to accelerate R&D in data lineage, autonomous investigation, endpoint and browser intelligence, and prevention of sensitive data misuse by AI agents. It is also expanding its North American sales operations and leadership. “Enterprise data security is at an inflection point. As AI agents increasingly operate alongside humans, the challenge is no longer just knowing where sensitive data resides, but understanding how it’s being used and acting before it becomes a risk,” said Tanglin’s managing partner Sankalp Gupta. Founded in 2023 by Keshava Murthy and Harsh Sahu, Matters.AI builds an autonomous “AI Security Engineer for Data” powered by its Data Detection and Response (DDR) platform. Matters.AI operates teams across Bengaluru and the San Francisco Bay Area. The startup claims to serve over 50 clients including major financial institutions, stockbroking firms, asset managers, retailers, and digital media platforms. It has raised around ₹175 Cr till date, including the latest round. As enterprises increasingly deploy autonomous AI agents, Matters’ platform helps identify sensitive data and trace how agents are moving it around by consolidating four typically fragmented enterprise functions – data security posture management, insider risk, activity monitoring, and data loss prevention – into a single platform. The platform discovers sensitive information across cloud, on-premises systems, SaaS applications, endpoints, and browsers. It tracks how the data moves using LLM-based fingerprinting, identifies risk signals and correlates them, and autonomously investigates and remediates policy violations. With the latest advances in generative AI, frontier models are now increasingly being used to find vulnerabilities and exploits in software within a fraction of the time it once took. The integration of AI into these systems, if not implemented with careful data governance and visibility, can create even more entry points for attackers. Concerns around cybersecurity have only become more prominent in recent weeks with disruptions to the tech infrastructure used by Microsoft, Apple, JPMorgan Chase and the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). Earlier this week, SaaS startup MoEngage, too, saw its cloud infrastructure breached via a compromised third-party vendor account.

When Ramayana – Part I was announced as a grand cinematic spectacle, its makers were clearly aiming to deliver an experience that audiences would want to watch on the biggest screens. But did anyone expect 3D to play such an enormous role in the film's box office success? A detailed analysis of our format-wise data reveals a fascinating answer.
As per the box office data available until November 23, 3:30 PM, Ramayana has collected an extraordinary Rs. 584.11 crores nett from 3D screenings across all languages and premium formats. That accounts for a whopping 65.07% of the film's Rs. 897.68 crore India nett total. In other words, nearly Rs. 2 out of every Rs. 3 earned by Ramayana in India has come from its 3D presentations!
However, the most interesting statistic emerges when we examine ticket sales. The 3D versions have sold approximately 1.75 crore tickets, accounting for 57.39% of the film's 3.05 crore admissions. Despite generating 57% of the footfalls, they have contributed 65% of the revenue. This difference reveals the tremendous financial advantage enjoyed by 3D screenings.
What makes this achievement even more remarkable is that standard 3D, without including IMAX, 4DX, ScreenX and other specialised presentations, has generated a staggering Rs. 510.28 crores nett. By comparison, standard 2D screenings have contributed Rs. 311.69 crores. This means standard 3D has generated approximately Rs. 198.59 crores more than standard 2D, an enormous difference that underlines its importance to the film's theatrical business.
The average nett realisation per ticket offers another interesting insight. Standard 3D has generated approximately Rs. 306 per admission, compared with Rs. 240 for standard 2D. That's a premium of nearly 27.5%. When all 3D formats are considered, the average rises to approximately Rs. 333 nett per ticket, compared with Rs. 241 across non-3D formats.
While standard 3D remains the biggest revenue generator, the more expensive premium formats have also made a substantial contribution. IMAX 3D alone has generated Rs. 54.15 crores nett, followed by 4DX 3D at Rs. 12.91 crores. ScreenX 3D, Dolby Cinema 3D, ICE 3D and EPIQ 3D have collectively added another Rs. 6.77 crores. Together, these specialised 3D formats have generated approximately Rs. 73.83 crores. The fascinating aspect is that audiences have not merely chosen between 2D and 3D. A significant section has also opted for more expensive premium presentations. Of course, these figures do not establish that the film would have earned exactly the same amount had 3D been unavailable. Ticket pricing, screen allocation, locations and the size of the audiences differ across formats. Nevertheless, the conclusion is difficult to ignore.
For a film mounted on the scale of Ramayana, 3D has proved to be far more than a technological attraction. It has become one of its biggest revenue engines.
And with Rs. 584 crores already generated from 3D alone, the numbers raise an interesting question for the industry: Will Ramayana encourage more Indian filmmakers to treat premium theatrical presentation as a major part of their box office strategy rather than merely an optional add-on?

What failure of COP31 reveals about a divided world
- Published
Some may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming.
Yet that is what happened in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday.
The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy. But it may tell us even more about the increasingly divided world in which the negotiations take place.
Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who led the negotiations, spoke of a backdrop constituting "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". The competing demands, he said, had become "unbridgeable red lines".
Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and the summit's president, was blunter. Governments should not disappoint people desperate for climate action, he suggested, by getting "hung up on one word or phrase".
And Kurum had a point. Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, there was agreement to transition away from fossil fuels. The proposed Antalya Pact failed to mention them at all.
Was it really worth sacrificing the agreement over two words, then?
The countries that rejected it said the distinction was fundamental. They argued that there was a world of difference between promising to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and committing to move away from the fuels responsible for most of them. Without that explicit commitment, they feared the new agreement would weaken the one made in Dubai.
Normally, it is difficult to establish exactly who has said what at these conferences. Much of the bargaining takes place behind closed doors, and governments are often reluctant to admit which proposals they have opposed.
This time, some of the opposition was public - mostly from oil-producing nations.
Mohammad Ayoub, a Saudi negotiator speaking on behalf of the 22 Arab League countries, argued that Arab nations had contributed less than 2% of historical greenhouse gas emissions. It was wealthy industrialised nations, he said, that bore the overwhelming responsibility for the problem.
He defended the Arab countries' right to choose how to tackle climate change according to their national circumstances.
Russia's delegate Sergei Kononuchenko went further. Cutting oil and gas supplies before demand fell, he warned, would cause shortages, higher prices and energy poverty.
"For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel," he said.
The wider political backdrop was still more revealing.
The US, which in previous rounds of talks had helped broker compromises - sometimes working alongside China - had no official delegation in Antalya. President Donald Trump has rejected the entire international climate process.
And while delegates argued over fossil fuels in Turkey, Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen that included a pledge to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products.
The priorities of some of the world's most powerful governments appeared very different from those being discussed in the negotiating rooms.
A majority that may yet offer hope
Yet, perhaps, the picture is more optimistic than it first appears. About 130 governments backed a demand for explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels - roughly two-thirds of the countries represented in Antalya.
Christiana Figueres, who led the UN negotiations that delivered the Paris Agreement, argued that countries were right to walk away rather than endorse a weaker political commitment that might undermine the progress already made.
Looked at this way, the collapse is not evidence that the world has lost its appetite for climate action. Quite the opposite - a substantial majority of governments were demanding more ambitious action.
So why not simply find a way for them to move ahead without waiting for the countries determined to block them?
The difficulty becomes clearer when you look beyond the dispute over fossil fuels.
Kononuchenko had another target in his sights: climate finance. Much of the money wealthy countries provide to poorer nations, he complained, comes as loans rather than grants. He said that developing countries ended up repaying more than they received.
"This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner," he declared.
Then, in a striking moment, he leaned towards the microphone and switched from Russian into English to address his criticism directly to the Europeans: "First of all distinguished representatives of the EU."
Russia has its own reasons for attacking Europe, but the complaint about finance is one that many developing countries share. They argue that they are being asked to pay for damage they did little to cause while receiving too little help to adapt to climate change or build cleaner economies.
The EU had ruled out significant new funding before the negotiations began. Mohamed Adow, the Kenyan campaigner who heads Power Shift Africa, accused Europe of rejecting a flawed deal while refusing to acknowledge its own responsibility for the failure on finance.
So is it possible for a majority of countries to outvote those blocking progress?
The UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, has acknowledged the need to "improve, modernise and reform" the process. Some governments have proposed introducing voting when consensus proves impossible. Others want countries prepared to move faster to make their own agreements outside the formal talks.
But there is a reason the UN climate process depends on consensus. International climate co-operation is largely voluntary.
Voting might produce more ambitious agreements on paper, but would it persuade the governments that had been outvoted to act? Consensus also offers some protection to smaller and poorer nations that might otherwise find themselves overruled by the most powerful countries.
Meanwhile, the failure to agree a summit declaration does not mean climate action stops. Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles are becoming increasingly competitive, while the upheaval in global oil and gas supplies is giving countries another reason to generate their own electricity rather than depend on imported fossil fuels.
The energy transition is moving forward, whatever happens in the UN negotiating rooms. The problem is that it is not moving nearly fast enough for the climate.

  - Published20 hours ago
- Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31 
  - Published19 hours ago
A rare moment of agreement
Perhaps the most poignant aspect of the failed Antalya Pact is what the countries had apparently been prepared to accept.
The final draft expressed "deep concern" that global warming was expected to exceed 1.5°C in the next few years. It warned that further warming would cause increasingly serious damage, some of it irreversible, and called for urgent action to limit how far temperatures rose above that threshold.
This remarkably strong language had survived into the final version, apparently without provoking the opposition that sank the agreement. Even countries bitterly divided over fossil fuels and finance seemed prepared to acknowledge the scale of the danger.
Yet they couldn't agree on how to respond.
And that, perhaps, is what Antalya tells us about the state of international climate co-operation. The problem isn't simply finding the right words or changing the voting rules. It is persuading countries with very different interests to take action that no international authority can compel them to take.
That was always going to be difficult. In today's divided world, it looks harder than ever.

Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
And now Kimi, who turned 20 only in August, has dominated F1 in only his second season, and become the youngest world champion in the sport's history.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he entered, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments, including pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He took the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli took six poles and six wins in the first 11 races, establishing a 50-point lead in the championship.
Mercedes lost their dominant form in the second half of the season in the face of challenges from first McLaren and then Red Bull.
But Antonelli remained a consistent threat at the front, and he killed off his Monza ghosts in the Italian Grand Prix with a stunning victory after an engine penalty led to him starting 19th on the grid.
He put in a drive of clinical excellence and, with help from a safety car, chased down and caught Russell in the final laps to take a win that will go down in folklore.
The extent of his turnaround in form has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not [fitting the stereotype of] a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says.
"We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said 'Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1'," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."
