Nasscom seeks AI transformation scheme for IT firms in Budget 2027-28
The industry body said generative and agentic AI are changing what clients want, how technology work is delivered and how IT firms charge for it
The National Association of Software and Service Companies (Nasscom) has asked the government to set up a dedicated scheme to help Indian IT services companies adapt to artificial intelligence (AI). This demand is part of its pre-budget recommendations for the Union Budget 2027-28.
The industry body said generative and agentic AI are changing what clients want, how technology work is delivered and how IT firms charge for it.
Building new AI products and retraining staff needs money upfront, it said, and companies have to spend it while still delivering for existing clients. Smaller companies are hit hardest as they struggle to fund development, hire specialists and free up staff to learn on live projects.
Nasscom wants the budget to commit to an “AI Services Transformation and Innovation Scheme” for an initial three years. Under the proposal, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and the finance ministry would design the funding and implementation together with industry.
Also Read: Nasscom pushes back on US green card freeze: ‘Immigration, talent mobility distinct issues’
“A Budget 2027-28 commitment to develop the AI Services Transformation and Innovation Scheme for an initial three years, with MeitY and the Ministry of Finance designing funding and implementation with industry. This would support technology development and commercialisation, including offerings earning licence, subscription, usage-based or outcome-linked revenues, built and operated from India,” said Nasscom.
The scheme would back AI offerings that are built and run from India and earn money through licences, subscriptions, usage-based fees or outcome-linked pricing. It would also tie training to supervised work on real projects, so existing employees can move into new roles and freshers get hands-on experience. Smaller firms would get shared technical facilities, specialist support and joint projects.
Cybersecurity support for MSMEs
Cyber cover for MSMEs, tax clarity for Global capability centres (GCCs)
Nasscom has also asked for a contributory cybersecurity programme with a capped first-phase allocation. It would help manufacturing and services MSMEs put basic cyber protections in place and keep them running. Many of these small firms work inside the delivery chains of bigger IT companies that handle client data and run critical systems for enterprises worldwide, it said. Weak links there could hurt trust in Indian service delivery, the body said.
Also Read: Should the government own a piece of AI companies?
Tax clarity for global capability centres
Global capability centres (GCCs) are on the list too. These centres are taking on complex engineering, R&D and leadership work, and that brings more overseas specialists visiting, more secondments (overseas staff temporarily posted in India) and more India-based executives running global teams. Nasscom wants clear rules so none of this creates a taxable “permanent establishment” for the foreign parent.
Under Nasscom’s proposal, overseas staff could visit for up to 90 days in any 12-month period without creating a permanent establishment. A secondment wouldn’t create one either, as long as the Indian GCC directs the work and pays the salary, and reimbursing the actual salary cost wouldn’t be taxed as fees for technical services.

Mental health concerns among refugee communities are linked not only to past trauma, violence and forced displacement but also to legal uncertainty, limited work opportunities, poor living conditions and social isolation in host countries, finds a study of Sri Lankan Tamil and Rohingya communities in India, published in the International Journal of Migration, Health and Social Care.
Titled ‘Building mental health capacity in protracted refugee situations: Empirical pointers from Sri Lankan Tamil and Rohingya populations in India’, the study looks at common mental health concerns and barriers to accessing care. It calls for training community members and health workers to recognise psychological distress, provide basic support and facilitate access to professional mental health services.

China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.
Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”
China is the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases by far, producing more than a quarter of the world’s total, so its push for electrification is significant.
At Cop31, countries are being asked to sign up to a target of deriving 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035. Australia, the president of the negotiations, and the host nation Turkey have pushed the target and on Friday night Australia and China signed a joint statement endorsing the “35:35” goal.
But in the second draft text of the probably outcome from Cop31, released on Thursday, the electrification pledge was downgraded to one of a suite of voluntary options countries can take up to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.
In an interview with the Guardian at the talks, Wang said: “China will do our best to realise clean end-use electrification, and also help other countries to improve. China has significantly reduced the cost of clean technology and products and we would like to share our experience with other countries.”
Experts have said electrification is the next vital step in the shift to a low-carbon economy, as the only way to diminish the close to 80% of fossil fuels still used for primary energy, mostly for transport, heating and industry.
While civil society organisations want any commitment made on electrification to specify that it must be met from clean sources, a pledge that leaves the choice to countries is likely to have more widespread support, as many – including China and India – are resistant to anything they feel smacks of “top down” interference in national plans.
But campaigners argue that allowing individual countries to decide risks leaving the door open to more gas-fired power plants. Some compromise language is also possible that would urge countries to decarbonise their power.
Last year, electricity made up nearly 30% of China’s energy use and it is on track to make that 35% by 2030. Electricity is several times more efficient than fossil fuels, meaning that it takes far less energy to run electric vehicles, heat pumps and industrial processes than their fossil fuel counterparts.
Wang said China was happy with the 2035 target, but that it would be harder to meet if the electricity was required to come entirely from low-carbon sources. “For this target, no problem. But if you think about ensuring clean electrification, that may be a little bit difficult, even for China. For other countries, it’s even more difficult,” he said.
China still has a large number of coal-fired power stations and is planning some new ones, though fewer than before. Wang said this would be used for back-up during the transition to clean energy.
One of the key issues at Cop31 is the “transition away from fossil fuels”, which was one of the resolutions passed at the Cop28 summit in Dubai in 2023, but which countries have failed to flesh out since. The phrase was included in the first draft of the “cover decision” outcome from Cop31, presented on Monday, but excised from the second draftissued on Thursday, to the dismay of many countries and campaigners.
Wang said: “We agree with paragraph 28 of the UAE consensus [the transition resolution]. But maybe different countries have different roadmaps. It’s very difficult to have only one unified roadmap for every country. So maybe we will help other countries to have their own country-based solutions, to realise their own national way of establishing a new renewable-based power system.”
China is also concerned about trade barriers to its clean technology exports, including the tariffs that the US under Donald Trump has placed on Chinese goods, and the “carbon border adjustment mechanism” (CBAM) imposed by the EU. The CBAM penalises imports from countries with looser regulations on carbon than the EU, which forces companies in high-carbon sectors to pay for their carbon emissions in order to level the playing field.
Some smaller developing countries have criticised the EU for its CBAM, warning that it will hamper their manufacturing industries. The EU said it had processes in place to ensure smaller developing countries were not hurt.
Wang called for more work on trade issues at Cops. “They must come together to find a unified approach,” he said. “China and other developing countries, including the global south, disagree [with the EU] on this. But that’s why we should continue to strengthen our dialogue.”
Jiangwen Guo, a senior research fellow at the Chatham House thinktank, said other countries could learn from China. “China has very consistent top-down policies [and] sets a clear direction with high consistency, then follows with learning by doing,” she said. “In the great energy transition, there is no one ahead of China. China is creating the model for the globe.”
Negotiators at Cop31, which was scheduled to end at 6pm on Friday, were sent home late on Friday after the talks stalled, with a new draft text of a “cover decision” marking the main outcome of the negotiations not thought likely to emerge until some time on Saturday morning. The talks are likely to continue into Saturday and potentially beyond.

Air alert sounds hours after attack on Russia-bound ship in the Gulf of Finland
The governor of Kaliningrad says a rare air alert sounded in the Russian exclave near Poland and Lithuania
KYIV, Ukraine -- A rare air alert sounded in Kaliningrad, the Russian exclave near Poland and Lithuania, according to the local governor, as claims circulated online of drone activity near a major naval base there.
The alert late Saturday in Kaliningrad came hours after a drone strike in the Gulf of Finland set fire to a Russian cargo ship bound for the region, which is a key base for Russia's Baltic Fleet. Finnish emergency services were still working to extinguish the blaze on Sunday.
Photos and video posted online show drone activity around the city of Baltiysk, where much of the fleet is stationed. But The Associated Press couldn't immediately verify the authenticity of the images.
According to local media, air raid sirens were heard in Kaliningrad for the first time since Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022.
The Kaliningrad governor, Alexei Bezprozvannykh, said that “a suspicious object coming from the direction of Lithuania” triggered the alert in the Nemansky district near the Lithuanian border, about 170 kilometers (105 miles) northeast of Baltiysk.
On Russian Telegram channels, posts by users saying they were Baltiysk residents described air defenses working there during the night. They featured photos and videos of bright streaks against the night sky, with crackling sounds heard in the background.
Kaliningrad authorities on Sunday denounced as fake one photo, supposedly from Baltiysk, that showed clouds of smoke rising into the night sky, while an orange haze glowed on the horizon. They told Russian state media that the photo “had nothing to do with the region.”
As of Sunday morning, Russian authorities reported no casualties or damage in Kaliningrad.
Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys wrote on X that Lithuania “categorically rejects false claims” regarding the country’s involvement in a drone attack against the region.
“The Republic of Lithuania has never authorized the use of its airspace for attacks against targets in the Russian Federation, including in the present case.”
Lithuania's authorities also said they hadn't recorded any drones or similar objects flying through the country’s airspace the previous night.
Meanwhile, emergency services tried to extinguish the fire aboard the Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland on Sunday morning, authorities in Finland said.
The Sparta II drifted into Finland's territorial waters following the attack, the Finnish Border Guard said. The contents of the ship’s cargo remain unknown.
A Border Guard representative told Finnish broadcaster Yle that the crew had been transferred to a Russian rescue ship. Once the fire is extinguished, the boat would be moved out of Finland's waters, the official said.
Both Finland and Russia have suggested that the drones that struck the ship were Ukrainian. As of Sunday morning, Ukrainian officials hadn't provided any comment.

The representative in the US House expected to chair the House Intelligence Committee in January, Jim Himes (D-Conn.), has threatened to withhold support for funding government-owned systems from SpaceX amid the ongoing inquiry into the use of Starshield in Ukraine.
“SpaceX’s potentially unilateral modification of a U.S. Government contract, combined with its lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight, calls into question every contract the U.S. Government has with SpaceX,” Himes wrote in a letter to SpaceX founder Elon Musk on Friday.
CNN first reported the letter’s existence. The network also reported that Himes sent a classified communication to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton with a similar message that it would be difficult for Congress to authorize funding for systems with SpaceX as the primary vendor.
The conflict in Ukraine
SpaceX has developed the consumer Starlink service over the last decade, which provides high-speed Internet from low-Earth orbit to user terminals on Earth. For government customers, SpaceX has also developed Starshield, a suite of satellite services that includes a militarized version of Starlink communications. The US government has purchased Starshield services and extended access to Ukraine, although the terms governing that access are largely classified.
During the last several weeks, a controversy has erupted over interruptions to Starshield service in parts of Ukraine, cutting off connectivity to drones used to defend against Russian attacks.
On October 19, for example, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said of Starshield on social media, “Unfortunately, we have established that the equipment stops functioning at speeds of 130–161 kilometers per hour in various sectors of the front. This is slowing down our frontline logistics and limiting the use of various types of drones, particularly mid-strike drones and interceptors of jet-powered ‘shaheds.’” Additional disruptions were reported a week ago.

This story originally appeared on Yale E360 and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
The world is now in the grip of a super El Niño: a Godzilla-sized version of a natural climate phenomenon that has already shriveled rivers, upended aquaculture, and flattened crops with drought. But the global organizations that keep an eye on food security are warning of even tougher times ahead.
The impacts of an El Niño can be far-reaching and catastrophic. In the late 19th century, one of the strongest El Niños on record helped to fuel multiyear droughts across Asia, Brazil, and Africa that spurred a global famine: Some 50 million people, or 3 percent of the global population, died. Thankfully, the ways we plan for bad weather and move food around the planet have improved massively since then, with organizations working hard to provide relief where it’s needed. But the impacts of bad weather on crops are still hard to avoid. After a strong El Niño hit in 2015, cereal yields across Southern Africa were 20 percent below normal; crop yields in parts of Ethiopia dropped by 90 percent.
This year’s El Niño has already, by one measure, topped those previous record holders in strength. And it’s still growing. By the time the phenomenon peaks in early winter, sea-surface warming in the tropical Pacific could be higher than anything seen in a millennium. In August, the World Food Programme warned that this El Niño might push an additional 49 million people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027, taking the total number to 274 million. Worryingly, this year’s event comes as global aid dollars are pinched and wars are making it hard to plug holes in global food systems.
“It’s a triple whammy of high fertilizer costs, high energy costs, and now massive droughts across the tropics,” says Berkeley Earth climatologist Zeke Hausfather, who is watching the situation unfold. “It’s not a great story.”
El Niño is one phase of a natural climate pattern called the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, which has a dramatic impact on global rainfall patterns. El Niño years are marked by unusually warm waters in the tropical Pacific, which weaken winds across that patch and alter global patterns of rising and falling air pressure. The results are complicated and variable, but they tend to bring dry conditions to some tropical areas—including the Amazon and parts of Australia and Africa—and rain to other places, including Florida. The other side of the oscillation, La Niña, is marked by cooler ocean temperatures and a different pattern of wet and dry. The planet swings between the two in irregular intervals of years, sometimes with neutral periods in between.
Both sides of this cycle can harm crops, though one prominent 2014 study found that El Niño affects a larger swath of the globe’s harvested land. While some places get more water, and some crops thrive, in many spots drought withers production. That same study found that an El Niño tends to improve global soybean production by up to 5 percent but suppresses maize, rice, and wheat by up to 4 percent. The numbers in any one country can be much more dramatic than that: Since 1980, South Africa’s maize output, for example, has averaged about 28 percent below normal during El Niño years.
Cereal disruptions, even if small, can hit hard if they come on top of other economic strains, says Stanford agricultural economist David Lobell. “When markets are tight, then if there’s a drought somewhere, that’s a much bigger deal.”
And the markets are, indeed, tight. Global average food prices have been trending upwards for about 20 years, says Lobell, thanks to climate blows stacking on top of each other. And this year has brought additional strains. When the U.S. and Israel launched an attack on Iran at the end of February, marine traffic through the Strait of Hormuz ground to a near halt for months. The transport of oil was choked, energy prices spiked, and the supply of fertilizer, which is most often made with hydrogen sourced from cheap natural gas, was severely pinched. The Middle East usually produces a quarter of the world’s fertilizer. Meanwhile, the ongoing war in Ukraine continues to play havoc with the cost of fuel and restrict the transport of wheat from a major hub on the Black Sea.
As of October, the warming in the mid-tropical Pacific that’s used to measure the strength of an El Niño hit 3.5 degrees Celsius—breaking the previous record of about 2.75 degrees Celsius—and is on its way to an unprecedented peak of around 4 degrees, according to Hausfather. “That’s scary,” he says. Broadly speaking, he says, the more powerful the El Niño, the more powerful its effects on weather events, including droughts.
Unusually, this year’s El Niño is the third “strong” El Niño event to hit within a relatively short span of 11 years, which means some areas have been hit repeatedly with drought. The higher-than-usual frequency of El Niños may itself be caused by climate change, some researchers have suggested—though this is still an area of hot debate, Hausfather says.
All these factors act together, with cascading impacts that can take months to develop and last for years. “The confluence of drought and conflict drives some of the worst outcomes we see,” says Richard Choularton, director of climate and resilience for the World Food Programme in Rome. A farmer can’t afford fertilizer; then his fields face drought. In anticipation of a bad year, he plants less and hires fewer people. The river used to transport his crop dries up, and the port that takes it overseas has been bombed out of commission. His cows have little to eat. A year later, he can’t afford to buy groceries or fuel his farming equipment. The lack of rain allows seawater to seep into aquifers, so fresh water gets rationed. Hydropower plants sputter. And on it goes.
While any year brings its own spates of bad weather—some of it random, and some made more likely by the pressures of climate change—plenty of events this year have been attributed to El Niño. Among the first to be hit was the Peruvian anchovy fishery, which was closed dramatically early this year to give anchovies a fighting chance in the face of warm waters and less plankton, one of their main food sources. This industry, typically worth between $2 billion and $3 billion, is a huge contributor to global feed for livestock and aquaculture. As of September, global fishmeal output was about half what it was the year before; fishmeal prices have spiked, with some European salmon farmers turning to cheaper chicken byproducts.
In Indonesia, palm oil mills stopped buying fruit from farmers because an ongoing drought shriveled the area’s main transportation artery, the Kapuas River. In Cambodia, a delayed rainy season is drying out rice fields. Panama has declared a national state of emergency (as it did for the 2023 and 2015 El Niños), and the Panama Canal is carrying less ship traffic and transporting less food in the face of dwindling rainfall. In northern Sudan, rainfall totals have been less than half of normal, which is expected to take a toll on both crops and livestock from March to August next year. El Niño-induced drought alongside record summer temperatures in Central America has eaten away at crop yields and threatens that region’s second planting cycle: The E.U.’s Joint Research Centre projects an 83 percent spike in people suffering from acute food insecurity in that area.
Perhaps surprisingly, the global food production outlook for this growing season isn’t as bad as one might think: The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) notes that the USDA projects worldwide production of maize, wheat, and rice for 2026-2027 to be just 2.7 percent below the previous year’s production, which will still make it the second-largest annual crop on record.
“Globally, food supply is not of high concern,” says FEWS NET advisor Amy Ostrander. “The concerns are production changes in some specific regions, such as Southern Africa, and food access.” Even if sufficient crops are harvested in those regions, in other words, some food won’t make it to market, and some people won’t be able to afford it.
An analysis by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization concludes that the highest risks from El Niño–prompted droughts will be in the Sahel, Southern Africa, South and Southeast Asia, and in Central America’s Dry Corridor and the Caribbean.
One good thing about an El Niño is that meteorologists can see it coming almost a year in advance, unlike freak weather events, which are harder to forecast. This gives agencies a fighting chance to protect people by distributing drought-resistant seeds, for example, securing deals for future emergency food supplies and transport, or setting up income assistance for struggling farmers.
The World Food Programme first tested its forecast-based financing program in Zimbabwe during the 2015 El Niño: Delivering cash to families in one district facing drought helped them to sustain their quantity and quality of food, while a neighboring district that didn’t receive cash aid saw a massive drop. This year, the WFP has been delivering cash and other assistance, including, for example, more than 3,000 airtight silos for farmers in Guatemala to help them safely store grain. As of October, the program says it has reached 28 million people across 15 countries with early warning information and assistance.
Cash is strapped for such programs, though. Funds for global aid were down 30 percent in 2025 from their 2022 peak and are still falling, making it hard for the WFP and others to do their work. In Somalia, the WFP helped 10 million people during a drought in 2022; today, in the face of similar conditions, says Choularton, they can afford to reach fewer than a million.
Advanced warning is good, says Lobell, but challenges will still abound, and even harder times may lie ahead as El Niños pile on top of climate change. The peaks of strong El Niños are almost always followed by record-breaking years for the global average temperature. The anomalously hot years of 1998, 2016, and 2024 (the current record holder) all followed hot on the heels of El Niño peaks the year before. While 2026 is warm, “2027 is going to be the record-shattering year,” says Hausfather.
Global warming, of course, also has impacts on food supply. Last year, Lobell published a paper showing that total wheat, barley, maize, rice, and soybean yields are now altogether about 5 percent lower overall than they would have been in a world without climate change. “To a lot of people, that sounds like a small number. But the kind of shocks that we talk about can be far smaller than that,” he says. “It doesn’t take much of a supply shift to have an important effect on people’s lives.”
Because the specific places that get warmer and drier during El Niños are different from the specific places that get warmer and drier from climate change, researchers caution that what we see in 2026 won’t be a precise forerunner of things to come. But how we deal with this temporary challenge does say something about the resilience of our food systems, says Lobell, and it will reveal how we might cope in the future with other climate disruptions to crops. “That’s one of the big questions,” he says. “How much can you adapt when the conditions are bad?”

Bewakoof cofounder and former CEO Prabhkiran Singh has launched Save8, an AI-powered shopping assistant that helps consumers compare prices and offers across ecommerce and quick commerce platforms. The venture comes months after Singh stepped down from Bewakoof, the D2C fashion brand he led for nearly 14 years. Singh is also looking to raise external capital for Save8 and has held talks with investors, including All In Capital, sources told Inc42. The proposed funding amount and the final investor lineup could not be ascertained. Questions sent to Singh about Save8’s launch, business model, and fundraising plans remained unanswered till the time of publication. According to its website, Save8 aggregates prices and offers across more than 1,000 online stores. It compares product prices alongside coupons, cashback, discounted gift cards, and bank offers to help shoppers identify potential savings. How Does Save8 Work? Users can compare offers by pasting a product link into Save8’s website, adding ‘save8.ai/’ before the product URL in their browser’s address bar, or sending the link to the Save8 app through a shopping app’s share menu. The platform lists Amazon, Flipkart, Myntra, Zepto, Blinkit, and Swiggy Instamart among the services it covers. Its comparison tools aim to help users assess purchase costs after accounting for available discounts and payment offers. Save8 is available through its website and mobile applications. Its Google Play listing says it displays available bank and payment offers but does not automatically apply them. Save8 operates under ThousandX Ventures LLP, according to its terms of service. Besides its deal-finding tools, Save8 facilitates the purchase of digital gift cards issued by brands or their authorised partners. Singh's Return To Entrepreneurship Singh cofounded Bewakoof in 2012. In February this year, he announced plans to step down as CEO at the end of March, citing personal priorities, including health and family. His departure ended a nearly 14-year stint at the company. Aditya Birla Group’s digital-first venture TMRW invested ₹200 Cr to acquire a majority stake in Bewakoof, with the transaction completed in February 2023. During Singh’s tenure, Bewakoof built a youth-focused fashion business catering to millennials and Gen Z shoppers, expanding beyond its own D2C platform into online marketplaces and offline retail. With Save8, Singh is moving from selling consumer products to helping shoppers compare where and how to buy them.

AI unicorn Sarvam AI has defended its Token Factory business, saying the platform runs on privately procured GPUs rather than government-subsidised computing capacity, while reiterating that developing homegrown AI models remains its core focus. In a post on X, cofounder Pratyush Kumar addressed questions about the startup’s government support, its decision to host global open-weight models, and whether its expansion into inference infrastructure signals a shift away from building indigenous models. Notably, Token Factory’s launch had sparked online debates about Sarvam’s use of government subsidised compute capacity and its ability to anchor India’s indigenous AI ambitions. Kumar said the IndiaAI Mission gave around 20 startups access to GPUs at a 40% discount. Sarvam used this computing capacity to train its 105-billion-parameter foundation model from scratch, completing and releasing it in February 2026, he said. He added that the government did not make direct payments to Sarvam. Instead, the subsidy went to GPU cloud providers, which supplied discounted computing resources to participating startups. Sarvam’s access to the government-supported GPU allocation ended in March this year. The startup said Token Factory operates on GPUs it procured privately. Under the IndiaAI Mission, Sarvam received access to 4,096 Nvidia H100 GPUs to develop indigenous foundation models. The six-month computing allocation was valued at around ₹247 Cr, including a government subsidy of ₹98.68 Cr. The Inference Business Case The clarification follows the launch of Token Factory, which hosts Sarvam’s own models alongside global open-weight models, including Google’s Gemma and China’s DeepSeek and Kimi, on GPU infrastructure in India. The platform lets developers and enterprises access multiple models through a single API, without procuring GPUs or managing model deployment themselves. It charges customers for the tokens they use. Kumar said open-weight models offer enterprises cost advantages and greater control over their AI systems. However, Indian businesses requiring data to remain within the country and fast responses for interactive applications need access to locally hosted models, he argued. He claimed Sarvam has optimised its data centre-scale inference infrastructure to offer token prices comparable to or lower than global providers such as Fireworks AI, Baseten, and Together AI. Kumar said India consumes a few trillion tokens daily, with most of this demand served from overseas. Building domestic inference capacity could reduce that dependence while creating a commercial opportunity, he argued. He added that Sarvam would continue reducing costs and widening access to inference services in India. Sarvam Reiterates Focus On Homegrown Models Kumar said building inference infrastructure does not conflict with Sarvam’s core mission of training its own models. Over the past few months, the startup has optimised its training systems for NVIDIA’s Blackwell GPUs alongside building Token Factory and expanding its enterprise offerings, he said. Using this infrastructure, Sarvam trained Sarvam-105B-1711, an upgraded version of its 105-billion-parameter model, which it released yesterday. The company claimed improvements in reasoning, tool use, Indian languages, and work tasks involving multiple steps. Kumar described it as one of the strongest models in the Flash-Lite category, which targets high-volume applications such as customer support and voice agents. Kumar said the model can power its agentic AI product Indus. Alongside the model weights, Sarvam is releasing training and inference recipes to help developers build on the technology. The startup plans to release more models across vision, speech, and edge AI over the next two weeks. It is also working with partners to bring the latest training-grade computing infrastructure to India for its next generation of larger models. Kumar said Sarvam aims to pursue larger models while building a sustainable commercial business serving enterprises and population-scale applications.

Kenya and DR Congo agree to restore ties after tensions over conflict
- Published
Kenya's President William Ruto and his Congolese counterpart Felix Tshisekedi have agreed to restore full diplomatic ties between the two countries following tensions over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
Relations between the two countries have soured since 2023 when DR Congo accused Kenya of hosting leaders launching a rebel alliance, including the M23.
This led DR Congo to recall its envoy to Nairobi. Relations deteriorated further when Kinshasa refusing to accredit Kenya's nominated ambassador.
On Sunday, the two leaders affirmed their commitment to "sovereignty, territorial integrity, non-interference in the internal affairs of states".
The agreement was announced in a joint statement issued after the summit held in the town of Oyo in Congo-Brazzaville, facilitated by the nation's President Denis Sassou Nguesso, with Togolese leader Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé as mediator.
Tshisekedi and Ruto also agreed to "good neighbourliness and peaceful settlement of disputes" as well as "strengthen cooperation within regional mechanisms".
DR Congo and Kenya are both members of the East African Community (EAC).
DR Congo, which joined in 2022, is the latest entrant to the bloc, but its membership has been complicated by its accusation that Rwanda, a fellow member, backs the M23 rebels. Rwanda denies the claims despite overwhelming evidence.
DR Congo has also accused Kenya of hosting Congolese political and rebel leaders whom it says are working to destabilise the country.
When the Congo River Alliance (AFC), a political-military alliance including the M23, was launched in Nairobi in 2023, DR Congo responded by recalling its ambassador to Kenya.
The tensions were stoked further in March last year after Kenya named a consul-general to Goma, the capital of DR Congo's North Kivu region, after it fell to M23 forces, who control many eastern parts of the country.
DR Congo said naming the envoy amounted to disrespect for the country's territorial integrity and seemed to legitimise the group's occupation.
- Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader 
  - Published31 October
Relations deteriorated further after Kenya hosted a meeting of Congolese opposition figures, including former President Joseph Kabila, in October 2025.
Kabila was in 2025 sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself.
He has since been named the leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), the new rebel coalition that took over from the AFC.
Sunday's meeting between Ruto and Tshisekedi also included other issues including deepening trade cooperation, economic development, and regional integration.
The two also sought to collaborate to control the spread of the Ebola virus.
On Sunday, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said the frequency of attacks across the country's east had increased since the end of October, seriously affecting the Ebola response.
Tedros said heavy fighting in an area close to where the Ebola outbreak first emerged had disrupted work and the wider Ebola response.
More than 5,700 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.
The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, has spread beyond DR Congo borders, with cases reported in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria.

Mushroom supplements promise health benefits. What does the science say?
Growing up in the French Alps, Julie Daoust fell for mushrooms early in life.
"So as a kid, we'd go out and forage," she recalls. "We'd come across species like lion's mane or reishi. And I became more and more interested in those species."
Daoust went on to get a Ph.D. in chemistry, searching nature for novel pharmaceuticals. Her work ultimately led her back to mushrooms, a group of organisms to which humans are more closely related than plants. And yet, many of our modern medicines and therapeutics come from plants.
"Mushrooms share a lot more in terms of their biochemistry with us than plants do," says Daoust, which means "you have more chances of finding something that's going to have bioactivity in a human than you would with other source organisms."
Daoust is now vice president of science and innovation at Monterey Nutra, a company that specializes in the genetics and cultivation of mushrooms and sells fungal extracts and powders. Her team focuses not on the poisonous varieties, nor the psychedelic ones that contain psilocybin. Rather, they are interested in the functional or medicinal mushrooms that Daoust likens to tiny cauldrons of potentially useful molecules.
"We love to look for soft things that can't run away very fast," says Daoust, "because they typically produce really interesting chemistry to defend themselves or to communicate with others in their environment to survive."
The claim
Daoust says that certain types of fungi may have specific uses.
For instance, lion's mane — a soft chandelier of a fungus — may aid cognition. Reishi and turkey tail, which are mushrooms that grow as hard brown scales on decomposing trees, could bolster immune health.
And on social media, influencers and advertisers promise that medicinal mushrooms, taken as supplements, can slow aging and improve energy levels, focus and immune health.
The evidence
Robust clinical trials proving such connections — and their safety — are largely lacking, according to Abby Langer, a registered dietitian based in Toronto. "In my opinion, I don't think that there's much evidence for functional mushrooms as of now," she says.
Langer says mushrooms accumulate and concentrate the materials in the ground they're grown in, both good and bad — so one has to be cautious.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
She grants that in certain communities (in parts of Asia, for instance), mushrooms have been incorporated into their healing practices for generations. However, "just because something has been used for a long time doesn't mean that it's safe, that it's effective, that the dosing has been established," Langer says. "There are a lot of unknowns."
Still, she acknowledges that empirical support for the potential positive impacts of mushrooms is growing. "The clinical research on specific functional mushroom products is young," she says, "but it's accumulating fast and already includes some impressive results."
Mushrooms are a good source of vitamin D2 and antioxidants. Their cell walls contain beta-glucan, which has been linked to gut health, including a lower risk of Crohn's Disease, and immune response. Research into the effects of mushrooms on cognition have been mixed.
In addition, there's work out of Japan looking at how PSK, a purified extract from turkey tail, improved immune response in cancer patients. A meta-analysis considered 8,009 patients in eight randomized controlled trials who had undergone surgical removal of a gastric tumor and in almost all cases chemotherapy. Those who were also given PSK showed a 12% reduction in risk of death.
"This is not something that we brush off," says Santhosshi Narayanan, an integrative oncologist based at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center who recognizes the potential of PSK.
Even so, she admits that this "does not mean that PSK or any mushrooms alone cures cancer. It just shows to us that we need to pay attention to these natural products." Narayanan says there's still a lot to figure out with this particular extract, especially for populations outside Japan with different genetics or treatment regimes who might experience unwanted side effects.
"We need to do more research and understand how we can use it," she says. "Like which people, which type of patients benefit from which type of mushroom — because that itself is a whole science."
Narayanan and her colleagues also surveyed 2,349 studies examining the relationship between medicinal mushrooms and cancer, but only 39 were robust enough to be included in their 2023 analysis. Of that subset, "31 studies showed beneficial effects of the mushrooms, resulting in improved quality of life, reduced [side effect] profiles of different chemotherapeutic drugs, improved anti-inflammatory and anti-metastatic effects, and improved [disease-free survival] as well as [overall survival] in a few trials," according to the report.
Six studies didn't reveal any advantage and two highlighted worse outcomes. Overall, the analysis was unable to make clear conclusions about "the complex biological effects of mushrooms on the immune system in cancer."
The bottom line
In Narayanan's estimation, there's not yet enough evidence to support routine clinical use in cancer treatment.
And Langer recommends considering a few nutrition basics before introducing a supplement for gut health or cognition. "Take a closer look at what you're eating, how you're eating, when you're eating," she advises, "and see if there's any tweaks that you need to make."
Maybe it's possible to eat more fiber or protein, reduce consumption of alcohol or sugar-sweetened beverages, skip fewer meals, or eat out less often, she says.
"There's so many things that people can potentially improve on," Langer says, "before adding something else that's promised to be this panacea for everything that ails you."

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows police officers beating two Muslim men, Junaid and Asif, with sticks, parading them on the road, and taking them away in Uttar Pradesh in connection with a harassment case. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Uttar Pradesh police beating two Muslim men with sticks and parading them on the road in connection with a harassment case.
Fact: The video shows police officers beating and parading Sahil Bhagoria and Sachin alias Ayush, who were arrested for opening fire outside the house of Sujal Khare in Valmiki Nagar, Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh, over an old dispute. Jitendra Solanki, sub-inspector at Madhav Nagar police station, confirmed to Factly that both accused are Hindus and that the incident has no communal angle and the video is unrelated to Uttar Pradesh. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple media reports (here, here, and here) featuring the same visuals. According to these reports, at around 3:30 am on 07 October 2026, Sahil Bhagoria and Sachin alias Ayush opened fire outside the house of Sujal Khare, a resident of Valmiki Nagar, Ujjain, over an old dispute. They were subsequently paraded from Valmiki Nagar to Desai Nagar, during which police officers beat them with sticks and pipes. A pistol was also seized from them. Jitendra Solanki, sub-inspector at Madhav Nagar police station, said police arrested both accused after CCTV footage of the incident surfaced. He further stated that the two men were criminals and had been arrested following a siege.
We then contacted Jitendra Solanki, sub-inspector at Madhav Nagar police station, who told Factly that both the accused are Hindus and that the incident has no communal angle. He dismissed the viral claim, clarifying that the video is from Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh, and not Uttar Pradesh.
To sum up, a video of police beating and parading two men in Madhya Pradesh is falsely shared as a Uttar Pradesh incident with a communal spin.

Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
- Published
The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.
The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.
The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.
Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.
Sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.
She conceded on Sunday, saying in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."
Hubbard, meanwhile, wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".
He added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."
Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx in the 2024 midterms by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa.
Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters.
President Donald Trump himself has suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses, as well as Vice President JD Vance.
Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website.
The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes.
Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law.
However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation.

President Trump took to social media Monday afternoon to announce that he has ordered the US military to halt plans to detonate 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. Trump claimed that the fate of the unstable, highly explosive material is now in the hands of a federal court and Rob Sand, Iowa’s governor-elect, who won’t be sworn into office until January.
The Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups. The explosion will launch a plume of toxic gases and neurotoxic lead that could reach up to 100 miles away from the Iowa facility, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP).
Iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand. The environmental groups, led by Earthjustice, claimed in an emergency court filing that the Army had not fully considered safer options for disposing of the lead azide before planning the detonation.
Late Thursday, a federal appeals court granted Earthjustice’s request to put a hold on the Army’s permit from the Environmental Protection Agency, which allowed for the controlled detonation to be carried out. Around the same time, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the detonation would be postponed until Monday so the military could communicate with Iowans about the situation and plans.
Lead azide risk
Documents released by the Army last week said that the military first learned in March that the lead azide had started to degrade and crystallize. Lead azide is used in detonators for munitions, but in crystallized form it becomes highly unstable and sensitive to physical movement or friction. The IAAAP is said to contain around 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of lead azide in barrels held in earth-covered containers.

It was the most simple of questions. On Monday afternoon, during a NASA news conference about the International Space Station, Space News reporter Jeff Foust asked about an upcoming launch of a Russian spacecraft.
“It’s my understanding there’s another cargo mission going to the ISS this week, a Russian Progress,” Foust said. “Can you confirm that, and give the date and time that will launch?”
This Progress MS-36 cargo launch, mind you, is presently scheduled for fewer than 16 hours from now, at 10:13 UTC (05:13 am ET) on Tuesday. It is going to a space station co-operated by the US space agency. But no, NASA would not provide this basic information about the upcoming Progress launch.
“Regarding the Progress launch, I would ask you to please reach out to Roscosmos directly for any questions tied to that vehicle,” said the senior NASA official on the call, Gaurang Patel, operations integration manager for NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program.
Effectively, this is a “Go f- yourself” response from NASA. Roscosmos typically does not reply to Western media outlets, and everyone knows this.
So why is a bog-standard Progress launch suddenly a state secret? It seems to be a recent policy change, because, historically, NASA has televised every one of these cargo flights from Russia’s main spaceport in Baikonur, Kazakhstan. But there is no information about the upcoming launch on NASA’s television schedule for upcoming “live” events.
As recently as September, NASA provided live television coverage of Progress launches from Baikonur. It even issued a media advisory promising to update its broadcast schedule once Roscosmos provided launch details. Two months later, NASA officials apparently are unwilling to confirm that another Progress launch is taking place.
Who made this decision?
The question is whether this decision was made by NASA or was a request from Roscosmos, and, ultimately, whether any of this matters. We can make some educated guesses.
It is probably safe to surmise that the decision here was originally made by state-sponsored Russian space corporation Roscosmos. The company has not been advertising the preparation of the Progress spacecraft as it customarily does, some local sources say. Russian space reporter Anatoly Zak confirms that Roscosmos has “dramatically curtailed” its coverage of all launch campaigns in recent months. There is no mention of the launch on Roscosmos’ Telegram channel.

Srinagar- The Border Roads Organisation (BRO) on Monday said that post-Amarnath Yatra road-widening works near Sheshnag Lake are being undertaken in accordance with prescribed safety norms and environmental safeguards, dismissing claims circulating on social media about new construction in the area as incorrect.

Tejasvi Dahiya has earned the reputation of being one of the best six-hitters in domestic cricket. He shares the top spot on the six-hitting charts in this season’s Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy (SMAT) with Jammu and Kashmir’s Abdul Samad, having blasted 20 maximums in five innings.
Almost half of those came on Sunday, when he smashed nine sixes in a 36-ball 95 to power Delhi to 232 for six and a 43-run victory over Haryana at the Holkar Stadium.
Dahiya said his work with Abhishek Nayar and the Kolkata Knight Riders (KKR) management last season helped him fine-tune his big-hitting game.
“Last season, with Nayar sir and the KKR management, we worked on keeping my base tight and firm, using long levers, and getting deep into the crease. That’s my go-to thing, and I just try to execute that in the last overs,” he said.
He demonstrated that in the final five overs, plundering 48 runs off 17 balls, including a 19-run assault on pacer Samant Jakhar in the 19th over, when he struck two sixes and a four.
After going unsold at the IPL 2025 auction, Dahiya enjoyed a breakout season in the Delhi Premier League (DPL), scoring 339 runs at a strike rate of 190.45 for South Delhi Superstarz. He hit 29 sixes, the second-most, and also struck a half-century off just 12 balls. His performances triggered a bidding war at the IPL 2026 auction, with KKR eventually snapping him up for ₹3 crore. However, he made only two appearances for the franchise before being released ahead of the IPL 2027 auction.
The 24-year-old, however, is not one to dwell on the vagaries of franchise cricket, preferring instead to focus on what he can control.
“It’s a management call. As a player, I just do my job and try to deliver what my team wants from me. It doesn’t matter whether I am playing in the IPL or domestic cricket; I try to make myself available for whatever my team wants. We are professionals, and it’s our job to play one match at a time, not think about the future but stay in the present.
“As a player and as a human being, I try to improve myself day by day. There were areas in which I was lacking, and I have worked on those things after speaking to my coaches and seniors about what I need to develop to dominate and play at a good level. I don’t give my energy to things that are not happening in my favour. I just try to get better every day,” he said.
When asked what aspects of his game he had specifically worked on, he said: “I worked on developing my power-hitting in the last 2-3 overs and playing square shots like sweeps and cuts against spinners,” he said.
He trains with Cosco balls to work on generating power. “They are soft, so you have to generate power from within,” he explained.
Dahiya helped South Delhi Superstarz win the DPL 2026 title. He was the team’s most expensive buy at ₹40 lakh, retained through the Right to Match (RTM) card, and stepped in as captain when Ayush Badoni was unavailable. He scored 291 runs in nine innings at a strike rate of 180.75, including three half-centuries. His good run has continued in the ongoing SMAT. “I am fortunate enough to experience that,” he said.

A new Nepal, an old neighbour - Balendra Shah's India test on first visit
- Published
Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India has raised hopes of a reset, marking the first high-level engagement between leaders of Nepal's new political generation and its giant neighbour.
It is Shah's first bilateral visit since his Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) swept to power in March, six months after a Gen Z uprising against corruption and nepotism toppled K P Sharma Oli's government.
The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, during which he will meet his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi and other senior officials.
The talks are expected to cover a broad range of issues, including economic and energy cooperation, the opening of new air corridors, and a reconstruction assistance package following the devastating flash floods that struck Nepal in August.
The disaster killed more than 1,450 in the Himalayan nation, while thousands remain missing and unaccounted for.
India and Nepal share close ethnic, cultural, religious and economic ties, with a largely open border stretching more than 1,750km (1,080 miles).
Wedged between India and China, Nepal is a strategic buffer and, analysts say, its stability has direct implications for India's security.
But over the decades the relationship has been strained by territorial disputes, allegations of political interference and resentment over what many in Nepal see as the dominant 'Big Brother' attitude of Delhi.
Nevertheless, analysts see Shah's visit as an opportunity for a reset.
"The new Nepali leadership says they do not have the political baggage of the past and they want to focus on development, diplomacy and economic partnership," Ranjit Rae, a former Indian ambassador to Nepal tells BBC.
"They seem to be more pragmatic, less ideological. I personally feel it's an optimistic moment," he adds.
Since Nepal abolished monarchy and became a democratic republic in 2008 three political parties dominated the governance.
Delhi has maintained close contacts with all of them – the Communist Party of Nepal (CPN – UML), the Nepali Congress and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre).
Nepal's communist parties were seen as closer to India's rival China, owing to ideological ties, and often criticised Delhi over what they viewed as unequal bilateral agreements.
Due to Nepal's strategic location, both Delhi and Beijing compete for influence in Kathmandu, leading to accusations the two Asian giants are meddling in the internal affairs of Nepal.
But Nepal's ties with India extend beyond diplomacy and strategic interests.
The Hindu-majority nations share deep social ties, with families straddling the open border and communities interacting daily.
Bilateral trade exceeds $9bn, heavily skewed in India's favour - a longstanding source of resentment in Kathmandu. India is also Nepal's main supplier of petroleum products and several food items, and a key transit route for its trade with the rest of the world.
One key area of co-operation is hydropower. India has approved projects to import up to 1,200MW of electricity from Nepal and is looking to expand imports further.
"India has a huge demand for electricity and Nepal has the potential to generate due to its water resources and geography. It's not just bilateral, Nepal also exports electricity to Bangladesh via India," says Rae.
India has often been among the first countries to assist Nepal during major natural disasters, including the 2015 earthquake and the flash floods in August this year.
Despite the close links, Nepal and India have their differences.
In 2019, Nepal was furious after India published a map that included areas claimed by Kathmandu, in a western region close to the border with China, as part of its territory. That raised heightened awareness in Kathmandu about the region.
The diplomatic wrangle escalated after Nepal published its own map which included those disputed areas.
"I hope Nepal's prime minister raises the border issue with Delhi this time. There may not be a resolution immediately, but they should start negotiations to settle the issue," Kanak Mani Dixit, a veteran Nepali political analyst, told the BBC.
Nepal has also long urged India to open additional air entry routes, allowing large aircraft to fly in from the west to its new airports at Bhairahawa, near the Buddhist holy site of Lumbini, and Pokhara, a major tourist destination.
Access to Indian airspace would mean shorter flights at lower cost and, with more flights, the airports would become commercially viable.
Some in Nepal also believe that Delhi is wary of the fact that the Gautam Buddha international airport was constructed by China's Northwest Civil Aviation Airport and the airport in Pokhara was built with Chinese financial assistance.
Shah has yet to make any overtures to Beijing, but sent a 20-member delegation of party MPs to China for an 11-day visit from 15 November, ahead of his trip to India - seen as an effort to balance ties with Nepal's two powerful neighbours.
Shah had pledged not to travel abroad during his first year in office, but devastating flash floods in August have changed the calculus.
His government estimates reconstruction will cost nearly $5bn, while international aid pledged so far has fallen short of expectations.
But some observers in Nepal believe that Shah's preparations for the high-stake India visit have been less than thorough.
"Prime Minister Shah and his advisors are young and fresh, but they do lack experience. Repeatedly they have exhibited a lack of gravitas in governance, which would be essential for diplomacy with an overwhelmingly powerful neighbour," says Dixit.
Shah is already facing criticism over some of his government's recent decisions, including to remove police chief Dan Bahadur from his post after he allegedly refused to comply with directives from the Prime Minister's office.
Police were sent to some news organisations to detain journalists for their news coverage triggering accusations of curtailing press freedom.
While Kathmandu has ambitions in advancing its ties with India, the real test for Shah would be to return home with tangible outcomes. Securing concrete commitments from Delhi on financial aid would be seen as a diplomatic success and could help blunt growing domestic criticism.

Bengal govt to amend land reforms law during Assembly winter session to ease acquisition
The BJP state government plans to introduce eight bills, including amendments to land reforms, MSMEs and ease of doing business.
The West Bengal government will introduce a bill in the Assembly during its winter session to amend the land reforms law to ease land acquisition for setting up industries in the state, official sources said on Monday.
With the winter session set to be held from December 4 to 14, the government plans to introduce eight bills, which include a proposed law on amendments to land reforms, as well as one related to MSMEs and another on ease of doing business to give a fillip to the state's dilapidated industry scene.
Though details of the proposed amendments to the land reforms law are not known yet, sources said the government was not planning to scrap the land ceiling, but would introduce provisions to make land acquisition easier.
The state government had been deliberating a lot since the BJP came to power in May to help industry get land without any political backfire.
When contacted, West Bengal Industry Minister Tapas Roy said he would be able to share details once the bill reaches him, and that it would not be proper to disclose them at this stage.
"Land pooling is a different matter, and the amendments may not include it," the minister said, but confirmed that the proposed amendments would try to ease land-related hurdles for industrial growth in the state.
Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari has said the government would neither forcibly acquire land from farmers nor stay completely away from acquisition and ask industry to buy land on its own.
The government has already begun a drive to acquire land on its own, including in Singur. Adhikari expects to acquire 8,000 to 10,000 acres in the short term through various means via the West Bengal Industrial Development Corporation (WBIDC).
Adhikari has said the government has adopted the 2013 land acquisition law and will also use land pooling as a new mode of acquisition.
An industrialist, who did not wish to be named, said the government has come out with an investment policy and has assured industry that it would address land issues through a new land policy. "So we are hopeful of some better news on this front," he said.
The West Bengal Land Reforms Act, 1955, caps maximum land holdings for a family or a trust at around 17.30 acres for agricultural land.

Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO after a whirlwind series of events.
His resignation followed reports of more than one extramarital affair and a board investigation into concerns he might have been the subject of a foreign-intelligence effort.
If you're having trouble keeping up, you're not alone.
Here is a timeline of everything that happened leading to Huang's bombshell disclosure of infidelity, resignation, and his surprising return to the company:
Spring 2026: Rubio's classified warning memo
Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of a "highly classified" memo in the spring warning about the Nvidia CEO's relationship, The New York Times reported.
The Times reported that the memo was based on electronic surveillance of a woman called Alice Huang. The memo was later shared among top Trump administration officials, according to The Times.
May: Jensen Huang boards Air Force One
Jensen Huang was not among the initial list of top executives set to join President Donald Trump for his May visit to China. News organizations pointed out the curious absence given that the Nvidia CEO had joined Trump on similar occasions.
In a seemingly last-minute decision, Huang joined the trip when Air Force One made a refueling stop in Alaska. Trump published a Truth Social post calling out CNBC for reporting Huang's absence.
"Jensen is currently on Air Force One and, unless I ask him to leave, which is highly unlikely, CNBC's reporting is incorrect or, as they say in politics, FAKE NEWS!" Trump wrote in the May 12 post.
Jensen Huang's name was not on a list of business executives that were part of a US delegation that a White House official sent Business Insider at the time. The Nvidia CEO later told reporters that Trump "asked me to come," CNBC reported.
October 29: Chinese spy allegations emerge
Questions about Huang's relationship publicly came to light in October.
On October 29, the Times reported that US officials had concluded that Alice Huang, or Huang Le, was "a Chinese intelligence asset" who "had developed a close relationship" with the Nvidia CEO.
The Times article included photos of the pair at a party in June 2024, which the publication said had been posted on LinkedIn. The article also recounted that in May 2025, Alice Huang had waited behind the Nvidia CEO as he spoke to reporters after leaving a restaurant in Taipei.
October 29: Nvidia calls meetings 'not unusual'
Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo was quoted in the Times report as saying, "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.'s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year."
October 29: Jensen Huang downplays interactions
The Nvidia CEO echoed the company's statements, downplaying his interactions with Alice Huang as routine business.
"Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual," he told Bloomberg News in a report published October 29.
Jensen Huang also told the publication that the US government hadn't told him about its concerns about Alice Huang, confirming another aspect of the Times reporting. In its initial story, the Times reported that the Nvidia CEO had not received "defensive briefings," the term for such formal warnings sometimes communicated to business leaders.
November 4: House GOP leaders seek briefing
Three House Republican committee chairs sent a letter to Jensen Huang on November 4 asking him to appear for a joint closed-door meeting about his interactions with Alice Huang.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information. The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress," the letter read. "It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk."
The letter, which described Alice Huang as a "publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset," asked for a November 18 meeting.
November 8: Jensen Huang admits infidelity
In a November 8 internal memo to employees, JensenHuang said he had been "unfaithful" to his wife of more than 40 years and said that his actions "hurt her and our children."
"I owe my family and all of you an apology," he wrote, adding, "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."
November 8: Nvidia opens probe
The same day, Nvidia's board of directors announced it was opening an investigation into whether Jensen Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort."
The board said a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the probe.
"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the board said.
Jensen Huang said he supports the investigation and "will cooperate fully."
November 8: Trump defends Jensen Huang
Later that day, Trump defended the Nvidia CEO, calling him an "honorable guy."
"I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it," Trump told reporters.
The president also said he thought Jensen Huang should remain Nvidia's CEO.
"He's done an amazing job for our country," Trump said.
November 9: Nvidia CEO off tech events lineups
In the wake of the scandal, Huang didn't attend an Anthropic-hosted private CEO forum in Montecito, California.
Huang was also removed from the lineup at the ElevenLabs Summit in NYC later that week, a spokesperson for the AI voice technology startup confirmed to Business Insider. He was scheduled for a fireside chat with ElevenLabs CEO Mati Staniszewski.
November 9: China denies allegations
The Chinese government has pushed back against claims that Alice Huang is a spy.
"The 'Chinese spy' allegation is purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters during a news conference on November 9.
November 11: Report emerges about a second affair
The New York Times published a report saying that Huang was involved in a second extramarital affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare, Kimberly Powell. The 48-year-old VP was a direct report of Huang, and the two worked together for over 18 years.
The report cited five company sources who confirmed the affair. The two were said to have been "captured on video being affectionate" at an Nvidia conference hotel in San Jose in March.
November 12: Huang is out; Colette Kress becomes interim CEO
On November 12, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned as CEO.
In a memo announcing his resignation, Nvidia said that Colette Kress, the company's chief financial officer, would serve as interim CEO "until a permanent successor has been named." Kress joined Nvidia in 2013 and has served as executive vice president and CFO since. Prior to joining Nvidia, she spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at companies including Cisco and Microsoft.
The board said in the memo that it would consider internal and external candidates as it initiated a search for a permanent chief.
November 12: Nvidia stock plunges
Nvidia's share price dropped 13% at market open following Huang's resignation, deepening the decline it had seen since the scandal came to light.
By late morning on November 12, the share price had partially recovered, trading about 5% below the market close the day before.
November 14: A petition to reinstate Huang gains traction
A petition to reinstate Huang as Nvidia's CEO received over 100,000 signatures as of November 14, including from employees, shareholders, and prominent tech leaders such as Replit CEO Amjad Masad.
November 16: President Trump backs Huang's return
Trump told reporters outside the White House that he would support Huang's return to Nvidia. He said Huang "learned a big lesson" and that he wouldn't mind if Huang were reinstated.
Other tech executives, including Elon Musk, similarly called for his return.
November 17: Huang says he would be 'honored' to return as CEO
On November 17, Huang broke his silence with a post on X, thanking those who had shown kindness to him and his family, and saying he loves the US and Nvidia. He admitted to making "serious mistakes" in his personal life and said he was committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation.
In the post, Huang also shared his interest in returning to lead the company.
"If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang wrote.
November 17: Nvidia chair says it doesn't intend to reinstate Huang
Nvidia reported blockbuster third-quarter earnings, beating on both top and bottom lines.
Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said during the company's call with investors that the board "unanimously accepted" Huang's resignation and "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."
November 23: Huang is reinstated as CEO
On Monday, Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO and Nvidia's stock soared more than 30%.
The chipmaker's board chair told employees in a brief message that Huang was returning "after careful consideration." Jones said he would remain board chair and Kress would return to her role as CFO. Hundreds of Nvidia employees reacted to the message with celebratory emojis.
President Trump said he worked behind the scenes to help secure Huang's return, speaking to the board both directly and indirectly, and felt "very strongly about it."
"I was talking to a lot of people" about Huang's return, Trump told CNBC. "The board decided to do what we wanted them to do."
Huang returned to Nvidia's headquarters in Santa Clara on Monday and was greeted by cheers and chants from employees.
"I'm gonna be a better CEO the second time around," he said, according to a person in attendance.
