An X account, MenToo (@MenTooSave), shared the video claiming that the woman in the video was leaning on the man, trying to record a fake molestation video just for views. Noting that such false narrative can put an innocent man’s life and reputation at risk, the post asks, “When will society stop treating every man as guilty by default?”
She filmed herself deliberately pressing her breast against a man’s hand while he visibly tried to create distance and protect himself.
If true, this wasn’t an accident. It was a calculated attempt to manufacture a molestation clip — just for views.
One video. One false narrative. And an innocent man’s life, reputation, and freedom put at risk for content.
This is not empowerment. This is weaponizing accusations. When will society stop treating every man as guilty by default?
Innocent until proven guilty — even when the camera is rolling.
#FalseAccusations #DueProcess #MenToo #JusticeForAll
— MenToo (@MenTooSave) November 19, 2026
Men’s rights activist Barkha Trehan shared the same video on her Instagram account (@barkhatrehan16) on November 20. She also claimed the woman was trying to manufacture a molestation video for views, and the incident was from Patna, Bihar.
Social activist Deepika Narayan Bhardwaj (@DeepikaBhardwaj) also shared the video on X claiming the woman was deliberately sticking to the man so that she could “cry molestation”.
Fact Check
A close examination of the video shows that there is a release announcement poster of a film, ‘Janak’ at the end of the video. Below is a screenshot of the last frame of the viral video:
We then searched for the trailer of the movie, ‘Janak’, and found it on the YouTube channel of Marathi Cineyug, where it had been uploaded on October 14, 2026. The trailer contains the visual that is now viral. The same two people, the same background, clothing and movements can be seen at the 0:49-0:50-second mark in the trailer.
In the process, we also found behind-the-scene photos related to the movie shared on Instagram by Anushka Pimputkar, the woman in the viral clip. In one of the photos, she is seen with Avinash Narkar, the actor who is standing next to her in the viral video.
To sum up, the viral video does not show a real incident of a woman trying to record a fake molestation clip on a bus. It is a scene from the trailer of the Marathi film, ‘Janak’. Social media claims presenting the footage as real are false.

Bayer reaches Roundup settlement that could cost the company billions
The agrochemical and biotech giant Bayer has agreed to pay billions of dollars to people who sued the company alleging the weed-killer Roundup caused their cancer.
On Friday, a judge in Missouri gave final approval to the nationwide settlement that could cost the company up to $7.25 billion in the coming years.
The money will go to thousands of people who have been or will be diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma — a blood cancer that they claim is linked to glyphosate, which is the main ingredient in Roundup.
Under the settlement in circuit court, people affected could receive anywhere from $10,000 to $165,000 in compensation, depending on whether their work in agriculture or other occupations exposed them to higher levels of glyphosate, the age when they were diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and other factors.
In a statement, the CEO of Bayer, Bill Anderson, called the settlement a "decisive milestone" that will "mitigate the risks" of pending and future litigation.
The presiding judge, Timothy Boyer, said it was "among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements."
Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in favor of Bayer, the German company that now owns Monsanto, finding that it could be shielded from lawsuits filed in state courts over claims that it failed to warn consumers about the cancer-causing effects of glyphosate.
Roundup is the most widely used weed-killer in the world.
The attorney representing the plaintiffs, Christopher Seeger, said in a statement that "Today's final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice."
The latest settlement comes in addition to a previous one in which Bayer agreed to pay between about $10 billion and $11 billion to settle more than 100,000 claims related to Roundup.
More than a decade ago, the World Health Organization's cancer agency concluded that glyphosate is probably carcinogenic to humans. Prominent scientists in the field of environmental health have echoed those concerns as recently as this year.
But Bayer has steadfastly denied that its product causes cancer.
The Environmental Protection Agency has also concluded it "did not identify risks of concern from glyphosate uses, including for cancer," though the agency is currently conducting a review of the evidence related to human health after facing intense pressure from advocates and some scientists.
Concerns about the safety of glyphosate has been an animating issue for supporters of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr and his Make America Healthy Again agenda.
However, the Trump administration has taken steps to support the herbicide-maker, siding with Bayer in the Supreme Court case and issuing an executive order to promote domestic production of glyphosate.
Several years ago, the company removed glyphosate from its U.S. products used in residential settings, although it's still in use in the agricultural industry.

FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database

The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media report citing two people briefed on the issue.
The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks. The BBC has contacted the FBI for comment.
This comes after string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyberattacks - but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with US President Donald Trump saying he was not good enough.
It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US.
In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.
After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.
In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) .
Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC said.
The USDA has not publicly commented on the issue.

The first round of seat-sharing talks between the Samajwadi Party (SP) and Congress for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections started in New Delhi on Monday (November 23, 2026), with leaders from both parties indicating that an alliance deal could be finalised soon.
The meeting held at the residence of Congress Rajya Sabha MP Pramod Tiwari in New Delhi lasted just about 20 minutes, and the two sides are likely meet again on Tuesday (November 24, 2026) to take the negotiations forward.
Samajwadi Party National General Secretary and Rajya Sabha MP Ram Gopal Yadav, who is leading the SP team, said the discussions were held in a cordial atmosphere.
“The meeting took place in a very cordial atmosphere. We listened to each other’s points of view, and we will soon finalise this alliance and inform you about it,” he told reporters after the meeting.
Uttar Pradesh Congress in-charge Rajendra Pal Gautam also said that both parties trust each other and will manage things jointly.
Sources have indicated that it is the first round of discussions, and the alliance will take time to reach an agreement on 403 assembly seats.
A Congress leader who was part of the negotiations said on condition of anonymity that the Congress shared a list of around 130 seats that it wants to contest in the alliance with the SP.
“We have shared our list of preferred seats. It is around 130-odd seats. We have done a detailed survey and the demand is based on the outcome of 2024 Lok Sabha polls and our performance in previous assembly elections,” he said.
“In the assembly segments coming under six Lok Sabha seats we won in 2024, we are very strong. The discussions will continue. Our broader objective is to defeat the authoritarian Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) regime, but our approach in selection of seats is evidence and data-based,” added the leader.
In the evening, a parallel meeting of the Congress party was under way, in which they discussed the response of the SP and how to move forward.
Sunil Singh Yadav ‘Sajan’, the SP spokesperson, said winnability will be sole criteria to decide which party will contest a particular seat.
“Winnability will be sole criteria to decide which seat a party will contest in the 2027 polls. There is a broader understanding between our leader Akhilesh ji and Congress leader Rahul ji about defeating the BJP. In our alliance, we are partners and we will collectively defeat the BJP,” said Mr. Sajan.
The SP team consists of National General Secretary and MP Ram Gopal Yadav, Lok Sabha MPs Rajeev Rai and Iqra Choudhary and state party chief Shyam Lal Pal. The Congress team consists of the party’s U.P. in-charge Rajendra Pal Gautam, state party chief Aradhna Misra, working president Imran Masood, and MLA Virendra Chaudhary.
Speaking to The Hindu on November 22, Mr. Rai said, “We don’t want to repeat the Bihar story. Winnability is the factor to decide which seat a party will contest in the 2027 polls. For every seat, our alliance partner needs to convince us how they can win that particular seat, who their probable candidate is, how the candidate fits in the social realities of the constituency, and how he can strengthen the alliance.”

Vote for the first BBC Men's Footballer of the Year

Voting is now open for the BBC Men's Footballer of the Year 2026 award, which will be presented at Sports Personality of the Year.
Fans from the UK can vote from the five-player shortlist of Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe, Rodri and Lamine Yamal.
The vote closes on Friday, 27 November at 09:00 GMT.
The winner of the award - new for this year - will be presented during the live Sports Personality of the Year show on Sunday, 13 December.
Alex Kay-Jelski, Director of BBC Sport, said: "From the drama and excitement of the men's World Cup to the moments that have captivated fans across the domestic and international game, 2026 has given us so much to celebrate.
"Our inaugural BBC Men's Footballer of the Year award is about recognising the players who have made this year so special, inspired fans and left their mark on the game.
"It's a fantastic shortlist, and I can't wait to see who the public choose as our first-ever winner."
The shortlist was selected by an expert panel comprising former international players and some of the BBC's most respected football voices, bringing together a wealth of experience and insight from across the game.
The panel included Cesar Azpilicueta (Spain), Scott Brown (Scotland), Olivier Giroud (France), Shay Given (Republic of Ireland), Hassan Kachloul (Morocco), Lucas Leiva (Brazil), Benni McCarthy (South Africa), Alan Shearer, Ellen White (both England) and Ashley Williams (Wales).
Read more on the five contenders and cast your vote below.
Jude Bellingham
Age: 23 Country: England
Club: Real Madrid Position: Midfield
Bellingham made history this summer as he became the first Englishman to score as many as seven goals at a major tournament.
In a superb World Cup for the midfielder, he memorably netted twice in back-to-back games to help the Three Lions beat Mexico and Norway.
That meant he joined exalted company as the first player to score two or more goals in successive World Cup knockout games since Diego Maradona in 1986, and the second youngest in history behind Pele in 1958.
Bellingham also became the youngest European player to make an appearance at four different major tournaments, and also reached the milestone of 50 caps at a younger age than any other England men's player.
The goals continued to flow for Real Madrid, too, with Bellingham notching his 50th for the club to move above the legendary Zinedine Zidane in the Los Blancos' all-time scoring charts.
Harry Kane
Age: 33 Country: England
Club: Bayern Munich Position: Forward
In a stunning year of goalscoring, Kane become the first Englishman for 25 years (and only fifth in history) to win the Ballon d'Or - awarded to the world's best footballer.
His tally of 73 goals in 65 matches for club and country during a stellar 2025-26 season has only been surpassed in one of Europe's top five leagues by Lionel Messi's 82 for Barcelona and Argentina in 2011-12.
Kane scored 61 of those goals in just 51 appearances for Bayern Munich as he helped the Bavarians to a league and cup double. His total was 19 more than any other player in Europe's top five divisions.
Already England's record goalscorer, he surpassed Peter Shilton's mark of 125 appearances to become the most-capped Englishman in history.

Age: 27 Country: France
Club: Real Madrid Position: Forward

Age: 30 Country: Spain

Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out

A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained along with his lieutenant by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.
Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.
Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.
Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores and his second-in-command, it added.
Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds.
The two detainees were subsequently flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said.
When he was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture.
Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico.
He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019.
The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019.
Meza Flores was originally a high-ranking member of the Beltrán Leyva Organization, but a split between rival factions led to a surge of violence and prompted him to establish his own cartel by 2013.
His organisation has also engaged in what US officials described as an "extremely violent turf war" with the Sinaloa Cartel, one of the most powerful drug trafficking gangs, which operates in the same region.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has taken a tougher stance on the country's cartels in a bid to resist US intervention on Mexican soil. Mexico has welcomed closer collaboration but resisted US boots on the ground.
Trump made stemming the flow of drugs into the US across its southern border one of his key election pledges.

Commons reasons your Android phone's icons won't move and how to fix it
It’s most likely your home screen settings.
Android phones offer plenty of customization options to help you organize your apps. Some settings, unbeknownst to users, can reorganize your phone's icons or prevent you from moving them at all. A home screen that keeps changing can be frustrating, but the good news is you can fix it without much troubleshooting.
Many Android phones can auto-arrange icons in your app drawer, usually called automatic sorting. This causes your phone to organize icons in alphabetical order, by install date or by other listed criteria. App or OS updates can also change your home screen grid, so don't be alarmed if icons rearrange after a major software update.
If your icons aren't moving at all, check your home screen and launcher cache settings. A locked home screen is the main culprit on most phones. However, if you're using a Google Pixel or stock Android without a locked home screen setting, clearing your launcher cache is another option. Employing either solution is fairly straightforward.
Fixing a locked home screen
The most likely cause of locked icons is a locked home screen. Many Android manufacturers enable locked home screens by default, preventing you from moving icons. You can fix this by going into your phone's home screen settings and turning the setting off.
Most Samsung phones let you access this setting by going to Settings and searching for "Home Screen." From there, look for the option "Lock Home Screen Layout." Toggle it off to enable icon movement again. If you are using another type of Android device, you can usually find this setting under the "Home" tab of your device.
Once you've unlocked your home screen, you might notice that your icons will sometimes reorganize themselves without your input. This could be due to some auto-sort options in your phone settings. You can find these sorting options in your home screen settings—on Samsung phones, under "Settings," while on some Android phones, under "Home." If your home screen layout is still not to your liking, consider resetting your home screen and restart your phone.
Clearing a bloated launcher cache
On Android devices without a locked home screen layout, such as Google Pixel phones, you may want to clear your launcher cache instead. Your phone's launcher cache saves all temporary data related to your home screen. If this cache gets bloated, it can make your phone more prone to crashing and cause inconsistent home screen behavior, including frozen icons.
Clearing the launcher cache is similar across Android phones, though the launcher app varies by manufacturer. Head to your phone's settings menu and look through your apps. You're looking for your phone's launcher. Google Pixel uses the Pixel Launcher; Samsung phones use One UI. Select the app and head to its storage settings. You should see an option to clear its cache. After you clear it, you should notice your home screen is more responsive. We also suggest rebooting your phone once you've cleared the cache to ensure it actually gets cleared out. If your phone remains unresponsive, restart your phone in safe mode to see whether a third-party app is causing the problem.

Why a shortage of clinical psychologists in Keralam govt hospitals is leaving people with intellectual disabilities waiting for certificates
As per the last Kerala Disability Census in 2015, there are about 80,000 persons with various intellectual challenges. However, government hospitals and medical college hospitals in the State currently have only 22 clinical psychologists to conduct IQ assessment tests
Updated - November 21, 2026 01:40 pm IST - Kozhikode
As per the latest disability assessment guidelines issued by the Union government’s Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, differently-abled children must undergo assessment tests at least thrice before they turn 18 to obtain permanent disability certificates. (file image)
| Photo Credit: K. Ragesh
People with intellectual disabilities in Keralam are struggling to obtain and renew disability certificates due to a severe shortage of clinical psychologists in government hospitals to conduct Intelligence Quotient (IQ) assessment tests.
As per the latest disability assessment guidelines issued by the Union government’s Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, differently-abled children must undergo assessment tests at least thrice before they turn 18 to obtain permanent disability certificates. During all these assessment phases, an IQ test is a must. However, there are only 22 clinical psychologists under the Directorate of Health Services (DHS) and the Directorate of Medical Education (DME) put together – 17 under the DHS and the rest under the DME.

Artificial intelligence has sped early-stage drug development work at some of the world’s largest pharmaceutical companies this year, cutting by as much as half the time it takes to produce new molecules and move them into the clinic, Reuters explains. The top scientists at Bristol Myers Squibb, Novartis, Eli Lilly, Sanofi, Novo Nordisk and AstraZeneca all say they have moved beyond less glamorous tasks for AI like preparing regulatory filings. They are now using the technology for designing molecules, sorting out the most promising ones, and identifying safety risks.
A few of the largest pharmaceutical companies have told a Congressional committee that they do not plan to start new clinical trial sites in the Xinjiang region of China or at hospitals affiliated with the Chinese military, STAT writes. The disclosure was made by the House Select Committee on China, which last June opened investigations into five companies — Merck, Eli Lilly, AbbVie, Pfizer, and Bristol Myers Squibb — over concerns about intellectual property exposure, military entanglements, and ethical standards at trial sites in sensitive regions of the country.

The Department of Medicine at Assam Medical College and Hospital in eastern Assam’s Dibrugarh has withdrawn an order advising postgraduate trainees (PGTs) of general medicine to defer “personal milestones such as marriage” until they complete their residency tenure.
Prasanta Dihingia, the Head of the Department, withdrew the order hours after issuing it on Wednesday (November 18, 2026). The withdrawal followed a backlash from a doctors’ body.
“With reference to the Order No.MED/2026/5700; Dtd. 18.11.2026, regarding the advisory issued to the PGTs of Dept. of Medicine concerning personal milestones during their residency tenure, it is hereby notified that the Office Order is withdrawn with immediate effect,” the order read.
“Accordingly, the above-mentioned order is cancelled and treated as withdrawn from the date of issuance of this notice. All concerned are hereby informed to take note of the same,” it further read.
Earlier, the Federation of All India Medical Association (FAIMA) condemned the “unreasonable advisory” and demanded its immediate withdrawal.
“What’s next? NOC from the HOD for marriage and family planning? By the same logic, HODs should stay in the hospital 24×7 until retirement. After all, commitment to patient care should apply equally to everyone!” FAIMA posted on X, sharing the controversial order.
The association advised administrators to regulate duty hours, not the resident doctors’ personal lives.
“Residency is a postgraduate course, not a vow of celibacy!” it stated.

It’s mostly been the subject of Hollywood movies, but one day, an asteroid or comet could collide with Earth and cause serious damage. We don't have to look all that far back for an example. In 1908, in an incident now known as the “Tunguska Event,” a space rock, likely a few dozen meters wide, exploded over Siberia. Though scientists weren’t able to visit the site for another two decades, the landscape was still scarred from the explosion.
Astronomers predict that in mid-April 2029, the asteroid Apophis will fly by Earth. The 450-meter-wide body will miss us at a distance of only 19,000 miles. That’s about 12 times closer to us than the moon and much closer than many satellites. It will even be visible to the naked eye.
In the past few decades, there’s been enormous progress in making these kinds of predictions. As space probes deepen our knowledge of small bodies in the solar system, astronomers have increasingly reliable and detailed data for finding potentially hazardous asteroids. Our ability to respond to such a threat, however, is another story. This is the missing and extremely important link—planetary defense technology that could allow us to deflect a dangerous object in time.
In a sci-fi flick, such situations are often solved with a nuclear bomb. But in the real world, blowing up a big space rock into tiny bits is not ideal. Instead, it’s better to alter the asteroid's orbit. Everything in the vacuum of space is in motion. Our own planet travels about 20 miles every second. If the object hurtling towards us can be slowed down and thus reach the meeting point a little later, it will simply miss the Earth.
Four years ago, this was essentially what NASA tested on a pair of celestial bodies known as Didymos and Dimorphos. Astronomers at the Kitt Peak Observatory discovered Didymos, an asteroid measuring 780 meters across, 30 years ago. A few years later, Czech astronomer Petr Pravec observed that this asteroid had a “moonlet” orbiting it about every 12 hours. This smaller body, measuring about 151 meters in diameter, was then named Dimorphos.
The paired objects were a perfect testing ground for the kind of deflection a planetary defense system would involve. Locked in on these targets, NASA launched the Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) in late 2021. Nearly a year later, the DART probe crashed into Dimorphos.
Scientists had hoped that the impact of the probe—which was barreling toward the asteroids at over 13,000 miles per hour—could shorten the period of the mini-moon's orbit by a minute or more. In the end, it was slowed down by 33 minutes. This major deviation was caused by the ejection of debris, leading to a much greater recoil than what was produced by the impact itself. In addition, the orbital speed of both asteroids around the sun also slowed. And in a sense, Dimorphos briefly became a comet—the debris released by the impact creating a long tail behind it.
But questions remain about the longer-term impacts of this test. In October 2024, the European Space Agency (ESA) sent off the space probe Hera to rendezvous with both asteroids. After a flyby of Mars, the probe began its arrival phase this past October. It took its first image about 800 miles away, and the first detailed image of Didymos was published in early November.
Now in their vicinity, Hera will study both bodies in depth. Though there’s much we can learn about asteroids by observing them from our planet, nothing can replace close-up exploration, and this will be the first time a binary asteroid system will be explored in detail. One of the mission's goals is to find out how such asteroid pairs form. Didymos is also interesting for its rapid rotation, turning once every 2.3 hours—placing it on the very edge of stability.
But of course, beyond this traditional astronomy research, which could also take place at another set of binary asteroids, Hera will investigate the consequences of the DART mission. This will include studying the impact site. Because there are so many knowns about the impact itself, scientists can also use this opportunity to understand craters more broadly, answering questions such as whether the strength of the material or gravity plays a more decisive role in crater formation.
Hera will also determine the exact mass of Dimorphos, an important detail in assessing the effectiveness of the DART mission as a test of planetary defense technology. The probe also contains a lidar instrument for mapping the asteroid's topography and instruments for investigating the chemical composition of the surface. Additionally, we can expect to see detailed images of the asteroids taken with a resolution of 1 meter per pixel.
The probe is also carrying two miniature, cube-shaped satellites, called “CubeSats” for short, which it will deploy in January 2027. In Earth’s orbit, CubeSats are often used for simple experiments, including student projects, and they can even be stacked together to create larger satellites.
Hera’s CubeSats, named Juventas and Milani, will attempt to land on the surface. Using radar capable of probing up to a depth of 100 meters, Juventas will focus on geophysical exploration of the asteroid Dimorphos. Additionally, a gravimeter on board will measure how the gravity on Dimorphos changes during its orbit due to the parent asteroid, Didymos. Meanwhile, Milani will carry out a detailed investigation of the asteroids’ surface composition and will search for traces of dust and the volatile substances contained within many space rocks.
According to current plans, this main phase of the Hera probe's mission is expected to last until the summer of next year, and findings from this probe will likely only become more relevant, not just as Apophis approaches, but even after it slings back into space. In the year 2000, we knew of only 300 near-Earth asteroids—those that approach Earth or directly cross its orbit. Today, we know of over 43,000.

Gilead Sciences said on Monday it had signed royalty-free deals with three generic drugmakers to make its experimental Ebola prevention drug available in 127 mainly low- and lower-middle-income countries if it succeeds in trials and wins regulatory approvals.
The deals with Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories, Eva Pharma and Ferozsons Laboratories cover obeldesivir, and include all African countries reporting cases in the current Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak. Obeldesivir has shown activity against several Ebola-related viruses in preclinical studies but is not approved for any use in any country.
A late-stage trial is testing the drug in people at high risk after exposure. The deals are intended to line up manufacturing and supply before trial results and regulatory filings.
Gilead is also expanding remdesivir licences to cover Ebola-related diseases if trial results are positive and regulators approve the drug. The company has donated more than 38,000 remdesivir vials to the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda and Kenya, including more than 2,000 recently sent to Kenya for investigational treatment and post-exposure prevention.
Remdesivir is not approved to treat or prevent Ebola Bundibugyo disease, and its clinical effectiveness has not been established.

WASHINGTON — Department of Health and Human Services officials announced Friday that 15 groups around the U.S. will test how well nutrition, exercise, and other lifestyle programs work to improve Medicare patients’ health and save the government money.
The MAHA ELEVATE program aims to generate evidence over the next several years that preventive efforts, such as cooking classes and nutrition coaching for people with chronic conditions, is worthy of Medicare coverage.
The U.S. spends trillions of dollars per year on health care, most of which goes toward treating chronic diseases. However, Medicare does not cover many of the lifestyle interventions that could help people improve their condition or keep them from getting sick in the first place.

Indore (Madhya Pradesh): The Food Safety Administration inspected three food establishments in Indore following complaints and collected nine food samples for quality testing. The inspections covered hygiene, cleanliness and food storage practices at the premises.
The inspection team visited Pushpak Restaurant at 56 Dukan in the presence of its operator, Arpit Jain. The team found inadequate cleanliness arrangements at the premises. Medical fitness certificates of food handlers and the water testing report for water used in food preparation were also unavailable.
The team collected five samples of tur dal, paneer, pav, pav bhaji gravy and soybean oil from the restaurant for quality testing. Officials are issuing a notice to the operator, directing him to rectify the deficiencies found during the inspection.
The team also conducted a surprise inspection at Ocean Grill Bar and Restaurant in Pipliyapala, where manager Manjeet Hora was present.
Officials directed the establishment to thoroughly clean its freezer and ensure proper cleaning and storage of raw non-vegetarian food items. They collected two samples of chicken manchow soup and paneer.
At Old Kolkata Roll, located at 56 Dukan, the team collected samples of veg Manchurian noodles and paneer.
The samples are being sent to a laboratory for quality testing. Officials will take further legal action in accordance with the rules after receiving the test reports.

Srinagar- Union Minister for Minority Affairs Kiren Rijiju on Monday said effective utilisation of the country’s more than nine lakh Waqf properties could bring significant socio-economic transformation in the Muslim community, stressing that the assets should be managed to benefit the poor and other needy sections.
“There are more than 9 lakh Waqf properties in the country. If all these Waqf properties are converted for the welfare of the Muslim community, it can transform the entire situation in the Muslim community,” Rijiju told reporters after attending the first-ever Waqf Day 2026 celebrations at Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology of Kashmir (SKUAST-K).
He said proper management of these properties could provide substantial support to poor, helpless and marginalised members of the Muslim community.
Referring to the Jammu and Kashmir Waqf Board, Rijiju said its work over the past three to four years had demonstrated how Waqf properties could be utilised for community welfare. He described it as the country’s top Waqf Board and said he had cited its functioning as a model for other state boards, including Uttar Pradesh.
The Union Minister also invited the J&K Waqf Board to submit comprehensive proposals for skill-development and employment-generation projects, particularly targeting educated unemployed youth.
He said the Ministry of Minority Affairs could consider dedicated funding for such initiatives, adding that proposals worth Rs 15 crore, Rs 20 crore or even Rs 50 crore could be examined.
Rijiju said the projects should promote local arts and culture while creating employment opportunities for young people in Jammu and Kashmir.
He also praised the restoration of the Hazratbal Shrine, saying the work had fulfilled the spiritual aspirations of devotees. He commended the Board’s initiatives in education and healthcare and congratulated its Chairperson, Dr Darakhshan Andrabi, and her team.
On the registration of Waqf properties, Rijiju said the government had already granted a six-month extension and would support genuine cases facing difficulties due to documentation delays.
He said the government would ask its counsel to support legitimate requests for further relief before tribunals and the Supreme Court to ensure that genuine Waqf properties were not adversely affected because of procedural delays.
Defending the amended Waqf law, renamed the UMEED Act, Rijiju said it was aimed at bringing transparency, accountability and better management of Waqf properties and was not intended to harass Muslims or take over their assets.
He said several Waqf properties across the country had remained unregistered, encroached upon or mismanaged for decades, making proper measurement and documentation necessary.
The Minister said the properties should ultimately serve their intended beneficiaries, including poor people, orphans, widows and other disadvantaged sections.
Recalling his earlier visits to Jammu and Kashmir in 2014, Rijiju said the region had witnessed considerable progress and expressed confidence about its future.
He said his visits at the time, when he was serving in the Union Home Ministry, were largely focused on security assessments in remote and border areas, with major public programmes and gatherings being rare.
“Given the situation in Jammu and Kashmir today and the pace at which it is progressing, I believe the future of Jammu and Kashmir and our country is very bright,” he said.
Rijiju also recalled his tenure as Union Sports Minister, saying the Khelo India Winter Games, conceived in Gulmarg in 2019, had developed into an event that athletes looked forward to every year.
He referred to initiatives promoting water sports at Dal Lake and adventure sports across the Valley, saying these had provided opportunities for young people to showcase their abilities.
Recalling his tenure as Union Law Minister, he also spoke about legal outreach programmes organised in remote areas, including Lolab Valley and locations beyond Baramulla, where legal-awareness camps and Lok Adalats were held to improve access to justice.
He said development initiatives in Jammu and Kashmir were being pursued through coordination among different ministries under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union Home Minister Amit Shah.
Emphasising the Prime Minister’s ‘Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas’ vision, Rijiju said inclusive development was essential to achieving Viksit Bharat by 2047, ensuring that no religion, caste or community was left behind.
The event was attended by Member of Parliament Mian Altaf Ahmad Larvi, BJP National General Secretary and J&K in-charge Dr Satish Poonia, SKUAST-K Vice-Chancellor Prof Nazir Ahmad Ganai, religious scholars, Waqf Board members, academicians and public representatives.

GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them. If widely used, our new research suggests these appetite-suppressing medicines could transform the global food system and free up vast areas of agricultural land.
The global food system is ultimately driven by demand. If people eat less, producers respond, affecting production, prices, trade, and how much land is needed. We used a powerful computer simulation to explore scenarios ranging from GLP-1 use concentrated in high-income countries to widespread global access.
With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land—an area slightly larger than Italy—for other uses.
The biggest effects, however, occurred when reduced calorie intake was combined with a shift toward healthier diets. In this scenario, up to 7 million deaths could be avoided each year by 2050, while around 46 million hectares of agricultural land would have become available for other uses. This suggests that alongside weight-loss medicines, we need to make healthier options more widely available, affordable, and more appealing.
The food system could respond in unexpected ways
Food systems are interconnected across countries. If demand falls in one part of the world, this can affect farming, trade, and food prices elsewhere, with consequences for people who are not taking the medications at all.
Lower demand from GLP-1 users, for instance, could make food cheaper. That sounds positive, but cheaper food could also encourage greater consumption among non-users, offsetting some of the intended benefit. The effects of widespread GLP-1 use, in other words, cannot be understood just by looking at individual patients’ weight loss. They ripple through the global food system.
It’s tempting to read these findings as an argument for putting more people on weight-loss medication. That would miss the bigger picture.

Suresh Mittal is 87. According to Uttar Pradesh’s latest draft electoral roll, his father, Vansh Mittal, is 23. Both are registered at house number 869 in booth 111 of the Dholana constituency in Hapur. The same roll lists Vansh as the son of Ajay, a 56-year-old in the same house.
Suresh is not an exception. Alt News found 1,10,875 voters in the Special Summary Revision (SSR) draft roll whose father or mother, registered in the same booth and the same house, is recorded as the same age as them or younger. The draft was published on November 17.
A Year of Revisions: First SIR, Now SSR
The draft comes at the end of a long year for UP’s voter list. The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the rolls began on October 27, 2025 and ended with the final roll on April 10, 2026. In those 166 days the state’s electorate shrank from 15.44 crore to 13.39 crore.
As per the process of SIR, every voter was supposed to be issued an enumeration form, which was supposed to be collected by booth-level officers (BLOs). The Election Commission’s software then allegedly went through the data looking for what it called logical discrepancies. One of these was a parent less than 15 years older than the voter. About 2.22 crore voters in UP were sent notices for such discrepancies, and the Commission says hearings were completed on all of them.
On October 15, six months after the SIR’s final roll, the Election Commission ordered a Special Summary Revision (SSR) in 17 states and Union territories, including UP. The SSR draft roll, which merges the SIR roll with all supplementary lists, has 13.58 crore electors. Claims and objections can be filed till December 16, and the final roll is due on January 4, 2027.
What We Found and How
The SSR draft rolls are machine readable. We took every voter whose entry names a father or a mother, and looked in the same booth for a voter with that name living in the same house. If that ‘parent’ turned out to be the same age as the voter, or younger, we flagged the entry.
We found 1,10,875 such cases spread across all 75 districts and 403 constituencies.
In 35,523 of these cases, parent and child are the same age. In the other 75,352, the parent is younger, and in 6,860 of them by 20 years or more.
Some of the cases are shown below for representation:
What did SIR Actually Achieve?
The SIR was designed to weed out exactly this kind of error. It had enumeration forms, BLO visits, software flags and hearings. A parent who is younger than their own child is perhaps the most basic inconsistency a voter list can have. This raises a larger question: if a process this elaborate left the most basic errors untouched, what did the SIR actually achieve?
Moreover, spotting these anomalous entries is no rocket science. Each one is a contradiction between two lines of the same booth’s roll, often on the same page: An 87-year-old whose father is 23, a 123-year-old woman whose mother is 45, two women who are each other’s mother. A simple check on the roll itself would have thrown them up. Either no such check was run, or nobody acted on what it found.
As of now, all 1,10,875 are in the draft, and the window for corrections closes on December 16.
The district-wise and constituency-wise count of such cases is given below. Kushinagar district has the most cases (3,646), and Fazilnagar has the most for a single assembly constituency (711).

Eight killed as speeding minivan rams into roadside tree in Tamil Nadu's Tiruchirappalli
Preliminary investigation revealed that the driver of the van, identified as Rajesh, lost control of the vehicle due to overspeeding
Eight people were killed and two others injured after a minivan lost control and rammed into a roadside tree in Tamil Nadu's Tiruchirappalli district on Sunday, police said.
The incident took place at around 4 pm in Musiri, which is located about 350 km south of Chennai, an officer said.

The minivan, a Maruti EECO, was carrying 10 passengers who were returning to Thirukattupalli in Thanjavur district after taking part in a relative's ear piercing function in Namakkal, investigating officers said.
Preliminary investigation revealed that the driver of the van, identified as Rajesh, lost control of the vehicle due to overspeeding, following which it collided into a tree. Five passengers – Manickam, Sangili, Murugan, Pavadaidied and the vehicle driver Rajesh – died on the spot, Jembunathapuram police officials told HT.

The other five passengers, who had sustained severe injuries, were rushed to the Musiri Government Hospital for treatment. However, three among them – identified as Sakthivel, Subramani, and Seetharaman – succumbed to their injuries at the medical facility. The other two remain hospitalised and are undergoing treatment.
The bodies of the deceased have been sent for autopsy. The police have registered a case under relevant sections and launched an investigation.

For 15 years, Sébastien Fontaine has been trying to kill dirt. The biochemist, who runs a lab at the French National Institute for Agriculture, Food, and Environment, wanted to know how much carbon is released by soil—just dirt alone, completely devoid of life. His team sealed dirt into jars and blasted them with sterilizing gamma radiation. Then they waited for the carbon dioxide released by the soil—a sign of ongoing microbial respiration—to drop.
They waited and waited and waited some more: weeks, then months. Under a microscope, the irradiated soil showed no signs of life, but it continued to emit carbon dioxide. The soil wouldn’t stop breathing.
Fontaine’s lab repeated the experiments and produced the same results. Finally, convinced that they weren’t dealing with an artifact of the experimental setup, they set out to find the source of breath in dead soil.
Now, Fontaine and his colleagues have reported that their soil samples continued to consume oxygen and spew carbon dioxide for six years. In a 2025 paper in Science Advances, they proposed that a metabolic process that powers much of life is also possible outside living cells. Their experiments point to how it could work in dirt, absent the living proteins that would typically organize it. If they’re right, some biochemical reactions, such as those that release the energy of carbon-rich sugar molecules, may not be unique to living things. Such reactions—known as metabolism when performed by cells—could even predate life on Earth, Fontaine said.
The experiments show “what happens to biomolecules when they’re left to their own devices,” said Joseph Moran, an organic chemist at the University of Ottawa who was not involved with the research. They’re finding that the chemistry of life is not exclusive to life, he added. “It’s the chemistry of geology.”
When he made this accidental discovery, Fontaine was trying to establish a baseline for carbon in lifeless soil. Using a sterile syringe, the researchers periodically sampled the air in a hermetically sealed jar containing soil and measured its carbon content using a mass spectrometer. After radiation wiped out the soil microbes, the carbon emission rate declined quickly but didn’t disappear. It remained stable for over 100 days.
When he shared the results with other researchers, they advised him to treat it as an experimental artifact—a source of error not worth ferreting out—and move on. But he couldn’t. He needed to understand whether a metabolic process only known to occur in biological cells—a precisely orchestrated sequence of chemical reactions, requiring several molecules and enzymes—was unfolding in sterile soil. To see what was happening, his team added a dash of enzymes extracted from yeast cultures. Immediately, the soil’s carbon emissions spiked. This, they speculated, was because the enzymes had ramped up a reaction that was already happening.
Convincing the scientific community, however, was an uphill battle. When Fontaine submitted the manuscript to journals for publication, some reviewers “were highly positive, and others were really suspicious, especially concerning the sterility of the soil,” he recalled. In 2013 the results were published in the journal Biogeosciences. Still, Fontaine could not rest. Bruised by the harsh reviews, he decided to definitively prove that his irradiated soil samples remained free of life. Over the following decade, his lab would, in fits and starts, chip away at their obsession.
They considered the possibility that the soil wasn’t really dead and tried to kill it harder with more radiation, pressure, and heat. Still, the soil continued to emit carbon for months.
Through an electron microscope, Benoit Kéraval, then a graduate student in Fontaine’s lab, found cells in the irradiated soil. But staining showed no RNA or DNA molecules, indicating that the cells were definitely dead. When they experimentally added microbes to simulate contamination, the cells rapidly recolonized the soil microcosm and released much more carbon dioxide. So what they were observing in the sterilized sample likely wasn’t a result of inadequate antiseptic measures.
By 2018, when Clémentin Bouquet joined the lab, the team was confident in its findings and ready to dig into the underlying mechanisms.
For six years, Bouquet and Kéraval studied two sets of sealed, irradiated soil samples—one of normal soil and one that was supplemented with glucose. For 142 days, they took regular air samples and saw the daily rate of carbon dioxide emissions decline but not disappear, just as they had before. Then the samples sat in an incubator for over 1,000 days, as the researchers focused on their other experiments into how microbes process and store carbon in soil.
When they measured the samples again, at days 1,606 and 2,442, the emissions had slowed further, but the soil was still breathing. The glucose-augmented samples showed higher emission rates, which strengthened Fontaine’s suspicion that nonbiological catalysts in soil can induce reactions that resemble the metabolic breakdown of sugar.
During metabolism, sugar is broken down into smaller carbon molecules, which feed the Krebs cycle—a series of reactions in which high-energy electrons are stripped from carbon-rich molecules. Electrons liberated by the Krebs cycle then pass through another set of reactions that consume oxygen. For some researchers, it was a stretch to suggest that this process could unfold outside a cell. Fontaine would need to show that soil can play the same role.
He devised a fuel cell that could detect electrons zipping through soil in the form of a current. His team added soil that had been irradiated almost five years earlier and then closed the circuit. A current passed through the soil that was several times higher than in a control setup involving a saltwater solution. According to Fontaine, the experiment demonstrated that sterile soil supports a flow of electrons indicative of processes that resemble the oxygen-dependent metabolism of the Krebs cycle.
It was once thought that the Krebs cycle cannot occur outside the controlled confines of a cell, which teems with enzymes that keep everything ticking along and increases the chances that biomolecules will bump into each other. In a 2025 preprint on biorxiv.org, Fontaine and colleagues reported observing four of the eight intermediate molecules known to be part of the Krebs cycle in 6-month-old sterile soil samples. Many of these molecules formed after the irradiation.
According to the authors, their results suggest that clods of earth can indeed catalyze these reactions without the presence of life.
For Joshua Schimel, a soil ecologist at the University of California, Santa Barbara, Fontaine’s findings were not too surprising. “Glucose naturally, in the process of being oxidized, is going to form some of these Krebs-cycle intermediates,” he said. Many soils are rich in iron oxides and aluminum oxides, which can catalyze this conversion, he added.
The idea that metals can catalyze biochemical reactions is central to a theory about the origins of life that has emerged over the last decade. Metals such as iron and zinc sit at the core of many of the most ancient enzymes found across life forms. Some researchers, including Moran, believe they might have catalyzed these reactions before life emerged. Studies, including his, suggest that the chemical reactions that break down and construct glucose derivatives, which are normally associated with life, might have existed before the enzymes and genes that enable them in living cells.
“There’s a handful of researchers like myself that think, actually, we should organize our thoughts about life in a different way—that we actually should put metabolism at the base of what life is doing and then genes are a way of controlling that at a higher level,” Moran said.
Cell-free metabolic reactions could be more common than previously thought and don’t need special conditions to get started, said Markus Ralser, a biochemist at Charité University Hospital in Berlin, who found some of the first enzyme-free metabolic reactions.
“This fits a bit into my thinking about how metabolism started in evolution,” he said of the new work. “If it would be very hard to do, then the planet would not be full of life now.” This idea is complicated, however, by the low-oxygen conditions in which life arose.
Another explanation for the observed results could be that enzymes, loosed from the irradiated cells, might be hanging around in the soil and continuing their biochemical jobs. Even when degraded, enzymes have stable backbones that might be capable of catalyzing reactions, said Sudha Rajamani, an astrobiologist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Pune who wasn’t involved in the study.
Ralser agrees with her. “My gut feeling is they still have a lot of enzymes there [in Fontaine’s irradiated soil], even after six years,” he said. To know whether metals and minerals in soil could spontaneously carry out these reactions, the researchers would have to eliminate enzymes from the mixture. But that’s really hard: They would have to get the soil so hot that it would damage the soil structure itself.
However, the activity of such enzymes diminishes “exponentially” after they spill out of cells, Bouquet said. Plus, no enzyme is known to last six years, Fontaine added. He doesn’t doubt that enzymes released by living and recently dead cells contribute to carbon emissions in real-world soils, but the long-term experimental results make it “very unlikely that the respiration we observed is due to enzymes,” he said.
For Bouquet, chasing this years-long obsession has highlighted that “even in a context as close and familiar to us as terrestrial soil, we are not always able to distinguish or recognize processes that indicate the presence or absence of living organisms.” Now a researcher at the Collège de France and the National Museum of Natural History in Paris, he is looking for prebiotic origins of other biochemical cascades.
“I find it particularly interesting to imagine the survival of processes that may predate life itself,” Bouquet said, “right there under our feet.”

The COVID-19 pandemic is having a devastating impact across the world. Efforts to contain the coronavirus are vital to the health of the world’s population, but they are also exposing children to increased risk of violence – including maltreatment, gender-based violence and sexual exploitation.
As leaders of organisations committed to ending violence against children, we come together in solidarity to share our deep concern, call for action and pledge our support to protect children from violence and reduce the impact of COVID-19 on children in every country and community.
A third of the global population is on COVID-19 lockdown, and school closures have impacted more than 1.5 billion children. Movement restrictions, loss of income, isolation, overcrowding and high levels of stress and anxiety are increasing the likelihood that children experience and observe physical, psychological and sexual abuse at home – particularly those children already living in violent or dysfunctional family situations. And while online communities have become central to maintain many children’s learning, support and play, it is also increasing their exposure to cyberbullying, risky online behavior and sexual exploitation.
The situation is aggravated by children’s lack of access to schoolfriends, teachers, social workers and the safe space and services that schools provide. The most vulnerable children – including refugees, migrants, and children who are internally displaced, deprived of liberty, living without parental care, living on the street and in urban slums, with disabilities, and living in conflict-affected areas – are a particular concern. For many, growing economic vulnerability will increase the threat of child labour, child marriage and child trafficking.
We must act now. Together, we call on governments, the international community and leaders in every sector to urgently respond with a united effort to protect children from the heightened risk of violence, exploitation and abuse as part of the broader response to COVID-19.
Governments have a central role to play. They must ensure that COVID-19 prevention and response plans integrate age appropriate and gender sensitive measures to protect all children from violence, neglect and abuse. Child protection services and workers must be designated as essential and resourced accordingly.
Working with and supporting governments, our collective response must include: maintaining essential health and social welfare services, including mental health and psychosocial support; providing child protection case management and emergency alternative care arrangements; ensuring social protection for the most vulnerable children and households; continuing care and protection for children in institutions; and communicating with and engaging parents, caregivers and children themselves with evidence-based information and advice. National helplines, school counsellors and other child-friendly reporting mechanisms enable children in distress to reach out for help, and must be adapted to the challenges of COVID-19.
Given the heightened risks of online harms, technology companies and telecoms providers must do everything they can to keep children safe online. This includes providing access to cost-free child helplines, age-appropriate services and safe e-education platforms - and using their platforms to share child online safety advice. They must also do more to detect and stop harmful activity against children online, including grooming and the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse images and videos.
As global organisations working to end violence against children, we will continue to advocate for and invest in effective child protection solutions. We will collectively develop and share technical resources and guidance for policymakers, practitioners, parents, caregivers and children themselves. And we will support the courageous health, child protection and humanitarian professionals working around the clock to keep children safe during these unprecedented times.
In recent years, the global community has made significant gains in protecting children from violence. We must not allow those gains to be lost during the current turmoil. We must do all we can to keep children safe now. And we must plan ahead together, so that once the immediate health crisis is over, we can get back on track towards the goal of ending all forms of violence, abuse and neglect of children

Virginia reported its first measles-associated death of 2026 on Friday, November 20, 2026, involving a child who tested positive for measles, the state health department said.
The department said the child was between 0 and 4 years old. It did not disclose additional details, including the child's vaccination status, citing the family's privacy.
Measles can cause serious complications, including pneumonia, brain inflammation, complications during pregnancy and death.
Virginia has reported 220 measles cases so far in 2026, including 40 among children aged 0 to 4 and 75 among those aged 5 to 12, state health department data showed as of November 19. Of those cases, 179 were in unvaccinated individuals, 39 were in people whose vaccination status was unknown and two were in vaccinated individuals.
Virginia health officials have reported increased measles activity driven largely by outbreaks in central region. Buckingham County has reported 127 cases, the highest in the state, while neighbouring Charlotte County has recorded 34 cases.
The death adds to a worsening national measles outbreak that this week cost the United States its measles elimination status after 26 years.
Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit U.S. state, reported an eighth measles-related death and confirmed 1,631 measles cases, as of November 20. Wisconsin has also reported two deaths, while New York state recorded its first measles-associated death, involving a child.
The CDC has confirmed six measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, though it does not specify the states where the deaths were recorded.
A discrepancy between state and federal death tallies arose earlier this year after the CDC, under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., began using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data instead of state figures.
The sharp increase in U.S. measles cases has coincided with declining immunization rates and rising vaccine hesitancy under Kennedy, who has for years spread doubts, without scientific evidence, about the safety of measles vaccines.
