Quick Answer
Ente Photos is a privacy-focused Google Photos alternative offering 10GB of free storage, end-to-end encryption, open-source code, selective album backups, cross-platform access, easy photo imports, collaborative sharing, and on-device AI features like face recognition and Magic Search.
When we think about a dedicated photo app, we instantly remember Google Photos or the default gallery on our phone. We do not have many trustworthy options. That’s when I came across Ente. Ente is a dedicated photo app available as a standalone app to install on Android, iOS, macOS, Windows, and Linux operating systems.
Is Ente the real challenger to the Google Photos app? Can we replace the gallery on our phones with Ente? Let’s find out.
Table of Contents
Features That Make Ente a Worthy Photo App
Ente has some exciting features that really make it stand out from the few others available. Here’s what makes it worthy.
Generous Free (Forever) Storage Plan
Ente offers a 10GB free storage plan for your photos and videos. Ente claims the plan is free forever. 10GB of free cloud storage dedicated to photos and video backup seems a good deal. That too without any ads.
Google offers 15GB of free storage space for each Google account. There is no dedicated storage space for the Google Photos app. As Google’s free storage is tied to all Google products as a whole, Ente’s 10GB looks big.
If you exhaust the generous free space on Ente, you can upgrade to a paid plan that offers storage starting from 50GB to 2TB for a monthly or annual subscription.
End-to-End Encrypted Backups
The photos and videos you back up on Ente are end-to-end encrypted by default. Ente claims they never use our data to train their models or spy on us.
The photos we back up via Google Photos are not end-to-end encrypted. Google may use our data to train their AI models, serve us customized ads, etc. You can prevent Google from using your data to show you personalized ads, but they can read your data. That’s where Ente succeeds.
The backup is end-to-end encrypted with keys before it leaves our device. The encryption keys are derived from our password using advanced key derivation functions. That means only the password you set can decrypt the data.
As the source code of Ente is publicly audited, the trust factor improves. When I tried to sign up on Ente, it provided me with a recovery key or the master key that I can use in case I lose my password.
The encryption process involves only us, the users, and they can never access the data. Even in the unfortunate event of a data breach, our data can remain safe as it is end-to-end encrypted.
Fully Open-Source Platform
Ente’s entire codebase for photos and its other apps is available for public audit on GitHub with more than 29k stars. The stars do not necessarily mean the project is good, but they give some form of trust.
The internet rewards the sensation. If someone had found a mismatch between Ente’s tall claims and the code, they surely would have flagged it and made an issue out of it.
Backup of User-Selected Albums
When you give permissions for Google Photos on our device, it backs up all the available albums, photos, and videos. We cannot select or ignore certain albums.
Ente, on the other hand, gives users the option to select which albums to back up. The albums that we choose not to back up are ignored by Ente as well. I loved this feature personally, as a lot of unnecessary data gets uploaded and wastes storage space. We can also customize the albums for backup anytime.
Easy Accessibility on All Platforms
Ente Photo has an app for every major operating system. We can install its app on Android, iOS, Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. If we do not want to install the app, we can use it on the web through Ente.com.
Import Data From Google and Apple
Just download the Google Takeout that only has Google Photos data, import it into the Ente desktop app, and you are all set. It’s that simple to import data from Google Photos.
If you are an Apple user, just install the Ente app on your mobile device. Ente will read the data directly from your iCloud library and import it.
If you have iCloud shared albums, select the photos you want to import into the Ente app, and then save them to your device library for Ente to read them automatically.
Better Sharing and Collaboration Features
Ente Photo app provides us with three ways to share albums with others. You can share with a person on Ente, create a public link and share it with non-Ente users, or create a collaborative link to let non-Ente users add photos without an Ente account.
This does not put pressure on non-users to create an Ente account before collaborating with Ente albums, unlike the Google Photos app.
On-Device Machine Learning Features
There are a few machine learning-based features, like Magic Search, where you can search for photos with descriptions of how you remember them, Face Recognition, Memory Lane, Map and Location, and Jump to Date. These are all the latest advances in AI features.
To protect and maintain your privacy, all the machine learning happens on your device itself and is never sent to Ente’s servers. The machine learning feature is not enabled by default. You have to enable it manually and choose to disable it whenever you need to do so.
Is Ente Photos safe to use?
Yes, the Ente Photos app is safe to use to back up your photos and videos. It provides end-to-end encryption based on your password, and only your password can decrypt the data. Once you forget your password and also lose the recovery key they provided, you may never get to access the backup. The entire codebase of the Ente Photos app is available for public audit on GitHub.
How do I transfer photos from Google Photos to Ente?
You can transfer photos from Google Photos to the Ente Photos app in two ways. You can either download Google Photos data from Google Takeout, or download the entire library from the Google Photos app and drop it into the Ente Photos desktop app. It will read the data and import it to back it up safely.

Former South Africa captain AB de Villiers has alleged that Australia tampered with the ball during the first Test of the 2018 series in Durban, suggesting the ball-tampering scandal extended beyond the incidents previously acknowledged by the players.
Australia captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and Cameron Bancroft received lengthy bans for their roles in using sandpaper to alter the ball during the third Test in Cape Town.
Former Australia batter Usman Khawaja, whose recent autobiography has reignited scrutiny of the scandal, had claimed that sandpaper was also used during the second Test in Port Elizabeth, now known as Gqeberha. Warner and Bancroft have since corroborated his claims.
However, De Villiers, who played throughout the series, has now alleged that the practice began in Durban.
“It started in Durban, by the way, not in PE,” De Villiers said on his YouTube channel ABD360. “I’m very happy for people to quote me on that.
“I see everyone is sort of admitting that in Port Elizabeth it also happened. I can very much tell you Durban was no different, in the first Test. Go look at the footage. Absolutely no doubt in my mind.
“We lost that first Test match in Durban with the ball reversing at a very, very interesting time. Way too early for anyone to reverse a ball at Kingsmead. Trust me, I’ve played a lot of cricket there.”
He questioned why the players involved had not fully acknowledged their actions, suggesting the Australian bowlers would have known what was happening.
“So whatever they did there, whether it was sandpaper or (a) nail, I don’t care. The fact of the matter is they were caught and everyone knew. Just stand up and say ‘we were wrong’. A lot is at stake now because they lied.
“The bowlers in particular knew because the ball doesn’t just reverse. It’s not your first Test match for Australia. So just stand up and say, ‘guys, we were wrong’.”
However, Bancroft disputed the allegation in a 4,000-word article last week, explicitly stating that sandpaper was not used in Durban. Mitchell Starc took nine wickets in the match as Australia secured its only victory of the series.
Australia’s bowlers and then head coach Darren Lehmann have consistently denied knowledge of ball-tampering during the series. Current Test captain Pat Cummins, who was part of the bowling attack, dismissed Khawaja’s claims as “100% wrong” and “utter nonsense” earlier this month.
De Villiers, meanwhile, said he had sympathy for those involved but criticised how the team handled the fallout.
“It’s become really personal for all the people involved and I do have sympathy for them,” he said. “Obviously not sympathy for what took place on that day and who knows how many games before then.
“I just feel they should have stuck together as a unit. They threw the guys under the bus and forced a situation like this to pop up again eight years later.”
He also acknowledged that he had pushed the boundaries during his playing career but insisted his teams had stayed within the rules.
“I’m not playing all innocent and saying that I’m the perfect person,” he said. “We all try and get the ball to reverse. We try and bounce it in. We try and do it in a legal manner and we try and push the boundaries as much as possible.
“We all have tried over the years to get the ball to do something, to get an edge, but obviously not being as stupid as to take an object onto the field and blatantly cheating.”
Cricket Australia has launched an independent forum for players and staff involved to voluntarily share their accounts. It is not a formal investigation and will not result in further penalties.

There's no denying that 2026 has been a slower year for the iPad lineup. Only the iPad Air and iPad Mini received updates (with nothing new for the iPad or iPad Pro since 2025), and in June, the entire lineup was subject to a painful price hike of either $100 or $200, depending on the model. For more shopping advice from our team of product testers and deal hunters, check out our Best Early Black Friday Deals, Best Amazon Early Black Friday Deals, and Best Early Black Friday Laptop Deals.
The Best iPad Deal: iPad Mini (2024)
Even though it's more than two years old at this point, the 2024 iPad Mini is the best iPad deal ahead of Black Friday. It's $100 off, bringing the price down to $499. That's just $50 more than the base iPad (the most affordable in the lineup), below. With its tiny size and weight, the iPad Mini is the perfect device to take on the go with you. You can also conveniently use it one-handed, which is especially helpful if you're using an Apple Pencil Pro in your other hand. Don't get me wrong: The improvements to the newer iPad Mini are substantial and worthwhile to the right person. The updated OLED screen is gorgeous; the chassis is even thinner; and the front-facing camera is better for video calls, having been moved to the side bezel. But because it's $300 more expensive, most people should stick with the older model—especially since the iPad Mini is better-suited for more casual tasks, like reading and note-taking.
iPad for $449
If you're trying to save the most cash, the base iPad is the absolute cheapest. You might appreciate the larger screen over the iPad Mini, too. While $50 isn't a huge discount—and it's also a fairly common price—hopefully we'll see deeper cuts in the future. Even so, this is a good buy right now, particularly if you're looking for a tablet to use immediately, whether for an upcoming flight or to keep kids busy on a long car trip.
iPad Air for $649
The iPad Air is the in-between iPad. It's not as cheap as the base iPad, nor does it have the Tandem OLED screen and high-end features of the iPad Pro. And yet, I find that it's the iPad people should buy if they intend to use it for work. That's primarily because it has both a powerful M4 chip and can be connected to a Magic Keyboard with full trackpad support. The most recent versions of iPadOS make windowing much easier, and Apple even made the cursor work more like macOS. After all, most people don't need an OLED screen to do some word processing, answer emails, and take the occasional Zoom call.
When you're ready to use it more like a traditional tablet, just pull it off its magnetic cover, and it's ready for your fingers or an Apple Pencil. The 11-inch model is still small enough to not feel overwhelming in your hands. And while the $649 sale isn't particularly rare, it's not a bad price for a tablet that functions pretty well as a laptop replacement.
Other iPads to Consider
iPad Mini (2026) for $699: The latest iPad Mini came out just last month, and it's not currently on sale. It's a significant upgrade from the 2024 iPad Mini, with its OLED display and improved performance. But as a small, one-handed tablet, the previous-gen model is the better deal right now—and the smart buy for most.
iPad Pro 11-inch for $1,099: It's a little surprising that the iPad Pro hasn't been discounted at all for Black Friday. At $1,099, it's cheaper than the 13-inch MacBook Air, which uses the same M5 chip. The difference? You still have to buy the Magic Keyboard separately to pair with the iPad Pro. All in all, the iPad ends up being a much more expensive device.

Jensen Huang received a “hero’s welcome” from employees on Monday after Nvidia’s board of directors reinstated him as CEO, according to people who were present. An outspoken faction of Nvidia’s workforce had demanded his return and greeted him with chants, raucous applause, and hugs at the company’s headquarters.
But other employees were quietly stewing. Several current and former Nvidia staffers had viewed Huang’s abrupt exit earlier this month as a rare opportunity to change the “one team” corporate culture of unfettered unity and minimal bureaucracy that he had cultivated over the past three decades, according to interviews with the workers, as well as internal correspondence and social media posts reviewed by WIRED. Most spoke on the condition of anonymity because they feared backlash from colleagues.
Some employees were alarmed by Huang’s alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a subordinate and another with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. But their frustrations extended beyond the CEO’s personal conduct. Current and former workers describe a culture at Nvidia in which allegedly abusive behavior was tolerated and challenging leadership was perceived as discouraged.
“Everyone agrees that mistakes were made, the question is what we are ready to forgive,” one employee wrote on an internal platform before Huang’s return. “I don’t know how comfortable I’ll be working at a place where such affairs are not taken extremely seriously.”
Another added, “If Jensen comes back, I’m not doing any HR trainings ever again.”
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
When Huang returned to Nvidia’s offices in California on Monday, he told employees who greeted him that he would do a better job with his second chance at CEO. (As of Monday afternoon, he had not yet sent a companywide note about his return, as he was still getting his laptop set back up.)

|---|
| Are you a current or former Nvidia employee who has information to share? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at Peard33.24 | 
US President Donald Trump said he played a crucial role in convincing Nvidia's board to bring back Huang. A person close to Trump calls him an irreplaceable CEO and says they expect him to exercise better judgement going forward.
Nvidia’s board announced it will continue an independent investigation into whether Huang had been a target of foreign intelligence services and that it will double down on plans to step up corporate governance.
It’s difficult to gauge how widespread dissatisfaction with Huang’s leadership may be at Nvidia. The company’s emphasis on unity has historically made it difficult for people to openly question his leadership or choices, workers say. “There's only one team at NVIDIA,” the chipmaker’s official website declares.
A public petition campaign known as Stand with Jensen garnered signatures from more than 10,000 Nvidia purported employees, according to its website. Nvidia has roughly 49,000 employees and 18,000 contractors overall, according to a person familiar with its workforce.
But inside Nvidia, one employee told colleagues that “some portion” of the signatures appeared to be “illegitimate,” noting that the names included “Satan” and media personality Mia Khalifa, who does not work at the chipmaker. The employee wrote that they found 75 suspicious names in an hour of checking. WIRED was unable to independently verify the findings. The petition’s organizers did not respond to requests for comment.
Huang’s supporters have praised how he made the company feel like a “big super family.” They credited him for minimizing bureaucracy, making himself available to staff, and supporting employees during difficult periods, including the Covid pandemic. A former employee who attended numerous meetings with Huang and other senior executives says the CEO was particularly adept at preventing bureaucratic infighting. He could detect corporate “politics and nonsense before it was even born,” says the worker.
There are also powerful financial reasons for Nvidia employees to feel loyal to Huang. His bets on chips and software for artificial intelligence have transformed Nvidia into one of the world’s most valuable companies and made many longtime employees wealthy in the process.
But for some employees, the revelations about Huang’s behavior have forced them to question that loyalty. Jason Sequeira, a longtime engineering leader at Nvidia, wrote on LinkedIn last week that he ultimately couldn’t decide whether he wanted Huang back as he weighed arguments from both sides. “Some believe his contributions to NVIDIA and the industry are so extraordinary that he deserves another chance,” Sequeira wrote. “Others argue that making exceptions for powerful leaders sets a dangerous precedent. … I don’t have a clear answer.”
Several current and former workers say that Huang’s management style could come off as overly harsh at times, including, for example, toward longtime colleagues he viewed as having grown complacent as Nvidia’s market value surged. Two former employees say that he regularly raised his voice at workers, sometimes in ways they found belittling.
Other employees were more concerned about whether Nvidia’s board would hold Huang accountable for allegedly misleading the directors about his affairs. “That’s something we can’t have,” one employee says.
Another source of frustration for Nvidia workers has been the growing influence of Huang’s two children and son-in-law, who all hold senior titles at the chipmaker. In March, his daughter, Madison Huang scolded a colleague on a call with about 100 other employees, according to a participant who didn’t believe the anger was warranted. “I’m disappointed you asked that, are you fucking stupid?” the employee recalls Madison saying in response to a question about workshops on OpenClaw technology scheduled for an upcoming Nvidia conference. “Your mom can build a claw.”
Madison and her brother, Spencer Huang, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.
Praveen Mhapsekar, a senior system software engineer who was let go last week after disputes with his managers and HR, says he and colleagues stopped feeling comfortable complaining about practices that concerned them because of the trouble they believe it brought on themselves.
“This organization requires greater discipline and structured processes,” he says. One of the world’s most valuable companies “cannot be managed like a private startup operating out of a garage, where personal influence takes precedence over established procedures.”
Huang’s return doesn’t eliminate the prospect of Nvidia evolving to quell frustrations. But with internal issues more public than ever before, maybe the days of one big family all cheering along together are mostly gone.
Additional reporting by Lauren Goode and Hugo Lowell.

- GTA 6 reportedly sold 44.9 million copies within four days of its November 19 launch.
- PS5 accounts for 33.7 million estimated sales, while Xbox accounts for 11.2 million.
- Alinea Analytics estimates GTA 6 generated over $4 billion in launch-weekend revenue.
Grand Theft Auto 6 was already breaking records before players even set foot in Vice City. This was thanks to GTA 6’s massive pre-release sales. Now that Rockstar’s long-awaited open-world game is out, the money keeps rolling in. A new report claims that GTA 6 has sold nearly 45 million copies in just four days, generating more than $4 billion in revenue during its launch weekend.
According to a new report from Alinea Analytics, GTA 6 has sold an estimated 44.9 million copies since its November 19, 2026 release. The figures were shared by the firm’s head of market analysis, Rhys Elliott on X, and cover sales across PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S through November 22.
Of the nearly 45 million copies reportedly sold, PlayStation 5 accounts for the majority of these sales, with an estimated 33.7 million copies sold, representing 75.1% of the total. Meanwhile, Xbox accounts for the remaining 11.2 million copies, or 24.9%.
The report also reveals that GTA 6 has generated over $4 billion in revenue in just four days, with more than $3 billion coming from PS5 sales alone. These estimates represent copies purchased by customers and exclude unsold physical copies sitting on retail shelves.
But the impressive numbers don’t stop at sales. Alinea estimates that around 40.8 million people played the game on November 22 alone, while nearly 9 million players have already spent more than 20 hours exploring Leonida in GTA 6.
But the game isn’t just breaking sales records. GTA 6 has already broken internet traffic records, while a separate report revealed that players spent over eight hours on average playing it on launch day.
With such an enormous opening weekend, GTA 6 is already on its way to becoming one of the best-selling games ever. And with a PC release still to come, Rockstar’s latest blockbuster has plenty of room to grow.

Budget jewellery startup Zavya has raised ₹22.6 Cr ($2.4 Mn) in a pre-Series A funding round led by Daksham Growth Ventures (DGV), the growth investment arm of Daksham Capital, with participation from existing investor Orios Venture Partners. The investment values the silver jewellery brand at approximately ₹191.5 Cr on a post-money basis. “With DGV joining us and Orios continuing to back us, we are excited to strengthen our presence across D2C and quick commerce, invest in long-term brand building and take our first steps into physical retail,” Zavya cofounder and CEO Poem Kabra said. Founded in 2021 by Kabra and Ravi Malani, Zavya offers silver jewellery targeted for 22-35 year old women. Its everyday 925 sterling silver jewelry, including products like individual rings, pendants, earrings, and anklets, are priced between ₹699-2,299. The startup claims to come up with over 50 new styles every month. Zavya operates through its own website and mobile application, alongside quick commerce platforms such as Blinkit and Zepto. It also sells through online marketplaces including Amazon, Myntra and Nykaa. For the fiscal year FY25, Zavya reported a net profit of ₹54.7 Lakh on a revenue of ₹6 Cr (up 38% YoY). While numbers for further periods are yet to be determined, the brand claims to have maintained EBITDA profitability while scaling. The five-year old brand sees a robust opportunity in scaling in the world’s largest silver jewellery market by fabrication volume. A report by Credence Research estimates India's 925 sterling silver jewellery D2C market at $614 Mn in 2025 and projects it to reach $2.28 Bn by 2035, growing at a CAGR of 14%. The report identifies online channels as the largest distribution segment, accounting for 60% of market value in 2025, while quick commerce is expected to be among the faster-growing channels. In this market, Zavya competes with legacy Beliram Legacy, TrueSilver, and Silver Emporium. Meanwhile, it is one of the up and coming new-age jewellery brands that bid to capitalise on the growing market opportunity and challenge the incumbents. Backed by strong venture capital backing, brands like Giva and Palmonas are also bidding to take on legacy giants with their select, premium-feel offerings at more affordable price ranges.

The Food and Drug Administration said Friday that it had rejected a cell therapy intended for patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy developed by Capricor Therapeutics.
The decision to block the treatment, called deramiocel, from reaching the market should have been an easy one for regulators to make. The targeted patient population — teenagers and young men with Duchenne who had already lost the ability to walk — have few treatment options today. Deramiocel didn’t help them either. Capricor conducted two randomized clinical trials. Both failed to show deramiocel could stave off heart failure or preserve muscle function in their arms.

On Nov. 23, Nvidia announced the tech company had reinstated cofounder Jensen Huang as president and CEO. In the hours that followed, people shared an alleged screenshot appearing to show that U.S. President Donald Trump had shared an altered image of Huang on Truth Social.
That altered image showed Huang standing in Trump's place at the site of the Butler, Pennsylvania, assassination attempt in July 2024. A flag bearing the Nvidia logo hangs on the right side. Huang's right hand — formerly Trump's pumped fist — holds a red bra, appearing to allude to Jensen Huang's affair with Chinese businesswoman and alleged government spy Alice Huang.
For example, people posted (archived) the purported screenshot from Trump's Truth Social account on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived) and X (archived).
(@atrupar via X)
Snopes readers also emailed us to ask whether Trump actually shared the altered image.
In sum, this was true. The altered image showing Huang holding a red bra in the Butler assassination attempt photo appeared in a Nov. 23 post on Trump's Truth Social account (archived).
(@realDonaldTrump via Truth Social)
The fake image displays a watermark for the user @grandoldmemes, who previously posted the same meme on Instagram and X, with the latter displaying a label for parody content. The user acknowledged that Trump's account had reposted the image.
Snopes emailed the White House to ask why Trump reposted the fake image and will update this article if we receive further information.
Huang reinstated, Trump's investments
The user @grandoldmemes posted the inauthentic meme shortly after Nvidia, which dominates the market for computer chips used by artificial intelligence models, announced its board of directors had reinstated Jensen Huang. Huang resigned earlier in the month after news media outlets reported on his relationship with Alice Huang.
The New York Times reported on Nov. 23 that Trump, who holds investments in the chip maker — as confirmed in various public disclosures — directed Nvidia's effort to reinstate Huang.
Last week, Congress announced Jensen Huang voluntarily agreed to appear before three House committees. He will likely face scrutiny over the affair and reports of Nvidia's advanced chips being diverted to China.

Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say
- Published
A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.
Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.
Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.
This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.
In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.
At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.
There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.
On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.
"We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said.
"The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."
Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari.
"Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," said Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).
Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.
In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".
Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.
Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.
In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.
Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.
According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.
Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it says.

Quick Answer
LastWave, Musify, Convx, Spotube, and SimpMusic are free open-source clients for YouTube Music and Spotify. They unlock premium perks without subscription fees or ad tracking, offering background playback, offline downloads, time-synced lyrics, lossless audio, and customized interfaces without locked controls.
Subscription prices are going through the roof. And when you stack multiple subscriptions together, it can put a big hole in your pocket. For listening to music, we usually depend on Spotify and YouTube Music. They are the default music streaming sources for millions across the globe. Though there are alternatives from which you can hear high-quality audio, they just can’t match the ease of popular apps. But you are bombarded with ads, and several features are locked behind a paywall unless you pay.
Thankfully, you don’t have to search the internet for free options. Developers around the world have built free apps that give you many of those perks. Below are five of the best, what each does well, and what to watch out for before installing.
Table of Contents
Why are open-source music apps worth a look?
To be clear, most of these apps are clients. This means that they don’t store any music themselves. They plug into a service like YouTube Music and show it in a cleaner, ad-free interface with extra features on top, which you’d usually get after paying for a premium subscription. For me, Spotify has been the go-to music streaming app, but slowly the app has become quite greedy.
After a few times, the next and previous song buttons get locked, and it asks you to pay to unlock them. I mean, what is wrong with companies today? Thankfully, I have now ditched Spotify and have picked one of the below open-source music options.
That has three practical effects:
- No ads and no subscription fees. Everything below is free.
- Most of these apps have no ad trackers or tracking SDKs.
- New features are constantly added, and some of them aren’t even available in paid apps.
The catch is that these apps rely on unofficial methods to fetch music, so they can break when YouTube or Spotify changes something. Treat them as great free alternatives, but not as rock-solid replacements. Let us take a look at the free alternatives.
Best free open-source music apps
LastWave
If you care about how your music sounds, LastWave is the one to install first. It’s a free YouTube Music client for Android, Windows, macOS, and Linux. Most of us would care about the free music that we get with LastWave, but you will soon appreciate the quality of music that it offers. And since it is a YouTube Music client, you are getting access to almost every song that is available on YouTube.
The headline feature is lossless FLAC audio, up to 24-bit/192 kHz. When you press play, the song starts playing right away on the fastest available stream, and while you listen, the app fetches the lossless version in the background and switches over once it’s ready. On compatible phones and headphones, LastWave also plays the Dolby Atmos version of a song automatically. For those who own a USB DAC or a pair of IEMs, there’s a bit-perfect mode that sends raw, unprocessed audio straight to your device.
The app is packed with features that normally sit behind a subscription. The lyrics are synced word-by-word and pulled from sources like Apple Music, Musixmatch, and LRCLIB. There’s a 10-band equalizer with presets for thousands of headphone models, and smart playlists that build mixes from your listening history. Plus, you have the option to import playlists from Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube Music in seconds, and even sync your Spotify liked songs.
Musify
Not everyone wants a hundred settings and toggles. Some people just want to listen to their favorite music without having to deal with ads and a hundred pop-ups about purchasing the subscription between two songs. Musify is for people who just want to open an app, search for a song, and press play. It’s a lightweight Android app built around Material You, which means its colors automatically match your phone’s theme and wallpaper.
Using it is fairly easy. You search for songs, albums, artists, or playlists and start streaming over Wi-Fi or mobile data. If you want to save data or listen on a flight, you can download tracks and play them offline. It lets you create your own playlists, rename and reorder them, or import existing ones from online sources. The player shows lyrics so you can follow along. You can also control the quality of the audio.
There are no annoying banner ads, no audio ads, no sign-up, and no tracking inside the app, and the interface is translated into dozens of languages by the community. I found this to be a great choice for older phones, or for a parent or sibling who finds complicated apps annoying.
Convx
While most open source music apps work well, there are only a few that also feel nice to use. Convx comes in the second category. If you like iOS’s “Liquid Glass” design, then you would love Convx. It brings iPhone’s Liquid Glass design to Android, with frosted, see-through menus, floating controls, and album-inspired colors that change with whatever you are playing.
Under the pretty surface, Convx is a complete music player. You can browse and stream music, save songs for offline listening, build queues and playlists, set a sleep timer, change playback speed, and tweak the sound to your taste with an equalizer. What makes it stand out among the heavy hitters is its DJ-style playback. You also get automix, crossfade, and smooth transitions between one song and the next. Lyrics are synced word by word and come from several providers, plus it gets animated artwork.
Convx can play local files and even songs stored on a home server or NAS through SMB and WebDAV. You can choose the option to import your Spotify playlists, show what you’re playing on Discord, scrobble to Last.fm, recognize songs playing around you, and use Listen Together to sync playback with friends.
Spotube
Spotube is the veteran here, with over 46,000 stars on GitHub, and it works differently from the rest. Instead of being locked to one service like Spotify or YouTube, it runs on plugins. You choose your own music sources, metadata, and playlists through plugins made by the community, or if you’re good with it, you can write one yourself.
The biggest advantage is that it works everywhere. Spotube runs natively on Android, Windows, macOS, and Linux. This means you can use the same app on your phone and your laptop. It’s small, fast, and light on data. You can import and sync playlists from popular music services or manage them locally. It gives time-synced lyrics from public lyric databases no matter which source you use. Offline downloads are supported, with proper metadata and ID.
Privacy is one of the biggest highlights of Spotube. It collects no telemetry and no user data. Installing it is also easy, because you can download it through winget, Scoop, Chocolatey, Homebrew, Flatpak, and F-Droid.
SimpMusic
SimpMusic is that one app that does everything. It’s a free YouTube Music client for Android and desktop that borrows many of Spotify’s best ideas. You can play music from YouTube Music or regular YouTube without ads, and it gets you background playback. You can browse the home feed, charts, podcasts and moods, search everything on YouTube, cache songs for offline playback and use Android Auto.
SimpMusic Wrapped gives you a year-in-music recap just like Spotify’s. Then there is monthly recap playlists and listening charts that stay on your device. There are three Now Playing styles, including one that looks like Apple Music, and the lyrics are synced in 12 languages. You can even share lyrics as an image.
You can switch to 1080p video with subtitles, skip sponsor segments with SponsorBlock, see dislike counts with Return YouTube Dislike, and use a 10-band equalizer with AutoEq headphone profiles.
Which one should you pick?
If you care most about sound quality, I would suggest LastWave. If you want something simple, pick Musify. If design matters to you, try Convx. If you want plugins and an app that runs on every device you own, choose Spotube. If you want the most features in one place, install SimpMusic. The best part is that all five are free and can be installed side by side, so you can try a few and keep your favorite. You will get access to unlimited songs from the best sources in good quality. Let us know which one you chose, and comment below if you have a different app that you use for listening to music.

Drone attack on Colombian police base injures civilians and damages homes
Explosive-laden drones have struck a police base in Cúcuta, Colombia, injuring two civilians and damaging 60 homes
BOGOTA, Colombia -- Explosive-laden drones struck a police base in the Colombian city of Cúcuta Monday, injuring two civilians and damaging 60 homes, authorities said.
Officials did not immediately say who was responsible for the attack on a base belonging to the Norte de Santander Police.
The attack came as President Abelardo de la Espriella steps up military offensives against rebel groups and drug gangs, increasing air strikes and acting on intelligence that has enabled the military to capture several midlevel commanders.
Armed groups have responded by attacking military bases and police stations with small drones, rockets made with gas canisters and roadside bombs. De la Espriella, a conservative who took office in August, has canceled peace negotiations with rebel groups that were underway with his predecessor Gustavo Petro.
Cúcuta, a city of half a million people a short drive from Colombia’s border with Venezuela, is a major trade hub and an important center for criminal groups that profit from the drug trade and other kinds of smuggling.
Rebel groups including the National Liberation Army and the FARC-EMC also operate in the nearby Catatumbo region, where they tax local businesses and promote the cultivation of coca, the raw material for cocaine.
A 2016 peace deal between the Colombian government and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia led to the demobilization of more than 14,000 fighters.
But violence has increased in some parts of Colombia, including many border areas, as smaller armed groups try to seize territory abandoned by the FARC, where the Colombian state has been slow to provide security and basic services.
A police station in the town of Curumani, in the department of Cesar, was also attacked with drones Monday. On Saturday, one soldier was killed and 12 others were injured during an attack with drones and rockets on a military base in La Jagua de Ibirico, also in Cesar. Officials said that both incidents remain under investigation.
According to the Ideas for Peace Foundation, a group that monitors Colombia’s conflict, illegal armed groups carried out 323 drone attacks during the first nine months of 2026, a 95% increase from the same period last year.

A 17-year-old girl in Keralam has developed a serious kidney ailment allegedly after using a fairness cream purchased online following its promotion by social media influencers, doctors treating her said on Saturday (November 21, 2026).
According to doctors at Aster MIMS Mother Hospital in Malappuram, the girl ordered the cream after watching promotional videos by Instagram influencers who claimed it could remove pimples, dark spots and pigmentation.
The girl told reporters that she contacted the sellers through a WhatsApp number provided on Instagram and ordered the product.
She initially found the cream effective and ordered several more bottles over a period of one year.
The girl said that she subsequently began experiencing health problems, including a sudden drop in blood pressure and fainting.
She also developed swelling in her legs, making it difficult for her to walk and climb stairs, following which she approached the hospital.
Nephrologist S. Gowri, who is treating the girl, told reporters that the detailed medical examinations detected dangerously high levels of mercury in her blood and body.
“Mercury can severely damage the filtering units of the kidneys,” she said, adding that the girl had developed membranous nephropathy, a serious kidney condition that could lead to further complications if left untreated.
Tests conducted on the cream allegedly revealed mercury levels of 12,500 parts per million (ppm), against the normal permissible level of less than one ppm, the doctor said.
She said the findings allegedly revealed that the mercury-containing product had caused the kidney ailment.
Dr. Gowri cautioned people against advertisements promising instant results or rapid improvement in skin tone through fairness creams.
Those experiencing skin problems should consult a dermatologist and seek proper treatment instead of relying on such products, she said.
The girl said she had informed the company about the health problems but received no positive response.
The company initially said its senior officials would be informed, but subsequently stopped responding to her messages, she alleged.
The girl’s family has decided to initiate legal proceedings against the company in the consumer court.
They have not disclosed the name of the cream as they are proceeding with legal action.

Lebanese villagers return to wrecked homes as the Israeli army pulls back
ZAWTAR AL-GHARBIYAH, Lebanon — After two decades of working installing vehicle air conditioning in Saudi Arabia, Atef Kadouh saved up enough money to build a house in his hometown in southern Lebanon.
He and his wife, Soumaya Yaghi lived in the house for 40 years and had five children — all born at home.
Now there are four.
A photo of the youngest, Adel, is propped up in a basket of dried flowers near the doorway.
Adel, clean-cut with a trimmed beard, was a sports teacher and a basketball champion who was planning to travel to France this summer to pursue his doctorate. When the war with Israel began this year, he decided to volunteer as an ambulance driver.
The Israeli military killed him and four other medics on March 28 in a drone strike as the first responders buried a 75-year-old man who had died in hospital.
"This one broke me," his father says. "He was my youngest son, 27 years old. There have been wars in every country in the world but there are rules for war … you attack a paramedic rescuing wounded people, children? He was not a fighter at the front."
He says he warned his son that Israel could not be trusted not to kill medical personnel.
"He would not listen to me. He said, 'Dad there are wounded children — we have to go rescue them,'" he says.
Lebanon's Health Ministry says Israel has killed more than 135 first responders and medical staff in the past two years.
Asked about this airstrike, the Israeli military replied, without providing proof, that militants routinely pose as paramedics and transport weapons in ambulances for the militant group Hezbollah and its allies.
It did not respond to follow-up questions pointing out the five were not killed in an ambulance but at a burial.
A test case
The Kadouh family returned to the village in July when it became the first and until now only test of a U.S.-brokered plan for Israeli forces to withdraw and the Lebanese army to take over.
The plan is aimed at keeping Iran-backed Hezbollah out of the area, after they started firing rockets across the nearby border in solidarity with the Palestinian militant group Hamas who launched a surprise attack on southern Israel in October 2023.
Israel responded with devastating air strikes and eventually a ground invasion, and says it has continued attacks in south Lebanon following a U.S.-brokered ceasefire this year to eliminate what it believes are continued threats to northern Israel. Israel's defense minister has acknowledged destroying more than 20,000 homes across the Lebanese border in a self-declared security zone.
When Kadouh and Yaghi returned to the village, they found that Israeli soldiers had occupied their house. And then it had been set on fire.
Wrecked home
Upstairs in the hallway, near scorched walls and shattered windows, what appeared to be a work roster was written on the wall in blue marker in Hebrew with the first names of Israeli soldiers.
Almost everything in the house had been destroyed. Appliances — the fridge, freezer and washing machine — had bullet holes in them. Some, along with furniture, had been pushed over the second floor balcony, smashing on the ground below.
Kadouh says they knew from satellite photos there was destruction in their village "but the level of destruction — we were not expecting that. Everything that could be broken they broke."
In the kitchen were shattered floor tiles and kitchen cupboards wrenched from the walls.
The fire appeared to be set as the soldiers were leaving. Blackened, burned food packets — fruit boxes and cans of energy drinks with Hebrew writing — were on the floor along with rotting sandwiches.
In their 18-month-old grandson's bedroom, soot from a scorched ceiling dripped down on walls decorated with images of hot-air balloons and teddy bears climbing ladders to the moon.
Yaghi shows a bullet — one of many she says she found throughout the house. The spent engine casing of a missile or a drone with English markings reading "propulsion unit – tactical" was found in one of the rooms.
There is no running water or electricity — Kadouh says the Israeli military destroyed the solar panels.
The Lebanese army told them that when it reentered the village many of the houses had been rigged to be blown up. It said it dismantled explosives left by Israeli forces in their house and others.
The Israeli army did not reply to NPR queries about why the house was damaged or set on fire. It said military policy bars burning homes or leaving explosives.
Unable to enter the village while Israeli forces were there, Kadouh said he saw a tank in their courtyard from drone images posted on social media.
Even the trees destroyed
Yaghi says the Israeli army used a bulldozer to uproot the trees — including the pine trees which yield one of their most prized cash crops: pine nuts. When they had killed the trees, she says they demolished the family's garage and destroyed their tractor.
"We are back to square one," Kadouh says. "Starting from scratch."
Even more precarious, though, than when they started decades ago. Despite a ceasefire, smoke rises from a nearby village where Israel is still attacking.
Amid all the damage, the destruction of the family's trees cuts the deepest.
"I tended to them as if they were small children — they were all dear to me," Kadouh says.
Yaghi points out where there were fruit-bearing cactus, olive trees, a fig tree one of her sons brought from Italy, avocado trees and fields of thyme, avocado.
Up until a decade ago, almost everyone here grew tobacco, diversifying crops when that market collapsed.
"We raised our children through hard work and thank God all of them were educated," Yaghi says, noting with pride that they all became professionals.
She maintains a visceral connection to the land.
"Record this," she asks, walking next to rose bushes that have begun to bloom again. "Our land is a paradise with everything in it. Our life is this land. Our life is our homes. Even if we were to die in our homes it would be much better than to live outside."
Villagers here feel abandoned by even their own government — and still in danger from nearby Israeli forces.
"Our homes were destroyed and no one came to check on us," Kadouh says. "Not the Lebanese state or outsiders or the parties," he says, referring to Hezbollah and its allies. "They just say 'Go back, go back' to the village. We came back and there are no essentials — no electricity, no water."
Kadouh has a son in the Lebanese army and another in national security services but he says, because the Lebanese army is deliberately underequipped to avoid presenting a threat to Israel, they have never been allowed to do their jobs.
"The Lebanese state never sent a soldier here to protect us," he says." That is why the parties and others came in — Hezbollah or Amal or even the Palestinian factions decades ago. "But the vacuum that the Lebanese state has left brought us to this tragedy" he says.
"We love the Lebanese army — let them bring us an army, but let them protect us," he says. "This army has a rifle — Israel has an F-35" fighter jet.
"But we would rather sit in the dirt," he says. "Our soul, our life is here, I was born here."
Kadouh says maybe someday there will be peace with Israel, but after all the deaths and destruction, not in his lifetime — and not with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"Netanyahu is the one who killed my son. Let him bring back my son," he says. "If just yesterday Israel killed my son, am I supposed to tell the Israelis, 'Put your hand in my hand'? If they want to be our neighbors they should do good. Instead they burn us."

Hospitals worldwide are ill-equipped to assess whether artificial intelligence (AI) systems deployed in their facilities actually improve patient outcomes, raising questions about the clinical and economic value of healthcare AI, Emmanuel Bacry, Scientific Director of France’s Health Data Hub, said at the Bengaluru Tech Summit.
“There are maybe six or seven hospitals in the whole world today that are able to evaluate medical devices deployed in their system,” Mr. Bacry said. Hospitals struggle to access and integrate patient information to track outcomes after discharge, including recovery rates and mortality, making it difficult to establish the actual impact of AI-based medical technologies.
“In hospitals, we don’t know how to compute that,” he said, referring to the return on investment of such technologies. “So imagine now, if they adopt AI.”
Unintended consequences
Mr. Bacry cited an alert system based on rules-based AI, or an expert system, designed to warn intensive care unit (ICU) staff about severe kidney failure. Despite functioning effectively, the system was associated with a doubling of deaths in two of the six US hospitals where it was deployed in 2022, he said. He did not identify the study.
While researchers had offered hypotheses, the precise cause remained unknown. Mr. Bacry suggested that the absence of a tested response protocol among hospital personnel could have contributed to the outcome.
“We just replaced the alert done by a human with the alert done by the medical device. And that changes the whole thing,” he said, underlining the importance of integrating AI into clinical workflows rather than treating it as a standalone technology.
He also cautioned against evaluating diagnostic AI tools solely through laboratory accuracy scores or comparisons with doctors. A system achieving 95% accuracy against a doctor’s 90% might not necessarily perform better in clinical settings. “When you deploy in real life, you can forget about these scores,” he said.
The black-box dilemma
Mr. Bacry flagged another concern: AI systems can identify patterns that even their developers cannot explain. Citing research, he said one model predicted ethnicity from chest X-rays with approximately 85% accuracy, while another inferred sex from eye images with 95% accuracy.
Such hidden correlations could influence medical decisions without clinicians understanding the underlying basis, potentially introducing unintended bias into diagnosis and treatment.
Western bias in healthcare datasets
In a separate interaction with The Hindu, Mr. Bacry warned that healthcare AI development was heavily skewed towards Western populations. By his estimate, nearly 70% of global healthcare AI training data came from male, white and Western populations.
“We are developing an Occidental AI and even narrow types of Occidental AI,” he said.
He advocated smaller, locally tailored AI models trained on representative population data, arguing that deploying large, general-purpose models without adaptation could have disastrous consequences, particularly in developing countries.
Mr. Bacry heads the Health Data Hub, established under French law in 2019 to facilitate secondary use of health data for research. He is also a research director at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) at Université Paris Dauphine–PSL.

In November, a rumor circulated that tech billionaire Elon Musk once said, "I'm not just MAGA — I'm dark, gothic MAGA," referring to U.S. President Donald Trump's campaign slogan, "Make America Great Again."
Musk donated more than any other political donor in the 2026 midterm elections — giving more than $445 million to Republican candidates, according to money-tracking nonprofit group OpenSecrets. Following Republicans' losses, he told The New York Times on Nov. 18, "I'm not MAGA" and that he felt "pretty foolish" for having spent so much money backing GOP candidates in the midterms.
Social media users across multiple platforms were quick (archived) to resurface a speech he gave in 2024 in which he purportedly called himself "dark, gothic MAGA."
The quote was correctly attributed to Musk, and both clips featured in the X post above also were real.
While speaking at a campaign rally in New York City on Oct. 27, 2024, Musk said, "I'm not just MAGA — I'm dark, gothic MAGA." He pointed to his hat, an all-black version of the typically red "Make America Great Again" cap popularized by Trump.
The other clip included in the X post was from a live interview Musk gave on Nov. 18 during The New York Times DealBook Summit. Though a crowd watched in person, Musk spoke remotely by video.
He said (at 13:11): "No, no but you can't just say broad-based, oh, MAGA or whatever. I mean, I'm not MAGA. Well, at least, I'm not like — I'm not sure what MAGA means."
In sum, the quote was authentic, as were the video clips comparing Musk's public statements in 2024 and 2026.

Appy fizz: Now build snazzy widgets right on your phone, no coding experience required
One of the biggest innovations of the Nothing ecosystem was the introduction of Essential apps that let users, even with no coding knowledge, make widgets. In the past, you had to access Essential Apps on a computer to be able to make these widgets. Now you can do so right on your phone. And it is as easy as easy peasy apple squeezie. Mind you, you still need to sign up for Essential Apps and be part of a waiting list before you can get into design mode. No download is needed – the Essential Apps app comes to your Nothing phone when you update the phone to Nothing OS 5.g
Get a gooey or an info-loaded lockscreen clock!
On to the really serious stuff now. Perhaps the most noticeable visual change in NothingOS is the addition of two lockscreen clock widgets – Gooey and Micrographics. The Gooey clock has a bold and fluid look, with numbers looking a little melted. It is very eye-catching and, well, different. Those who want a truckload of information on their lockscreen and who opt for Micrographics get details like day, date, weather, temperature, upcoming appointments, and, of course, the time, all in rows that give it a very business ticker feel. This is how you clock into this feature:
- Long-press on the lock screen of your phone. This will show a Customize lock screen text bubble. Tap on it, and then tap on the fingerprint scanner to get into the Lock screen edit zone.
- Tap the clock widget space, which shows the time, and you will see Clock face options.
- Gooey is the second option, and right next to it is Micrographics. Choose the one you want, and also tweak its color as per your wish.
- Tap on Done, and hey, it’s, well…done.
Our own preference is the Micrographics widget, which is incredibly handy. We hope they add email and other notifications to it as well.
Split those notifications and quick settings
In the past – as on many phones – swiping down on a Nothing phone showed one new notifications, and swiping further down gave one access to Quick Settings (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Brightness, Torch, et al.). Well, you can split them into two separate zones if you wish. Once done, swiping from one side of the top will give you access to Quick Settings, while swiping from the other will show notifications. To do this segregation, just follow these steps:
- Open Settings and go to Notifications
- Go to the Notifications and Quick Settings Option
- You will see two options: Separate and Combined (classic).
- Select Separate, and now Notifications and Quick Settings will occupy different parts of the top panel.
Find out how long you have been away from your phone
One of the coolest new widgets on Nothing OS 5 is the Away Time widget, which lets you know how long you have kept away from your phone, and shows it in a simple, clean widget that can be placed on your home screen or your lock screen. It is a nice way to know about the “me time” you have given yourself away from your phone. Getting it is as easy as pressing on any place on the lock screen or Home Screen, and then selecting the Away Time widget option. We suggest going for the larger (4 x 2) one because it just looks so much better, especially with that zen-like blue background.
Keep what matters on the Home Screen – use Collector
Another widget (yes, Nothing seems to really like them widgets) that is very handy is Collector. You just open it and place images of what you want to keep seeing or consider important in it, and it automatically cuts out what it sees as important and keeps it handy on the home screen. It has a wonderful fridge sticker vibe, and keeps what matters close at hand. Just long-press on the home screen and select it from the widget collection!
Glyph Interface? There’s an app for that – finally!
The Glyph Interface has been one of the most eye-catching features of Nothing’s phones. This is basically a collection of LEDs on the back of the phones that light up in different patterns, showing notifications and battery levels, letting you know who is calling, controlling volume, setting timers, and doing more, all on the back of the phone. There was a catch, though. The Glyph UI had to be controlled from the settings of the phone, which seemed to be a rather roundabout way of doing things. This has now been fixed with the Glyph app, which gives one direct access to the Glyph Interface, letting one tweak it without having to get into the Settings. No downloads needed – the Glyph app appears on your Nothing phone the moment you update it to Nothing OS 5.
Lights, camera action…with both front and back cameras
Nothing OS 5 gives you the option to shoot videos using the rear as well as the front camera simultaneously. One can choose from having the footage one below the other, or having the selfie camera in an inset and the main camera in the larger part of the display. To access the option:
- Launch the Camera app
- Scroll across to More and choose Dual-View Video
It would have been nice to be able to take some stills with this feature, but as of now, it is limited to video.
There’s a glassy, classy “translucent” theme
Yep, your Nothing phone is now on the glass UI bandwagon. Mind you, this option is not turned on by default. You will need to follow these steps:
- Go to Settings, and then choose Customization
- Choose Theme & Style, and then choose Translucent. You can opt to have a dark theme in this if you wish.
- Honestly, it is not exactly eye-popping as of now. The translucence seems mainly to be around the widgets, and the app icons are not translucent. But it is a good starting point.
Scan that QR code, even if it wobbles
This is a pretty minor and yet handy change in Nothing OS 5. While camera icons have all been polished, a tiny yet useful tweak is in scanning QR codes, especially when using the scanner in crowded places or in slightly wobbly situations (think of paying in a moving vehicle). Now, when you use the camera to scan a QR code, the link it leads to remains on the screen, even if your hand moves and the QR code goes off or the code itself wobbles a little. So scanning codes is a whole lot easier, and you don’t have to bother about lining up the camera with the QR code all the time.
Send images to THAT friend with the iPhone easily (no app needed)
With Nothing OS 5, sending images to iPhones is pretty easy. Here’s how you do it:
- Ask your friend to switch on AirDrop on their iPhone and allow everyone to send images to it.
- Select the images you want to send on your Nothing phone.
- Select the Quick Share option, and then select the Use QR Code option.
- Scan the QR code with the iPhone’s camera. The images will be transferred.
Get the new font, Geist
Nothing’s marketing communications look very distinct because they use a font called Geist. Well, with NothingOS 5, you can now use Geist as the default font on their Nothing phones. This is how one does it:
- Head off to Settings again, and this time go to Display.
- Choose Font & Display Size.
- Once there, you can choose Geist as your default font.
- Once again, the difference is not going to jump out at you, but will become apparent as you use the phone.

A report published by Dainik Jagran newspaper is being shared on social media (here, here, here), claiming that Mayawati has announced her support for the BJP in the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections. The report quotes Mayawati as saying, “Supporting the BJP in 2027 is the right decision for the stability, development and social harmony of the country and the state.” Let’s verify the claim made in the post. 
Claim: Dainik Jagran reported that BSP chief Mayawati would extend full support to the BJP in the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections.
Fact: The alleged Dainik Jagran newspaper clipping is AI-generated. We could not find any such report in the newspaper’s 11 November 2026 e-paper editions or any announcement supporting the claim on Mayawati’s social media accounts. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A relevant keyword search did not yield any such report. The viral screenshot mentions 11 November 2026 as the publication date and identifies the day as Tuesday. However, 11 November 2026 was a Wednesday, raising suspicions about the screenshot’s authenticity. Further, we found no such report in any of the November 11 e-paper editions available on Dainik Jagran’s website. We also reviewed BSP supremo Mayawati’s Facebook and X accounts but found no posts supporting the viral claim.
To further verify its authenticity, we analysed the viral screenshot using various AI detection tools. OpenAI’s Verify tool and Sightengine AI both identified the newspaper clipping as likely AI-generated.
To sum up, the viral Dainik Jagran clipping claiming Mayawati’s support for the BJP in the 2027 UP elections is AI-generated.

Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
- Published
Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.
His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media.
Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales.
The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".
The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.
Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.
Paolo Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.
The Bulgari family favoured bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected colour combinations to set them apart from the delicate asethetic associated with Parisian jewellery houses.
The business broke into luxury markets and diversified beyond jewellery into watches, perfumes, leather goods and hotels.
"Paolo Bulgari began collaborating with his father in 1960, specialising in the knowledge of precious stones, of which he was one of the world's leading experts, and refining the sensibility and aesthetic sense that are at the root of the Bvlgari style," the Bvlgari company posted on social media., external
"He poured his heart into his craft and into nurturing the talents of young designers, leaving an indelible mark on the world of jewellery.
"Thank you, Mr. Paolo, your legacy as a brilliant beacon of creative inspiration will continue to inspire generations to come."
The post included a quote from Paolo Bulgari: "Everything can be a source of inspiration. There are no rules in creativity. Never."
The designer brand's celebrity clients have included Elizabeth Taylor, Audrey Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe, Ingrid Bergman, Sophie Loren, Anne Hathaway, Zendaya and Rihanna.
In 2011 the family sold its controlling stake to the French luxury group LVMH, in a deal worth about 3.7 billion euros.
In 2019, he and his wife established the Paolo Bulgari Foundation to support young people through schooling and job training in disadvantaged neighbourhoods on the outskirts of Rome.
The funeral will take place in Rome on Monday, 23 November in the Basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.

It’s a rare thing for a film sequel to match or even surpass its predecessor; The Godfather Part II and Terminator 2: Judgement Day are the best known examples on a pretty short list. Go ahead and add Godzilla Minus Zero to that list. Director Takashi Yamazaki’s sequel to his critically acclaimed Godzilla Minus One (2023) is everything one could want in a Godzilla movie: human pathos, great special effects, and, ultimately, two giant kaiju duking it out over who gets to destroy Japan (and eventually the world) the most.
(Spoilers for the first film below. Spoilers for Minus Zero but no major reveals until after the gallery. We’ll give you a heads-up when we get there.)
As I wrote previously, Yamazaki wanted to return to Godzilla’s filmic roots with Minus One, setting the events in postwar Japan and tapping into the monster’s symbolic representation of the Japanese perspective on the 1940s nuclear holocaust—while also incorporating all-too-human themes of guilt and redemption. That first film focused on kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who struggled with survivor’s guilt after he failed to take action when Godzilla attacked the Japanese base on Odo Island in 1945.
Knocked unconscious, Kōichi survived and awoke to find his parents and many others were killed in the World War II bombing of Tokyo. Kōichi rebuilt a life with a woman named Noriko (Minami Hamabe) and the orphaned baby she rescued, Akiko (Sae Nagatani). But then Godzilla re-emerged, and Kōichi resolved to die fighting the monster to atone for Odo Island. Kōichi saved the day and lived to tell the tale. He reunited with Noriko, who had a strange black bruise on her neck. And we saw a chunk of Godzilla’s remains start to regenerate, leaving things open for a sequel.
Godzilla Minus One was a massive hit, both in Japan—where it remains one of the highest grossing Japanese films ever—and worldwide, racking up $116 million globally and winning an Oscar for best visual effects. Yamazaki said in interviews at the time that there had as yet been no talk of a sequel—while also hinting at future directions a sequel might explore. He later admitted it was way of planting a seed for what would become Godzilla Minus Zero.

The 60th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu looks at key developments in public including healthcare financing, reproductive health, antimicrobial resistance, tuberculosis, environmental exposures and diabetes care.
Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, The Hindu, discuss the latest National Health Accounts estimates for 2023–24, which show a substantial increase in government health expenditure and a decline in the share of household out-of-pocket spending nationally. The episode also examines the contrasting trends in Keralam, where household healthcare expenditure has increased and the share of government spending has declined.
The episode looks at the drug regulator’s direction to pharmaceutical companies to comply with revised prices for 137 anti-cancer drugs and the potential implications for treatment costs. It also examines concerns over an illegal human egg collection racket in Telangana, including questions about informed consent, women’s safety and the regulation of assisted reproductive technology centres. Developments in Karnataka’s proposed mid-life women’s health programme and mandatory gynaecological check-ups for girls are also discussed.
Marking World AMR Awareness Week, the episode explores the growing challenge of antimicrobial resistance and the need for appropriate antibiotic use, timely diagnosis, infection prevention and surveillance. It also discusses phage therapy, which uses bacteriophages to target bacterial infections, and its potential role in addressing infections that do not respond to conventional antibiotics.
The discussion also examines tuberculosis through the lens of social and economic vulnerability, highlighting the importance of nutrition, housing and social support alongside diagnosis and treatment. It looks at the latest figures on domestic funding for India’s TB response, which now accounts for 86% of total spending, even as external funding declines.
The discussion also examines the health risks of extreme heat for pregnant women and newborns. A survey of healthcare professionals across five countries found that 98% of Indian clinicians surveyed had treated pregnant women and newborns whose health they believed had been affected by extreme heat.
The episode also looks into how fear of diagnosis may discourage people from screening and discusses a Chennai initiative that uses dietary counselling by staff nurses to improve blood sugar control and support long-term diabetes management.
The episode can also be viewed on The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap

A controlled detonation of hazardous materials stored at an Army facility in Iowa is on hold pending an appellate court decision and the agreement of the state’s incoming Democratic governor, President Donald Trump said Monday, warning that the delay raises the risk of “a large, spontaneous explosion.”
At issue are 68 drums of lead azide, which had been used as a primary explosive in munitions and stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant.
Without a favorable court decision and the consent of Governor-elect Rob Sand, “we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation,” Trump wrote.
The president’s announcement follows multiple postponements of the detonation.
The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club asked the US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit to halt the detonation, which had been scheduled for Nov. 20, and challenged the Environmental Protection Agency’s authorization of it. The groups contend that the open-air detonation of lead azide would create a hazardous plume of lead dust that could affect communities dozens of miles from the site in Middletown, Iowa.
In a Nov. 20 letter to Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, EPA Region 7 Administrator Jim Macy said the Army had determined “recrystallization of the lead azide in long-term storage had occurred” and posed “a risk of spontaneous explosion due to the material’s sensitivity to friction and shock.” The service determined that a controlled detonation was the only viable option, he wrote.
The Army said Sunday that the detonation had been rescheduled for Wednesday, Nov. 25 “to allow for more optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced.” 
Trump said experts believe “there is a substantial chance that this material will explode of its own volition, perhaps sometime in the near future.”
Spokespeople for the Army and for Sand’s transition team did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The Army, EPA and the Department of Health and Human Services said in a joint statement on Nov. 20 that the entire government was working to ensure the safety of the planned detonation. Last month, the Army held a consultation with officials and residents of Middletown to answer their questions about the controlled detonation.
“Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized,” the statement said.

Henry Patten ends partnership with Harri Heliovaara to team up with fellow Briton Neal Skupski
Henry Patten and Harri Heliovaara were crowned the best men's doubles team of the year at last week's ATP Finals after winning Wimbledon for a second time in July; the pair have won three Grand Slam doubles titles together but will go their separate ways in 2027
Monday 23 November 2026 22:29, UK
Henry Patten has ended his world No 1 doubles partnership with Harri Heliovaara in shock fashion in favour of teaming up with British compatriot Neal Skupski for 2027.
Patten and Heliovaara celebrated being crowned the best men's doubles team of the year at last week's ATP Finals after they claimed a second Wimbledon success together back in July.
However, in a post on Heliovaara's blog, the Finnish player revealed Patten phoned him on Friday to say their three-time Grand Slam-winning partnership was over - despite a previous agreement they would continue.
"After the trip to Turin, I didn't even have time to get into the holiday mood when the weekend took a rather unexpected turn," Heliovaara said on his own blog website. "Henry completely unexpectedly announced that he had changed his mind about next year.
"I picked up the kids from daycare on Friday afternoon and we were just opening presents when I got a call from Henry. Without going into too much detail, the message was clear.
"He didn't want to play together again next year, even though we had agreed to do so during the fall. The announcement came as completely as it could come and I couldn't help but listen with my mouth open in horror and say that I don't agree at all.
"I'm unlikely to ever fully understand what and why this ultimately happened.
"The emotional scale in my head was quite violent at first, a shocking situation in any case.
"The two-and-a-half years with Henry have been by far the best time of my career, for which I am eternally grateful to him, but now the main feeling was heavy disappointment and even anger."
Heliovaara confirmed in his blog that he would team up with another British player Julian Cash, while Patten is set to partner Skupski in 2027.

Doctors tell the BBC about the targeting of Sudanese hospitals by paramilitary fighters
A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.
UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings "deeply disturbing".

The health minister of the group's civilian-affiliated government, Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud, dismissed the allegations as propaganda.
