Donald Trump and Anthony Albanese have heralded plans for new joint Quad military exercises designed to push back on China’s expansionist ambitions, with the US president promising the grouping with India and Japan will guarantee “peace through strength”.
Albanese met Trump, India’s Nahrendra Modi and Japan’s Sanae Takaichi in Manila late on Tuesday in talks about enhanced cooperation on AI, critical minerals, infrastructure and maritime security.
“These nations represent some of the most important partnerships in the entire world,” the US president said.
“They’re among the most successful nations in the world, and in certain ways among the most powerful nations of the world. Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific.”
Trump said: “As we continue to protect peace through strength, we are also working together to advance super intelligence, SI, the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the industrial revolution.”
The Australian prime minister praised Trump and said a new Quad business forum to be held in 2027 would build economic growth across the region.
Leaders in the group – established as China seeks to build its military might and exert influence across the region – say they will cooperate to maintain peace and stability with Beijing.
“When we work together for our common view in the Indo-Pacific of peace, security, stability, and prosperity, then the world will be a safer and more secure place, and the Quad has a critical role in achieving that,” Albanese told the summit.
The plan for new military exercises involving maritime patrol aircraft is likely to prompt strong criticism from China.
Albanese said Australia would deploy its P8-A Poseidon and P3-C Orion maritime patrol aircraft as part of the operation in early 2027.
Asked what he would tell Chinese leader Xi Jinping later this week about the plan, Albanese said military exercises were common.
“We want peace and security in the region. That’s the objective here. It’s not about any one country. It’s about our own sovereignty, but also about peace and security in the region,” he said
The Quad leaders want the group to present a multilateral coalition of resistance against Beijing, seeking to undermine its dominance, including in the South and East China seas.
Takaichi said the Quad would help shape the future of the region.
“We would like to realise a free and open Indo Pacific by strengthening resilience of countries in the region and promote their freedom to decide for themselves across a wide range of areas including maritime security, economic security, energy and critical and emerging technologies.”
Before the meeting, as the four leaders posed for a group photo, Trump praised Modi and Takaichi as “tough”, before gesturing to Albanese and saying: “We’re OK too.” Albanese laughed at the remark.
The first meeting of the Quad leaders since 2024 came as Albanese and Trump both prepare for setpiece engagement with China’s president later this week. Albanese will visit Xi in Shenzhen on Friday, a day after three-way talks between Trump, Xi and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
Trump said he wanted talks with the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, but conceded he was not the host of the China summit and it was up to Xi to issue an invitation. The US president said he could have a one-on-one meeting with Putin “if it’s available”.
Quad military exercises would build on progress from the recently completed Malabar joint exercise near Japan, where sailors completed anti-submarine and anti-surface warfare drills.
Trump also talked up the Aukus nuclear deal with Australia. “We make the greatest submarines anywhere in the world, and we’re working with Australia and others on that,” he said.
Trump said the US was poised to catch up to China on rare earth production within 10 months, backed up by speedy progress from Australia, Japan and India.
He was accompanied by cabinet members Marco Rubio, Scott Bessent, Howard Lutnick and Jamieson Greer, as well as his new chief of staff, Stephen Miller.
Privately, officials believed the meeting alone showed the group was progressing. Australian officials welcomed the engagement of Trump in regional affairs as he enters the final two years of his presidency.
Trump took credit for reinvigorating the grouping, and said he placed a premium on relations with Albanese, Modi and Takaichi.
“When they have difficulty, when they want to tell me something, my phone is always open, and the Oval Office is always open to you, and you know that,” he said.
Albanese said before the meeting he would push Trump on ending the war in Iran, a conflict which has produced an unprecedented global energy shock and badly distorted conditions in the Australian economy.
It was Albanese’s first meeting with Takaichi since a weeks-long saga about comments he made on a podcast about her gift of melons presented to him during a visit to Australia in July.
Earlier, Albanese took part in the East Asia Summit where he called for regional partners to work together to boost AI protections. Trump, who calls the technology “superintelligence”, said it represented “the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution”.

“It costs what it costs” is a mindset I’ve found useful when encountering a sizable, but highly necessary or desired, expense. The sentiment encourages me to accept the price because that’s the accepted value of the gadget, app, or service that I really need or want.
But with surveillance pricing, that comfort is no longer a given. I could end up paying more for my TV because of where I am or more for a software subscription because of my age.
Surveillance pricing leverages data collected from our web history, smart devices, and apps with the goal of getting us to pay more. That obfuscates the value of products, challenges smart shopping and budgets, and makes it harder for people to get products and services at a fair price.
Surveillance pricing versus dynamic pricing
Surveillance pricing, according to the nonprofit Electronic Privacy Information Center (EPIC), is an algorithmic pricing practice that charges individuals or groups of individuals different prices “for the same goods or services.”
“The goal of surveillance pricing is to infer the highest price that the customer is willing to pay, based on consumers’ personal data and other market data,” EPIC explains.
Instacart previously practiced surveillance pricing, also called personalized pricing. In 2025, Consumer Reports found that, “based on how much Instacart says the typical household of four spends on groceries, the average price variations observed could translate into a cost swing of about $1,200 per year.” Instacart has since removed its surveillance pricing tools.
Dynamic pricing, or surge pricing, differs from surveillance pricing in that, instead of relying on consumer data, it uses changing market trends, like supply and demand, inventory levels, and competitor pricing, to set prices.
While dynamic pricing may charge you more for an Uber ride when it’s very busy, surveillance pricing can feel less reasonable.
For instance, Target’s app was previously accused of using location data to charge users $100 more for a TV if they bought it while standing inside a Target store. At the time, Target said that it would match lower prices presented by customers, but many customers wouldn’t think to look for pricing discrepancies. In another instance from 2012, Orbitz was found to more prominently feature expensive hotels to people using macOS. Companies often dispute whether their practices truly qualify as surveillance pricing. But these examples all reflect companies using data about their customers to influence the prices they show them.

Chemicals found almost everywhere in modern life pose a "global and growing threat" to human health and the environment, a landmark report based on over a decade of research has warned.
The report on "endocrine-disrupting chemicals" (EDCs) released by the United Nations Environment Programme and World Health Organization "conservatively" estimates the health and environmental costs of EDC exposure at over $1 trillion annually.
"The scientific evidence is clear: EDCs are a global and growing threat to human and environmental health," warns the report written by international scientists, calling current regulations "uneven and insufficient."
EDCs are chemicals that interfere with, mimic, or block the hormones that regulate the development and behaviour of our organs.
They are in everything from toys and makeup, to building materials and clothing.
The report released late Tuesday is the first such comprehensive look at EDC impacts in 14 years, and finds increasingly clear links between them and a range of diseases.
"The evidence is so strong that it's irrefutable at this point," said Laura Vandenberg, report co-author and professor of environmental health sciences at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.
The report examined thousands of studies on chemicals like bisphenols, phthalates and parabens.
Evidence of links between these chemicals and disease is strongest for certain neurological conditions and reproductive problems including sperm decline.
But there is also growing confidence that EDCs are linked to diseases like type 2 diabetes and asthma that have spiked globally.
"Because these changes are occurring rapidly, they are unlikely to be explained primarily by genetic change," the report says.
Sufficiently worrisome
Scientists looked at associations between EDC exposure and health conditions, as well as the mechanisms by which exposure could cause harm.
The findings vary, with "strong evidence" of developmental and neurobehavioral effects, but "emerging" links between EDCs and cardiovascular disease.
However, the overall risk is strong because EDCs are so ubiquitous and likely to impact health at tiny levels, Vandenberg said.
Among those most at risk are workers in the chemicals and recycling industries, particularly in countries with weak regulations.
A 2024 study by the International Pollutants Elimination Network NGO fitted participants with silicone wristbands that absorbed chemicals.
Lab tests of the wristbands found that plastic waste and recycling workers in Thailand and Kenya were exposed to over 20 hazardous chemicals, while even control subjects working in offices were exposed to at least 11.
There are around 1,000 identified EDCs, but experts say many chemicals have simply not been tested properly and their impacts remain unknown.
They are also concerned about "synergistic" impacts -- the way exposure to multiple chemicals may amplify health effects.
The "proverbial million-dollar question" is what level of EDC exposure triggers any given health impact, said Frederic Leusch, professor of environmental toxicology at Australia's Griffith University, who was not involved in the report.
But even absent an answer, Leusch believes "the hazard is sufficiently worrisome that we need to take action to reduce our, and our environment's, exposure."
It scares politicians
Many countries have regulated certain EDCs, often targeting bisphenol A, particularly in children's products.
But regulators have struggled to determine which chemicals should be regulated, and what an appropriate exposure level might be.
"It scares politicians, to some extent, because it's such a complicated area," said retired professor of environmental chemistry Ake Bergman, who worked on the previous editions of the EDC report in 2002 and 2012.
Like other experts, he warned there is no known safe exposure level for most EDCs.
"We have some that are really acting at extremely low concentrations."
In a statement, the International Council of Chemical Associations industry group called for "science-based" approaches to regulation that protect health and the environment "while enabling society to benefit from the products, technologies, and innovations that are essential to modern life and sustainable development."
Many EDCs are in plastics, and experts say oil firms are increasing plastic production as demand for fossil fuel energy falls.
"We need to stop the expansion of plastic production,... reduce exposures to EDCs, and ban the worst actors," said Tracey Woodruff, report co-author and professor at Stanford University.
"While more science is always needed, we don't need more science to act."

You can give the gift of creativity with this do-it-all digital music maker. Akai’s portable sampler, beat maker, and all-around sound machine blends tactile quick keys and pads with an onboard screen so musicians can build it all in a box and send the results to their DAW of choice.
Nimble SharePower Portable Charger
For those who enjoy clever devices that just work, we give you Nimble’s “breakable” SharePower Portable Charger. The magnetically joined power bank quickly snaps into a pair of 20W batteries, letting two people charge their phones, or works as a single 10,000mAh unit for larger top-offs.
New Zealand artist Aldous Harding has another eccentric album on her hands with this year’s Train on the Island. The slow-burning LP is gorgeously recorded and delightfully weird, and it feels tailor-made for vinyl, making it an easy pick for Harding fans (or anyone who loves quirky indie jams).
Ninja Crispi Microwave & Air Fryer
For those in smaller dwellings, efficient living means maximizing space. That’s where combo appliances like Ninja’s newest microwave / air fryer combo come in. The handy countertop gadget lets you zap your food, then crisp it at the end so your pizza or French fries don’t turn into a soggy mess.
Perhaps no game in history is more anticipated than the latest entry in Rockstar’s sprawling, intricate, and absolutely bonkers open-world series. Grand Theft Auto VI is said to offer a more obsessively dense map, more realism in details like weather and passing time, and more realistic NPCs (non-player characters) than ever before. Here’s hoping those 13 years were worth the wait.
Shokz OpenFit Pro
Open-style earbuds aren’t just for the sporty; they’re an entirely different way to listen that keeps you environmentally aware without the plugged-up feeling of traditional buds. The OpenFit Pro take a balanced approach, with seamless open-ear performance and even a touch of noise reduction to dampen the din on crowded commutes.
The old Ironman Timex was a staple for ’80s and ’90s kids, and while you can’t bring back those carefree days, remakes like the Retroware can bring back that carefree feeling. No smarts, no notifications, just a takes-a-licking Timex watch with tactile keys, 50 meters of water resistance, and totally tubular digital graphics.
Serious gamers need a serious controller, and few take gaming more seriously than 8BitDo’s Elite-style Xbox gamepad. From its drift-proof TMR joysticks and motion support to its customizable buttons and remappable bumpers, the Ultimate 3E is the gift for that lovable control freak in your life.
Play-Doh Blooms
There’s regular Play-Doh for kids, but did you know that Play-Doh makes kits for adults, too? We’re not scoffing. The new Blooms sets take on Lego’s floral bouquets with more realistic-looking flower arrangements, and they include a vase. They’re equal parts nostalgic kitsch and stylish decor.
Insta360 Luna Pro
For on-the-go creators, it’s all about capturing the moment in the highest video quality possible. Insta360’s Luna Pro steadycam offers plenty of features to get the job done right, including 4K vertical video, swift file transfers, four hours of battery life, and a detachable touchscreen that doubles as a remote.
The new Fitbit Air provides the same great fitness tracking we’ve come to expect in a comfortable design that virtually disappears on your wrist. Google’s AI Coach can be overly assertive, but the tracker’s great battery life and metrics for everything from sleep to blood oxygen make it an excellent gift for anyone who needs a healthy hand.
Razer Kishi V3 Pro XL
Most mobile controllers have a serious size limit. Not Razer’s Kishi V3 Pro XL, which lets you throw a big ol’ tablet between the handles for a major visual upgrade. It also has high-quality joysticks, great grips, and customizable keys for USB-C tablets, along with haptics for Android models.
KPop Demon Hunters (4K Blu-ray)
So what if you’ve heard “Golden” more times than you can count? Netflix’s massive animated hit is a lot easier to gift now that it’s officially available on 4K Blu-ray disc. The story about three pop stars who band together to save humanity from a demonic boy band is an instant classic, with fantastic music and striking animation.
Blissbury Ear Pillow
If you’re contemplating a pricey pair of sleep buds for your loved one, we urge you to halt and consider a softer (and cheaper) alternative. Piercing pillows, designed with pockets for freshly pierced ears, also work great for regular earbuds. Blissbury’s comfy and adjustable Ear Pillow is our favorite. Problem — and sleep issues — solved.
Keychron K2 HE keyboard (Concrete Edition)
The Concrete Edition of Keychron’s K2 HE is not your average mechanical board. Cased in actual concrete, it offers standard keycaps to match its industrial aesthetic, both Bluetooth and 2.4GHz connectivity, and several other advanced features. This includes the ability to adjust the actuation distance of the individual Hall effect switches (hence the “HE”).
We all do it: pay a ton for a monthly streaming service for just a few series. It’s better to own the real thing, and Hacks, a hilarious drama that follows a comedian (Jean Smart) and her young writer (Hannah Einbinder) in the tumultuous “biz,” is one of HBO’s best series in years.
Hoto’s soldering iron is super cool — and by that we mean hot, as it’s able to reach nearly 400 degrees Fahrenheit in about three seconds. The cordless, adjustable iron makes the perfect gift for your favorite DIYer, especially since it features customizable presets for virtually any job.
Knockaround Premiums sunglasses
For the person on your list whose hatred for smart glasses runs deep, Knockaround’s hip, tech-free sunglasses should hit the spot. They’re available in a variety of fun styles and offer lightweight frames and polarized lenses, with both UVA and UVB shielding for attractive eye protection.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
The first 3D Zelda game has been remade for the modern era. And if you fear it will diverge too much from the Nintendo 64 original, fear not: This carefully crafted remake delivers updated graphics and improved controls alongside the same stellar adventure we remember.
Wuben G5 rechargeable flashlight
Everyone needs a good flashlight, and perhaps your recipient’s next one should ditch the replaceable batteries. Wuben’s rechargeable G5 has a pocketable, spy-tech-inspired design, USB-C charging, and adjustable brightness. More importantly, the 400-lumen light is super compact, making it easy to stow or clip onto your bag.
If you haven’t been bombarded by the Hulken yet, it’s a rolling tote that’s blown up online. Designed to hold everything from laundry to an impromptu picnic, the durable bag is beloved for its seemingly bottomless capacity and colorful style, making it a thoughtful gift for fashionable folks on the move.
Xteink X4 Pro e-reader
If a Kindle won’t quite fit into your favorite traveler’s tight pack job, consider the Xteink X4 Pro. The tiny e-reader is easy to pop into your bag or pocket thanks to its 4.3-inch display, and the latest model offers a backlit touchscreen for a more intuitive way to explore the literary world.
Ember Mug 3 (14-ounce)
For the coffee or tea lover in your life who’s always headed to the microwave for a heat zap, Ember’s fancy-schmancy smart mug is a luxurious way to keep things toasty. With the ability to set the temperature on the mug or in the app, the Mug 3 makes it simple to keep liquids perfectly hot indefinitely.
Nalgene Narrow Mouth water bottle (16-ounce)
Not all reusable water bottles are created equal. Give the gift of a narrow-mouthed bottle, like this 16-ounce Nalgene pick, which makes it easy to take measured sips on the go. Take this advice from someone (me) who bought the wide-mouthed version and regularly spills water all over themself.
If your giftee is into New York City memorabilia or wants a more unique way to light up a room, this cube-shaped lamp, designed around the old MTA entrance beacons, is sure to delight. Locals will recognize the vintage symbol, which still survives in the wild, and everyone will dig the old-school vibe.
Pokémon Pokopia
Pokopia brings Pokémon to life in a cozy worldbuilding game that borrows the best from predecessors like Minecraft and Animal Crossing. The twist? The slow-burning Switch 2 title eventually rolls into an expansive adventure that lets you customize as you go.
Petkit Fresh Element Solo Automatic Feeder
When it comes to keeping your pet happy and healthy while you’re away, the details matter. Petkit’s most basic auto feeder offers peace of mind with dual-power protection, meal monitoring via the Petkit app, and a generous 12-cup capacity that should keep an adult cat fed for up to 15 days.
Fairphone 6 Plus
Electronics are becoming more sustainable, and Fairphone is leading the way. The Fairphone 6 Plus may seem like a regular Android phone on paper, but the ability to repair and replace its internals, from the screen to the battery, makes it anything but average.
In many ways, the Pebble Index 01 is the gadget of our times. The stripped-back smart ring has a microphone and, with a tap of a button, records and sends your thoughts to the Pebble app over Bluetooth. You can also use it to start a timer or even add a calendar event to your phone.
Cast iced tea glass
Sure. You could put iced tea in them, but no one’s stopping you from sipping pulpy OJ or rich chocolate milk from Kinto’s stylish glassware, which was crafted with an “uninterfering design” in mind. Needless to say, a full set makes a lovely addition to any minimalist’s ensemble.
The hippest thing in audio right now is… the hippest thing from a long time ago. Enter the modded iPod Classic from Player Mods, which refreshes Apple’s media player with some 21st-century upgrades. The 5th-gen model can be customized with several color options (including a transparent case) and up to 2TB of storage.
GuliKit TT Pro controller
For those tired of experiencing Joy-Con drift with their Nintendo Switch (or stick drift on any controller), there’s the TT Pro. Loaded with the latest anti-drift tech for joysticks and customizable triggers that let picky gamers have it their way, GuliKit’s customizable wireless controllers work with PlayStation, Nintendo, PC, iOS, and Android devices.
Voicemod Key Pocket
Do you like… scary movies? That’s just one of many catchphrases that pair well with the Key Pocket, which can alter voices in real time. The tiny device sticks to the back of Apple or Android devices via magnets, granting you multiple effects for gaming, voice calls, or streaming.
OhSnap Grip Stand
Pricey yet endlessly useful, this is the kind of item you might not buy for yourself, which makes it a fantastic gift. Offering a brilliantly thin yet durable framework in a stand that also hangs, pops, and never needs to come off, it’s the ultimate phone accessory.
If someone on your list collects Game Boy, Game Boy Color, or Game Boy Advance cartridges, the GB Operator might be the perfect gift. The slick, transparent USB-C device makes it easy to play and manage classic titles on a macOS or Windows machine via emulation, with or without achievements.
Dock & Bay Picnic Blanket
Dock & Bay’s blankets are a great choice for almost everyone. They provide a soft space on which to relax or entertain, whether at the park or on your hardwood floors at home, and they’re incredibly easy to pack. Plus, they have a water-resistant bottom and come in an array of fun colors.
Sonos Beam Ultra
This radical upgrade of the middle child in Sonos’ soundbar lineup may be the best (little) soundbar you can buy. It delivers musical sound, surprisingly full and cinematic bass, and brain-tricking immersion thanks to drivers that now point every which way; it can also expand or connect with other Sonos speakers and stream almost anything.
Instruo Pocket Scion Bio-Feedback Instrument
The Pocket Scion is unlike any musical instrument you’ve witnessed before, one that uses the “biofeedback” from plants to trigger built-in synths. The device offers MIDI-out to send digital signals to outboard synths, and it includes an app for both macOS and Windows, finally giving you a way to make your favorite fern a rockstar.
Alienware AW3426DW QD-OLED Gaming Monitor
Your favorite gamer needs an awesome monitor, but there are 10 billion options. Alienware’s 34-inch Penta Tandem QD-OLED delivers top-end picture quality, with vibrant colors and perfect blacks, plus a swift 280Hz refresh rate. Best of all, it’s not nearly as expensive as you might think.
Lego PlayStation
Few devices evoke more sheer nostalgic joy than Sony’s OG PlayStation console from ’94. If you know a gamer, Lego’s latest replica brings it all flooding back with several brick-ified details, including a pop-up hinge, a gamepad, and a number of hidden surprises waiting to be discovered.
Fi Ultra dog tracker
Nothing can replace our furry friends, so for pets that tend to wander, only the best tracking tech will do. Enter the Fi Ultra, which uses Starlink technology via T-Mobile to track pets almost anywhere, even in cellular dead zones.
If your favorite cinephile is looking to get off the streaming carousel, the Kaleidescape Strato E is the key. The premium player lets library builders locally store and play their favorite films and TV shows in lossless 4K resolution with Dolby Atmos for sterling entertainment that’s all theirs.
Gardyn Studio 2
If there’s someone on your list who loves plants but can’t seem to take care of them, the Gardyn Studio 2 can bring life to their living room. The smart hydroponic garden is easy to set up and features automated, AI-powered lighting, helping anyone maintain a green thumb.
Bissell ProHeat 2X Revolution Pet Pro carpet cleaner
You create a home for your pets; they create a mess for your home. It’s the circle of life (or carpet, anyway). Thankfully, Bissell’s pro-grade cleaner uses a concentrated stream of formula and 12 rows of rotating brushes to do the dirty work for you, keeping your carpets in good order.
Have you broken something fragile that seems impossible to mend? Maybe all you need is a Kintsugi Repair Kit, which provides the Japanese method and a special lacquer to repair and restore broken ceramics to good health. The resulting golden scar is merely to remind us that rebuilding is possible.
Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro
Soundcore makes some of the best wireless earbuds you’ve never heard of — and the Liberty 5 Pro may be its best pair yet. The sleek buds deliver powerful noise cancellation, good sound, and surprisingly fabulous call quality for way less than Apple’s latest AirPods Pro.
Matic robot vacuum
It’s time for a smarter robovac. Thankfully, there’s the Matic, which looks less like the rambling discs that pervade the space and more like an actual robot that, well, vacuums. It doesn’t get under beds, but it also doesn’t get stuck under them, and it does a great job providing truly no-fuss cleaning thanks to its superb mapping.
OhSnap MCON controller
There’s no shortage of mobile gaming controllers, but few are as stealthy or as compact as the MCON. The sliding gamepad quickly attaches to any MagSafe- or Pixelsnap-ready phone, letting you game with a set of satisfying controls that feel more natural than most rivals.
Big Walk
It can be hard to keep in touch with friends, but Big Walk might be the game that gets the gang back together. The cooperative multiplayer title drops players into a wacky world as spherical humanoids who must solve puzzles by chatting and teaming up. You’ll want at least two copies, and sessions support up to 12 players.
The future is now, so of course we’ve got screens in sunglasses. The Viture Pro 2 are a slick pair of augmented-reality shades with speakers, micro-OLED screens, and a bonus feature: diopter-adjusting dials, which can sharpen the focus of whatever they’re mirroring from a phone or other device over a USB-C tether. Fancy!
BYOK
The BYOK (Bring Your Own Keyboard) is a distraction-free way for creatives to get their thoughts down without the allure of silly YouTube videos or notifications about their dog’s flea meds. No frills, just a low-resolution LCD screen that works with most keyboards and provides plenty of power for the long haul.
The Switch 2 leverages the same ideas as its predecessor, only with a larger, 7.9-inch display, a faster chip, and a bevy of new social features. However, its most important trait is that it’s the newest Nintendo console, which means access to a host of weird, beautiful, family-friendly games that only Nintendo could dream up, now on a better screen.
WiiM Sound smart speaker
WiiM is a popular Sonos alternative, thanks in part to excellent software that works across its multiple streaming amplifiers and other products. The WiiM Sound is the brand’s sharpest smart speaker, with accessible controls, Alexa and Google smarts, and the ability to connect to other WiiM gear in surround sound or throughout your home.
When it comes to jotting down notes, there’s nothing like the pen and paper. At least, that’s what we thought before we tried the Remarkable Paper Pure. Offering a strikingly realistic writing experience that saves everything in the digital realm, this tablet is a brilliant way to bridge the gap and save paper.
KitchenAid Artisan Plus Series 5 stand mixer
Once The Great British Baking Show becomes an obsession, only a serious stand mixer will do for replicating recipes at home. This mixer’s timeless design adds new features in what KitchenAid calls its biggest upgrade since 1955, with a new half-speed setting and a control lever that lets you set speeds between its standard settings.

The Telangana Standards Authority for Food and Essential Drugs (TG SAFE) has issued show-cause notices to 90 medical shops across Hyderabad for violations involving the sale of habit-forming drugs and antibiotics without following prescribed regulations.
The notices were issued following a special enforcement drive conducted by the drugs wing of TG SAFE, along with its enforcement wing and excise enforcement personnel, on Thursday (November 19). The department said it would initiate further action, including suspension or cancellation of drug licences, against the establishments found violating the rules.
The inspections were carried out at medical shops in areas including Koti, Abids, Basheerbagh, Nampally, Khairatabad, Panjagutta, Ameerpet, SR Nagar, Sanathnagar, Erragadda, Yousufguda, Madhura Nagar, Jubilee Hills and Banjara Hills.
Officials detected violations such as selling prescription medicines without valid prescriptions issued by registered medical practitioners, failure to maintain prescription and Schedule H1 drug registers, and dispensing medicines in the absence of registered pharmacists. Medical shops were also found selling drugs without issuing bills and failing to maintain or produce sales and purchase records.
The enforcement drive focused on the illegal sale and diversion of habit-forming drugs, including Tramadol, Alprazolam, Nitrazepam, Codeine-containing cough syrups, Tapentadol, Pregabalin and Zolpidem. Officials also checked the indiscriminate sale of antibiotics. Decoy operations and test purchases were conducted to verify whether such medicines were being sold without prescriptions.

On the heels of recent news reports on how keratin-based hair-straightening products containing glycolic acid derivatives led to severe kidney injury in women, researchers from Kerala have reported a series of cases wherein, the use of fairness creams has been linked to nephrotic syndrome.
(For top health news of the day, subscribe to our newsletter Health Matters)
In a study published in the latest issue of Kidney International (‘NELL-1 associated membranous nephropathy linked to skin fairness cream use — insights from an Indian case series’, ) doctors describe a series of 15 cases of Membranous Nephropathy, reported by Aster MIMS Hospital, Kottakkal, Malappuram district, that were traced to the regular use of fairness creams.
Heavy metal screening of the blood and urine samples of these patients revealed high levels of mercury, the toxic effects of which are well-known. An analysis of the fairness creams also showed that these contained high levels of mercury -- in some instances, 10,000 times above the permissible limit of 1 ppm.
Since 2021, Ranjith Narayanan, a nephrologist practising at two busy private hospitals in Kozhikode, had noticed a specific pattern in cases of membranous nephropathy diagnosed amongst his patients. They all had non-specific symptoms — fatigue, mild edema and frothy urine — but high levels of proteinuria, in the range of 6.5-22.2 g/day.

Tom Jackson, a cornerstone of the Denver Broncos’ “Orange Crush” defense who went on to forge a lengthy career with ESPN following his playing career, has died at 75.
ESPN announced his death on Sunday, indicating his family informed the company that he had passed away on Friday. No cause of death was released.
Jackson played 14 seasons with the Broncos after being selected in the fourth round of the 1973 NFL draft out of Louisville. The three-time Pro Bowl selection (1977-79) was a first-Team All-Pro in 1977 and second-Team All-Pro in 1978.

24 dead in Nigeria when boat capsizes while carrying people to a funeral
Nigeria's emergency services say that a boat carrying people to a funeral has capsized and that at least 24 people have died
ABUJA, Nigeria -- A boat carrying people to a funeral has capsized in southern Nigeria, killing at least 24 people, emergency services said on Saturday.
The boat was taking passengers from one community to another for a burial ceremony when it sank on Friday in Bayelsa State in the country’s South South region, Nigeria’s National Emergency Management Agency spokesman Manzo Ezeki said in a statement.
He said that search and rescue operations were ongoing without specifying how many people were missing.
Police spokesman Musa Mohammed said on Friday that another 24 people had been rescued and sought medical assistance.
Authorities haven't said how many passengers were believed to have been on board.
Mohammed said that preliminary reports suggested that the boat suffered a mechanical problem.
Passengers asked the boat operator to steer towards land, but he allegedly declined, according to Mohammed. The boat operator then reportedly fled the scene, while the manager of the boat was taken into custody.

At this year’s World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, US President Donald Trump stated that people from Somalia have low IQs. “I always say these are low-IQ people,” he said in his speech. His son, Donald Trump Jr, made a similar statement about Haitian people in 2024 (Trump’s government has since ended the protected status of both Somali and Haitian migrants in the US).
These statements and their consequences are symptoms of a growing trend in Western politics: the re-emergence of racial views of human nature that have been largely in hiding for the past 70 years. Narratives about the innate intellectual inferiority of black or brown people compared with white people—which can still be found in academic journals today—are fuelling far-right propaganda in some of the world’s largest democracies. Such claims underpin misinformation strategies on social media and bolster political movements.
These narratives are sometimes euphemistically referred to as “race science” or more recently “race realism.” But, as we argue, they are not actually scientific. One member of this community, Nathan Cofnas, recently attracted public attention by accusing the late Jason Arday of plagiarism.
What got less attention was that Cofnas has links to a network of people who make supposedly scientific claims about the innate intelligence, criminality, or sexuality of different racial groups. Some within this network are affiliated with universities, giving their work the mask of legitimacy.
This group produces work that has the appearance of science, but which is methodologically deeply flawed and fails to engage with rigorous scientific research. Yet they regularly succeed in publishing this work in (a handful of) mainstream academic journals.
How do they manage to do this, and what are the consequences?
Scientific shortcomings: biology and genetics
Contemporary race scientists position themselves as persecuted but legitimate scientists who are prevented from pursuing their work for ideological reasons. They sometimes refer to what they defend as hereditarianism. This is the idea that genetic differences play a key causal role in determining differences in human behavior and intelligence between human groups—such as races—over purely environmental differences.
Yet scientific evidence has shown repeatedly and from many points of view that hereditarian thinking is both flawed and wrong. Race scientists make extremely simplistic claims such as: “Black people have innately lower intelligence than white people, because selection pressures resulted in the evolution of higher intelligence in white people.” No part of this claim can be scientifically supported; not from the point of view of genetics, evolutionary biology, or psychology.
In the 1970s, the influential evolutionary biologist Richard Lewontin famously showed that there is more genetic variation within human groups than between them. Socially defined racial groups just aren’t that genetically different from one another. There is genetic variation—though we’re actually a relatively genetically similar species compared to closely related primates. But this variation doesn’t fall neatly into clusters that correlate with how we typically categorize races.
Skin tone and color do vary between geographical locations. So do some other physiological features like hair texture, or the ability to process oxygen or milk products. But these differences are associated with characteristics of the environment rather than with racial groups. Some genetic variants associated with white skin color, for example, may have originated in Africa. Similarly, the ability to digest milk is seen in some populations in Europe, Africa, and Asia, rather than being an exclusively “Aryan” characteristic, as far right groups sometimes claim.
We now know considerably more about the human genome than Lewontin did in the 1970s, but his conclusions are supportedtoday. Knowing someone’s race just doesn’t tell us a great deal about their genetics.
Recent scientific advances allowing us to examine ancient DNA from archaeological sites help explain why genetic differences do not fall neatly along racial lines. This research paints a picture of constant mixing between human groups, as waves of migration washed to and fro across the globe. It ultimately makes any belief in the genetic “purity” of European or African populations meaningless.
While human genetics is fascinatingly complex, race scientists ignore this complexity in favor of a far-too-simplistic view of humanity. And this view is not supported by the work of scientists who have used rigorous scientific methods to further our understanding of our species.
Challenges from social science
When race scientists say that black people have lower intelligence than white people, they typically base that on claims of differences in IQ test results. But the data underlying these claims is often shaky, to say the least.
Hereditarians have relied heavily on a database that claims to provide average IQs for countries worldwide: the “national IQ” database. Researchers have repeatedly demonstrated that this database is deeply methodologically flawed. It isn’t possible to measure intelligence in the same way in very different cultures, with different exposure to formal education. That’s because we know that education is one of several other factors linked to differences in IQ.
The methods used to put the database together did not come even close to meeting typical standards of scientific rigor. There’s even analysis suggesting that low IQ samples were deliberately chosen to represent sub-Saharan Africa, to make the IQ for black populations artificially low.
Meanwhile, the Flynn effect, showing that IQ has risen considerably during the 20th and 21st centuries, clearly demonstrates that IQ scores are heavily determined by the environment we’re in. Such a rapid rise over a short period of time must have environmental, not genetic, causes.
What’s more, intelligence is a contested topic—something that is hard to define and measure. IQ tests only measure specific cognitive abilities, ignoring things like social intelligence or creativity, for example. In fact, social intelligence features heavily in mainstream research on the evolution of human intelligence.
As one of us recently outlined in a peer-reviewed paper, race scientists are largely silent on the social brain hypothesis—the view that humans evolved remarkable intellectual abilities to manage social issues. In every group, there is strong social competition around resources, mating, and status. These are the things humans spend the most time navigating—the complexities of our rich social lives.
Not one of the prominent mainstream views on the evolution of human intelligence concludes there are innate cognitive differences between racial groups. Factors that have been put forward range from our cooperative child rearing to our heavy reliance on culture and learning. These all involve our social relationships, and all have received equal lack of attention from race scientists.
Mainstream opinion in the evolutionary behavioral sciences is that cognitively, all human groups are the same, though of course individuals within groups differ. Our amazing behavioral diversity stems from our species’ ability to adapt flexibly to our environment. This is especially because of our reliance on culture and social learning—not because we have evolved different psychologies to suit different environments.
Rather than drawing on this mainstream research, race scientists use simplistic “just-so” stories to explain how race differences in traits such as intelligence supposedly evolved. Their “cold winters theory,” for example, claims that the challenges of cold winters in Europe and east Asia created evolutionary selection pressures for greater intelligence after human groups migrated out of Africa. In doing so, they make unsupportable assumptions about environmental differences between Africa and the rest of the world. They also fail to acknowledge half a century of research on the evolution of human cognitive ability.
Yes, we needed to learn new food gathering practices and methods for dealing with environmental challenges as we migrated across the world. But the same was true as humans migrated across the large and ecologically diverse continent of Africa. Race scientists provide no evidence for their arguments. They don’t rely on archaeological evidence, nor do they use typical methods from evolutionary biology to understand evolutionary processes. Using the methods of race scientists, it would be equally easy to make the argument that challenges posed by hot summers drove the evolution of higher intelligence, and equally without scientific backing.
No matter which way you look at these issues—from the view of genetics, anthropology, evolutionary biology, or psychology—hereditarianism does not hold up.
A short history of race science
To understand the potential consequences of these views, it is important to see them in historical context. Early in the 20th century, race science was mainstream. Overly simplistic and biologically deterministic views about the origins of differences between human groups—not just race but class—were widespread (if not universal) and important to the eugenics movement.
If disadvantaged groups owe their disadvantage to some fault within them, and not to the structural conditions they experience, then some argue society is not responsible for helping those people. Such arguments led to eugenic sterilization laws that aimed to “improve” society by preventing—without their consent—the reproduction of those considered likely to pass on their innate “defects” to future children. And it was ultimately behind the Nazis’ “solution” of trying to eliminate “undesirables” entirely.
In the decades after the Second World War, the horrors of the Nazi regime led to a decline in the popularity of eugenics in mainstream research and a rejection of race science. But the belief that science supported eugenic claims was already collapsing, even as the Nazis were trying to implement a race-based society. As we learned more about human biology and genetics during the 20th century, it became obvious that human genetic variation was too complex to be mapped into socially recognized racial (or class) categories. Advances in science meant race science dropped out of mainstream thinking.
Yet those committed to a belief in a biological hierarchy of races, regardless of what the science said, wanted venues in which they could continue their discussions. In the 1960s, the pseudo-scientific journal Mankind Quarterly became their venue. Mankind Quarterly was funded by the Pioneer Fund, a nonprofit foundation set up in the 1930s by a US textile magnate who chose to use his fortune to fund research on race science and fight desegregation in the US.
The Pioneer Fund continued to fund race science into the 21st century—including supporting Mankind Quarterly—when it was taken over by the current network of race scientists. They channeled its remaining funds into a new company, the Human Diversity Foundation, subsequently rebranded as Polygenic Scores LLC.
How race science still persists
Given all this, how is race science still being published in mainstream academic journals? To be clear, race science does not typically get published in genetics or evolutionary biology journals. Most academic journals operate peer review, meaning papers only get published after evaluation by experts in the field. The overall absence of race science in genetics or biology journals is a clear signal that it does not meet contemporary standards of scientific rigor in genetics or biology.
Instead, race scientists continue to publish in para-scientific journals. But race science also makes it into a growing number of mainstream social science or humanities journals. Psychologist Andrew Winston, an expert in the history of race science in psychology, has described it as a “community project… with its own networks, mentorships, journals, funding, conferences, heroes, origin myths, martyrs, defenders, and historiography.”
Behind the network of writers producing race science sits a community of editors, peer reviewers, and others in gatekeeping roles, which too often allows race science to be published in mainstream journals. This is particularly in the subfields of psychology interested in intelligence and individual differences, and evolutionary psychology.
Editors of Intelligence, the mainstream journal that has probably published the largest quantity of race science, have occasionally publishededitorials defending their publication of race science in the name of ensuring robust academic debate even on controversial topics.
There have been sanctions. Philippe Rushton, one of an earlier generation of race scientists, faced sanctions from his university in Canada but kept his job apparently owing to the intervention of Edward O. Wilson, arguably the most famous biologist toward the end of the 20th century.
Cofnas created justified controversy over his call for a “hereditarian revolution” after which it will be acknowledged that black people are innately intellectually disadvantaged compared to white people. But he kept his postdoctoral fellowship at Cambridge University (though his affiliation with a Cambridge college was ended). He has also kept his postdoctoral position at Ghent University after using the opportunity provided by excessive news coverage of Arday to publicize his hereditarian views (though some sanctions have been imposed, such as restrictions on teaching). Cofnas has defended his views by saying he’s been misunderstood and is entitled to free inquiry.
Moreover, when University College London discovered that the race science community had been holding conferences on its premises (the “London Conferences on Intelligence”), without their knowledge of the subject of the conferences, they acted to prevent further such conferences being held. The publisher of the journal Intelligence, Elsevier, has recently appointed new editors, who have stated their commitment to publishing both rigorous and socially responsible science. Race scientists are increasingly publishing in evolutionary psychology journals rather than Intelligence.
However, the London Conferences on Intelligence continue, though not at UCL. Race scientists also have a media arm, Aporia magazine, which promotes race science using much more overt language and with more obvious policy focus than publications in academic journals. One Aporia article, for example, argued for eugenics as a solution to Africa’s lack of economic development, noting in a post that some may find it “distasteful.” It claimed—relying on race science’s unscientific arguments—that artificial selection for higher intelligence is needed to improve the continent’s innately unintelligent populace.
Race science may not have the respect of the scientific community, but it does have funding and influential backers. A report by Hope not Hate revealed that the network of race scientists received significant funding from the US businessman Andrew Conru, who withdrew his funding after the report was released.
The US Ambassador to Belgium even intervened when Ghent University set up an investigation into how Cofnas was hired.
Race scientists are far from the victims they claim to be. Race scientists in this and previous generations have worked hard to ensure their messages are heard beyond academia. And in this generation, they are successfully using social media to spread their beliefs, especially Elon Musk’s X.
But what about academic freedom? Isn’t it good for science to discuss any hypothesis to ensure free exchange of ideas? Academic debate is productive only if it involves methodologically rigorous research. Science will not progress if one side of any debate consistently uses poor-quality, methodologically flawed work. Nor is it necessary to continually debate topics that have long since been settled.
We believe it is unequivocal that race science is fundamentally pseudoscience. In our view, it’s critical to call attention to not only the scientific flaws underlying this body of work but also the real target it’s aimed at: political actors and everyday readers who ultimately decide the direction that science, and society, goes in.
The Conversation is an independent source of news and views, sourced from the academic and research community. Our team of editors work with these experts to share their knowledge with the wider public. Our aim is to allow for better understanding of current affairs and complex issues, and hopefully improve the quality of public discourse on them.

Your older, discontinued AirTags can still serve a purpose
Before you toss your original AirTag, here are a few ways to keep it useful.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
Earlier this year, Apple introduced the first new generation AirTag since the original debuted in 2021. And while you might still be able to find first-generation Apple AirTags for purchase on some websites, Apple doesn't sell them anymore. The company is now focusing solely on the new model and leaving the original AirTag behind. But the old ones are still supported in the Find My app, so there's lots of ways you can continue to use them.
The newer Apple AirTag offers an expanded finding range thanks to the second-generation ultrawideband chip, upgraded Bluetooth chip, improved Precision Finding from up to 50 percent farther away and a louder speaker. Given how cheap Apple AirTags are ($29 on Amazon) and all the upgrades with the second-gen model, you'll probably want to grab a few for your most precious items.
But that doesn't mean you should toss your old AirTags. They can be relocated to secondary items, kept as backups for your most important gear or handed down to friends and family.
Use them for secondary items
An AirTag that still works is worth hanging onto. Use newer AirTags for your keys, purse, wallet, child's backpack and maybe even pet collar and move your old AirTags to secondary items. Toss one in your glove compartment or trunk of your car in case of theft or to keep track of your newly licensed teen if they turn off location sharing in Find My. Or put one in your luggage as a secondary method of tracking its location if it's lost or misplaced.
Keep one in your child's jacket pocket so they're still trackable if they don't have their backpack (some parents even stitch them into their kids' shoes). Clip one secondary set of keys you often misplace in the house, like the key to the back door or home office filing cabinet. While the range is farther and the speaker louder on the new AirTag, both are still sufficient on the older model for finding items within the home. My son used Precision Finding with an old AirTag the other day to locate his house keys and it worked perfectly well.
You could also get creative and affix one to the inside of your headphones case or toss one in your dressy purse, clutch or wallet so you don't have to move the new AirTag back and forth when you switch. Or keep one with items that are tough to find in a cluttered space, like holiday decorations in the attic, a toolbox in the garage or a small remote in the game room. AirTags use easily replaceable CR2032 batteries that last about a year with normal usage and under normal conditions.
Other things you can do with an old AirTag
Since the new Precision Finding benefits of the second-generation Apple AirTag are only supported with iPhone 15 and newer models, you won't be able to use one if you have an older phone. In this case, it's still worthwhile to continue using a first-gen Apple AirTag until you upgrade your phone. Standard Precision Finding works with iPhone 11 through 14 models, so consider handing over the old AirTag to a friend or family member with an older iPhone, like a parent or grandparent. They can use it for their wallet, purse, eyeglasses case or other item they often misplace.
If you want to be extra diligent, use a second older AirTag with a new battery as a backup in case the battery in your new AirTag dies before you get the chance to replace it. A second AirTag can also add security. Think putting the new AirTag under your bicycle seat and the older one under the bike's bottle cage or inside the bell. A thief might find one and dispose of it, but likely won't find both.
Some buyback sites in certain countries also purchase old AirTags. While Apple doesn't accept AirTags for trade-in, sites like Sell Techs in the UK and BuyBackWorld do. So you could make a bit of cash by selling them. Just because older AirTags are slowly becoming obsolete, that doesn't mean they don't still have their use.

Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.
In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.
Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.
At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.
“We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said.
He said Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.
“You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he said.
“We want them to build it here.”
With many Americans turning against the datacenters being built near their homes, the US tech industry is making a show of conciliation by promising to take fewer government handouts, to be more transparent, and to give more money to towns and cities willing to allow server warehouses to be built.
The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced US computing chips and servers, in a move it said was designed to limit China’s ability to use US chips to train its artificial intelligence models – though a House committee said on Wednesday the US had signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months.
China’s ability to obtain advanced AI chips made by the US firm Nvidia, in which Trump is an investor, has been spotlighted in recent weeks after its CEO, Jensen Huang, was fired over his affair with a woman alleged to be spying for China.
In the same press conference, Trump was asked about reports Iran was planning to potentially detonate an explosive laced with nuclear material – a so-called “dirty bomb” – in Washington DC. The president called it a “rumour” and said: “If they do, we’re going to fight.”
He added: “We know a lot about what’s happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We’ll find out about it.”
Responding to a question about reports of a rift with Vance, Trump said the vice-president’s remark blaming the Republican collapse on the Iran war was “a very accurate statement”.
“I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” the president said. “I would have added one other thing if it were asked … would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”
Trump was asked whether Vladimir Putin could really be considered a friend to America since Russia is a close ally of Iran.
“I can’t speak to America,” he said, adding: “I consider [that] I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that.”
He praised Putin as he repeated his grievances over the Department of Justice’s investigation into the Russian attempts to influence US voters ahead of the 2016 presidential election.
“I’ve been dealing with Putin … [since] the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax,” he said.
Trump also spoke about two prominent Democrats. He said Gina Hinojosa, who won the race for Texas governor over Trump’s Republican ally Greg Abbott, called him. “She was really nice,” Trump said. “It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border, and I think we’ll be able to work something out.”
And he said Hakeem Jeffries – who Trump previously called a “thug” but is now in line to be the next speaker of the House, and the first Black speaker – is “a smart guy. He’s a streetwise guy.”

New Delhi, Nov 23: Scholars and delegates from Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) member states and dialogue partners discussed ways to strengthen cooperation in preserving, digitising and translating India’s rich manuscript heritage at a session organised under the Gyan Bharatam Mission in New Delhi. The session on “Language, Literature, Script and Manuscript Traditions” was held on November 22 at Purana Qila as part of the first SCO Civilization Dialogue Forum, which concluded on November 22.
The Ministry of Culture organised the session to explore opportunities for international collaboration in manuscript preservation, translation, research and digital access.
Addressing the participants, Inderjeet Singh, CEO of Gyan Bharatam and Joint Secretary in the Ministry of Culture, briefed delegates on the mission’s objectives and operational activities, including manuscript survey and cataloguing, conservation, capacity building, digitisation, translation, research and publication.
He highlighted the use of artificial intelligence (AI) through initiatives such as Gyan-MitramAI, Pandulipi Darpana and BharatiyaGPT. He also said more than 1.26 crore manuscripts had been reported through the National Manuscript Survey.
Describing the mission as an opportunity for international cooperation, Inderjeet Singh said it was both a responsibility and an invitation to work together. He underlined the importance of Indic scripts across the SCO region and the need to build a global digital repository of knowledge.
The session, moderated by Prof Anirban Dash, Project Director, Gyan Bharatam, discussed four major themes, including India’s linguistic and script heritage and its influence on Asian languages, the transmission and translation of Indian literature across Asia, the global presence of Indian manuscripts and the role of digital technology in reconnecting dispersed knowledge.
Prof Rajnish Kumar Mishra of Jawaharlal Nehru University highlighted India’s diverse linguistic and script traditions and their influence on Asian cultures. He referred to the spread of Indian cultural and intellectual traditions through communication networks and the Silk Route.
Prof K K Mishra of the University of Calcutta stressed the need to expand digitisation, translate manuscripts into more languages and use AI to improve global access. He also referred to international archival institutions and cooperation with countries such as Thailand, Vietnam, Mongolia and Russia.
Dr Viswajanani J Sattigeri, Head of the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) Unit, highlighted the need to protect India’s traditional knowledge from piracy and misuse. She emphasised intellectual property rights, standardised metadata and controlled digital access to prevent duplication and misappropriation.
Prof K Rama Subramaniyam of IIT Bombay underlined the importance of preserving manuscripts and ensuring that translations remain free from bias. Citing the example of the Panchatantra, translated into more than 50 foreign languages, including Arabic and Persian, he said manuscripts carried not only knowledge but also the history and traditions of the societies that preserved them.
Delegates from Iran, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Cambodia, Uzbekistan, Laos and Nepal shared their countries’ initiatives in manuscript preservation and expressed interest in collaborating with the Gyan Bharatam Mission. The session concluded with a commitment to strengthen cooperation in manuscript conservation, script training, comparative literary studies, translation, cataloguing, academic exchanges and joint research.

Every year in Delhi, the arrival of the winter months also signals the beginning of what residents widely call “pollution season”. A thick toxic smog shrouds the city, home to 30 million people who have no choice but to breathe the poisonous air as they go about their daily lives, often while suffering from wheezy coughs, nausea and itchy eyes. While successive state governments have brought in measures intended to improve air quality, the situation has remained the same for more than a decade. Delhi is widely regarded as the world’s most polluted city. Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Pollution season usually begins around the same time as Diwali, the Hindu festival of light. Amidst the plummeting air quality, people still gather in the markets for festival shopping and at festivities outside. Diwali is also known to cause a surge in the pollution levels, due to the tens of millions of cars that hit the roads and the use of firecrackers for the celebration. In previous years, firecrackers were banned, but this year the state government has allowed “green” firecrackers”. However environmentalists argue that these are still highly polluting.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The causes of Delhi’s apocalyptic pollution are multi-faceted. In recent years, one of the biggest causes has been vehicle emissions, from the almost 10m cars, rickshaws, motorcycles and trucks on the city’s roads. It is also the season where farmers in the neighbouring states of Haryana and Punjab often burn their fields to ready them for the next crop. These fires are illegal but still occur. Factory emissions, dust from construction and rubbish burning also contribute to the toxic air quality levels.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
So far, the air quality index (AQI) has already soared above 650, more than 30 times the limit the World Health Organization (WHO) deems to be safe. Air pollution is linked to numerous serious diseases, particularly respiratory, and hospitals have already reported a surge in patients suffering from breathing difficulties.The pollution season is expected to last until January, when the weather warms up.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
Millions of Delhi’s residents are poor families or migrant workers, who have no choice but to go out to work in the toxic air, often suffering long term impacts on their health. Doctors and campaigners have described the pollution as a “health emergency”. According to a study last year, at least 15% of deaths in the capital are linked to air pollution. Pollution now kills more people in Delhi than obesity of diabetes.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
As in previous years, the state government has introduced various restrictions to try and bring air quality levels under control. Coal and firewood have been banned as fuel. Construction has also been halted and so have older diesel and petrol cars. Offices have been instructed to get people to work from home to limit traffic on the roads. Trucks can often be seen spraying water on the roads. However, it is widely acknowledged that, so far, these restrictions have had little impact on the pollution levels. Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
The pollution has been a problem for so long in Delhi that it has become normalised and people carry on with their daily lives in the toxic smog.Residents rarely wear masks outside and the parks will still be full of families and children and people exercising outside.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
While rich and middle class families will buy air purifiers for their homes, they are unaffordable for most poorer families who often live in makeshift tents or informal homes. As a result, breathing clean air during pollution season has become a luxury privilege in Delhi.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The pollution is not restricted to Delhi alone. All across north India, in states such as Punjab and Haryana, the air is also toxic due to coal-powered plants, vehicles and farm fires. Cities such as Amritsar in Punjab, on the border with Pakistan, also suffer from extremely dangerous air quality levels during the winter months. Photograph: Narinder Nanu/AFP/Getty Images
Campaigners say more money needs to be invested into proper public transport and better vehicle emission regulation in Delhi to tackle the root causes of pollution. Every year, the number of cars on Delhi’s roads keeps rising, releasing more harmful pollutants, and yet few the percentage of electric vehicles remains very low.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Delhi has an extensive bus and metro network, but it is not sufficient to cope with the huge daily demand and still has poor connectivity in many areas. Most people still rely on polluting rickshaws, cars and motorcycles to get them to the bus stops or metro stations. Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
Delhi’s topography – a city built in a bowl-like valley, which has little breeze or rain in the winter months – means most of the emissions get trapped over the city as the cold weather hits and cloak the city in brown smog. Some call it Delhi’s “death shroud”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
In past years, the state and national government has been accused of manipulating the data to disguise how bad pollution levels are in the capital. Last year, it was found that water was being sprayed around the air quality monitors, allegedly to bring down the readings. Campaigners and opposition politicians have alleged that a lot of data from the air quality measuring stations has gone “missing”.
Environmental campaigners have argued that much more extreme measures are needed to bring pollution under control, similar to how Beijing successfully cleaned up its air in recent years. However, others have argued this would have an economic cost that India, as a developing country, can not afford.Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
One of the plans being prepared by the government this year is to experiment with “cloud-seeding”, to create rain which would clear the skies. But many residents and campaigners say that until the root causes are tackled, these plans are nothing more than a “gimmick”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images

San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
- Published
Lauren Goldboss is busy. The owner of a small San Francisco dog-walking company, she has been hiring staff and buying vans.
Fuelling the growth is her new office dog-walking service Paw Perk, popular with some local AI start-ups.
Her business is an example of how the AI boom in San Francisco is benefiting other sectors.
The city saw an exodus of residents during the pandemic and its downtown was weakened by remote work, but it s now enjoying a rejuvenation, with AI being the major driver.
Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.
Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up, external in San Francisco.
Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.
But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn, external that this was a possibility.
Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (£49bn).
- Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting? 
  - Published4 days ago
- Wealthy AI workers send San Francisco house prices soaring 
  - Published9 July
What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco – no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles – be preparing for a possible crash?
One AI worker, employed by one of the largest companies in the city, is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come down… and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.
He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.
But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"
Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".
Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.
"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."
If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.
That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.
One study, external found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.
But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.
For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.
"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.
Ted Egan, the chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, adds that "because of AI, it is a good time for tech again in the city, but we are not seeing tonnes of overall tech job growth".
Despite the expansion of the AI sector, the city remains about 35,000 jobs shy of its pre-pandemic peak, estimates Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley.
Instead, much of the spending by AI firms in the US is going towards data centres and computing power, relatively little of which are located in the Bay Area. San Francisco might be the brains of the AI boom, but it isn't the brawn.
Nonetheless, a significant correction could still be "very painful" for San Francisco, warns Moretti. Less AI hiring and potential layoffs would ripple through the local service sector, likely to affect jobs in everything from restaurants, to retail, to personal services like dog walking.
"It is the spillover on service jobs that would actually be the main effect," he says.
Office vacancies could also rise, reducing downtown foot traffic, while rents and house prices could weaken.
But AI isn't the only force driving San Francisco's recovery. Healthcare and tourism – which the city has been working to encourage, including by improving downtown safety and cleanliness – are also growing,, external which may help cushion against a possible AI downturn.
"Tourism is not fully back, but the growth has been healthy," says Egan, adding that it is a sign of confidence in San Francisco.
All told, Egan doesn't expect an AI crash to fundamentally alter San Francisco's economic trajectory.
"The city's economy has not been screaming during this AI boom, so I wouldn't expect it to grind to a halt if there was a slowdown in AI spending," he says. "I think of it primarily as a hiccup that we should expect, rather than a major course correction for the city's economy."
As to whether and how San Francisco's city government should prepare, there are limits to what it can do, note Bellisario and Moretti. But encouraging growth in sectors beyond technology and maintaining financial reserves could help.
For Goldboss, the dog-walking company owner, her philosophy is to "build while it is here". If the next tech bust comes – "always a reality in San Francisco" – she will try to adapt to what the market needs. "It is just the risk you kind of have to take," she says.
