For years, a rumor has asserted that drinking Hawaiian pink salt mixed with lemon in water helps people lose weight.
Several posts on Facebook shared a recipe for the drink, claiming it supported weight loss (archived):
One user on TikTok demonstrated in a July 2025 video how she prepared the concoction, to which she also added vinegar and pepper (archived). But this claim dates back years. In 2022 a TikTok influencer who said he helped women older than 40 lose weight posted a video explaining the alleged science behind the claim (archived):
The claim is false, however, and the explanations internet users shared to support it were based on mistaken beliefs rather than science.
Snopes reached out to Allison Childress, a clinical dietitian and an associate professor of practice in the Department of Nutritional Sciences at Texas Tech University, asking for clarifications on this claim.
Childress said the trick is ineffective for weight loss. Rather, it could result in weight gain. "This will not do anything significant to benefit weight loss," she wrote in an email. "In fact too much sodium can lead to water retention which may actually lead to weight gain (however this would be fluid gain, not fat gain)."
Asked if there was any possibility, even remote, that it could at least support efforts to lose weight, she said that "in theory," it could increase hydration, leading to a sensation of fullness that may help a person eat less. "But this is a far reach," she added.
Childress did expound on the nutritional benefits of pink salt, saying that it contained more electrolytes than regular table salt. "However, most people do not need additional sodium," she warned. "In fact, Americans consume more than 50% more than the recommended amount of sodium already."
Asked if there were dangers to consuming too much pink salt, Childress said that the consequences of increased sodium in the diet could be dire, especially for people with certain health issues, "people who have heart, kidney and/or blood pressure issues as increased sodium intake can exacerbate these conditions."
Further, she warned against replacing table salt, which is enriched with iodine, with other types of salt. "There is little to no iodine in pink salt", she said. "Table salt is typically fortified with iodine which helps prevent deficiencies. While iodine deficiencies are relatively rare in the United States (most likely due to our consumption of iodized salt), we have seen a rise recently due to people consuming more pink salt, sea salt, kosher salt etc. instead of table salt." Iodine deficiencies can result in thyroid problems, including an enlarged thyroid (goiter) or hypothyroidism — an underactive thyroid.
Finally, when asked if there were better ways to lose weight, Childress listed the following:
- High-protein meals and snacks, which help create a sensation of fullness for longer.
- Good hydration, as dehydration "can mimic hunger signals and can derail weight loss efforts."
- Exercise, especially "resistance training," she said. "Strength training two to three times per week can preserve lean body mass during weight loss."
- Good sleep. "Poor sleep increases ghrelin, our hunger hormone, which can lead to cravings, specifically for high-calorie foods. Good sleep hygiene can aid in hormone regulation, lead to healthier food choices, improved metabolism and provide more energy for physical activity."
Other tips Childress mentioned included avoiding highly processed foods to favor whole foods, which are more nutritious with a lower caloric density, and monitoring food intake with "a food log or app" to "increase awareness and accountability."
In other words, no single trick can result in weight loss the way healthy lifestyle and habits can.

Following a terrorist attack on November 11 at a Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) checkpoint in Jammu and Kashmir’s Kulgam district, a video went viral on social media with the claim that retired Indian Army officer and journalist Pravin Sawhney described Indian military and counter-terrorism drives in the valley as “false flag operations”.
Social media users claimed that Sawhney said that operations against the Kulgam attack, the Balakot airstrikes, and Operation Sindoor were orchestrated for political gains.
X user @RedDeFactoIND (Red Vanguard) shared the viral clip, which shows an interview conducted by The Wire. (Archive)
𝗘𝘅-𝗔𝗿𝗺𝘆 𝗢𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗲𝗿 𝗗𝗿𝗼𝗽𝘀 𝗕𝗼𝗺𝗯𝘀𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗹🚨: Pravin Sawhney in Recent Interview for Wire said, “Another false flag, just like Pulwama and Pahalgam,This is a pattern”
Indian journalists and influencers are now openly questioning the government’s narrative.
The voices from within are getting louder.
#CRPFSoldiers #CRPFCampAttack #kulgamattack #Kulgam #KulgamTerrorAttack
— Red Vanguard (@RedDeFactoIND) November 12, 2026
In the viral clip, the interviewer can first be heard saying (translated from Hindi): “Sushant, I want to know from you…the theme of your latest essay is the politicisation of army…During the false flag operations like Balakot and Pahalgam, the way the Bharatiya Janata Party used the military for political gains. My second question is that today while there is a war-like situation in the world…is testing the Pralay missile is an indication of a new false flag operation?”
“On one side China is occupying [Indian land], on the other there are CJP protests…Rahul Gandhi…,” the interviewer goes on to say before his voice is abruptly cut off.
The interviewee then seems to respond with, “Two things are very clear. One, for false flag operations like Balakot and Pahalgam, Operation Sindoor was launched but the Indian army failed. Second, my answers are within your questions.”
Several other users on X and Facebook also circulated the same video with identical claims. Among them were X handles @KaurUdhoke3 and @HinduReformer, along with multiple public Facebook pages focusing on South Asian geopolitics. [Archives: 1, 2]
Fact Check
A closer look at the viral video reveals noticeable lip-sync discrepancies and an unnatural, monotonous cadence in the voices of both men in the interview, which are salient features of AI-generated audio manipulation.
Further, columnist and strategic affairs expert Sushant Singh has been misidentified in the viral video as Pravin Sawhney. In the viral video itself, the interviewer refers to the interviewee as Sushant, and not Pravin. Below is an image of Sawhney, who does not appear in the viral clip.
On November 13, Singh himself took to X to debunk the clip, clarifying that the video was AI-generated, and highlighting that users had also misidentified him.
This is AI generated video of an old interview, which completely fabricates my conversation with @ashubh. This Pakistan-made AI video clip not only gets my identity wrong but creates what was never said.
The original full interview of March 2025 is here: https://t.co/Y6teNLJDfg
— Sushant Singh (@SushantSin) November 13, 2026
In his post, Singh also attached a link to the original YouTube interview from which the visuals were taken. Alt News examined the original video uploaded on The Wire’s official YouTube channel in March 2025.
Comparing the viral clip with the March 2025 interview confirms that the visual frames, including Singh’s attire, the background setting, and lighting, are identical. However, the audio track in the viral clip has been changed using AI.
In the original interview, Singh makes no mention of Kulgam, Pulwama, Balakot, or any ‘false flag operations’. Instead, he is heard discussing civil-military relations and institutional oversight.
To sum up, a manipulated video of journalist and strategic affairs analyst Sushant Singh is circulating on social media with users misidentifying him as journalist and FORCE editor Pravin Sawhney. The claim that the speaker in the video termed India’s counter-terrorism measures in Kulgam and Pulwama ‘false flag operations’ is false as well.

5 lakh guests, 150 dishes, Thar as prize: Anant Singh's daughter's big fat wedding
Anant Singh has added a Thar-prize horse race to his daughter Shivangi's November 25 wedding. The celebrations combine lavish gifts, a vast feast and rain-hit preparations for lakhs of guests.
A Rs 3-crore Land Rover Defender for the groom? Check.
A brand-new Mahindra Thar for whoever wins a horse race? Check.
Five lakh guests, 150 varieties of food and hundreds of workers making sweets through the night? Check.
Former Bihar MLA Anant Singh is clearly not doing things by halves for his younger daughter Shivangi Singh's wedding. And just when the celebrations could not get any bigger, he has added a horse racing competition to the festivities, with a Thar waiting for the winner.
The only uninvited guest causing trouble so far is the rain.
Shivangi is set to marry Rishikesh Kumar, also known as Ankit, on November 25. Her wedding preparations have turned Anant Singh's ancestral village into a massive celebration ground, with grand pandals, elaborate food arrangements, a Jaipur-style mandap and a 12-bigha field being readied for the horse race.
The celebrations have already delivered some memorable moments. At the haldi ceremony, Anant Singh, popularly known as 'Chhote Sarkar', was seen dancing to 'Rangbaaz Raja', even giving his trademark moustache a twist. At the tilak ceremony, he presented his future son-in-law with a white Land Rover Defender reportedly worth around Rs 3 crore.
And if the groom's gift was not enough to get people talking, the wedding guests and horse racing enthusiasts now have another reason to watch out for November 25. The winner of the race will get a Mahindra Thar, the runner-up a motorcycle and the third-place finisher a scooter.
In short, this is one wedding where the gifts are not limited to the bride and groom.
FROM 'RANGBAAZ RAJA' DANCE TO A RS 3-CRORE DEFENDER
The wedding festivities began with traditional family rituals, but it was Anant Singh's haldi appearance that gave the celebrations their first viral-style moment.
As 'Rangbaaz Raja' played, 'Chhote Sarkar' joined the dancing, matching the music with his signature style and a flourish of his moustache. The politician, known for his outspoken personality, was seen enjoying the occasion as a father celebrating his daughter's big day.
The celebrations then moved to the tilak ceremony at a resort in Danapur, Patna. Before leaving for the function, traditional rituals were performed in the ancestral village. The family then travelled to the resort in a convoy reportedly comprising around 100 vehicles.
Rishikesh Kumar welcomed Anant Singh and his family with a bouquet of flowers. The tilak and faldan ceremonies were performed in the presence of relatives and family members.
But the gift that stole the spotlight was the white Land Rover Defender presented to the groom. The luxury SUV is reportedly worth around Rs 3 crore. And the Defender was not the only expensive present. Rishikesh also received a 100-gram gold chain and an 80-gram gold bracelet, along with silver utensils and other gifts.
NOW, A HORSE RACE WITH A MAHINDRA THAR AS THE TOP PRIZE
With the groom already having received a luxury SUV, Anant Singh has turned the wedding celebrations into an opportunity for horse racing enthusiasts to win a vehicle of their own.
A competition is being organised on a field spread across around 12 bighas, with the winner set to take home a Mahindra Thar. The second-place finisher will get a motorcycle, while the third-place winner will receive a scooter.
The race is scheduled for November 25, between 2 pm and 4 pm. Horse owners and riders from Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand, Rajasthan and other parts of the country are arriving for the event.
More than 50 horses had reportedly reached the village by November 22. Among the horses attracting attention are Lal Badshah, Khagaria Express, Babar, Rocket and Sikandar. Their names alone are enough to add a little drama to the competition.
The excitement is not limited to the organisers. Horse owners and riders arriving with their animals have made their intentions clear: they want to win the race and take the Thar home.
Temporary stables have been arranged for the horses, with provisions for their food, water and care. The horses are being looked after ahead of the competition, while the track is being repaired after rain left the ground muddy and waterlogged.
For the riders, this is no ordinary wedding invitation. There is a brand-new SUV waiting at the finish line.
FIVE LAKH GUESTS, 150 DISHES AND MILK TANKERS FOR THE SWEETS
If the horse race is the sporting attraction, the food arrangements are a spectacle of their own.
Around five lakh people are expected to be served at the wedding, with more than 150 varieties of dishes planned for the feast. Over 500 halwais, along with hundreds of other workers, are involved in preparing the food.
Four to five pandals have been set up for the preparations, with artisans and workers busy making sweets day and night. The scale of the operation is such that milk is being brought in tankers to meet the requirements of the kitchens.
The work has continued late into the night, with workers focused on getting the sweets and other preparations ready in time. At the earlier tilak ceremony, guests were treated to desi ghee laddoos, other sweets, fruits and traditional delicacies.
The wedding venue itself is spread across around 10 to 12 bighas. A grand mandap inspired by Jaipur's palaces is being constructed, while a large stage is being prepared for the jaimala ceremony.
A helipad has also been arranged for VIP guests. However, even that has not escaped the weather's interference, with rain leaving the helipad wet and workers now busy getting it ready again.
RAIN TRIES TO PLAY SPOILSPORT, WORKERS KEEP GOING
For all the grand plans, the biggest challenge facing the organisers has come from the weather.
Rainfall ahead of the wedding left the grounds waterlogged, with mud accumulating at the sites prepared for the pandals, wedding ceremonies and horse racing competition. The horse track also suffered damage, while the helipad for special guests needed maintenance.
Anant Singh personally inspected the preparations after the rain disrupted the work. JCB machines were brought in to clear the affected areas, while additional soil was laid to repair and level the ground.
The organisers have also adapted the construction work to deal with the wet conditions. Instead of relying on the ground surface, iron rods are being used to raise the pandals and stages.
At night, some work has been stopped, but essential preparations are continuing. Workers have been seen making sweets and putting the finishing touches to the arrangements even after dark.
The musical programme wrapped up at around 9.30 pm, after which workers returned to their respective tasks for the wedding day. The lights, meanwhile, have turned the house and surrounding area into a brightly illuminated spectacle.
Even late at night, visitors continue to arrive at Anant Singh's residence to meet him. Supporters have taken charge of arrangements at the village entrance, managing the movement of people arriving for the celebrations.
FROM VIP GUESTS TO AN OPEN INVITATION
The wedding is also expected to attract prominent political and social personalities, besides Bhojpuri film stars.
Names such as Pawan Singh, Akshara Singh and Gunjan Singh have been doing the rounds among those expected to attend, although their presence has not been confirmed.
Anant Singh has extended an open invitation to people, conveying that they can attend the celebrations even if they have not received a formal invitation card. With the guest count expected to run into lakhs, arrangements are being made to manage the crowds and ensure food and other facilities are available.
The scale of the event has also meant that preparations are spread across several areas, from the wedding pandals and kitchens to the horse racing ground and helipad.
NOVEMBER 25: A WEDDING, A FEAST AND A RACE TO REMEMBER
From dancing to 'Rangbaaz Raja' at his daughter's haldi to handing over the keys of a luxury Defender at the tilak, Anant Singh has made every stage of the celebrations a talking point.
Now, the countdown is on for November 25. The bride and groom will begin their new journey, lakhs of guests are expected to arrive, and dozens of horses will compete for a Mahindra Thar.
The workers are racing against time, the kitchens are working through the night, and the horse track is being restored after the rain. The weather may have forced the organisers to bring in JCBs and extra soil, but the preparations are continuing.

What's next after no deal at COP31 climate talks?
The COP31 climate summit in Turkey has officially come to an end after countries failed to come to a consensus on a new deal.
The European Union and some other countries rejected a fourth draft agreement over its failure to mention a need to phase out fossil fuels, the largest driver of global climate change.
An EU representative accuses some oil states of hijacking talks, as Russia defends opposing the inclusion of such a commitment and levels direct criticism at the EU in its speech.
The talks have been the longest-running in the summit's history, with negotiations breaking down two days after they had been due to end.
BBC climate and science reporter Esme Stallard reports from Antalya, in Turkey.

Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive officer, reversing its decision to remove him just 11 days earlier following revelations about his reported extramarital relationships, including one involving a woman suspected by US officials of having links to Chinese intelligence. The announcement triggered a sharp rally in the company's shares, adding $952 billion to its market value in a single trading session.
The reinstatement followed an extraordinary intervention by US president Donald Trump, who mobilised senior administration officials, including vice president JD Vance, to persuade Nvidia's board to bring Huang back. Trump personally contacted board members to vouch for the executive, whom he considers critical to America's artificial intelligence ambitions and its economic competition with China.
According to people familiar with the matter cited by CNN, Trump had been concerned about the impact of Huang's departure on the stock market and the broader US economy. He ultimately concluded that restoring the Nvidia chief was necessary to stabilise investor confidence and prevent the country from losing a key figure in the global AI race.
The decision marked a reversal after the company’s board had publicly described his conduct as “inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms”.
Vance led White House pressure campaign
Trump tasked Vance with working directly with Huang and Nvidia’s board to facilitate the reinstatement. The vice-president became the administration’s principal emissary, using his connections in Silicon Valley to persuade board members to reconsider their position.
The Associated Press reported that Vance stepped up his involvement over the weekend to make Trump’s case to the board.
The person familiar with the matter told AP that the White House believed Vance, who had worked in Silicon Valley before entering politics, had the stature to help board members overcome their reservations about bringing Huang back.
CNN reported that Vance coordinated directly with Huang over 72 hours, assuring the board that the government had found no evidence that the CEO had committed anything illegal or threatened national security.
Commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury secretary Scott Bessent were also involved in the effort, according to CNN. Their involvement came amid reported disagreements within the administration over the handling of Nvidia chip sales to China.
Trump also contacted Nvidia’s board directly to vouch for Huang, whom he considers an important adviser on AI policy and a key figure in maintaining America's technological advantage over Beijing.
According to news agency Reuters, US attorney general Todd Blanche and director of national intelligence Jay Clayton also played roles in determining Huang was not a security risk to the US and did not see any evidence that he did anything illegal or untoward related to US national security.
Speaking to CNBC on Monday, Trump acknowledged his role in the decision. “I believe my intervention was very important,” he said.
Trump added that he had spoken to Huang on Sunday and that the executive had promised to work harder following his return.
“The board decided to do what we wanted them to do,” Trump said.
“I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it,” he added.
The president also said, “I think we have one of our great stars back in play.”
Scandal and China concerns
The intervention followed concerns about Huang’s reported extramarital relationships, including one involving Alice Huang, a woman US officials suspected could have links to Chinese intelligence. Another relationship reportedly involved a direct subordinate.
Alice Huang was an executive at Megaspeed, a company that purchased Nvidia chips, which US officials feared could subsequently have reached China. The precise nature of her alleged intelligence connections remains unclear.
Nvidia’s board said it would complete its investigation into the national security concerns. Meanwhile, the Commerce Department is adding Megaspeed to the US Entity List, restricting its access to US exports, according to a notice scheduled for publication in the Federal Register.
The financial implications of Huang’s return were immediate. Nvidia shares surged more than 30%, recording their third-best trading day on record and adding $952 billion to the company's market value. The Nasdaq Composite rose 6.51%.
Forbes estimated Huang’s fortune at approximately $143 billion, a single-day increase of $33 billion.
Huang is scheduled to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next Thursday, where questions about his conduct, Nvidia’s China strategy and the administration’s intervention are expected to remain under scrutiny.

Cumin-laced fizzy sodas are giving cola giants a tough fight in India
- Published
It began as an impromptu kitchen experiment.
Saurabh Munjal, Nikhil Doda and Saurabh Bhutna - three cousins in India's north-western Punjab state - were messing about at home post dinner one evening, when Doda casually brewed up a tangy cumin-flavoured fizzy soda using regular pantry ingredients.
They enjoyed its earthy, piquant taste so much that they decided to explore options to sell it commercially.
Cumin-laced sodas had always been sold at street-side stalls in India, but it was a broken market of local companies. Not many had built a carbonated beverage brand around the flavour.
The trio persuaded their families to invest some capital and launched Lahori Zeera in 2017. Zeera is the Hindi name for cumin.
Almost a decade on, the drink has become a bit of a sensation in India, challenging the entrenched monopoly of global cola giants, especially in the all-important mass-market ten-rupee ($0.11; £0.078) beverage category - it will close this year with revenues of $115-120m.
Its popularity reflects a growing consumer preference for distinctly Indian flavours and drinks perceived to be more healthy, say analysts.
Lahori Zeera is one of several cumin-flavoured soda brands that have mushroomed across the country over the past decade.
There's Jeeru from Mumbai-based Xotik Frujus, Campa Jeera from billionaire Mukesh Ambani-owned Campa Cola and at least half-a-dozen other variants from regional players including Fizz Jeera Masala from House of Bindu.
Bindu launched their cumin soda nearly 25 years ago, but sales were flat until some years ago, according to Megha Shankar, a director with the company.
"Now it is the fastest growing category among carbonated beverages," Shankar told the BBC. "Its contribution to our revenues has doubled from 20% to 40% in the last five years."
Soaring demand for the product has pushed House of Bindu to widen its footprint across the country, after being largely based in southern India for over two decades.
Parle Agro, external, one of India's oldest consumer brands, also rolled out its own cumin soda brand Dhishoom nationally last year after exclusively selling it in rural markets since 2012.
Online orders for these fizzy drinks, meanwhile, were up 900% this summer according to a report from one of India's online delivery companies.
The cumin frenzy is reshaping India's non-alcoholic beverages market, which was valued at $32 billion in 2024 and projected to double by 2033.
According to a report from Kotak Mutual Fund earlier this year, Lahori Zeera, Campa and other smaller challengers - now dubbed as India's "ethnic beverages market" - collectively doubled their share of India's carbonated soft-drinks market to around 15% by September last year, while the combined market share of Coca-Cola and PepsiCo fell from roughly 93% to 85%.
"This is a "Jio moment" for beverages. Just as telecom incumbents bled market share when data prices crashed, beverage incumbents are bleeding volume," the Kotak report said, drawing an analogy to the disruption caused by the entry of Reliance-owned Jio Telecom in India's telecoms market in 2016.
"In global markets, established duopolies rarely lose more than 1-2% share annually; an 8% swing in less than a year is a structural disruption."
Saurabh Munjal, CEO of Archian Foods which manufactures Lahori Zeera, told the BBC that the company has "always been in a situation where we are sold out each year. We've doubled our capacity to 1.2 million bottles per day last year and are still unable to meet demand".
For decades, the colas have had a dominant presence in India, appealing to the aspirational part of the population as lifestyle products that were cool to consume.
With millions of dollars in marketing budgets splashed out on billboards, Bollywood stars and cricket championships, they sold a very western idea of hydration to India, says Munjal.
But home-grown brands are now mounting a serious challenge with a combination of smart distribution, attractive pricing and a turn towards nostalgic Indian flavours such as cumin, raw mango, kokum fruit and tamarind.
Munjal says that for long, there has been a tendency among consumer brands in India to either westernise Indian products or "Indianise" western products. But with Lahori Zeera, which uses the tagline "apna desi thanda", meaning India's own cold drink, his desire is to change that.
Shankar says her brand has also recently launched a zero-sugar version of their cumin soda to capture the growing market for healthier non-cola drinks.
This success notwithstanding, sustaining this winning trajectory will not be easy for these ethnic beverage brands, say analysts. The very factors that propelled their rise could also limit growth.
"The million-dollar question is how big can the cumin-flavoured drink market become. And I suspect it won't become as big as the colas," Rajiv Agarwal, a professor at Mumbai-based SP Jain Institute of Management, who advises family businesses on strategies to succeed against multi-national corporations, told the BBC.
The 10-rupee price point, which accounts for the bulk of sales volumes in India's cumin-flavoured carbonated drinks market, is another double-edged sword.
While it has driven up sales, the soaring cost of plastic, packaging, sugar and other raw material amid the global energy shock could start to hit margins, which are already very thin.
Raising prices, meanwhile, could affect volumes, forcing brands to further reduce bottle sizes, something the cola companies had resorted to a few years ago.
Then there is always the threat of bigger, deep-pocketed players coming in to disrupt the category.
"Competition is extremely aggressive," says Agarwal. And the established global players are better organised in terms of systems, processes, distribution channels and bottling arrangements.
Coca Cola, which had acquired the cumin-flavoured Rimzim brand in the 1990s, is strengthening its play in this category and reportedly doubled production last year.
But the challenges haven't deterred the ambitions of the homegrown players.
"Indian flavours need to find a global spotlight," says Munjal, who is looking to tap the global market in the coming years.
"For generations, we've grown up drinking colas of the world, but I hope the next generations will drink the zeeras of India."

The reproductive-autonomy jurisprudence as evolved by the Supreme Court under Article 21 of the Constitution is rich yet narrow, focusing primarily on one side of the problem. In Suchita Srivastava v. Chandigarh Administration (2009), the Court held that reproductive choices may be exercised to procreate as well as to abstain from procreating. In X v. Principal Secretary, Health and Family Welfare Department (2022), the Supreme Court extended the right to abortion to unmarried women as an exercise of ‘decisional autonomy’.
These, and nearly all other landmark cases are concerned only with an existing pregnancy. The freedom to pursue parenthood through medical treatment, however, has surfaced only at the margins. The Delhi High Court, in 2023, allowed parole of a life convict to attempt IVF, by recognising a “right to parenthood,” but only as a claim against a barrier the State itself had erected. No court has yet asked whether the State may leave a citizen’s access to infertility care entirely to their own purse. Can a right available to the fertile but structurally withheld from the infertile be called a universal right?

Forward JJ Gabriel, who has recently turned 16, walked out on Manchester United in September and now has a verbal agreement to join Real Madrid.
Before even playing a senior game - barring friendlies - he has told Spanish newspaper Marca his "dream is to win the Ballon d'Or".
Gabriel's real name is Joseph Junior Andreou O'Cearuill - with Cypriot and Irish lineage - but he changed his name, reportedly for commercial purposes.
His father, London-born Joe O'Cearuill, played twice for the Republic of Ireland - but the highest level he played at club level was a loan spell with Brighton in League One and one minute in the Uefa Cup with St Patrick's Athletic. He has been actively involved in his son's career.
Gabriel was scheduled to become Manchester United's youngest ever player in the Carabao Cup against Brighton on 16 September, but had told the club he planned to leave by then.
How long will Gabriel have to wait for a first-team debut now? In the past 10 years Real have only handed two debuts to 17-year-olds and none to a 16-year-old.
When Real boss Jose Mourinho was asked about Gabriel on Friday, he said: "I don't have a feeling [about Gabriel]. I don't have a feeling with players who don't work with me."
In fact, Real have not even announced anything yet - despite Gabriel posting a 50-second video montage on social media saying goodbye to United this week.

Why did Real Madrid want Gabriel?
For a while now Madrid have been getting the best young talents early and turning them into Galacticos before they cost in excess of 100m euros.
Vinicius Junior and Rodrygo came that way, then Endrick - and Gabriel is seen as the next.
It fits the policy run by Jose Angel Sanchez, the director general, and Juni Calafat, head of scouting. It is a long-term bet on one of the most promising young players in the international game.
Barcelona looked at him too, and backed away because the commissions were too high. Madrid believe in the player so much that they were willing to pay whatever it took to get the deal done.
The expectations are very high and the aim is for him to reach the first team. They want him at Castilla - Real's reserve team - but the situation right now does not allow it.
Castilla and Real Madrid C cannot sign players until January, so for the time being he is expected to play for the Juvenil - the under-18s.
Madrid also learned from the Martin Odegaard period that training with the first team while playing for the B side is a bad idea. So the plan is a spell in the B side, and when he is ready, Gabriel jumps straight into the first team.
Where Madrid are less happy is with how things have unfolded. Madrid wanted to set the timing themselves and be discreet, because they do not want problems with Manchester United and do not want to upset anyone. At Real Madrid, nobody is bigger than the club.
The idea was to keep everything quiet until January and announce it then. But with Gabriel already training in Madrid, the secret was never going to last.
The super-agent behind the move
Who is Gabriel's new agent, Ali Barat?
"Players are moving to him because his reputation is that he'll get you a move to a bigger club," one Premier League club source told BBC Sport.
Dubai-based Barat does not just consider himself a super-agent, but a "boutique" super-agent.
Born in Iran and raised in London, Barat says he fell into football almost by accident after many years in international business.
After initially working as an intermediary at low-level clubs, he founded Epic Sports in January 2020.
His major football experience before that? The football game Championship Manager.
"I was always trading players," he told ESPN this year. "I was obsessed with every single player around the world."
This was not just about living out a fantasy in the real world. Barat was drawn into the profession because of the vast sums agents can earn in commission.
What makes his agency "boutique"? Unlike the top operations which have a huge number of players on their books, Epic Sports aims to have just 22 - two for each position.
This, Barat argues, ensures there is never any conflict of interest in how he represents his players.
Barat offers bespoke management of a player's career and came to prominence in the summer of 2025 when 15 of his players moved on.
This included Dean Huijsen joining Real Madrid, Nicolas Jackson moving to Bayern Munich and Xavi Simons signing for Tottenham Hotspur. Noni Madueke left Chelsea for Arsenal, and the Gunners signed Piero Hincapie.
This led to Barat being named Golden Boy Best Agent for the second time in three years.
Yet he is largely the figurehead, with agents working on his behalf around Europe. For instance, Epic has three other agents registered with the English Football Association (FA).
Barat, who also brokered Moises Caicedo's move to Chelsea, says he uses social media, and in particular influencer Fabrizio Romano, to amplify stories and agree transfers on his terms.
He is an unashamed self-publicist, too.
"Ali Barat redefines the game again," read an Epic Sports press release to announce Jackson's loan move to Bayern. No other agency seems to promote itself in this way.
The largely AI-generated video which announced Gabriel had joined Epic Sports was right on brand.
Gabriel's deal is part of a new venture: Epic Future - and this presents an ethical problem.
"It is about targeting the biggest young players, especially where they're not necessarily on the longest contracts," a Premier League source said. "And move them overseas for cheap fees.
"The original club will get a few 100,000 euros if that, and everyone else will hoover up millions and millions and millions - including his family."
Transferring a player to Europe also opens the door to future sell-on fees for an agent, which is against FA regulations.
It is this new focus on younger players which has started to cause friction at some top clubs.
No club wants to lose players they have spent years developing for nothing, only for an agent to reap the rewards.
Why is he leaving Man Utd?
Manchester United had to work hard 18 months ago to convince JJ Gabriel and his family that Old Trafford was the right place to further his football education.
The big question is, did they overpromise in doing so?
Sources close to the player eventually felt they were let down and United did not deliver on what was expected.
Certainly around Gabriel's pre-season minutes and presence in the squad for the Champions League opener against Azerbaijan title winners Sabah FK, which it was felt would be a perfect opportunity for the youngster to make his debut.
By the time the Carabao Cup tie against Brighton came round, there was no faith Gabriel would be brought on. Given United lost 3-2, there is merit in that stance.
The secondary elements are where will Gabriel develop the most?
United's academy is one of the best in England at producing young players, but given his size, will the forward benefit more from being in a less physical environment?
There has been a lot of sniping around his decision to leave United, but his stats are impressive and he is clearly a player of huge potential. United would certainly have wished the situation had not unfolded the way it has.

- In early and mid-November, people shared videos allegedly showing what they called "jellyfish UFOs" flying over various cities, beginning with a repost of a genuine video recorded in Anchorage, Alaska, in June.
- The person who recorded the Anchorage video contended the object was not a kite or balloon. However, a woman with decades of experience in flying kites, including participating in a kite-flying group in the same area, told Snopes she believed that the clip "definitely" and "100%" showed an inflatable octopus kite.
- Research of the many videos users shared found no conclusive evidence of the objects involving extraterrestrials. Rather, some clips appeared to show popular jellyfish- or octopus-shaped kites (or balloons), while others displayed signs of generative artificial intelligence.
- This story involved three kinds of videos, including some clips appearing to quite clearly show kites or exhibit signs of AI, as well as others that looked blurry and lacked conclusive information about their purported originating date and location — making the content difficult to research. As such, Snopes has not rated this article.
In early and mid-November, people shared numerous videos online appearing to show jellyfish- or octopus-shaped objects hovering high in the sky. Users referred to the alleged phenomenon as "jellyfish UFOs," with some alleging the objects were the secret reason for the U.S. air travel ground stop and other service outages.
However, Snopes' investigation of the clips failed to uncover any definitive proof of aliens. Rather, of the many videos people shared, those with identifiable locations appeared to line up with parks or beaches, suggesting the clips simply captured people flying jellyfish- or octopus-shaped kites (or balloons). Some of the clips also appeared to have been created with artificial intelligence; for example, one video clearly displaying an AI-generated content label.
Snopes has not added a fact-check rating to this article, as our standards require comprehensive details and conclusive proof to establish a rating. This matter involves numerous videos, including some quite clearly showing kites, as well as others exhibiting signs of AI or lacking definitive information about their date and location.
We contacted a handful of users appearing to originally post some of the videos and have included the responses below.
Clips' spread started with Anchorage video
People have discussed supposed "jellyfish UFO" sightings for years. For example, a video from 2024 showed an object appearing to hover above a U.S. military base in Iraq.
Going back decades, The Associated Press, citing the Russian news agency TASS, reported (archived) about an event in Petrozavodsk, Russia, on Sept. 20, 1977, involving "a huge mass of light" that "hovered over the city in the form of a jellyfish sending down a multitude of fine beams." People now refer to that story as the Petrozavodsk phenomenon.
The wave of "jellyfish UFO" videos circulating in November appeared to begin with reposts of a video recorded in Anchorage, Alaska, in June, followed by some news media outlets reporting on the matter.
For example, a Nov. 3 Reddit post (archived) of the video displayed the title, "Video taken in Alaska of a strange jellyfish object. (Kite?)."
Video taken in Alaska of a strange jellyfish object. (Kite?)
by u/FrankMurphys in InterdimensionalNHI
The Reddit user linked to Facebook user Sara Jane Osborn's original post (archived) from June 15.
We identified Osborn's location in Google Street View after seeing the words "Alaska Geologic" on a building near the end of her video — matching the west side of the Alaska Geologic Materials Center. Osborn shared with us an image of the exact location where she recorded her video while her husband, Peter Osborn, sat in the driver's seat, confirming they faced directly east.
The object hovering in Osborn's video appeared clearer than the distant mountain haze, suggesting its closer proximity to the camera.
Using Google Earth, we moved directly toward where the object hovered, traveling over or very near at least three different parks or fields — nice spots for flying kites — first the large Russian Jack Park (about 1 mile east of the Osborns' location), then Creekside Park (about 2.4 miles east) and the Muldoon Elementary School athletic field (3.3 miles east).
Interviewing Sara Osborn
In an interview via Messenger, Sara Osborn said she and her husband were driving in Anchorage and stopped to take photos of a rainbow just after 10 p.m. (Sunset in Alaska occurs around 11:30 p.m. in June.)
She sent to us multiple photos, the video and metadata proof to help confirm she didn't use AI or other editing tools to create or manipulate her content. One photo, shown below, features the object hovering at 10:13 p.m.
(Sara Jane Osborn via Facebook, Snopes illustration)
Sara Osborn said she and her husband checked some nearby parks and kept searching but didn't locate the object again. She said she didn't believe it was a kite or balloon: "It was after 10PM… People were at home, getting ready for bed to go to work the next day." She added, "Only God & the government know what it is."
In 2010, Joint Base Elmendorf–Richardson, a military base located farther north and not in the same area of the hovering object's location, reported about launching weather balloons on an Alaskan island. Those weather balloons appeared white and round, and not in the shape of a jellyfish.
A spokesperson for the military base told us via email, "We are aware of a video circulating on social media regarding a reported aerial sighting near Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson from June 15, 2026, but have no additional information to provide at this time."
Local kite group member says 'definitely' octopus kite
To learn more about the Anchorage video, we reached out by phone to Debbie Wik, who represents the Alaskiters kite flying group and lives just southwest in Kenai.
Wik, who said she's been flying kites since about 1990 and has attended kite festivals for years, told us she believed the object in Osborn's video was "definitely" and "100%" an inflatable octopus kite, "probably at least a 50-meter inflatable black and white octopus." She also said she has no knowledge of anyone in her group flying that night.
She pointed us to recent photos and videos of her flying kites over Kenai in the daytime and LED-lit kites at night. Regarding the night flying Wik said, "I thought we were gonna cause an accident because everybody was pulling over and it was really cool."
The group created an interactive map in Google Maps identifying both Russian Jack Park and Creekside Park, as well as an area just south of Creekside Park, as prime flying locations.
Other 'jellyfish UFO' videos
Several social media accounts posted collections of various "jellyfish UFO" sightings. One of those collections began with an object resembling the two distinctly striped arms of an octopus foil kite that Amazon (archived) sells with 328 feet of string.
Another collection began with a video that the Pangram AI-detection website determined contained at least some inauthentic elements. That clip possibly originated from a Facebook post. We contacted that account to ask if the user created the clip. (Snopes does not entirely rely on AI detection tools to make conclusive determinations.)
The second clip in the collection, also a slideshow, featured two women looking at two jellyfish- or octopus-shaped kites, imaking fun of people who might believe the objects are aliens. The @swanvr Threads account recently claimed ownership of that clip, saying it dated back to 2024 and that "they're kites." The remaining four clips all appeared to show kites, as well.
A third collection displayed six still images of purported "jellyfish UFO" sightings, beginning with one from Osborn's Anchorage video. As one example, a search for the text caption's words, specifically "In the skies over Nashville," located a Facebook video appearing to show the man recording the clip of a "mysterious squid," including saying, "Nah, I think it's a kite."
Another example video (archived) out of Buffalo, New York, appeared to show the view out of a hospital window toward Ralph Wilson Park, also suggesting a kite.
One of the AI-generated videos
Another video showing a dark, octopus-shaped object flying in the sky displayed the words, "Clearest video to date thanks to my Canon EF-S 55-250mm Nov. 13th Arlington, Texas."
TikTok user @silversagag told us in a private message that he used AI to generate that video using images from two sources. The clip displayed an AI-generated content label, as well.
According to an AI prompt screenshot that the user shared with us, those two sources included Facebook user Deon Morris' post (archived), in which Morris claimed he found one of the supposed "alien babies" in his backyard, as well as a December Reddit post (archived) found on an Augusta, Georgia, subreddit mentioning Columbia County and "Evans Park."
In other words, the AI-generated video appeared to originate from some authentic content — meaning photos and videos genuinely recorded in reality — though the purported Augusta-area video still showed an object resembling a kite.
(Deon Morris via Facebook)
One close-up video (archived) that Morris recorded showed fibers, with commenters believing it was an old, dirty dog toy — potentially a rope dog toy that had unraveled or a no-sew octopus dog toy. We sent a private message to Morris to ask about his post and will update this story if we receive further information.
For further reading about similar untrue, fantastical matters, we recently investigated whether a video showed a pterodactyl flying in Mexico.

De Villiers claims ball-tampering from first 2018 Test
- Published
Former South Africa batter AB de Villiers has alleged Australia were ball-tampering from the first match of their controversial 2018 Test series.
Australia captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and batter Cameron Bancroft received long-term bans for their roles in using sandpaper to alter the ball during the third Test in Cape Town.
Former Australia batter Usman Khawaja, whose new autobiography has re-started scrutiny of the scandal, has previously claimed that sandpaper was also used during the preceding Test at at Gqeberha, then known as Port Elizabeth.
Warner and Bancroft have both corroborated Khawaja's claims about that match, but De Villiers has now suggested the ball was altered during the series opener in Durban.
"It started in Durban, by the way, not in PE," De Villiers said on his YouTube channel ABD360. "I'm very happy for people to quote me on that.
"I see everyone is sort of admitting that in Port Elizabeth it also happened. I can very much tell you Durban was no different, in the first Test. Go look at the footage. Absolutely no doubt in my mind.
"We lost that first Test match in Durban with the ball reversing at a very, very interesting time. Way too early for anyone to reverse a ball at Kingsmead. Trust me, I've played a lot of cricket there.
"So whatever they did there, whether it was sandpaper or (a) nail, I don't care. The fact of the matter is they were caught and everyone knew. Just stand up and say 'we were wrong'. A lot is at stake now because they lied.
"The bowlers in particular knew because the ball doesn't just reverse. It's not your first Test match for Australia. So just stand up and say, 'guys, we were wrong'."
In a 4,000-word article last week, Bancroft said sandpaper wasn't used in Durban, where left-arm paceman Mitchell Starc finished with match figures of 9-109 as he bowled Australia to their one victory in the series.
"Casting forward to the first Test in Durban, sandpaper was not used," he wrote. "There were more traditional methods of maintaining the ball, including saliva. I cannot say with certainty whether mints or lollies were involved. Probably quarter-seam picking, this practice became so normal after my first Test."
Australia's bowling attack in the three Tests and Darren Lehmann, their head coach at the time, have consistently denied any knowledge of ball-tampering during the series.
Current Test captain Pat Cummins, who was part of the bowling attack, labelled Khawaja's claims as "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense" at a news conference earlier this month and has received backing from Cricket Australia to continue in his role.
Cricket Australia has launched an independent "forum" for players and staff involved in the scandal to voluntarily share their version of events, but it is not a full investigation and will not involve any new penalties.
"It's become really personal for all the people involved and I do have sympathy for them," added De Villiers, who played in every match in the series and retired from international cricket after its conclusion.
"Obviously not sympathy for what took place on that day and who knows how many games before then.
"I just feel they should have stuck together as a unit. They threw the guys under the bus and forced a situation like this to pop up again eight years later."
De Villiers also acknowledged that he was not an "angel" during his playing career but insisted his side had stayed within the rules of the game when working on the ball.
"I'm not playing all innocent and saying that I'm the perfect person," he said. "We all try and get the ball to reverse. We try and bounce it in. We try and do it in a legal manner and we try and push the boundaries as much as possible.
"We all have tried over the years to get the ball to do something, to get an edge, but obviously not being as stupid as to take an object onto the field and blatantly cheating."
Cricket Australia has been contacted for comment.

- The claim that the Pentagon cannot account for $2 trillion in taxpayer money is based in truth but missing some context.
- It is more accurate to say that the Pentagon cannot comprehensively account for about $2.14 trillion worth of assets, based on a November news release from the Department of Defense about its annual department-wide audit. As of this writing, DOD remains the only federal agency that has never passed an audit.
- We have left this claim unrated for several reasons, including the fact that the department is composed of many agencies, and some of them are still undergoing audits as of this writing.
- Congress passed an act in 2023 mandating that by 2028 the Pentagon must obtain a clean audit, a term used to describe when auditors find no issues with an organization's financial records. The Pentagon celebrated the progress made toward that goal in 2026, despite significant issues remaining.
- Federal auditors said that while some audits are still ongoing, the Pentagon has maintained or improved records for at least some of the agencies it oversees. However, the auditors also said that while the number of high-risk issues with financial reporting identified under "material weaknesses" may seem lower, that's because DOD has consolidated its audits, not because it's fixed the underlying issues.
Social media users claimed in mid-November that the U.S. Department of Defense is unable to account for $2 trillion in taxpayer funds.
"The military is unable to account for $2 trillion in tax payer money, but somehow forgiving student loans would be 'unfair to the American tax payer,'" one post on Facebook read. Users shared similar posts on X and other platforms.
This rumor began after the Department of Defense released its annual agencywide audit Nov. 16. The Pentagon said in a news release that more than 56% of the department's assets received a "clean audit," meaning auditors from the department's Office of the Inspector General and from independent public accounting firms found no issues with the agency's financial records for that percentage of its assets:
For the first time in Department history, clean audit opinions will cover more than 56 percent of DoW [Department of War, the Trump administration's preferred name for the Department of Defense] assets and over 90 percent of its liabilities. These figures include audit opinions expected in January and February of FY 2027.
The Pentagon has $4.87 trillion in assets, according to its fiscal year 2026 financial report (Page 19). In other words, about 44% — or about $2.14 trillion — of its assets, or resources owned and controlled by the Defense Department, are not comprehensively and cleanly accounted for.
We have left this claim unrated as the Department of Defense is composed of many agencies, and some of them are still undergoing audits as of this writing, as DOD notes. Those audits combined is what determines the Pentagon's departmentwide audit opinion.
The lack of a clean opinion also does not necessarily mean that the Pentagon has no idea where its assets are — just that it can't keep a detailed, transparent record of how it moves money around. Furthermore, reader opinions may differ on whether $2 trillion in assets are the same as $2 trillion in taxpayer money, given that the amount those assets cost at the time of purchase may be different from their current value.
We also asked department's Office of Inspector General for more information about the percentage of assets that did not receive a clean audit and await a detailed response. DOD did not immediately return a request sent outside of the agency's working hours to explain the exact details behind its 56% calculation. 
A related rumor circulating online claimed the Pentagon can't account for $31 billion worth of F-35 aircraft parts. That's a reference to a real Government Accountability Office report — separate from the audit — that found DOD's "records of its F-35 parts are outdated, inaccurate, and incomplete." The OIG's audit echoed that conclusion, finding that DOD "has not yet established an accurate, complete, or financially reportable population of F-35 property, nor implemented an IT environment capable of supporting reliable reporting."
DOD celebrates audit progress, despite major issues
Overall, DOD received a "disclaimer of opinion" rating, which means the condition of the agency's accounting is so poor, it is impossible to assess its financial records.
However, it is worth noting that the percentage of assets accounted for in 2026 is technically progress for the Pentagon, which remains the only federal agency that has never passed an audit. The Pentagon has received a disclaimer of opinion rating on every departmentwide federal audit since they began in 2018.
"This is a really big deal for us," said Jules W. Hurst III, the department's undersecretary and chief financial officer, in DOD's news release. "For the first time, by February 2027, we will have clean opinions on a majority of our assets and over 90% of our liabilities."
A clean opinion, or clean audit, means auditors have found no issues with an organization's financial records. At least one fund that the Pentagon oversees, the Medicare Eligible Retiree Health Care Fund, received the first clean opinion in its history this year.
The department's Office of the Inspector General said in the introductory memo to its report that while the Pentagon's disclaimer of opinion rating remained the same, the Department of Defense has taken "deliberate steps" to meet a congressional requirement to receive a departmentwide clean audit by 2028. For example, DOD has increased spending on auditing and overhauled its strategy toward a clean audit.
The Government Accountability Office, which has had the Department of Defense's financial management on its "high risk" list for fraud and management since 1995, said in May that DOD's "renewed focus" on a clean audit was "encouraging." However, the office said the new strategy's efforts to consolidate standalone audits of agencies under DOD oversight "potentially risks limiting accountability and transparency."
In fact, the Department of Defense Office of the Inspector General said that while the audit results seemed to suggest fewer material weaknesses — in other words, severe issues that result in a high risk of inaccurate financial reporting — that reduction comes from consolidation, not from actual resolution of the problems.
For more on the DOD's history of spotty financial records, see our in-depth look examining what the Pentagon's audit ratings actually mean.

Can a US-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo?
- Published
As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not thinking about critical minerals or billion-dollar investments.
She is thinking about getting around more easily.
The railway runs through Catumbela, near the Angolan city of Lobito, on the Atlantic coast.
For Julia, it has made travelling cheaper and more convenient.
"Before, I had to use a taxi, which is much more expensive. Now it is cheaper and easier to travel," she says.
But the railway has ambitions far bigger than improving local transport.
It is part of the Lobito Corridor, a US-backed effort to secure access to Africa's critical minerals and promote regional economic cooperation, which Washington hopes will help bring peace to conflict-torn eastern DR Congo.
Under agreements brokered by US President Donald Trump, DR Congo and neighbouring Rwanda have committed to greater economic cooperation, including more transparent mineral supply chains and regional infrastructure development.
The wider plan envisages linking these initiatives to the railway, which transports minerals from Central Africa to Western markets via Angola, rather than east to China as most do currently.
The hope is that formalising the mineral trade and encouraging investment could help curb illicit markets that have helped finance armed groups and fuel instability.
But can a railway built to move minerals to global markets also deliver peace and prosperity?
The Lobito Corridor links DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast through the Benguela Railway and the Port of Lobito.
Its importance has grown as demand for copper and cobalt rises, driven partly by the global transition to cleaner energy, as both are critical ingredients for all kinds of electrical components.
"The timing matters," says Johannesburg-based political risk analyst Wellington Muzengeza
"Electrification and the energy transition have increased the strategic importance of copper, cobalt and reliable mineral supply chains."
DR Congo is the world's largest producer of cobalt and one of its biggest copper producers, along with neighbouring Zambia. The US sees the corridor as a means to diversify mineral supplies and reduce reliance on China, which dominates much of the world's processing capacity.
A US-DR Congo strategic partnership identifies the route from the Congolese town of Sakania to Lobito as a priority for mineral exports, while the economic framework agreed by DR Congo and Rwanda envisages connecting regional infrastructure and trade initiatives to the corridor.
The project has attracted over $750m (£570m), including funding backed by the US International Development Finance Corporation and the Development Bank of Southern Africa to upgrade railway tracks, signalling systems and trains.
The railway, built in 1902 under Portuguese colonial rule, was originally designed to transport goods and minerals from Central Africa to the Atlantic coast. After years of disruption during Angola's civil war, it was rebuilt and fully reopened in 2015.
The US first got involved in the project under former President Joe Biden but backing has continued under Trump.
At Lobito's mineral terminal, the renewed ambitions are already visible.
When the BBC visited, a train carrying about 12,000 tonnes of copper cathodes from DR Congo had arrived. Workers moved the refined copper sheets into a warehouse before they were loaded on to ships bound for international markets, mostly the US.
The cargo is handled by Lobito Atlantic Railway (LAR), which has a 30-year concession to operate freight services along the corridor and manage the mineral terminal.
Chief operating officer Nicholas Gregoir says freight volumes have more than doubled since the company took over in January 2024.
LAR expects to transport about 200,000 tonnes of copper through the corridor in 2026.
For mining companies, the railway offers a shorter route to international markets.
"The Lobito Corridor is the shortest route for both Zambia and the DRC," to the Atlantic, says Kátila Vanessa Monteiro da Silva Neto, executive director of the Lobito Port Authority.
Zambia, Africa's second-largest copper producer, also plans to connect its Copperbelt to Lobito through a proposed 830km (515 mile)-railway.
But a more efficient route to market does not automatically translate into economic transformation.
"Joining a corridor is not the same as industrialising," Muzengeza says. "The test is not simply whether Zambia gains another route to the sea. It is whether that route helps build a stronger economy."
Some Angolans believe the railway's greatest value could lie in what it offers businesses and communities beyond mining.
"I call it a corridor of development," says businessman Adérito Areias.
The railway passes through some of Angola's most productive agricultural regions.
Better transport links could help farmers reach larger markets and reduce losses.
"If there isn't an artery carrying products from the interior to where there is demand, those products simply rot where they are produced," Areias says.
But the challenge is turning that ambition into reality.
The Port of Lobito handled about 1.8 million tonnes of cargo in 2025, of which around 158,000 tonnes was minerals. Its mineral terminal can handle up to 3.6 million tonnes annually.
"The port already has the capacity," says Neto. "What we need now is sufficient railway capacity and rolling stock."
For residents along the route, the benefits have been immediate.
State-owned railway operator Caminho de Ferro de Benguela (CFB), which runs passenger services, carried a record 1.6 million passengers in 2025.
LAR says it directly employs nearly 1,000 people, 98% of them Angolan.
"This job allows me to support my family," says Domingos Canhama, a father of four and a forklift operator at CFB.
"I can put food on the table, maintain a home and help support my father," he says.
Muzengeza argues that the bigger opportunity is developing local businesses in engineering, maintenance, warehousing and agricultural processing.
"Businesses in Angola need access to the railway, not just proximity to it. That means feeder roads, electricity, storage and predictable services," he says.
But can minerals and their movement along the railways line help deliver peace to eastern DR Congo, where the battle for control of mineral resources has fuelled decades of conflict?
Most recently, this has seen the M23 rebel group seize control of many mineral-rich areas.
The Congolese government says neighbouring Rwanda is backing the M23 in order to gain access to DR Congo's mineral wealth. Despite overwhelming evidence, Rwanda denies backing the M23.
The Trump-backed agreements between DR Congo and Rwanda seek to promote transparent mineral supply chains, cross-border investment and regional infrastructure, with the aim of ensuring mineral wealth does not finance armed groups.
"The US wants reliable access to minerals essential to defence, advanced technology and energy systems, while reducing dependence on supply chains in which China has substantial influence," says Muzengeza, the political risk analyst
"Lobito is therefore more than a railway but an infrastructure that can reshape trade routes and commercial power."
At a meeting in Paris in November, DR Congo urged the US to turn its strategic partnership into tangible investments, arguing that success should be measured by completed projects rather than signed agreements.
"We want the partnership to support local mineral processing, electricity access for households and businesses and peace in the east," said DR Congo's Economy Minister Daniel Mukoko Samba.
Even if more minerals move through formal channels, better infrastructure alone would not resolve the political and security tensions driving the conflict.
There is also the question of who captures the wealth. Much of the copper and cobalt transported from DR Congo through Lobito is destined for processing and manufacturing outside Africa.
While Angola can earn transit fees and create logistics jobs, much of the higher-value activity takes place elsewhere.
"When you export raw materials, you are also exporting jobs and knowledge," Angola's Foreign Affairs Minister Téte António tells the BBC.
Areias shares that concern.
"We should not export lithium but export batteries," he says, arguing that the corridor should help develop local processing and manufacturing rather than simply accelerate raw material exports.
Back in Catumbela, such debates can feel distant from everyday life.
For Julia, the railway already means cheaper journeys and easier movement.
But its ultimate success will depend on whether it can deliver more than faster mineral exports.
Whether it can also help secure lasting peace in eastern DR Congo, where the minerals are mined, remains the bigger test.

Williams, a provider of gas power to several Meta data centers, met with Environmental Protection Agency leaders in the period leading up to the agency’s recommendation to waive acid rain regulations for data-center power plants, documents obtained by WIRED show.
The oil and gas infrastructure company’s private discussions with the agency come as the Trump administration loosens a number of environmental requirements for data centers and the natural gas plants being built to power them.
“The administration is trying to relax, if not suspend for all intents and purposes, a range of regulatory requirements for these data centers,” says Joseph Goffman, the former assistant administrator at the EPA’s Office of Air and Radiation. “What this administration is trying to do, either explicitly or de facto, is take layers [of regulatory protections] away.”
In response to a list of questions from WIRED, Williams spokesperson Alex Schott said in an emailed statement that the company “is committed to developing energy solutions to enhance America’s position in the global competition for AI, while prioritizing environmental protection—including addressing legislation and regulations to modernize construction and implementation timelines.” Meta declined to comment.
In July, the EPA announced new federal guidance for states around participation in the Acid Rain Program, following inquiries from “companies and States.” The decades-old program was designed to reduce harmful emissions of chemicals that cause acid rain. Power plants that fall under the program need to submit a permit application two years before a facility comes online, and then regularly monitor emissions to ensure compliance.
That month, the EPA said that it recommends that “islanded” power plants—which are increasingly being adopted by data centers across the country—be exempt from the program. Because the program was designed for facilities that sell electricity to the grid, the EPA said, power plants that exclusively power data centers wouldn’t need to comply.
Documents obtained by WIRED from the EPA show that Williams was one of three private companies that asked regulators for guidance on the program.
In a February letter sent to the Utah Department of Environmental Quality and obtained by WIRED, Williams director of permitting Steve Hall wrote that the “current regulatory uncertainty” around power plants being built solely to power data centers has created “obstacles … for data center development in the United States.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams sent the agency this letter.
Hall wrote that the company believed its power plants “are not subject to the Acid Rain Permit program requirements, as this program was never intended to apply to sources that do not sell power to the public grid.” Getting federal guidance, he wrote, would “accelerate deployment of critical infrastructure” and “support national goals for digital infrastructure and energy reliability in the global AI race.”
The EPA said in its July announcement that the new guidance was in keeping with orders from the White House to encourage data center developers to build their own power, in order to avoid increasing utility rates for consumers. However, data center developers are also increasingly turning to private power because it’s often quicker to build their own infrastructure than wait for a grid connection. These private power plants often create more emissions than many of their on-grid counterparts.
Williams, one of the top oil and gas infrastructure companies in the country, has emerged in recent years as a power provider for data centers. As of November, Williams had at least six data-center power plant projects in states across the country. Meta is the client for at least four of those projects: four in Ohio, and one in Utah.
Calendar invites provided by EPA show that Hall and other executives were invited to at least two meetings with EPA officials, including at least one with Aaron Szabo, then the chief of the agency’s Air office, earlier this year. In an external meeting request form filed with the agency in April, Williams indicated that its request to discuss projects in Ohio and Utah—sites where it is building power plants for Meta—was “urgent.”
The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams “requested regulatory guidance for both projects” in Ohio and Utah, and that the meetings “broadly discussed air regulations.”
“EPA program offices regularly meet with stakeholders in their areas of jurisdiction,” the agency added.
Williams’ materials submitted to regulators did not specifically reference its relationship with Meta. But in its official letter on the rule recommendations, the EPA used an example provided by an unnamed company that is building a planned 500-megawatt power plant of simple-cycle natural gas engines “to exclusively power an adjacent, third-party-owned data center.” Williams’ project in Utah and two of its projects in Ohio to power Meta data centers are around 500 megawatts each.
Williams first publicly proposed the exemption to the Acid Rain Program in September 2025 in testimony to the House of Representatives from Mark Gebbia, then the company’s vice president of environmental, permitting, and regulatory affairs. In the testimony, Gebbia made several suggestions as to how EPA should change or clarify the implementation of the Clean Air Act, including exempting behind-the-meter data centers from Acid Rain Program requirements. He noted that the long timelines for the permits are “not feasible given the urgent need to install and operate gas-fired generation for AI data centers.”
The Acid Rain Program has long been considered a regulatory success that’s ensured coal plants reduce emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, pollutants that help create acid rain. The law created a cap-and-trade program for power plants, allowing them to buy and sell credits for emissions to keep national levels of the pollutants low.
Natural gas plants emit lower levels of these pollutants than traditional coal-fired power plants. The permit application for Williams’ facility to power Meta’s data center in Utah, for example, shows that it could emit a maximum of around 100 tons of nitrogen oxide and 11 tons of sulfur dioxide each year. A 500-megawatt coal plant, meanwhile, can emit thousands of tons per year of each of those pollutants.
Other local and national restrictions may limit how much of these pollutants come from natural gas plants. But Acid Rain Program regulations also created crucial reporting requirements that are now in jeopardy for data-center power plants. In the early 1990s, Congress passed an amendment to the Clean Air Act mandating that power facilities monitor and report various emissions in order to establish the program. The reporting requirement covers sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, as well as carbon dioxide, the main driver of climate change.
The Obama administration later set up a program that would separate CO2 reporting requirements, though the Trump administration has made moves to repeal that program.
Now, exempting data-center power plants from complying with the acid rain regulations may jeopardize how much information regulators eventually get about data center emissions—including CO2 emissions, Goffman says.
“If the Trump administration was not deranged, and the greenhouse gas reporting program was operating, I think the EPA would be either interpreting that program’s existing requirements to cover these gas plants, or they would be promulgating new regulations to ensure these new gas plants were reporting their greenhouse gas emissions,” he says.
Both Goffman and Carrie Jenks, who directs the Environmental and Energy Law Program at Harvard Law School, agree that the EPA’s guidance on the Acid Rain Program for data centers seems to stick to the letter of the law. The program, they say, was explicitly intended to apply only to power plants that sold power to the grid. (Some environmental groups disagree with Goffman and Jenks: Earthjustice and the NRDC sent a letter to the EPA in September challenging the agency’s interpretation of the law in its July recommendation.)
When the program was created in 1990, though, wealthy tech companies weren’t rushing to build hundreds of megawatts of private fossil-fuel power that may not ever be connected to the grid. “No one expected it to be economical to develop a bunch of power plants that wouldn’t sell the product they were creating. No one envisioned this,” Jenks says. The program “was never designed to address behind-the-meter generation,” she says.
Some estimates show that there’s more than 110 gigawatts of planned behind-the-meter gas projects in the US, with some facilities—like Amazon’s 7-gigawatt facility in Texas, and SoftBank’s 9.2-gigawatt project in Ohio—on track to be some of the largest natural gas plants in the world. Even if those facilities don’t technically qualify for the Acid Rain Program because they’re not on the grid, lawmakers could move to change requirements to make sure that these massive facilities are covered by the program.
“Congress should have the ability and the authority to say, we have this situation, it wasn’t anticipated, here is the law,” Jenks says. “If the world were working, that’s what should happen.”
