Even as Christian communities continue to face attacks allegedly from Hindutva groups across various parts of West Bengal, Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) state president Samik Bhattacharya on November 15 issued a warning to Christian missionary school, saying it they were found promoting “anti-India activities”, they would not be allowed to function.
“If any Christian missionary school, due to religious reasons, promotes anti-India activities, we will not let that school run,” he said while addressing a gathering at Birsa Munda’s birth anniversary celebrations in New Alipore, Kolkata.
“Guardians should become alert that an official at a school placed a Pakistani flag on the table of his chamber… in a school here in Kolkata. Please correct yourselves… We will let this happen in West Bengal no matter how powerful they are. All Christian missionaries can take to the streets; we are not opposed to any religion, but sitting in our state, in our country, we will not let you insult saffron [colour]… We will not allow it.”
Prior to issuing the warning, Bhattacharya claimed that a woman BJP worker was prevented from entering a “prestigious school in Kolkata” for wearing a saffron saree. “A prestigious school in Kolkata…I am not naming the school right now because a few days later I will sit outside its gates. One of our sisters, our BJP worker who was seen wearing saffron attire…was told [by the school] that ‘wearing these saris, you cannot come to school, you cannot pronounce the name of lotus flower while teaching the students.’ This is happening in the land of Kolkata where several eminent personalities have walked,” he said.
He further went on to insinuate that Christians were continuing to uphold British mentality in India. “It’s been 75 years since the British left the country, but the mentality has not left. You have come here; you are holding your establishments; you are Catholics, you are Protestants; you can propagate your religion. But remember, this government is not Babur’s government. This government is not trying to uphold British legacies. West Bengal has an independent government,” he said.
A report published by The Telegraph stated that the BJP president alleged that a reputed college in Kolkata was carrying out religious conversions in Asansol forcibly through “allurements”. “There is an obhijato (elite) college in Kolkata whose principal is carrying out religious conversion in Asansol. This cannot be allowed to continue. This is not the government of the Trinamool Congress, this is not the Left Front government…We are against political intervention in any educational institution. We want schools to create their own curriculum,” the report quoted him.
Bhattacharya, however, did not name any Christian missionary schools or colleges or provide any evidence behind the severe allegations he levelled against the community.
Upon being asked about Bhattacharya’s allegations against Christian missionaries, chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on November 17, Tuesday, told the media, “…I get information on this and verify the facts. If the information is true and a written complaint is filed, if an individual did it, action will be taken against the individual; and if it was done institutionally, we will withdraw the NOC given to the institute.”
Murshidabad, West Bengal: On a Christian missionary school in Kolkata bars a teacher from wearing a saffron sari, Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari says, “…I will verify the facts. If the information is true and a written complaint is filed—if an individual did it, action will be taken against the individual; and if it was done institutionally…”
— IANS (@ians_india) November 17, 2026
Christian Bodies Condemn Remarks, Issue Statements
The Bangiya Christiya Pariseba (BCP) in a statement on November 18 reacted to Bhattacharya’s statement saying “sweeping accusations without evidence” maligned a peace-loving community and endangered social harmony, and demanded “specific facts, accountability, and immediate legal action”.
BCP posed eight questions to Bhattacharya and the state administration, questioning the lack of legal action against alleged perpetrators of illegal conversion, if any, and the silence over recurring vigilante attacks on Christians. It asked why attacks and vandalism of prayer meetings by ‘militant groups’ had not been condemned, whether such groups were allegedly being used to intimidate Christians, and sought the status of FIRs filed in connection with alleged threats and attacks against the community in the state.
ALSO READ: Christian families in Bengal attacked, allege ‘rape and death’ threats by ‘Bajrang Dal’ members
The BCP also demanded documentary evidence of alleged conversions in Christian-run educational institutions, pointing out that millions studied in these schools, and urged ruling party leaders educated in missionary institutions to share their experiences.
The association further questioned the administration’s silence on around 50 alleged attacks on Christian prayer gatherings over the past four to five months, contrasting it with their vocal responses to issues like an official allegedly displaying a Pakistani flag or wearing a saffron saree, without conclusive evidence.
Concerns Ahead of Christmas
Following Bhattacharya’s remarks, Paritosh Canning, moderator of the Church of North India and bishop of the Calcutta diocese, on Sunday sought chief minister Suvendu Adhikari’s intervention against the rising number of attacks against the Christian community in West Bengal. Issuing a statement under the banner of Bengal Christian Council, he urged Adhikari to take appropriate measures to ensure the safety and security of Christians, churches and places of worship, to uphold the constitutionally guaranteed right of practising one’s faith.
“Our concerns are not without reason. Reports of attacks, intimidation and disruption of Christian religious activities have emerged from several districts of Bengal…These reported incidents include attacks on priests, pastors and worshippers, vandalism of churches and crosses, disruption of prayer meetings, intimidation of Christian families and interference with religious activities,” the statement read.
“These developments have caused considerable anxiety and apprehension among members of the Christian community. West Bengal has traditionally been a land of communal harmony…With Christmas approaching, the apprehensions of the Christian community have become particularly serious…the prevailing atmosphere of insecurity has raised genuine concerns about whether Christians will be able to observe their religious services and celebrate Christmas without fear or disruption,” the statement added.
Condemning Bhattacharya’s remarks, representatives of BCP and the West Bengal Association of Christian Schools held a joint press conference on November 16, Monday. Representatives of the associations dismissed the allegations of forceful religious conversion as baseless. They demanded that Bhattacharya name the two institutes and provide evidence to back his claims against Christian missionaries.
ALSO READ: Another attack on a Christian family in Bengal: Woman alleges mob assault, desecration of Bible
“A viral video has recently come to our attention. While we cannot verify its authenticity at this moment, the remarks recorded in it feature four grave allegations: claims of widespread religious conversions, an accusation that a…principal is involved in conversion activities; an allegation regarding a person wearing a saffron sari coming to a school; and a sweeping insinuation that even though the British have left, Christian missionary school administrators continue to carry a ‘British mentality,” read a statement by the representatives.
“At a time when vigilantes and hooligans are taking the law into their own hands across various districts — vandalising and launching brutal attacks on peaceful prayer meetings under the false pretext of forced conversions and desperately trying to build a fabricated narrative — the Christian community is both shocked and deeply angered to hear such an incredible, hate-mongering and aggressive speech from a usually balanced and sagacious leader like Samik Babu,” it added.
Speaking to Alt News, Moloy D’Costa, secretary of the West Bengal Association of Christian Schools and vicar-general of the Roman Catholic archdiocese of Calcutta, said, “The comments made by Mr Bhattacharya are vague. Every school has its own dress code, and there is no universal colour code. The authorities should either provide evidence or identify specific institutions and take appropriate action against them, rather than making general statements that vilify an entire community and a network of institutions.”
D’Costa also pointed out, “Several leaders in the party attended Christian missionary institutions; have they converted to Christianity? Converting to Christianity is a lengthy process. Simply visiting a church or sprinkling water is not part of that process. Accusations of forced conversion are being made from all sides, yet not a single case has been reported where anyone has been proven guilty of such actions.”
National Christian Council (NCC) state general secretary Arpan Rana strongly condemned Bhattacharya’s remarks on Christian missionary institutions, stating that “sweeping allegations without evidence” risk fostering suspicion and hostility towards the Christian community.
Rana told Alt News that Christian institutions were primarily invested in “education, humanitarian service, moral development and nation-building, not forced religious conversion,” adding that students from diverse religious backgrounds have studied in these institutions without abandoning their faiths. “Thousands of students from Hindu, Muslim, Christian and other communities have received education from these institutions while preserving their respective religious identities,” he said.
He also termed the portrayal of Indian Christianity as a legacy of British colonialism ‘historically misleading’, noting that Christianity existed in India long before colonial rule. “We expect scholarly arguments backed by evidence, not broad political claims. If any institution is found to engage in unlawful conversion, we support impartial investigations, but the entire Christian community should not be collectively accused,” he added.
Akin to other Christian associations in the state, Rana, on behalf of the NCC, urged the state government to protect Christian institutions, churches and communities, and ensure they can celebrate Christmas peacefully.
As precautionary measures, the BCP also advised churches to inform local authorities about upcoming programmes, establish a community alert system, ring church bells thrice if suspicious groups enter church premises, immediately notify police, and install CCTV cameras at vulnerable points. It also urged members to seek legal aid from BCP, maintain discipline and peaceful conduct, refrain from retaliation, and involve neighbours of all faiths and civil society members in Christmas celebrations to foster communal harmony.
Alt News has been documenting instances of hate crimes against the Christian community in West Bengal since early this year. Instances of violence, attacks, vandalism, and intimidation have often been carried out by Right-wing groups including Bajrang Dal, Vishva Hindu Parishad, and others, against individuals practising Christianity, house churches, and small Christian communities. However, in most of the cases we have reported, police action has been sparse, with fresh instances of harassment emerging regularly.

Fury reveals schizophrenia diagnosis
- Published
Tyson Fury says he was diagnosed with schizophrenia soon after his world title win over Wladimir Klitschko in 2015.
British heavyweight Fury, 38, says he heard voices in his head threatening to hurt him and his family.
In a documentary which will be released by Netflix on Friday, Fury and wife Paris describe how he was diagnosed after being admitted to hospital with a suspected heart attack in June 2016.
"Words can't explain the darkness I was in," Fury says.
"It was like a living version of the pits of hell. I thought I would end up in a padded room with the door locked, and that scared me so much.
"The anxiety was crippling me. I just could not overcome it and that's when I went and saw the psychiatrist down in London. She asked me a gazillion questions, and I ticked all the boxes. Depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder."
Doctors said Fury had suffered an anxiety attack.
Fury recalls hearing the radio talking to him, and begging Paris to get him out of the hospital because "the Illuminati" wanted him.
In the period after his victory over Klitschko, Fury gained weight and struggled with drug and alcohol addiction.
"It got that bad I was hearing voices in my mind," he says.
"I wouldn't be able to sit and have a conversation because I'd be hearing stuff in my mind.
"I didn't know where to turn and no-one knew what to do. I really needed help, or check into rehab or something.
"I never got a break from it for years. I wanted to be what I thought was normal again."
After Fury was released from hospital, a diagnosis of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder was confirmed.
The NHS describes schizophrenia, external as a form of psychosis, and symptoms can include hallucinations, delusions and muddled thoughts and speech. It says the main symptom of bipolar disorder, external is extreme changes to your mood.
Fury describes a "turning point" in 2017 when he was on a night out for Halloween.
"I went out and I was embarrassed by how I looked," he says.
"I was a fat mess and I had a glow-in-the-dark skeleton suit with full face mask on.
"I looked around and could see all the young people and I thought, 'I had the world in my hands and I threw it all away, and now I'm a fat mess addicted to alcohol'."
He says that was the beginning of a comeback which led him to focus more on his family and to return to training.
It resulted in another world title when he beat Deontay Wilder in 2020.
Fury is preparing for the long-awaited all-British heavyweight fight against Anthony Joshua in Cardiff on 11 December.
The fight will be broadcast live on Netflix.

‘CJP here to stay’: Dipke vows to fight for Goa’s land, identity; seeks scrapping of Section 39A
CJP ruled out entering electoral politics, but said it would set the agenda for the youth of the country.
The Cockroach Janata Party said it is here to stay and will continue to function as an independent pressure group to hold those in power accountable, its leaders said at an event in Panaji on Sunday.
The outfit ruled out entering electoral politics, but said it would set the agenda for the youth of the country, while adding that it would prepare a manifesto for the upcoming Assembly elections in Goa in 2027.
CJP convener Abhijeet Dipke said the movement would make the scrapping of Section 39A its “top priority”, while the outfit's spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka said the members were in it “for the long run.” Ranka highlighted remarks like “CJP it's done bro”, saying these would keep happening, but said the outfit was “here to build India.”
"'CJP is done, bro!' This will keep on happening. Because we’re here for the long run. We’re not just here to save India, we’re also here to build India. The youth of the country and the future of India is not the 75 years old mahamanav (great man)," Ranka said.

He further dispelled notions that the movement had been formed for a single protest. “A lot of people, even our own volunteers, members think it is about one movement, one protest, one resignation. CJP is here for the long haul. CJP is out to fight the long game. Cockroaches will never die,” Ranka said. He added that the outfit had been “silent” for a month because its members were on a break.
“We've been trying to spend time with our families on Diwali and already there is a small section that is writing our obituary,” he said.
Dipke vows fight to ‘save’ Goan identity, targets Section 39A
CJP convener Dipke said the organisation would back the people of Goa in their “fight” to “save” their identity, adding that the scrapping of section 39A of the Town and Country Planning Act would be the movement's top priority in its manifesto.
Section 39A, a newly introduced amendment to Goa’s Town and Country Planning Act, allows for reclassification of individual plots on Goa’s regional plan, thus opening lakhs of square metres of lands otherwise classified as orchard, agricultural or eco-sensitive for construction and development.
Dipke claimed the “loss of culture” in Goa, while claiming that the state's towns and cities had become like “any other metropolitan city.”
“The first time I came to Goa, I saw the ocean. I saw the paddy fields, I saw the gold houses, the true architecture of Goa. But now, when I landed here, it doesn't feel like I have come to Goa," Dipke said. He added, “And I think that is the biggest loss of Goa: the loss of its identity, the loss of its culture, the loss of its beautiful, beautiful architecture in its houses.”
Dipke further claimed that this “starts when they take away your land.” “First, they take away your land. Then they take away your tradition. Then they take away your culture, and at the end, they take away your anger. And this is what politicians, with the help of their land sharks, are doing,” he claimed. He further alleged, “They are here just to make money by stealing away your identity, and that is what we have to protect.”

The CJP convener responded to Goa chief minister Pramod Sawant's earlier remark wherein he said the outfit's protests in Goa were mainly led by “outsiders”. “We can ask Pramod Sawant, who always claims people are coming from outside, you are the one weho is selling Goa to your friends from outside. And that is why it is very necessary for all of us to unite,” Dipke said. He said that CJP “will stand with each and every Goan who wants to save Goa.”
“This is the promise from us that we will fight with you to save Goa, and to save your lands. Because remember, without your land, you are nothing,” Dipke added..
‘Vote chori began in Goa’: Dipke accuses BJP of ‘stealing MLAs’
CJP's Dipke, speaking at the event in Panaji, claimed “vote chori began in Goa,” while accusing the Bharatiya Janata Party of “stealing MLAs” in the state.
“Vote chori began from Goa. These people call us anarchists saying we don't believe in the constitution. I want to warn these people – in what part of the constitution is it written that the party which gets twelve seats can steal and form the government by stealing MLAs from the other party. What constitution are you following?" Dipke said. He further said, "How are we (CJP) unconstitutional? It is you who are unconstitutional, who is murdering democracy every single day.”
Dipke was allegedly referring to repeated “defections” which has helped prop up the ruling BJP government in Goa, with the party not having won a simple majority in Goa since 2012. Dipke mentioned the 2017 Assembly elections in Goa, claiming that the people's mandate was “far away” from the BJP then. In 2017, the BJP with 14 MLAs was able to form a government despite not being the single largest party.
“The murder of democracy started from Goa in 2017, when the mandate of the people was far away. That is the reason we all have to unite because if there is no value in our vote, then who are we? Who are we for them? We are just cockroaches and parasites for them," the CJP convener said. He added, "If we don't have the same rights, we are nothing but cockroaches and parasites, just like the Chief Justice of India said. And it's the reflection of their mentality that they think of us as a citizen.”
‘Not here to change the government’: CJP says will continue to function as independent pressure group
Dipke reiterated that the CJP movement was only intended as a pressure group and had no desire to seek power or contest elections.
“I just want to make it clear: we are not here to change the government. We are here to change this country for the better," Dipke said. The CJP convener said the movement would seek accountability from future governments as well.
“Tomorrow somebody else will sit on the PM chair, and he might do the same things because power corrupts. Power corrupts everybody, and that is why an independent pressure group like CJP is needed -- one that does not take power, but makes sure whoever is in power cannot take us the people of India be the people of India for granted,” Dipke said, “Because if we don't keep them accountable, they will take our land, our mountains, all our resources, just like they have been doing, not just in Goa but all over India, all over India. We need to save that. We need to save our country.”

The Prime Minister said he commends all the stakeholders whose efforts have ensured this remarkable feat.
The nationwide HPV vaccination campaign provides free, voluntary and single-dose vaccination to 14-year-old girls at designated government health facilities with parental consent.

Dalal Street emerged as a founder’s paradise in 2025, with 18 Indian startups listing on the bourses and collectively mopping up a record ₹41,248 Cr from the public markets. The surge was driven by a combination of macroeconomic tailwinds and regulatory support. While robust GDP growth projections helped revive investor appetite, SEBI’s reforms played a key role. Measures such as simplified DRHP filings reduced red tape, while more flexible ESOP rules allowed founders to retain meaningful ownership. Retail investors also fuelled the frenzy as demat accounts crossed the 20 Cr mark. The OFS component dominated public issues last year, providing liquidity to the early backers of the new-age tech companies. Post-listing performance also followed the usual curve, with investors rewarding companies that prioritised profits, sustainable growth and governance over hype. “Besides the readiness that startups showed in their unit economics, there is also an increase in the founders committing to their businesses for next couple of decades and grow their businesses by adding adjacent profit pools – something that the public markets reward handsomely,” said Ashish Kumar, cofounder and general partner at Fundamentum Partnership. Building on the momentum, seventeen new-age tech companies have already made their D-Street debut so far this year. Of these, ESDS Software Solution, Klassroom, RentoMojo, SEDEMAC, Kissht, LEAP India and Shiprocket made a bumper debut on the bourses. Nevertheless, the IPO pipeline remains strong. Twenty five startups have already filed their DRHPs with SEBI, while over 25 are in various stages of finalising their IPO plans. Unicorns like OYO and Razorpay alone could raise nearly ₹20,000 Cr in 2026, making it one of the biggest years for startup IPOs. However, recalibration is likely to define 2026 as investors are expected to prioritise strong fundamentals, profitability and low cash burn when backing new-age tech companies. “IPO-bound startups in 2026 will be increasingly defined by their ability to demonstrate predictable cash flows, sustainable unit economics, and operational discipline rather than headline growth alone. Public market investors will place greater emphasis on governance, capital efficiency and long-term value creation, favouring companies that balance scale with financial prudence,” Orios Venture Partners’ managing partner Rehan Yar Khan told Inc42. There are other challenges as well. Average retail subscription levels are moderating, while foreign institutional investors (FIIs) are pulling back in droves, reflecting caution amid geopolitical tensions and muted secondary market performance. The ongoing conflict in West Asia has further complicated the situation. Yet, the overall outlook remains bullish for new-age tech IPOs. Maturing business models, deeper domestic capital pools and an evolving regulatory framework favouring transparency position India as a leading startup IPO hub. Capital Markets, DAM Capital Startups That Have Taken The IPO Plunge In 2026 AceVector Founded by Kunal Bahl and Rohit Bansal, AceVector traces its roots to 2010, when the duo founded ecommerce platform Snapdeal. Over the years, this umbrella company expanded to include listed ecommerce enablement startup Unicommerce and house of brands Stellaro Brands. The three companies unified under the AceVector banner in 2022. Now, three years on, the consolidated entity is gearing up for a public market debut. Kicking off its IPO proceedings, AceVector filed its confidential DRHP with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) in July 2025. The regulator greenlit the offering in November 2025. Almost a year later in September 2026, AceVector filed its red herring prospectus with the SEBI, which outlined a fresh issue of shares worth ₹287 Cr and an OFS component of up to 4.16 Cr shares. It had also set a price band of ₹30-₹32 per share, valuing the company at up to ₹1,741.4 Cr at the upper end of the spectrum. Subsequently, AceVector’s public issue was oversubscribed 4.93X, receiving bids for 36.61 Cr shares against 7.42 Cr shares on offer. The company eventually made a weak debut on the exchanges on October 5. Shares of AceVector listed at ₹28.30 on the BSE, a discount of 11.6% to its issue price of ₹32 per share. On the NSE, the stock debuted at ₹28.32, an 11.5% discount to the IPO price. On the financial front, AceVector’s operating revenue rose 29.2% to ₹510.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹395 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, losses also shrank nearly 64% to ₹45.5 Cr versus ₹126.3 Cr in FY25. Amagi Founded in 2008 by Baskar Subramanian, Srinivasan KA and Srividhya Srinivasan, Amagi offers a comprehensive cloud-based suite that enables broadcasters to create, manage, distribute, and monetise content worldwide. The platform also provides advanced broadcast and targeted advertising tools tailored for both traditional TV and streaming services. The company filed its DRHP with SEBI in July 2025 and secured the markets regulator’s approval in November that year. In January 2026, Amagi filed its red herring prospectus (RHP), detailing a fresh issue of ₹816 Cr and an OFS component of up to 2.69 Cr shares. Subsequently, the public issue closed with an oversubscription of 30.2X. The company had set a price band of ₹343–361 per share for its public issue, valuing it at ₹7,966 Cr (nearly $885 Mn) at the upper end of the spectrum. The SaaS major’s shares made a lacklustre debut on the stock exchanges. The stock listed at ₹317 apiece on the BSE, a discount of 12.2% to the issue price of ₹361. On the NSE, it listed at ₹318 per share, 11.9% below the issue price. Financially, Amagi turned profitable in H1 FY26, reporting a net profit of ₹6.5 Cr as against a net loss of ₹66 Cr in H1 FY25. Operating revenue rose 35% YoY to ₹704.8 Cr. Aye Finance Founded in 2014 by Sanjay Sharma and Vikram Jetley, Aye Finance is an NBFC that leverages its AI-powered credit assessment platform to offer loans to small businesses across India. The company has raised $500 Mn to date from marquee investors such as Google, ABC Impact, and Dutch development bank FMO. In December 2024, Aye Finance filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, and received the markets regulator’s approval for its listing in April 2025. Nearly a year later in February 2026, the NBFC filed its RHP with SEBI for an ₹1,010 Cr IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹710 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹300 Cr. The company’s public issue closed with an undersubscription of 97%, with investors cumulatively bidding for 4.42 Cr shares against 4.55 Cr shares on offer. Shares of the company made a flat debut on the bourses, listing at the issue price of ₹129 on the BSE and the NSE. On the financial front, Aye Finance’s net profit declined 40% YoY to ₹64.6 Cr in H1 FY26, while operating revenue rose 21.8% YoY to ₹843.5 Cr during the year-ago period. ESDS Software Solution Founded in 2005 by Piyush Somani, ESDS provides cloud computing, data centre, managed services, and AI-led digital solutions to government and enterprise customers. It operates five data centres in Navi Mumbai, Nashik, Bengaluru, Mohali, and Noida. The data centre company claims to have served 2,501 customers in the fiscal year ended March 2026, with an average revenue per customer of around ₹19 Lakh. Backed by ace investor Ashish Kacholia, ESDS Software Solution has raised nearly $47.3 Mn in funding to date. ESDS first attempted to go public in September 2021 but the plan failed to materialise due to aftershocks of the pandemic. The company then refiled its papers in March 2025 and received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in December 2025. As per its RHP, ESDS Software Solution’s public issue consisted solely of a fresh issue of shares worth ₹720 Cr. Its public issue, which stretched between August 28 and September 1, closed with an oversubscription of 135.88X. Subsequently, shares of the company made a stellar debut on the bourses, listing at ₹757 on the NSE, a premium of 76.5% over the issue price of ₹429. On the BSE, the stock listed at ₹746.30, marking a gain of nearly 74% over the issue price. On the financial front, the company reported a consolidated net profit of ₹120.8 Cr in FY26, up 117% from ₹55.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Its operating revenue rose 30.7% to ₹472.2 Cr from ₹361.3 Cr in FY25. Fractal Founded in 2000 by Srikanth Velamakanni, Pranay Agrawal, and Ashwath Bhat, Fractal is a SaaS unicorn that offers AI-powered analytics solutions to enterprises globally. Backed by TPG Capital, Khazanah Nasional, and Apax Partners, the startup has raised $800 Mn to date. It achieved unicorn status in 2022 and was last valued at more than $2 Bn. In August 2025, the SaaS unicorn filed its DRHP with SEBI, and received the markets regulator’s approval in November 2025. The company’s ₹2,833.9 Cr IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹1,023.54 Cr and an OFS worth up to ₹1,810.4 Cr. The public issue closed with an oversubscription of 2.66X, with investors placing bids for 4.95 Cr shares against 1.86 Cr on offer. Fractal’s shares made a lacklustre debut on the exchanges and listed at ₹876 on the NSE, a discount of 2.7% to the issue price of ₹900. On the BSE, the shares listed flat at ₹900. On the financial front, Fractal’s profit declined about 3% YoY to ₹70.9 Cr in H1 FY26, while operating revenue grew 20% YoY to ₹1,559 Cr. Kissht Founded in 2015 by Ranvir Singh and Krishnan Vishwanathan, Kissht is a digital lending platform that offers personal and business loans up to ₹5 Lakh. It uses AI and machine learning to assess creditworthiness. It also offers health insurance products and credit against property. The startup has secured over $140 Mn till date from investors such as Vertex Growth, Brunei Investment Agency, Endiya Partners, and Ventureast. The lending tech startup filed its DRHP in August last year and received SEBI’s nod to proceed with its public listing in January 2026. As per its RHP, its IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹850 Cr and an OFS component of up to 44.4 Lakh shares. It had set a price band of ₹162-₹171 for the public issue, which was oversubscribed 9.5X. Subsequently, Kissht made a stellar debut on the bourses on May 8. The lending tech startup’s shares listed at ₹191 a piece on the BSE, a premium of 11.7% to the issue price of ₹171. On the NSE, the stock listed at ₹190, up 11.1% from the issue price. On the financial front, the company reported a net profit of ₹199.3 Cr in 9M FY26, while operating revenue stood at ₹1,569.9 Cr during the period under review. Klassroom Founded in 2016 by the mother-sons trio of Alka, Dhruv, and Dhumil Javeri, Klassroom is an edtech startup that operates at the intersection of offline and online coaching. It operates 30 offline partner centres that cater to both academic and skill-development needs. It also collaborates with state governments, private companies and education institutions to deliver academic and skilling programmes. The edtech startup also offers an AI-powered education OTT app that features over 100 courses for classes 8 to 12, and claims to have a footprint of over 4 Lakh registered users across the country. The startup raised over $2 Mn in private rounds from the likes of actor Suniel Shetty, ah! Ventures, LetsVenture, CPT Family Trust, Growth Sense and others. Kicking off its IPO proceedings in February 2026, Klassroom filed its DRHP with the BSE for an SME IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of up to 19.89 Lakh shares and an OFS component of up to 4.66 Lakh shares. The startup subsequently received the in-principle approval from BSE to move ahead with its public offering in May 2026. It had set a price band of ₹151 to ₹159 for the issue, looking to raise ₹39 Cr at a valuation of ₹148.1 Cr. Subsequently, the startup’s public issue closed with an oversubscription of 1.46X. Shares of Klassroom listed on the BSE SME on August 7 at ₹170, a premium of 6.92% to the issue price of ₹159. With this, the company became the second listed edtech startup in the country, after PhysicsWallah. On the financial front, Klassroom posted an operating revenue of ₹23 Cr in FY26, up 128% from around ₹10 Cr in the year prior. Meanwhile, net profit jumped nearly 162% to ₹7.6 Cr from ₹2.9 Cr in FY25. LEAP India A brainchild of Sunu Mathew, LEAP India provides supply chain solutions through asset pooling, enabling companies to share pallets, containers, and other assets. Founded in 2013, the platform also offers inventory management, transportation, returnable packaging and tool repair. It also sells electric and fossil fuel-powered forklifts through its subsidiary TRON. LEAP India has raised over $184 Mn till date from investors like KKR and Sixth Sense Ventures. The startup first attempted to list on the bourses in 2022, eyeing a ₹1,000 Cr listing. But the plan was later shelved amid market volatility. Reigniting its IPO plans, the logistics tech startup then filed its DRHP with SEBI in August 2025, and received SEBI’s nod in December 2025. In August 2026, the company filed its RHP with SEBI for an IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹480 Cr and an OFS component of up to ₹2,000 Cr. The company then set a price band of ₹151 to ₹159 for its public issue, which eventually closed with an oversubscription of 8.38X as investors bid for 96.32 Cr shares as against 11.49 Cr shares on offer. Shares of LEAP India eventually made their debut on the bourses on August 14, listing at a premium of about 4.4% to the issue price of ₹159. The stock got listed at ₹166 on the BSE and ₹165.90 on the NSE. Financially, LEAP India’s net profits zoomed 65.3% to ₹62.3 Cr in FY26 as against ₹37.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, operating revenue climbed 56.4% to ₹729.5 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹466.5 Cr in FY25. Moneyview Founded in 2016 by Puneet Agarwal and Sanjay Aggarwal, Moneyview started off as a personal finance platform before pivoting to digital lending. Today, it offers services such as UPI payments, gold SIPs, fixed deposits, digital gold, home loans, BNPL and insurance. The company claims to manage over ₹19,800 Cr in AUM and has raised more than $250 Mn in funding. It competes with players like listed fintech MobiKwik, IPO-aspirant Navi, and MoneyTap. It entered the unicorn club in 2024. In March 2026, the fintech startup filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO. It then received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in late-June 2026. In September 2026, the fintech unicorn filed its RHP. outlining an IPO with a fresh issue of shares worth ₹750 Cr and an OFS component of up to 10.04 Cr equity shares. The startup’s public issue then closed with an oversubscription of 98.46X, led by QIBs and NIIs. The digital lender made a bumper debut on the exchanges on October 1, with its shares listing at ₹55.6 on the BSE, a premium of 64% over the issue price of ₹34. On the NSE, the stock listed at ₹55, marking a premium of nearly 62% over the issue price. Moneyview’s operating revenue grew 43.3% to ₹3,351.2 Cr in FY26 from ₹2,339.1 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. Meanwhile, net profit rose a marginal 1% to ₹242.7 Cr in the fiscal under review as against ₹240.3 Cr in FY25. Purple Style Labs Founded in 2015 by Abhishek Agarwal, Purple Style Labs is an omnichannel luxury house of brands featuring fashion labels like Pernia's Pop Up Studio & Shop, Wendell Rodricks, and Hemant Trevedi. It operates over 12 Pernia's Pop-Up Studio experience centres across India. Backed by Alchemy Capital Management, Bajaj Holdings and Investment, and Minerva Ventures, the startup has raised more than $78 Mn to date. In September 2025, the D2C brand filed its DRHP with SEBI for its public issue and received the markets regulator’s nod to float its IPO in January 2026. It then filed its RHP with SEBI in August 2026 for a public issue, which consisted entirely of a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹680 Cr, with no offer for sale component. Subsequently, Purple Style Labs’ public issue opened for subscription in late August 2026 and closed with an oversubscription of 1.29X, receiving bids for 88.54 Lakh shares against 68.49 Lakh shares on offer. Shares of the company made a muted debut on the bourses on September 7. The stock listed at ₹535 on the NSE, 6.96% lower than the issue price of ₹575. On the BSE, the shares listed at ₹539, representing a discount of 6.26%. On the financial front, the startup’s consolidated net loss widened 51.5% to ₹285.4 Cr in FY26 as against ₹188.4 Cr incurred in the previous fiscal year. Operating revenue for the fiscal rose nearly 14% to ₹557.8 Cr from ₹489.9 Cr in FY25. RentoMojo Founded in 2014 by Geetansh Bamania and Ajay Nain, RentoMojo is an omnichannel rental platform to lease appliances, furniture, and furnishings. The startup operates an app, website and physical stores. It operates 20 warehouses and 82 offline stores across 29 cities. Backed by Accel, Chiratae Ventures and Bain Capital, the startup has raised over $45 Mn in funding to date. Hopping on the IPO bandwagon in March 2026, the rental platform filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO and received SEBI’s nod to float its public issue in July 2026. In September 2026, the startup finally filed its RHP with SEBI for an IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹150 Cr and an OFS of up to 2.7 Cr shares. It had also set a price band of ₹384-₹404 per share for its IPO. The public issue opened for bidding on September 9 and closed on September 11. The IPO was oversubscribed 72.88X, receiving bids for 158.68 Cr shares against the 2.18 Cr shares on offer. Shares of RentoMojo made a strong stock market debut on September 17. The stock listed at ₹482.45 on the NSE, a premium of 19.42% over its issue price of ₹404. On the BSE, RentoMojo opened at ₹480, up 18.81% from the issue price. The IPO opened despite RentoMojo cofounder and former COO Nain earlier filing a petition before the NCLT’s Bengaluru bench to stall the IPO proceedings. Alleging oppression and mismanagement, the plea claimed that incomplete or inaccurate information was shared with him and sought to declare his 2023 sale of 2,223 shares void ab initio. On the financial front, RentoMojo reported a profit after tax of ₹104.3 Cr in FY26, up 142% from ₹43.1 Cr in the previous fiscal, aided by a tax credit of ₹36.6 Cr. Meanwhile, operating revenue rose 45.5% to ₹387 Cr during the year under review from ₹266 Cr in FY25. SEDEMAC Founded in 2007 by IIT-Bombay professor Shashikanth Suryanarayana and his students Pushkaraj Panse, Amit Dixit, and Manish Sharma, SEDMAC designs electronic control systems for mobility and industrial applications. The deeptech company produces motor control units, integrated starter generators, fuel injection systems, genset controllers, and small industrial powertrains. On a sweltering July morning, in the middle of an empty playground in suburban Denver, two extremely fit, sweaty, shirtless male influencers are tussling in the dirt.
“The guy on top who’s in control, we call that position riding,” one of the grapplers, Carlos Monteon Jr. pauses to explain to a group of eight similarly fit, sweaty, nearly all shirtless men who are watching the action in a circle. Monteon is a wrestler and influencer from Arizona, with pomelo-sized biceps, glossy shoulder-length hair, and more than 675,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram. He turns to his demo partner, Johnny Cole, a rangy, then 28-year-old content creator (59,000 TikTok followers) with a penchant for slutty tank tops. “And this one is called the Saturday night ride.”
Monteon and Cole continue scuffling. The match ends with Monteon straddling Cole, their faces inches apart, their torsos glistening. The scene looks like a JV wrestling match.
The other men pair up to take turns grappling. Two cameramen circle them as a drone hums overhead.
“Yes, testosterone!” one influencer yells.
“And estrogen!” Cole adds. “Both of them together, as one!”
I’m at Hey Brother House, a content incubator that hosts weeklong retreats for male social media influencers. The organization teaches men and boys “to embody healthy masculinity, fully process emotions, embrace authenticity, and show up as compassionate, empathetic community leaders,” according to its website.
Cole, the founder of Hey Brother, helms the project with two other house leaders. Jonathan Jacobs, an affable 37-year-old who owns a digital marketing agency in Los Angeles, is wearing a brown cap that says “Male Friendship.” Matthew Echelman, a 35-year-old Brooklyn-based filmmaker, has hired two crew members to film the whole thing for a possible future documentary. Funded by a grant of more than $180,000 from an initiative called the Young Men and Media Collective, Hey Brother House’s goal is to flood 18-to-25-year-old men’s social media feeds with content that will (hopefully) make them less terrible.
The house itself is a rented stucco McMansion next to the Green Valley Ranch Golf Club, a residential community just outside Denver. In some respects, it looks like your average fratty domicile: There’s a Nintendo Switch console in the living room, where the boys play Mario Kart; a basement decked out with fitness equipment, a sauna, air hockey, and Foosball; and a makeshift indoor putting green. But there’s also a strict house alcohol ban, remote-controlled bidets, a box of wigs, swag boxes filled with fuchsia “Redefining Masculinity” T-shirts, and a wall covered in Post-Its of “gifts” the men can give each other, including “laying down on couch or blanket in park with my head on your lap.” There’s even a room—the “Man Box”—for testimonials, where the “cast members” can speak directly to the camera about their day. It’s reminiscent of reality TV, except most everyone is aware of bell hooks’ All About Love: New Visions, and they are explicitly here to make friends.
These guys are all in Denver because, as Cole puts it while he smokes Marlboro Lights on the porch, “men and boys are not doing well. And they have not been doing well for a long time.” The evidence supporting this is manifold: Young men are less likely than their female counterparts to finish high school and then enroll in college. They’re dropping out of the job market, and they’re more likely to report loneliness and isolation, as well as more likely to die by suicide.
Part of the problem is the manosphere, the social media ecosystem populated by looksmaxxers, incels, AI-touting hustle bros, and peptide-injecting fitness influencers. Initially a relatively fringe coalition, the “manosphere” has evolved into an online force to be reckoned with, thanks to the massive success of influencers like Jordan Peterson, a former academic who has advocated for all-meat diets and climate-change denialism; and, later, Andrew Tate, a failed kickboxer turned minor webcam impresario, who is currently facing more than 40 criminal charges in the UK and Romania, including trafficking and sex crimes. By preaching traditional masculinity as a path toward self-empowerment, so-called manosphere influencers have appealed to an audience of young men disillusioned by the rise of identity politics. Social media algorithms have happily amplified that message: By 2023, clips featuring Tate had more than 13 billion views on social media platforms.
During the 2024 election, an estimated 67 percent of white male zoomers voted for Trump, resulting in a flurry of discourse about the manosphere’s power in channeling the frustrations of young men. “[They’ve] never had brotherhood or friendship,” Cole tells me. “They’ve never had another man look them in the eyes and say they’re worthy.” Men like Tate are successful, he says, because they “weaponize this insecurity and this fragility and give them a scapegoat and say, ‘If you buy my course and you learn how to drop-ship, or come to my alphas-only elite men's circle, then you’ll become a high-value man.’”
Of the three Hey Brother House leaders, Cole is the only one in the demographic the creators are trying to reach. He’s 6'4" and built like a varsity swimmer, with translucent green eyes, gray-painted nails, and light brown hair, which he dyes green and magenta for a short while after he leaves the house. He characterizes his work trying to reach young men as something akin to a divine calling.
“I’m a white man who was a college rugby player, and I do jujitsu, but I also wear earrings and talk about feminism online,” he tells me. “Some of these guys think I’m performative, but in my experience, when I work with men and boys in person, they love me. They've never experienced a man who's a near peer who calls them into accountability, who offers them hugs and encouragement and support. In a looksmaxxing world, for these young guys I’m someone to look up to, literally and figuratively.”
This is where the Hey Brother House comes in: to teach progressive-leaning, male creators how to create content that captures the attention of the Kick-streaming, Zyn-sucking, butt-cut-sporting contingent. The goal is to adopt the visual hallmarks of the manosphere—slick editing, dynamic hooks, fast-paced montages—and apply those to what the house calls “healthy masculinity” content: dudes thrift-shopping together and picking out outfits, or guys playing golf while also wearing pink. “What we're not gonna do is stand in front of a camera, wag our fingers, and say, ‘I think that the patriarchy is the fucking worst thing in the world,’” Cole says.
Of course, there’s plenty of content for young men on social media that does not encourage men to become webcam pimps or forcefully hit themselves in the face with hammers, a la Clavicular. But much of the content in the “healthy masculinity” space is filled with academic jargon and feminist buzzwords. Or it’s more along the lines of Joe Rogan–infused, “Thunderdome-style” masculinity. (Think Instagram posts of white men with tribal tattoos weeping in the desert, with a caption promoting an online crypto investing class.) The Hey Brother House aims to teach male influencers how to promote values like empathy and vulnerability, via content about wrestling or fitness or style or financial advice. “It’s sugar with the medicine,” Cole says.
In selecting the initial cohort for the Hey Brother House, Cole, Echelman, and Jacobs had to strike a delicate balance: They wanted creators who would be “mission-aligned,” as Jacobs put it, but who don’t exclusively make political content. Out of more than 130 applicants, they selected eight men. Some were leftist commentators like Jerry Zeng (133,000 Instagram followers), a 29-year-old, tatted, Jacquemus shorts-wearing video essayist from Houston, and Ian Lightfoot (1 million Instagram followers), an immaculately-eyebrowed, now 26-year-old whose Instagram bio proffers “positivity, popcorn, and bite-sized politics.” Others were more conventional lifestyle influencers like Sean Jones, a premed student who makes cute date-night videos and productivity vlogs, and the Houston-based trainer Stephen Marmolejos (180,000 TikTok followers), who posts fitness content and does sponcon for brands like Corona and Thayers. One, the artist and dancer Mars Wright (195,000 TikTok followers), is a trans man who has never lived in a house with cis men before. “I kind of feel like I’m entering the cafeteria scene in Mean Girls,” he told me before he got to Denver.
I arrive at the house from my hotel to find the guys midway through a vulnerability exercise in the living room. (For four days, I was given almost total access but was politely asked not to attend the first day of exercises, so the men could bond.)
I quietly take a seat on a corduroy couch as the men stand in two parallel lines, facing their partners and taking turns answering the question: “What would you know if you really knew me?” All speaking at once, they say things like: “my father,” “my angry feelings,” “even my best relationship,” “Weight Watchers.” They are mic’d, and the cameras are out in full force, zooming in as the men embrace and thank each other for listening. Some are crying.
Later, the guys sit in a talking circle—one of many I would witness—and unpack their feelings. This is the first time some of them, particularly the brawnier health-and-fitness influencer types, have had such intimate conversations with other men, talking about their marriages, surviving domestic violence, trauma, addiction. “I started out with vague surface-level things that were quirky,” Monteon says afterward, “but at the very end I felt safe enough, and I revealed way more than I expected to.”
Cole, who leads the exercise, nods empathetically. “You can’t heal if you don’t reveal,” he says, the men snapping in assent. (There is a lot of affirmative snapping at the house; there is also repeated use of terms like “aligned,” “affirmed,” and “container,” a reference to a therapeutic trauma-processing modality. I heard about containers a dozen times, only once in the context of a physical vessel.)
The next morning, when I meet the guys for the first full day’s activity—a trip to a thrift store where the men select outfits for each other—approximately 40 percent of them are hungover from karaoke the night before, as well as the day of emotional disclosures. (As Zeng put it to me, “there’s been a lot of trauma-dumping.”) But they seem genuinely psyched for the activity, which is intended to culminate in filming a wholesome “dress your bro for a night out”–type video.
“It’s a lot of pressure. I’ve never shopped for another dude, [or] heard a man compliment another man’s outfit,” Chris Petrone (1.6 million TikTok followers), tells me. “At first I was nervous, but then I was like, let’s get funky.” A baby-faced 31-year-old who lives in Florida, Petrone is one of the most successful creators in the Hey Brother House, thanks in part to a 2021 viral video in which he advocated for men to stock tampons in their bathrooms for female guests; for about a year, he had “the CEO of tampons” in his bio.
If they are nervous, they don’t show it. Monteon, who arrives in a Movember cap and brown sweats, leaves with jeans and a brown and white geometric-patterned button-down, looking like a 1970s Tiger Beat centerfold. And when Lightfoot tries on a purple and yellow cropped windbreaker, Wright and Josh Kennedy, a 29-year-old mustachioed, Wichita-based personal trainer, snap in assent. “That was literally made for you,” Kennedy says.
The Hey Brother House was conceived, at least in part, as a content incubator. But aside from the documentary film crew being present for almost every activity, not a ton of content is actually being made. Occasionally, I turn a corner and see guys editing footage on a laptop or someone filming multiple takes of a house tour in the foyer.
Instead, the dudes seemed focused on … being dudes. They played Mario Kart and went for runs. They talked about what dog breeds they would be. “I am not a scary dog,” Jones said. “And I do believe I am majestic at times.”
Even Wright, who was initially anxious about living in a house with cis men—some of whom had never met a trans man before—quickly bonded with the other members. “I've always wanted to be in community with other men and feel like I belonged and like I was one of them,” he says. “And honestly, I didn’t really believe that a lot of men were having these conversations until I was behind closed doors with them.”
The bros are sitting in the living room for a content brainstorming session. They are watching a slew of manosphere clips, which Cole says embody the three “Rs” of masculinity: “relentlessly rich and ripped.” He then shows a few examples of Reels that he identifies as “really brother-core coded”: a challenge video of men guessing the drinks that have been thrown in their faces, or tips for how men can protect their girlfriends from drink-spiking at bars. The goal, says Jacobs, is not to “attack the messenger” by making fun of Andrew Tate or Jordan Peterson because “that puts people on the defensive.” The men volley around a few ideas, which are similarly wholesome and tongue-in-cheek: golf cart racing, a parody of Jordan Peterson, rating each other’s hugs.
Then Wright pitches an idea for an “ask a trans person” video series, and the warm brotherly vibes start to shift. Wright prefaces his pitch by saying that, during his time in the house, a few of the other members had unintentionally “asked him questions that you should never ask a trans person.” Though he doesn’t name names or call anyone out specifically, he proposes that the snafu serves as a teaching moment for cisgender men watching Hey Brother House content.
“Trans people don’t believe that any cis men care about them at all,” Wright says. “I want to show my community that there are men who care for them and would stand up for them and would be willing to be put in a situation that makes them a little uncomfortable.”
Many of the guys are on board, but Cole visibly bristles at the suggestion, saying the idea causes him “reservation [and] anxiety” due to the possibility of it generating backlash from LGBTQ viewers.
“I wasn’t worried about being canceled,” he tells me later. “I was worried about the emotional and energetic impact of that series when we, as a container of men, had not addressed the emotional and energetic impact of things that had been said offline.” But this wasn’t how Wright interpreted it. “I was really shocked he reacted like that,” he says. “He’s one of the few cis men to say that trans people really belong, and he invited me here, which was a dream come true. And it’s so gut-wrenchingly painful to see somebody react to you like, ‘Well, I don’t know how this is going to make me look.’”
The impact of the conflict doesn’t become clear until the next day, when members of the House are abruptly summoned upstairs for a “tribunal.”
The vibes are off almost immediately. The House members clearly have no idea what the purpose of the meeting is and are even more flummoxed when one of the camera crew members asks them to head back down and come up again, so they can get a better take. They sit in a circle, baffled, as Echelman, not Cole, opens the meeting by reading a seven-minute statement off his iPhone. Echelman, the documentarian, has largely been absent from the House activities. He occasionally chimes in during meetings and with video pitches during the brainstorm, including “a haunted house, but the ghosts are subverting gender expectations.”
“In line with safety and consent, some things have arisen over the course of the house around conflict that I think it's important to not shy away from, but welcome and embrace and talk through,” he reads. “Rather than let that pass quietly, we want to name how we hold conflict here. Conflict isn't a failure of this space. It's where we practice communication, accountability, and care. And holding space means letting someone name their experience without filtering it.” Then Echelman opens the floor for questions.
Immediately, someone says that they’re confused. “I echo that sentiment,” Cole says. “Are there things that you would like to name that you have observed in this space which prompted you to write that and call this meeting?”
Echelman’s explanation lasts an additional five minutes, over the course of which two things gradually become clear to everyone present: (1) this meeting is about Cole, and (2) he had no idea. Echelman accuses Cole of unintentionally abusing his leadership position to shut people down, and he brings up a critique raised by one house member that the “dress your bro” thrifting activity could be perceived on social media as “poverty porn” or depriving resources from low-income communities. (Echelman’s own “haunted house for toxic masculinity” pitch is not specifically mentioned.) “In a leadership position, it's our responsibility to, even if we’re feeling something in the moment, not to make it about us but someone else being so vulnerable and opening up to us,” he says.
The tribunal, several house members told me afterward, was a disaster. As the men splinter off to go rock-climbing or golfing, Lightfoot tells me, “It felt less like an authentic conversation and more like a reality TV show.” A visibly upset Wright says he had confronted Cole privately about the brainstorm and specifically told Echelman that he did not want to have a meeting in front of the cameras with the group about what happened. To hear him tell it, he was less angry than disappointed. “Their hearts are in the right place,” he says of the House leaders. “They’re working tooth and nail, day and night, to make a difference. But we’re still so far from where we need to be.”
Later, Echelman will dispute others’ characterization of the tribunal: “Plenty of people after the conversation said that we broke the glass ceiling, because we could finally be open and honest with one another,” he tells me later.
He isn’t entirely wrong. After the initial confrontation with Cole, some of the men brought up their own minor conflicts from Hey Brother House. Without exception, they had been addressed graciously and without grandstanding. There was no bluster for the cameras, no aggression, no dick-measuring; none of what you would come to expect from a group of men in conflict with each other. They listened. They affirmed. They told each other how grateful they were for the experience of being there together. Even if the house leaders were in conflict, the creators themselves were “synced up completely,” Wright tells me. “I look at any one of them, and I know they would make me feel safe and comfortable.” It didn’t necessarily make for compelling content, but it did seem like they had taken Cole’s earlier lesson to heart: you can’t heal if you don’t reveal. (Snaps).
Cole, Echelman, and Jacobs are now selecting the cohort for the next House, which will take place in Austin in December, followed by a third in Atlanta. Nearly all eight are already confirmed, including leftist bodybuilder Colin Davis and trans former NCAA athlete Schuyler Bailar. The leaders have apparently hashed things out and are working to correct some of the mistakes they made with the Denver House, enlisting the services of an in-person, trained men’s group facilitator to mediate conflicts. “This is a test-and-learn pilot,” Jacobs tells me. “While we are comfortable with swings and misses, we also want to ensure we don’t keep taking the same swing.” Cole’s friend, whom he describes as a “professional race car driver and videographer,” will also be on hand to record social media content. “He's 22 and has a really vibey aesthetic,” he says. “He knows what's t-u-f-f, tuff.”
All told, the creators at the Hey Brother House produced somewhere between 65 and 70 videos. The main focus was on bonding activities and group discussions. The highest-performing video was a clip of Wright injecting himself with testosterone as the other men cheered him on, which got 689,000 views. After the tribunal, the House also produced his “Ask a Trans Man” video series, which overperformed on both Instagram and Wright’s YouTube channel; in one, Cole and Wright, who have since made up, were prominently featured.
Little of the content from Hey Brother House went viral, but for a handful of the creators, their audience now skews more male; Wright, for instance, says some of his content from the house reached a predominantly male audience. But in reaching their target demo—men from 18 to 25—they saw little success. “There are some ways in which our content was too on the nose,” says Cole. In the future, he says they’ll make more of “the type of stuff that young men want to see” — such as the wrestling videos, which he says overperformed. For this reason, they’re trying to recruit a much younger cohort for Austin, who focus less on political commentary and more on skits and lifestyle content. They’re having some difficulty: many younger male creators often have to juggle their content creation with school. A lot of them have talent managers who don’t want their clients to “get too political,” or have turned down the House because they can’t pay them that much.
But there are signs pointing in the direction of a healthier version of manhood being promoted on social media—or, at the very least, an exhaustion with older models. Following the midterm elections in November, men like senators-elect Abdul El-Sayed, James Talarico, and Sen. Jon Ossoff emerged triumphant at the polls, proffering a kindler and gentler (not to mention hunkier) model of masculinity than any proffered by a Clavicular or an Androgenic. Perhaps even more tellingly, white men between the ages of 18 and 29, who had previously helped deliver the 2024 election to Trump, swung overwhelmingly left. According to one analysis, 54 percent of this bracket voted for Democratic House candidates.
There was also one video that came out of Denver that did indeed perform well with the target demographic of Gen Z men. A simple, five-second looping Instagram Reel shows Kennedy and Cole locked in an embrace. “When’s the last time you got a hug longer than 5 seconds?” the onscreen text reads. It has garnered 500,000 views, mostly from 18-to-24-year-olds.
I am reminded of something Cole told me the first time we spoke about how to solve the toxic masculinity crisis. “I know so strongly in my soul that more men and boys just need more hugs,” he said. “No matter what you’ve been through, no matter who you are. You just need more hugs [and] safe touches and affirmation and encouragement.” At the time, this struck me as cringe, and maybe a bit too simplistic. Watching the Reel with Kennedy and Cole embracing, I feel the same. But that doesn’t mean it’s not also true.

The Best Power Banks for Keeping All Your Devices Charged
Featured in this article
I hate running out of power. Everybody does. While our gadgets have advanced in many ways, battery technology has been slow to improve. That’s why you’re looking to buy a power bank. A good portable charger is a handy backup that can keep your smartphone, tablet, and maybe even your laptop going for longer. I’ve been testing power banks for years. I’ve tested more than 100 portable chargers. But you only really need one or two.
Most folks should buy one of the first four power banks I recommend, but there are a few other unique use cases, so I’ve included a few extra options. Read the Best MagSafe/Qi2 Power Banks for more magnetic wireless chargers, and Best Laptop Power Banks or Best Portable Power Stations for more power.
Updated November 2026: I added power banks from Anker, Peak Design, Nitecore, and Iniu, removed some older devices, and updated links and prices.
Other Portable Chargers I Tested
There are so many portable chargers out there. Here are a few more I like that just missed out on a place above for one reason or another. We also have separate guides for the Best Laptop Power Banks, Best MagSafe Power Banks, and Best Portable Power Stations.
Don’t Bother With These Power Banks
These portable chargers I tested aren’t necessarily terrible, but you can do better.
UGreen MagFlow Pro for $90: I actually quite like this magnetic, wireless charging power bank (Qi2 25W) with its Matrix-style screen that animates to show charging status. But considering the 10,000-mAh capacity, the price is absolutely bonkers. The marketing talks up its cooling properties, but it got very warm when I used it. The attached USB-C cable (45W) was annoyingly obtrusive when it was stuck to the back of my iPhone.
OnePlus Slim Magnetic Power Bank for $70: Sleek in silver-gray aluminum with a chamfered edge, this power bank looks lovely, but the 5,000-mAh capacity is just over half that after inefficiency takes a bite.
Iniu Portable Charger for $20: It’s very small for a 10,000-mAh capacity. You can charge at up to 45 watts from either of the USB-C ports or 18 watts from the USB-A (recharging was slow), it fell short of the stated capacity, and the display sometimes failed to update correctly.
FansDreams MChaos for $46: I love the idea of a wearable power bank, and this one comes in lime green with a carabiner that makes it easy to attach to a bag, but recharging is slow, and you’ll be lucky to get one full charge for your phone. It's also currently sold out.
iWalk Portable Charger for $22: The 4,800-mAh capacity won’t come close to fully refilling your device, but it's tiny enough to keep in a bag at all times.
What Features Should I Look for in Power Banks?
There are a few things worth thinking about when you’re shopping for a portable charger.
The capacity of a power bank is measured in milliampere-hours (mAh), but this can be a little misleading because the amount of power you get depends on the cable you use, the device you’re charging, and the charging method. (Qi wireless charging is less efficient.) You will never get the maximum capacity from any power bank. You can generally expect to get between 60 and 80 percent after energy loss through heat and conversion. Some manufacturers list a “Rated Capacity” that’s lower than the overall capacity to give you an indication of what to expect in real-world use. We try to provide a minimum estimate of what you’ll get in terms of charges for devices.
The charging rate for devices like smartphones is measured in watts (W), but most power banks list the voltage (V) and the amperage (A). Thankfully, you can calculate the wattage yourself simply by multiplying the voltage and amperage. Unfortunately, getting that maximum rate also depends on your device, the standards it supports, and the charging cable you use. Many smartphones, including Apple’s iPhones, support the power delivery standard, meaning you can use higher-power power banks to recharge the device with no issues. A few phones, such as Samsung’s Galaxy S range, support a supplementary PD protocol called PPS (programmable power supply) that goes up to 45 watts. Many phones also support Qualcomm’s proprietary Quick Charge (QC) standard. There are also other proprietary fast-charging standards, but you won’t generally find power banks that support them unless they come from the smartphone manufacturer.
Your device will need pass-through support if you want to charge your power bank and use it to charge another device simultaneously. The Nimble, GoalZero, Biolite, Mophie, Zendure, and Sharge portable chargers listed support pass-through charging. Anker discontinued support for pass-through in some of its products because it found that differences between the output of the wall charger and the input of the device being charged can cause the power bank to cycle on and off rapidly and shorten its life. Monoprice does not support pass-through charging either. We would advise caution when using pass-through, as it can also cause portable chargers to heat up.
Can I Take a Power Bank on a Plane?
It’s safe to fly with a power bank, but there are two main restrictions to keep in mind when you board a flight: You must have the portable charger in your carry-on luggage (it cannot be checked), and it must not exceed 100 watt-hours. If your power bank has a larger capacity than 27,000 mAh, you should check with the airline. Below that should not be a problem.
Some airlines introduced stricter rules in 2025, so always check with your chosen airline before you travel. For example, some airlines prefer you not to use or charge power banks during a flight, some require power banks to be in your hand luggage under the seat in front of you and not in the overheads, and some limit the number of power banks you can have on board.
Why You Should Avoid Cheap Power Banks
Many years ago, the Samsung Galaxy Note 7 gained notoriety when its batteries caught fire in a series of incidents. There’s been a steady stream of similar, though isolated, incidents ever since. Despite the high-profile coverage of batteries gone wrong, the vast majority of lithium-ion batteries are safe.
The chemical reaction that occurs inside a lithium-ion cell is complex, but as in any battery, there’s a negative and a positive electrode. In lithium batteries, the negative is a lithium-carbon compound, and the positive is cobalt oxide (though many battery makers are moving away from cobalt). These two compounds cause a reaction that is safe when controlled and delivers energy to your devices. When the reaction gets out of control, though, you end up with earbuds melting in your ears. What changes a safe reaction to an uncontrolled reaction can be any number of things: excess heat, physical damage during use, physical damage during manufacture, or using the wrong charger.
The three basic rules that have kept me safe through testing dozens and dozens of batteries are these:
- Avoid cheap cords, chargers, and outlet adapters;
- Make sure batteries aren't exposed to excessive heat (above 110 degrees Fahrenheit);
- Regularly inspect batteries for signs of damage.
Avoiding cheap wall-outlet adapters, cords, and chargers is the most important rule. These are your most likely sources of problems. Those chargers you see on Amazon for $20 cheaper than the competition? Not worth it. They probably got the price down by skimping on insulation, leaving out power-management tools, and ignoring the basics of electrical safety. Price alone is no guarantee of safety, either. Buy from reputable companies and brands.
Then there’s heat. Too much of it can cause all manner of problems, both in terms of discharge and safety. Avoid heat, and pay attention to your batteries when they’re charging. If your device gets overly hot when charging, this can be a sign of problems. Similarly, beware of any swollen, bulging, or otherwise misshapen batteries.
Why Is My Power Bank Charging Slowly?
I’ve explained charging rates and capacity above, but several factors can cause charging speed to be slower than expected. The rate is determined by the device being charged, so your phone will request a certain wattage, which changes depending on how full its battery is, on-device settings, and the battery temperature.
All devices charge more slowly when they are completely empty, when the battery approaches full, and when they overheat. The cable you use will also have a maximum charging rate, and so will different ports on the power bank. Wireless charging is more convenient, but also slower than wired charging.
How We Test Power Banks
I’ve been testing power banks for close to two decades, and my home office has stacks of ’em at any given moment. I test every portable charger that comes in for at least two weeks. I always check how many times it can fully charge my test phone (currently an iPhone 16). I’ll also try charging my Pixel 10 Pro XL and Samsung Galaxy S24+ to test charging speeds, and whatever else I have in. For larger-capacity power banks, I test-charge an iPad Mini and a MacBook Air. I test how long it takes to recharge each empty power bank.
Aside from these standard tests, I try to use the power banks in my everyday life, just to see how they feel, and my wife and kids often help out and share their opinions. For some of our top picks, I continue to test over months to get a sense of their reliability and durability, though it’s not possible to do this for every device that lands on my desk. Beyond function, I take form and usability into account. I keep an eye on user reviews and consider the warranties and customer service of each manufacturer.
How Does WIRED Select Power Banks to be Reviewed?
I often scan the latest releases to seek out worthy prospects, whether from an unknown new brand or an established favorite like Anker. I also get pitched many power banks every week. I sometimes reach out to those companies to ask for the product but never promise any kind of editorial coverage—that would go against WIRED’s editorial policies. While WIRED usually earns affiliate revenue if you purchase a power bank using our link, this is not factored into the decision on ranking.
There are too many power banks for me to test everything, so I tend to stick to known, reputable brands, but there’s always room for something new if it has a compelling new feature or price, and I cover as many as I can. (Leave a comment or send me an email if you want me to test a power bank from a certain brand!) Once testing is complete, I typically donate power banks to a local charity. I try to hang on to some of our top picks for comparison purposes and to test their longevity.

Seven streaming services reported that they received 920 grievances in October 2026, including 676 received by Amazon Prime Video, nearly three-quarters of the total. According to Amazon Prime Video’s grievance report, the plantform disposed 677 grievances but it classified only 673 of them. The difference in grievance disposal remains unexplained in its disclosure.
The streaming platforms disclose how they handled grievances each month under Rule 18(3) of the IT Rules, 2021. The 920 grievances cover seven streaming platforms like Netflix, Apple, JioHotstar, ShemarooMe, ETV Win and Sun NXT along with Amazon Prime. However, not every streaming service in India is present. The figure amounts to about 29.68 grievances a day. These figures are the platforms’ own disclosures, not audited by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (MIB) or a self-regulatory body.
What the seven streaming services reported
- Amazon Prime Video received 676, disposed of 677, and ended the month with 39 pending, down from 40 pending at the start of October. In its grievance report, the company classified eight disposals as related to the Code of Ethics, the content rules for online publishers. However, the streaming platform only agreed to and took action against five of them, the rest it didn’t agreed to.
- Sun NXT received 109 grievances, disposed of all of them and reported none pending. It filed the self-regulatory body’s form, rather than the publisher appendix.
- Netflix began October with 24 pending grievances and received new ones during the month, taking its total to 81. The streaming giant disposed of 56, leaving 25 pending at the end of October. It classified 11 disposals as related to the Code of Ethics and agreed with one.
- Apple reportedly received 50 grievances in October 2026, and disposed of all of them, with none pending at the end of the month. Additionally, the streaming giant didn’t classify any grievance as related to the Code of Ethics. Its disclosure is titled “Monthly Grievance Disclosure” and does not say it covers only Apple TV+.
- JioHotstar received 18 grievances in October and disposed of seven, leaving 14 pending. However, it uses a form which does not classify grievances by the Code of Ethics. Its grievance officer upheld none and dismissed seven; no appeals were filed with its self-regulatory body and that body issued no orders.
- ShemarooMe reported that it received 10 grievances in October and disposed of all with none pending. Its six-column form records zero under Code of Ethics grievances but does not specify whether that column counts grievances received or disposed of.
- ETV Win received no grievances in October 2026. It is a streaming service filing a news-publisher form, which does not give a comparable disposal or Code of Ethics classification.
The total count of grievances received by streaming platforms in October 2026 does not include SonyLIV, hoichoi or aha; as they have not published a monthly grievance report yet. ETV Bharat reported 16 grievances in October and replied to 13 of them, as per their report on the news-publisher form. But it remains outside the scope of this article because it is designated as a news site, not a streaming service.
The classifications do not add up
Amazon Prime Video’s opening and closing balances reconcile with receipts and disposals. But its 665 disposals marked unrelated to the Code of Ethics and eight marked related account for only 673, four short of its reported disposals. Its report also records four orders or advisories received and four complied with.
JioHotstar’s closing balance reconciles with the three pending grievances at the end of September, although it did not report an October opening balance. Because the publishers classify grievances differently, their received counts can be added, but their Code of Ethics classifications and grievances upheld cannot be totalled on a like-for-like basis.
Rule 9(1) and Rule 9(3), which require observance of the Code of Ethics, remain under an interim stay; Rule 9(2) was not stayed. The disclosures do not establish how many grievances across the seven publishers concerned the Code of Ethics, or whether every disposal was classified.
