On October 26, Charles Massner, the mayor of Mediapolis, Iowa, got an email from the US Army. It described “an intentional, controlled detonation” of “a quantity of degraded lead azide … in the near future” at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, some 20 miles south of Mediapolis.
The email, which was reviewed by WIRED, provided no details about when this explosion would happen, how much material the explosion would destroy, or what steps officials should take to protect the public from a possible toxic fallout. But it did request that public officials allow for environmental testing on public lands before and after the event, which the town granted in a November 2 meeting.
Massner says the next time he heard anything was early last week, when the Army published a press release on its website saying it would explode the lead azide in just a few days. That press release included a map of potential exposure from the blast. Mediapolis was directly in the path of exposure, covered in a reddish-yellow cloud with a hot pink border.
“There was really no communication, so to speak, other than what was on their website,” he says.
Massner wasn’t alone in being caught off guard. The sudden announcement that the Army would be exploding 9,500 pounds of lead azide with seemingly little to no notice caught nearly all of Iowa by surprise. Governor Kim Reynolds’ office said last week that they’d learned about the explosion the same way Massner did: via the press release sent out by the Army on November 15.
Now, despite a court order blocking the detonation, the Army announced late Sunday night that it plans to blow up the lead azide on Wednesday, a day before the Thanksgiving holiday. (On Monday, President Donald Trump posted that he was ordering the Army not to detonate anything without court approval.) Many Iowans are left with more questions than answers. Iowa’s unofficial state subreddit is filled with posts from people trying to plan holiday travel and safety around the event, which has switched dates twice in the past week. One local official in the path of a potential fallout told WIRED on Friday that she was leaving the area and staying at a hotel with her immunocompromised child.
Peter Thorne, a professor of environmental health at the University of Iowa who has studied exposure to lead in his laboratory, says his lab has been “deluged with concerns,” with everyone from pediatricians to parents to people who run cleaning facilities and are worried about their staff exposure reaching out. Like most Iowans, Thorne also heard about the explosion from the Army’s press release.
“My first reaction was, They’re going to do what?” he says.
The 68 barrels of degraded lead azide at the Middletown site have been there for more than 20 years. In March, according to a document released by the Army on November 18, the material was officially labeled hazardous waste, and officials began looking into how to dispose of it. In a court filing published Saturday, the Army says that there is an “immediate risk” of the material exploding by itself after temperatures drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit. It is now invoking emergency powers to detonate the barrels by November 24.
“In short, a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion,” the filing states.
The Army did not immediately respond to a list of questions sent by WIRED.
The Army does seem to have looked into other options besides blowing up the azide. The New York Times reported Friday that the Army awarded a contract in late March to a private company to handle cleaning up the chemicals onsite. However, that contract was pulled two months later; the company told the Times that the Army did not give a reason for changing its mind on the cleanup. A contracting officer in the Army told the company that the Army’s decision to pursue detonation “was not based on deficiencies” with the company’s science.
In a letter sent to Governor Reynolds on Friday, the EPA Region 7 administrator said that the agency only learned that the material had degraded to a dangerous state in March. The letter also listed a number of strategies the EPA had considered besides detonation, including chemical cleanup, which also risked causing an explosion.
The Army has blown up expired munitions before, although not at the scale of what it plans to do in Iowa. Thorne says that any exposure to lead from the explosion is expected to be “quite a bit lower” than lead exposures in communities exposed to legacy pollution sources. But “there is no safe level for lead, especially for young children,” he says.
The Army did have some public meetings and communications in late October with officials in Middletown, where the explosion will take place and where it has recommended temporary evacuation measures for some neighborhoods. But it’s not clear why its initial direct outreach around public health didn’t extend to towns in potential fallout ranges for a blast, including Mediapolis, beyond asking for permission to test soil samples. (The Army did include recommended public health measures in its November 15 press release.)
Thorne, a former chair of the EPA’s Science Advisory Board, says that a successful public health outreach program has lots of opportunity for public engagement for all affected areas.
“You have public meetings. You answer questions. You have extensive Q&A and FAQs, and you have people speaking to why this is the only choice, what are the burdens, and some kind of a cost-benefit comparison between the options, and then you roll it out through the media, through social media, through many ways,” he says. “Best practice is not what they’ve done—I think this is closer to worst practice, from a public health perspective.”
For his part, Massner, Mediapolis’s mayor, said on Friday that he planned to take “standard precautions” and follow the Army’s public health recommendations. (The Army has not released fallout modeling for a Wednesday explosion, but if winds carry the material south, it would be possible for Mediapolis to no longer be in the affected zone.) But Massner says he understands why people in his town were freaked out.
“What people saw was the map they drew, which showed a [red] cloud going over everybody’s head. I don’t think that was the intent of the map,” he laughs. “When you see a map covered in red, you’re supposed to run for shelter immediately—your life is in danger.”

The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) has levied a total of ₹2 crore penalty on Star Health and Allied Insurance Co. for violations of certain regulations.
In its order, arising from an inspection by the regulator from January 31-February 11, 2022, IRDAI said a penalty of ₹1 crore is being imposed as the claims processed by the insurer were, in a manner, inconsistent with its own policy terms and conditions and a violation of IRDAI Circulars on Covid Claim settlements and Regulation 27 (v) of IRDAI (Health Insurance) Regulations, 2016.
The insurer is advised to ensure all policies are serviced as per the terms and conditions of the policy documents and no arbitrary deductions/denial are made to the claim without proper justification, IRDAI said.
IRDAI levied one more penalty of ₹1 crore, on the insurer, for various violations, including resorting to arbitrary deductions and not communicating its decision to repudiate the claims to the policyholders and by not mentioning the specific terms and conditions under which repudiations were made. The insurer has violated Regulation 27(v) and 33(d)(ii) and (iv) of IRDAI (Health Insurance) Regulations, 2016; Regulation 21(3)(c)(i)(c) of IRDAI (TPA – Health Services) Regulation, 2016, it said in the order.
The penalty of ₹2 crore pertained four of the eight charges. For other charges, IRDAI issued a caution and advisory; warning and direction; warning and advisory; while not pressing a charge.

Two potential vaccines against the deadly Ebola strain gripping the Democratic Republic of Congo are set to enter trials in the outbreak's epicentre next week, the World Health Organisation announced earlier this week.
There are currently no vaccines or treatments for the less common Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the explosive outbreak declared in May, triggering an international public health emergency.
A total of 5,568 deaths out of 11,376 cases have been confirmed in the vast central African country's worst-ever Ebola outbreak, according to the WHO.
"We expect two candidate vaccines developed specifically for Bundibugyo virus to begin testing as early as next week," WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus told a press conference at the UN health agency's headquarters in Geneva.
The so-called Tumaini trial in the DRC is a single framework that can test the safety, efficacy and ability to trigger an immune response of multiple vaccines. The trial uses ring vaccination: immunising contacts deemed to be at high risk of infection.
Ervebo, a vaccine already approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, kicked off the Tumaini trial on October 23, at the full-scale Phase 3 level, to determine if it also offers any protection against Bundibugyo.
Different vaccine types
The trial will now also incorporate the two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines, which have both gone through earlier-stage, smaller-scale Phase 1 clinical trials.
One is a ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector jab developed by the University of Oxford; the other, mRNA-1469, was developed by the US-based Moderna group using the mRNA technology made famous during the Covid-19 pandemic.
Meg Doherty, head of the WHO's science for health department, said Phase 2 clinical trials with the candidate vaccines are scheduled to begin on November 26 or 27 in Bunia, the capital of the DRC's northeastern Ituri province at the epicentre of the outbreak.
If the safety and immune response data from the Phase 2 trial pass the next stage of review, the candidate jabs can move forward to a full-scale Phase 3 trial.
Children paying 'terrible price'
Doherty said that more than 140 people were enrolled in the Tumaini trial, with thousands of contacts ultimately expected to sign up. The trial will also eventually expand beyond the current single site in Bunia.
Ebola, which spreads through contact with bodily fluids and causes a haemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.
Tedros said 400 to 500 new cases were still being reported every week, with two-thirds of confirmed deaths still taking place outside Ebola treatment centres.
"Children are paying a terrible price. They account for more than a quarter of confirmed cases and one third of deaths," he added.

Srinagar- The use of heavy machinery near the ecologically fragile Sheshnag Lake in south Kashmir’s Anantnag district has triggered widespread concern, with political leaders, religious figures and environmentalists calling for an immediate halt to the activity.
A video showing an excavator operating in close proximity to the high-altitude glacial lake along the traditional Amarnath Yatra route has gone viral on social media, prompting concerns over the potential ecological impact of construction activity in the fragile Himalayan region.
Sheshnag Lake is among 14 high-risk glacial lakes identified across Jammu and Kashmir and is monitored for environmental vulnerabilities.
Former chief minister and Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) president Mehbooba Mufti termed the issue painful and accused the government of remaining silent over environmental concerns.
“The government itself is having Chinar trees cut down. At the university, they are cutting down our old walnut trees. They just watch as spectators and don’t say a word. Our Kashmir will become another Uttarakhand. What can we say? When they built roads and expressways for the Char Dham Yatra, look at how many storms and calamities strike there today. It is very bad,” she said.
Mufti said speaking out against such activities could invite accusations of opposing the Amarnath Yatra.
“If we talk about it, they will say we are against the Amarnath Yatra. What can I say? They try to polarise everything,” she told reporters.
National Conference Lok Sabha MP Mian Altaf said Kashmir’s lakes, rivers and forests must be protected.
“I have not seen that, so I cannot say anything to you about it. I will just say that Kashmir’s lakes must be saved. They must be saved at any cost. Its rivers must be saved, its forests must be saved. That is essential for all of us, essential for Kashmir, for Kashmir’s tourism, for Kashmir’s environment, and for our health,” he said.
Former Srinagar MP Ruhullah Mehdi criticised the activity, saying Kashmir’s mountains should not be treated as spaces for unrestricted construction.
“A party that wins votes in the name of faith is now taking JCBs to a holy lake. First, the BJP pushed motor roads up to the Amarnath cave. Now heavy machinery is digging at Sheshnag, a high-risk glacial lake,” Mehdi said in a post on X.
“Stop this now. Kashmir’s mountains are not BJP’s real estate,” he added.
CPI(M) leader and Kulgam MLA Mohammad Yousuf Tarigami also expressed concern over the visuals, describing Sheshnag as a glacial lake surrounded by loose moraine and steep slopes.
“It is already listed among the 14 high-risk glacial lakes in Jammu and Kashmir. Disturbing such terrain with heavy machinery is an invitation to disaster,” he said.
Tarigami said nobody was opposed to development or improved facilities for pilgrims, tourists and local residents, but stressed that infrastructure development in the high Himalayas must be environmentally sustainable and in harmony with nature.
He said works in such sensitive zones should be preceded by scientific studies, proper environmental impact assessments and consultations with experts and local communities.
Warning against human interference in glacial zones, Tarigami said the consequences could affect downstream areas, including Pahalgam and communities along the Lidder river in south Kashmir. He urged the government to intervene without delay.
Kashmir’s chief cleric Mirwaiz Umar Farooq also expressed concern over the construction activity, saying the visuals of heavy machinery operating near Sheshnag Lake in the glacial zone of Pahalgam were disturbing.
He said the activity had raised serious concerns over the ecological impact of construction in the fragile Himalayan region, particularly at a time when glaciers were retreating and recent glacier-related floods in neighbouring Nepal had highlighted the vulnerability of mountain ecosystems.
“Improving facilities for pilgrims has never been an issue. But not at the cost of our fragile ecosystem,” Mirwaiz said in a post on X.
He said the government owed an explanation to the public over the environmental concerns and called for the activity to be stopped.
“Our precious mountains, glaciers and water bodies need protection, not plunder, for now, and for the future generations. So this must be immediately stopped,” he said.
Apni Party president Altaf Bukhari sought clarification from the authorities over the authenticity of the video and the nature of the work being carried out near the lake.
“If the video is genuine, the government owes the public a clear explanation: What is such heavy machinery doing in an ecologically fragile zone, especially around a high-altitude glacial lake?” he said.
Bukhari said Kashmir had already suffered environmental damage due to unchecked construction and human interference, warning that further damage to natural habitats and water bodies could not be afforded.
Environmental activist Raja Muzaffar Bhat also questioned how heavy machinery had been allowed to reach the glacial area, describing the activity as a disaster.
Meanwhile, the Border Roads Organisation (BRO), the executing agency for the works, said the activity was part of post-Amarnath Yatra operations and was being carried out in compliance with applicable safety norms and environmental safeguards.
The BRO said it was taking measures to ensure safe disposal of excavated material, protect natural drainage and minimise disturbance to the surrounding terrain. It also said the works were confined to existing tracks and aimed at improving safety and easing congestion for pilgrims.

Marco Penge claims maiden PGA Tour win: Englishman triumphs from four-way playoff at RSM Classic
Three-time DP World Tour winner Marco Penge was in danger of losing his PGA Tour card after a 2026 season disrupted by a viral illness; the 28-year-old Englishman secures his card in stunning fashion with his maiden triumph at year-ending RSM Classic in thrilling four-way playoff finish
Monday 23 November 2026 20:17, UK
English golfer Marco Penge claimed a stunning maiden win on the PGA Tour as he emerged victorious from a four-way playoff at the season-ending RSM Classic.
Penge, a three-time winner on the DP World Tour, had gone into the tournament at risk of losing his PGA Tour card for next year after a rookie season disrupted by a viral illness placed him outside of the top 100.
With a top-four finish required to retain his spot, the 28-year-old found form at the best possible time at the Sea Island Golf Club this week, and a final-round 65 earned him a spot alongside Haotong Li of China and Americans Michael Thorbjornsen and Max Greyserman in a playoff decider - all four locked at 16 under.

Penge's five-under 65 on the Seaside Course included six birdies, including one at the last, and a single bogey, while he birdied 18 again to clinch victory in the playoff after nailing his approach to 10 feet.
"I always seem to play my best golf when my back's up against the wall," Penge said following his stunning win.
"I've been through this before on the DP World Tour, keeping my card in the last event and dealing with adversity and coming back from health issues, all that stuff.
"So I knew I could do it, I just wasn't sure I ever had the game this week to be able to do it and thankfully I did."
Rasmus Hojgaard, who had held a share of the lead - on 13 under with Thorbjornsen - heading into the weather-delayed final round on Monday, ultimately finish tied fifth.
The Ryder Cup star posted a disappointing final round of 69 to end two shots off the pace on 14 under, level with Jackson Koivun.

Recently, I was out doing some window shopping with one of my friends. We checked out some of our usual places — a makeup store, a clothing store — but the place where my friend’s eyes really lit up was a toy store. There were floor-to-ceiling displays of Labubus and Funko Pops, Jellycats that looked like croissants, and just about every Hello Kitty product you could imagine.
Adults are buying more toys than ever. You should too.
Legos, Pokémon, Jellycats — and the case for never growing up.
What really got my attention about the space was not the sheer volume of toys, but the lack of kids. It was mostly people our age, with the same excitement that I saw in my friend. This makes sense when you look at a breakdown of the current toy market: It’s an industry projected to be worth over $130 billion worldwide this year, and as of this summer, American adults with no kids bought more games and toys than households with children. There’s even a name for grownups who aren’t ready to put away the toybox: kidults.
According to Mia Sundstrom, CEO of the National Institute for Play, there’s a reason for our enduring fondness for toys. “The drive to play is actually biologically hardwired into our subcortex,” she told Vox. “Because of that subcortical location, the drive to play actually lasts across the entire lifespan, which means that we’re never too old to play. But our society deeply misunderstands that. We’ve slowly started to take play away as we grow up, and yet that drive is still there.”
So what does play actually do for our brains, and how can we add the playfulness of childhood back into our adult lives? We answer that and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me, Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.
Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Sundstrom, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545.
Adult consumers are making up the lion’s share of the toy industry now. What is happening in our adult brains when we play with toys?
Neuroplasticity means that our brains can adapt across our entire lifespan. Some of the similar benefits that children have with playing with toys, we actually still have as adults.
The primary reason is because of the hand-brain connection, which is essentially a two-way neurological highway. When we do fine motor movement while we’re playing with toys, it stimulates the brain regions that are responsible for our cognitive function, our emotion, and our focus. It activates these deep neural networks that go completely unused when we’re engaging in, say, passive screen time.
When we’re playing with a toy, we’re often doing something we’ve never done before, because play is a space where experimentation and risk-taking and mistakes happen. That is actually stimulating new neural pathways in our brain that support our long-term cognitive health.
The second big one is our amygdala, which is a key part of our emotional processing center in our brain, is relaxed in the state of play. A lot of us live in a stress response right now. Social media doesn’t really take us out of that stress response. It often leaves us feeling more stressed out or drained when we’re done.
I absolutely have experienced that.
But that’s not the case with the toys. When we engage in this play state with toys, our amygdala actually calms down. The amygdala is responsible for our stress response. So our stress, our anxiety, our emotional defensiveness are significantly reduced, and we enter that restorative state, which for a lot of us is really hard to access on the day-to-day.
Toys are a pathway to helping us access that more relaxed emotional state based on the reactivity of our amygdala.
When do we start being told that we’re too old for toys? What do we lose when we accept that?
Sadly, I think we’re being told that we’re too old for toys starting quite early. Specifically, when we hit the teenage years, a lot of play is replaced with, “If this doesn’t have an immediate purpose for my future career, it’s not worth the time.”
That free space to experiment, say, with Lego and even with collections and other things that stimulate our imagination and allow us to enter this world between imagination and reality, starts to slowly dwindle out, almost imperceptibly.
Parents think that they’re doing their children a service by replacing that free play time with structured sports or structured activities. Unfortunately, what happens is, slowly, the intrinsic motivation to do something gets replaced with extrinsic motivation, which very quickly leads to burnout.
It sounds like when we stop playing with toys, that’s when the optimization culture kicks in.
Exactly. We see playing with toys as extra, as a hobby, as something that doesn’t have an immediate purpose toward helping us achieve whatever our goals are. And yet paradoxically, it’s one of the most productive things we can do.
One of the things that I like to ask people is, “Where are you when you get your best ideas?” Now, the shower is the most common answer, but the second most common answer is when they’re playing with toys. You know how no one answers that question? “When I’m at my desk at 10 am answering emails.”
The creative mind flourishes in the space in between, and the space in between is the time that is spent playing with toys. But until people see it like that, it becomes really hard to fit into the hustle culture and the grind of the daily schedule.
How do we relearn how to play?
“Here’s the good news: Even 30 seconds to five minutes a day makes a difference.”
The first step is to think back on our earliest memories of playing, because play is who we were before the world told us who we have to be. The second, which is a derivative of that, is understanding your own play style. For some people, building a Lego set is going to be totally playful. For other people it’s going to be a puzzle or it’s going to be a game night with a board game or a sports league.
And third, this is not about adding more to our plate. Nobody has time for that.
That’s so funny. My first thought is, “I need to put play on my to-do list.”
And that is totally contradictory to the purpose of play!
Here’s the good news: Even 30 seconds to five minutes a day makes a difference. You can put play objects and toys in visible places around your environment so that you reach for that instead of your phone.
If you just crack the door open a little bit with those micro moments of play in your routine, your brain will automatically enjoy it and start looking for more opportunities to play. Just start really small and know that that’s enough.
What do you think the world looks like when adults embrace that playful spirit more?
The world looks more joyful. This isn’t all sunshine and rainbows, and play doesn’t take away from the hard things that it means to be human. Play is a healthy way to express those challenges and to express the full range of emotions.
Play can look mellow and play can look lower-energy, but what it looks like is humans honoring what it means to be human and feeling more connected with your authentic self. When we’re more connected with our authentic self, we’re more easily able to connect with the people around us and establish meaningful relationships. So I see this as a tool for societal flourishing, specifically in a technologically dominated world.

Pentagon takes fresh aim at Canada's military readiness, defence spending priorities
Washington accuses Ottawa of putting economic interests ahead of security
The Pentagon has fired a further salvo at Canada, saying the country isn't meeting its international obligations to either NORAD or NATO and is prioritizing "parochial economic and commercial interests" in its defence build up.
The complaints are contained in a U.S. Department of War fact sheet covering U.S.-Canada defence relations, which was posted online Monday.
Axios, a U.S.-based news website, was first to report the contents on Sunday.
The fact sheet takes aim at the readiness of different branches of the Canadian military, saying the air force only has 41.9 per cent of its fleet ready for operations in the current budget year and that directly affects the country's ability to contribute to the air defence of North America.
It also cites low army and navy readiness figures.
"Canadian political leadership continues to pursue unfocused global commitments, resulting in personnel and platform overextension, deferred modernizations for key equipment and low readiness rates," said the fact sheet.
"Ottawa’s prioritization of parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization introduces further uncertainty for NORAD and will further burden our Joint Force and the American taxpayer."
The fact sheet does not spell out precisely how Canada is not meeting its NATO commitments, but does point to the sorry state of the navy's submarine fleet, where only one of four boats is operational. It also mentions the ongoing review by the government of Prime Minister Mark Carney about whether to proceed with the full purchase of U.S.-made F-35 fighters.
The release of the document comes just two days after a report surfaced in the Washington Post that U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth had issued a classified directive restricting military co-operation between the United States and Canada.
A leading U.S. senator, Mike Rounds, who sits on the armed services committee, told the Halifax International Security Forum that the restrictions were largely symbolic in the sense that they don't affect day-to-day military operations, intelligence sharing and defence planning.
"It does limit general flag officer meetings to those that advance [U.S. Department of War] objectives," he said.
U.S. defence officials — uniform and civilian — must seek permission before attending social events or think-tank conferences.
The memo follows the suspension last fall of meetings between the countries through the Permanent Joint Board on Defence (PJBD), a decades-old organization that met infrequently to co-ordinate North American security.
No one in Defence Minister David McGuinty's office was immediately available for comment.
The fact sheet said Canada "has yet to articulate a resourced path" to reach the NATO target of defence-related spending of five per cent of gross domestic product by 2035 "and is deferring the largest increases needed to actualize NATO targets until after the 2029 federal election."
The latest federal budget, released Nov. 5, contains spending plans going up to 2030-31. But absent was any clear sense on what the precise rearmament plans are for the Canadian military — beyond equipment that is already on order.
The fact sheet contained the Pentagon's advice: "Canada can maximize its limited but growing defence funds by prioritizing missions important for its homeland defence and meeting NORAD and NATO obligations by committing to the best military platforms."
Retired Canadian major-general Scott Clancy, speaking on CBC's Power & Politics late Monday, said there's an undeniable political and strategic tension between the United States and Canada that — for the moment — hasn't affected day-to-day co-operation.
"I think we're seeing a continuous deterioration of that relationship," Clancy said. "So, at the operational level, my friends are telling me the relationship is as good, if not better than before, but there are some cracks" that are making it increasingly difficult to maintain the business-as-usual approach.

Delhi residents may soon have access to a wider selection of premium liquor brands at upgraded retail stores, with a committee clearing the way for the rollout of a new policy, the Times of India (TOI) reported.
However, the overhaul could also make alcohol more expensive in the national capital, as the Delhi government plans to raise both excise duty and retailer margins, a senior official told the newspaper.
According to sources cited in the TOI report, the proposed policy aims to expand the availability of premium liquor, introduce more brands, and revamp the format and facilities of retail outlets—all while boosting the government’s revenue from liquor sales.
According to the TOI report, two key financial tweaks under consideration are expected to push up retail prices across the city.
At present, excise duty is levied at varying rates based on the liquor category and wholesale price, ranging from 30% to 300% across Indian spirits. The government, the TOI report said, is planning to increase these rates.
Currently, sellers receive a fixed profit margin of ₹50 per bottle on Indian-made foreign liquor (IMFL) and up to ₹100 per bottle on foreign liquor.
Raising these margins is intended to incentivise outlets to stock and promote pricier, premium brands—though the added cost is likely to be passed on to consumers, the publication said.
Under the proposed framework, the Delhi government does not plan to bring private companies into retail operations, the Times of India reported. Maintaining the existing setup, the four Delhi government agencies will continue to manage the city's more than 700 liquor shops.
Instead, the official told TOI that reforms will centre on upgrading the size, facilities, and overall functioning of these outlets to improve the shopping experience and expand premium offerings.
The revenue push comes as Delhi looks to scale up collections: liquor sales fetched roughly ₹6,300 crore in 2025–26, while the target for the current financial year has been pegged at ₹7,200 crore.
While Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta discussed the policy with her cabinet colleagues last Friday, TOI sources said that the actual rollout may take some time.
The upcoming Punjab assembly elections are believed to be a key factor behind the potential hold-up. With drugs and liquor serving as major political flashpoints in Punjab—where the BJP has repeatedly targeted the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) government over the issue—sources told the TOI that unveiling a new liquor policy in Delhi at this juncture could hand the opposition fresh political ammunition.

For a woman who has been a witness to some of the most significant political moments in modern Indian history, Sonia Gandhi likes to insist her life has been far from remarkable. “Oh, I don’t know that I would say it’s an extraordinary story,” she says, shifting uncomfortably.
It’s hard to reconcile this modest characterisation with the course her life has taken over the last 79 years. Born to a working-class family in a small town in northern Italy, today she sits at the heart of Indian political power, having weathered assassinations and personal tragedy to become one of the country’s most influential figures. She held Indira Gandhi’s bloodied body after the then-prime minster, her mother-in-law, was gunned down at their home in Delhi in 1984. She then became India’s first lady when her husband, Rajiv Gandhi, took his mother’s place as prime minister. And when Rajiv, too, was killed, she threw aside her distaste for politics to step up and lead his fragmenting party. In 2004, having taken Congress to electoral victory, she famously turned down the prime minister post. She can still boast of being the longest-serving president of Congress, both when India’s oldest political party was in power and later, when it became the flailing opposition. When Gandhi stepped down in 2017, her son Rahul was appointed her successor.
Gandhi’s entrance into Indian politics began in Cambridge in the 1960s when, at 18, while she was studying at a language school, she fell in love with a bright-eyed boy at a Greek restaurant. At the time, she had no idea that Rajiv was heir to India’s most consequential political dynasty. “It was a coup de foudre,” she says. “After that, nothing else really mattered. He was, first of all, a handsome man. But I think his eyes told of the way he was – of his inner self. He was loving, he was comforting, he was caring. Everything I could have possibly dreamed of.”
Only later would she learn that Rajiv’s grandfather was Jawaharlal Nehru, Indian freedom fighter and the country’s first prime minister, and his mother was Indira Gandhi, who in 1966 became India’s first female prime minister.
Does she still recognise herself in that innocent Italian girl who was swept off her feet and transplanted to an alien land and culture? “Not really,” she says quietly. “Too much has happened, too much has changed.”
We meet at the grand white Delhi bungalow she has lived in for 36 years – a relic of British colonial rule, where peacocks roam the grounds. It was in this house in 1991 that Gandhi heard her husband had been assassinated by Sri Lankan Tamil separatist terrorists. Over the years, as she took on the mantle of Congress leader, her home became the centre of party operations.
The ghosts of Congress leaders past loom large in her study. A painting of Nehru, photographs of Rajiv, a carved stone bust and portraits of Indira line the walls, while a painting of Mahatma Gandhi, the freedom fighter who shaped the ideology of Congress, also hangs prominently. Heavy gilded tomes fill the floor-to-ceiling wooden bookshelves, and a long meeting table dominates the space, but the vibrant rugs, patterned blinds and scattered antiques suggest Gandhi’s own light touch.
In a dark blue sari and maroon blouse, her signature neat grey hair pushed back with a black headband, Gandhi looks every inch the composed Indian political matriarch as she sits on the sofa. The only hint of her heritage is softly accented English and recognisably Italian gesticulation.
She has, she confesses, been very nervous and tense about our meeting. Gandhi has not done an interview in a decade, and throughout her life in the public eye, has tried fiercely to maintain her privacy. She has only agreed to this rare meeting to discuss her forthcoming memoir, a strikingly personal account of her life, and has asked her daughter Priyanka, also a senior Congress leader, to sit in for moral support.
India’s media has often cast her as cold and aloof, yet today she seems warm, open and often a little unsure of herself. She’s anxious about how personal the book is, worried it will be eviscerated by the Indian media, but suggests that after years of “horrible and crazy things written about me”, it will be comforting for people to know “the truth”.
Gandhi has good reason to be nervous of the press. In today’s India, the mainstream media landscape has been crushed into submission by the hardline, rightwing Modi government and is largely devoted to promoting the prime minister’s agenda, while mercilessly attacking the Congress party, in particular the Gandhi family. She does not hold back on criticism of Narendra Modi – accusing him of being an “authoritarian force bent upon changing the very nature of our country” – and of his party, BJP, which she says has “systematically dismantled our democratic institutions”.
The Hindu nationalist vision of India that Modi has enacted over his 12 years in power is directly opposed to the pluralistic, secular India that was championed by successive Congress leaders and which remains enshrined in India’s constitution. It has led to well-documented oppression of the country’s minority groups, in particular its 200 million Muslims.
“More than disappointing, it’s very painful, having known a different India,” Gandhi says. “In parliament, we are not allowed to debate. In the past, there were discussions, there were meetings between the opposition and the government, there was consultation. Now the opposition counts for nothing.”
Since Modi came to power, she has had barely any interaction with him; he tends to avoid eye contact when they’re in a room together – a stark contrast to the past, when opposition leaders would often meet the government and “treat each other with cordiality”.
A “Congress-free India” is one of the openly declared goals of Modi’s BJP, resulting in highly personal attacks on Gandhi and her children, who have found themselves with numerous police cases filed against them. As we talk, Gandhi’s phone lights up with a call from her son Rahul – later, we learn a judge has just cleared him of defamation in one of these many cases, this time for criticising Modi’s home minister back in 2018. “They are very vindictive and vicious. There doesn’t seem to be a heart there,” Gandhi says.
So effective is the BJP’s crackdown on any form of dissent or criticism – what Gandhi describes as an “atmosphere of fear” – that her memoir almost didn’t see the light of day in India. Penguin Random House India were originally meant to release the book domestically, but after she sent them the manuscript she was met with a deafening silence. Gandhi says simply that Penguin were “uneasy in general with the criticism of the government” and that after she refused to make certain suggested edits, the publisher dropped the book, just a week before it was due to be announced. It will now be published by another imprint. In a statement, the publisher denied dropping the book, adding, “Any suggestion that Penguin Random House India decided not to publish Belonging because the author declined editorial changes does not accurately reflect the circumstances.”
Gandhi admits she was disappointed, though not altogether surprised, at what she sees as an attempt to censor her book. It is far from an isolated incident. In the days before we meet, Gandhi’s 26-year-old grandson, who is an artist and curator, is forced to take down dozens of his photographs depicting political protests that had been due to go on show in Delhi.
Gandhi had an early insight into the difficulties and loneliness of being a female leader in India’s deeply patriarchal society. When she arrived in India in 1968, she and Rajiv moved in with his mother, who at that time was two years into her first term as prime minister. Her husband, also a politician, had died years before.
They lived all together in another crumbling colonial Delhi bungalow, in relatively close and modest quarters. To outsiders, Indira was often seen as severe, an “iron lady”, and Gandhi admits that, to begin with, she was deeply intimidated by her formidable mother-in-law. Yet while Indira was imposing in public, she could be vulnerable in private, once confiding to Gandhi how terrified she was when she first bcame prime minister.
“In the newspapers she was portrayed as tough or harsh, but at home she was just like any other mother,” Gandhi says – although Indira’s notoriously explosive temper, frequently directed at political colleagues, would erupt through the house on occasion. Gandhi’s memoir recounts one incident where Indira lost her temper during a family dinner and threw her thali plate across the table.
Gandhi’s book documents the hostility Indira grappled with, both from political opponents and rightwing groups, but also from the old guard of her own party. “I saw her work day and night, constantly under pressure, constantly attacked,” Gandhi says. “It did affect her, like it would anyone. And of course, in that position, there is a loneliness. She had many interests and many friends, but it is a lonely kind of life.”
For several years, Gandhi says, her own life was “carefree”. She and Rajiv were madly in love, often embarrassing their children with public displays of affection that were highly unusual in Indian households at the time. “For this man, I was ready to do everything, to lose even my Italian identity,” she says. Rajiv was working as a commercial airline pilot, and as relations warmed with her mother-in-law, Gandhi set about redecorating the austere Delhi bungalow with some Italian flair, and learning how to cook Kashmiri food. After a traumatic miscarriage, she gave birth to two children, who were doted on by Indira. Even her pangs for fresh Italian ingredients, impossible to find in India in those days, eventually ebbed.
But in 1975 Indira would make the most controversial decision of her political life. Amid mounting political unrest, economic hardship and a concerted effort by the opposition to bring down the Congress government, Indira decided to impose a state of emergency on the country, in a bid to instil order. The repercussions were profound: the constitution was suspended, civil liberties and democratic freedoms abandoned, the media silenced and opponents detained en masse without trial. It lasted for almost two years, and is still seen as the darkest period of India’s democracy; it is regularly used to tarnish the Congress party today.
According to Gandhi, the family was split on the decision. Rajiv was against the move, telling his mother to wait for the next election, but her hotheaded younger son Sanjay pushed for it, arguing at one family dinner that the opposition would destroy his mother and telling her, “They must be stopped.” Sanjay’s forceful influence over his mother was a great source of public controversy at the time. Gandhi recalls that it inflamed tensions within the family, too; Rajiv attempted to confront his mother, but she refused to listen. “Keeping Sanjay in check could have prevented much of the damage that followed,” Gandhi writes in her book.
Today, she says it was a mistake for Indira to call the emergency, and that she believes her mother-in-law came to feel the same. “I always feel that Mrs Gandhi was a democrat at heart,” she says. “I know that many would laugh at this, but I believe she was never comfortable in the course of the emergency. I think it was sitting heavy on her.”
In the following years, Indira would lose one election and be returned to power in another. Rajiv would also be persuaded to enter politics after the premature death of Sanjay. But by 1984, darkness came to their door again.
Months of escalating violence had stricken the north Indian state of Punjab. As separatist militants prepared to declare an independent Sikh state, Indira authorised a military operation at one of the holiest sites in Sikhism, the Golden Temple in Amritsar, where the group were hiding out. The operation caused cataclysmic damage, killing Sikh pilgrims as well as militants, and led to desecration of the temple by tanks and heavy weaponry. Gandhi says that when her mother-in-law was shown images of the devastation, tears rolled down her face.
For Sikhs in India, it was a profound and painful attack on their religion, and Indira was inundated with threats. “She told us what to do in case she died – so she knew,” Gandhi says. “She was making preparations for her death. She told Rahul he must be brave and not to cry.” That summer Indira took her grandchildren on a trip to her ancestral home of Kashmir; Gandhi believes this was to “say goodbye”. Indira also defied advice to remove her Sikh bodyguards – something that turned out to be a fateful decision.
Gandhi was at home on 31 October when she heard what sounded like fireworks going off. Sprinting over to Indira’s office next door, she was confronted by her mother-in-law’s bloodied body, riddled with bullets, lying on the ground. Indira’s own Sikh bodyguards had opened fire on her in retribution for the attack on the Golden Temple.
What came next remains seared on Gandhi’s memory. After Indira was put into a car, she held her bleeding body and tried to revive her mother-in-law as they raced to the hospital. “There was blood everywhere and I realised she wasn’t replying to my questions. It seemed as if she had already gone,” she says.
Even after so many years, the story is clearly painful to recount and she speaks hesitantly, her soft voice growing even quieter. “I remember the drive from the house to the hospital was excruciating. There wasn’t much traffic, but it felt so slow. I also knew that because she wasn’t speaking, it must be over.”
Gandhi admits there are still parts of that experience she can’t bring herself to discuss. “I never talk about it. Only if I’m asked, then I struggle to.” Indira would be declared dead at the hospital. Her body was still lying there, cold, when Rajiv broke the news that he had been asked to step in as prime minister. Gandhi had begged him to stay out of politics and describes that conversation as a “knife going into my heart”.
In the aftermath of Indira’s death, she was traumatised and depressed, living “like a ghost”. Rajiv, too, had no time to grieve. Newly announced as prime minister, he immediately had to deal with deadly anti-Sikh riots that erupted after Indira’s death. He would later be accused of not doing enough to stop the bloodbath. “Rajiv never really showed his pain,” Gandhi says. “I remember seeing him in his mother’s study, on one of the chairs where she sat, with tears. But in public he felt he had to hide it.”
Fear took over their lives. The house became a fortress, with uniformed commandos stationed in the children’s bedrooms. Rahul and Priyanka were pulled out of school and no longer allowed to roam freely. She would worry if Rajiv didn’t come back from an engagement on time. He, meanwhile, would always want her by his side. “Fear was a very real thing,” she says. “My thought was always: he will be killed next.” By 1991, her premonition had come true.
A silence settles over the room as Gandhi struggles to recall how she went on living after Rajiv’s death. A Sri Lankan separatist militant had set off a suicide bomb while he was on the election trail, killing him instantly. Throughout our conversation, she still refers to Rajiv as “Papa”, as he is known to their children.
Priyanka, who sits on the sofa with us, interjects gently. She tells me how her mother would sit in the dark all day, listening to Mozart’s Requiem, engulfed by grief. “You were angry at him,” she says, speaking to her mother. “When you used to cry, you used to shout: how has he left me, why did he leave?”
Gandhi sits quietly for a moment. “After my mother-in-law was killed, we thought that, as we were always together, if something happens to one, it will happen to the other one,” she says. They had even written notes on how they wanted their funerals.
Yet when Gandhi’s sister pleaded for her to return to Italy, the thought was unfathomable. “India was my home, my children’s home,” she says. Gandhi last went back to Italy four years ago, when her mother died.
She found out later that, prior to the attack, Indian intelligence had intercepted death threats against Rajiv by the Sri Lankan separatist Tamil Tigers, angered over India’s intervention in the country’s civil war. However, these had been ignored by the newly elected government, who instead took away his top-level security. She still believes the truth of a wider conspiracy behind his death has yet to come out. The most recent commission to investigate it was shut down by the Modi government. “I don’t think we will get the truth now,” she says with a sigh.
Crucially, just as the foundation of her world was shattered, a wind of change was blowing across north India. A claim that a mosque in the city of Ayodhya was built on the ruins of an ancient Hindu temple had been gaining traction among hardline, rightwing Hindu nationalist organisations and political groups. In December 1992, supporters of the movement – including BJP figures – violently tore down the mosque.
Gandhi recalls crying as she witnessed the demolition on television. She says she knew then that they faced “a long battle for the secular nation that Mahatma Gandhi, Nehru and their colleagues had strived to build”. She accepts that failures of her own party in part contributed to the rise of the BJP and its hardline Hindutva politics. “I think we have been too complacent in many ways. There was a laissez-faire kind of an attitude,” she says. In 2024, Modi delivered on the BJP’s longstanding promise and inaugurated a vast Hindu temple in the place where the mosque had once stood.
Throughout her memoir, Gandhi is open about her distrust of politics, describing it as “menacing”, driven by “ambition, greed and hypocrisy”. But with Congress facing an existential threat and looking likely to fracture, Gandhi succumbed to mounting pressure and agreed to become its president in 1998. It was a decision, she says, driven by a sense of duty to her lost husband. Not only did she have to fight against her own ingrained shyness, she also had to take on political opponents in Hindi, her third language.
She insists she never had political ambition. Despite helping the party to win the most votes in the 2004 election, she shocked everyone by refusing to become prime minister. “It was clear in my mind I would never do it,” she says. “It was just not me.” Nonetheless, until she stepped back from the day-to-day of Congress leadership a few years ago, she had little time for herself. She would carry books to political events, history and autobiographies, to read on the way home. Music, both Indian classical and European operas, also became her solace. Having previously studied art restoration, “once in a while, I would slip away to an art exhibition”.
Today she stays out of the messy day-to-day of politics, though is still kept in the loop by her daughter and attends the occasional meeting. She finds joy in her small vegetable patch, but more than anything in spending time with her children and two grandchildren. Theirs has always been a dog-loving family (Priyanka once had seven golden retrievers) and Gandhi is devoted to her two jack russells, Noorie and Lapo, who were gifts from her son.
Nonetheless, the fortress of security that surrounds her home is a stark reminder of the restrictions still imposed on her freedom. Armed police man the barricades on the road outside, and my car is thoroughly inspected by security before I am allowed to drive through a towering metal gate and into her driveway.
While she was once credited with reviving the fortunes of Congress, over the past decade the Gandhi family have overseen its calamitous decline. Their previous government, in power till 2014, was marred by allegations of rampant corruption. (“In almost every single instance, the ministers resigned,” is Gandhi’s defence.) After taking over from his mother, Rahul lost the last three general elections to Modi, and Congress remains in power in only a few states. Meanwhile, the BJP’s Hindutva has become the country’s dominant political ideology. As the family has maintained its control, Congress has been unable to shake off allegations that it is nepotistic and run by political elites.
Why can’t Congress free itself from the Gandhi family’s leadership, I ask? She is dismissive, perhaps a nerve touched. “You would have to ask the party,” she says. Gandhi also skates over the question of nepotism, simply saying, “We all fight elections: we win them, we lose them. All of us have.” But after so many losses, can a Gandhi-led Congress still be a credible alternative to the BJP? While she is adamant they can, many in the country remain unconvinced.
It is true that we are meeting at an interesting moment, for both Modi and the bruised opposition. As gen Z youth erupted on to the streets in protest against the government over the summer – satirically calling themselves the “Cockroaches” after an online joke transformed into a serious political movement – the long-crushed space for dissent has opened up.
In recent weeks, young Indians have once again been taking to the streets against the government, despite being met with draconian state force. The question of whether they can shake the BJP’s grip on power remains to be seen; so far, the Cockroach movement has kept its distance from the opposition alliance. But “what encourages me is young people are coming out and demonstrating,” Gandhi says. “With determination, they’re calling out the government on things that are not right. I feel like this is a real shift.”
Congress, too, has become more energised than it has been for many years. Images of Rahul and Priyanka being manhandled by police as they tried to protest against the government have gone viral in recent weeks. After once pleading with her children to stay out of politics, Gandhi now says, “It’s good that they’re there. Now more than ever before.” The Gandhi family, it seems, are not done just yet.

Thanks to commercials starring actor (and former part-owner) Ryan Reynolds, Mint Mobile has become one of the most popular mobile carriers. According to J.D. Power, Mint ranks highest in overall customer satisfaction among wireless carriers. Its prepaid cell phone plans, with no contracts or early termination fees, appeal to many customers, especially those with basic needs. Mint operates on parent company T-Mobile’s network, which has the best 5G coverage among the big three operators. You can bring your own unlocked, compatible device, or purchase a new phone from Mint, including the latest Google Pixel 11, Apple iPhone 18 Pro, or Samsung Galaxy S26 FE.
Mint doesn’t always offer extra discounts in the form of codes or coupons, but its low-cost plans with minimal monthly commitment appeal to groups that need budget phone service, such as seniors on a fixed income or young adults transitioning off their parents’ service. However, it runs promotions that are automatically applied at checkout. Right now, Mint is running an anniversary special that gives you up to 71% off its six-month plans. We like that Mint Mobile makes its plans easy to understand, thanks to a nutritional-value-style breakdown of pricing and fees. If you’ve been looking to switch carriers and have your eye on Mint, you should definitely consider these Mint Mobile promos when you decide.
Mint Mobile Savings for Seniors: 6 GB for $15 a Month or 50% off 6-Month Plan
While Mint Mobile doesn’t offer a specific discount for customers age 55 and older, its low-cost standard plans should appeal to anyone on a budget or who simply wants to pay less for phone service. For seniors who don’t need much data per month, the 6-GB plan is plenty for casual browsing, streaming, app downloads, and emailing. Plus, it includes unlimited talk and texting, which may be more valuable to this age group than doomscrolling on social media.
The 6-GB plan costs $15 a month for three months, plus taxes and fees. Mint plans never require a contract, but you must pay the full $45 upfront. The plan renews for another three months, but the price increases to $25 a month, so it’s $75 plus taxes and fees. It’s still affordable compared with legacy carriers. You don’t have to deal with monthly charges, and there’s no commitment after the three-month term if you wish to cancel. You can switch to a different plan for potential greater savings. Note that Mint doesn’t refund unused months if you cancel outside the seven-day cancellation period (seven days after activation).
To save more, and if their budgets allow, seniors should consider Mint Mobile’s longer-term plans. While they cost more upfront, they save more in the long run. For example, Mint Mobile is currently running an anniversary special on its six-month plans. Seniors can lock in the 6-GB, 17-GB, 23-GB, or unlimited plan for $10 a month for six months. Afterward, the price increases to only $20 a month if you renew the 6-GB plan for another six months, or you can switch to a 3- or 12-month plan. Note the varying upfront costs required.
For the best savings, consider the 12-month plan. It has a higher upfront fee of $180, but it breaks down to $15 a month. Unlike the three-month plan, it stays at $15 after it renews (subject to potential price increases, which are very possible given the nature of subscription services). You pay more at first, but you save even more over time.
Perhaps the best feature for seniors is Mint Mobile’s customer service, staffed by live agents by phone during select hours or available 24/7 via online chat. While many companies are increasingly moving toward AI-based systems, having humans who can help guide customers through issues is refreshing.
Mint Kids: Mobile Discounts for Children
Like seniors, Mint Mobile doesn’t offer plans or discounts for kids. Instead, parents can choose a low-cost option that fits their children’s mobile habits. If they rely mostly on Wi-Fi at home, school, or the library, they may not need a high-data plan. If they binge on streaming entertainment and are constantly on social media, Mint offers 17 GB, 23 GB, or unlimited data plans at $20, $25, or $30 per month.
As mentioned above, the different monthly terms (3, 6, and 12 months) require different upfront payments, and prices may also increase after the initial entry price. The best approach is for parents to determine their child’s needs, then browse Mint’s plans that fit their budget. It can get costly as you move up in data and monthly tiers, plus the higher upfront costs, but parents could still save money in the long run compared with a legacy carrier, and without a contract. If additional children also need a phone plan, parents should look at family plans offered by other service providers. Mint Mobile doesn’t offer a traditional family plan, but you can sign up for multiple plans and mix and match based on your needs. Again, do some price comparison to see if you would actually save money.
Something Mint Mobile doesn’t offer is a smartwatch plan. Instead of phones, a popular trend is for parents to give their kids a cellular-enabled Apple Watch. So if this is what you’re looking for, sadly, Mint Mobile won’t work for this purpose.
Bundle Your Home Broadband and Phone Plan With This Mint Mobile Promo
Mint offers home internet from its parent, T-Mobile. Like its phone plans, Mint offers Home Minternet packages in 3-, 6-, or 12-month terms, each with an upfront payment. Prices start at $40 per month for a three-month term ($120 upfront).
Right now, Mint Mobile is offering a 12-month plan for $45 per month ($540 upfront) that bundles 12 months of unlimited data—a $300 savings compared with buying both separately. Since home internet can easily cost double what Mint charges, this could be a significant cost-saver for those with modest internet needs that T-Mobile’s 5G network can handle.
What to Do if Your Mint Mobile Promo Code Is Not Working
Mint Mobile keeps its offerings easy to understand, whether you're looking at standard pricing or promotions. With its transparent pricing model, Mint Mobile doesn’t usually require codes. Any listed promotion should automatically apply at checkout. Just make sure you note the total, including any fees and taxes, before you place an order.
If you are unsure, Mint offers live, human customer service via phone (limited hours) or online (24/7).

Qazi Faraz Ahmad is the Deputy News Editor with Hindustan Times. With more than 18 years of experience in hardcore journalism, he has been extensively reporting on policy, politics, and governance from the Hindi heartland of Uttar Pradesh. Based in Lucknow, Faraz is part of the Hindustan Times UP Bureau, where he reports on key beats. He has closely tracked and covered major electoral battles, including the 2012 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections, the 2014 Lok Sabha elections, the 2017 UP Assembly elections, the 2019 Lok Sabha elections, the 2022 UP Assembly elections, the 2023 Karnataka Assembly elections, and the 2024 Lok Sabha elections. His sharp analysis and on-ground insights have made him a trusted voice on Uttar Pradesh politics and national policy matters. Faraz brings rich experience from reputed organisations such as Press Trust of India (PTI), CNN-News18, Dainik Jagran Group, Oman Tribune (Muscat) and other leading media houses. Known for his in-depth ground reporting and copy-editing skills, he combines journalistic rigour with a deep understanding of northern India's sociopolitical landscape. A passionate traveller and trainer associated with initiatives like the Google News Initiative, he continues to deliver credible, impactful journalism on critical developments shaping the region and the country.
Samajwadi Party, Congress form 4-member panels each for seat-sharing talks in the run-up to UP polls
The two parties will hold 2-day talks in Delhi on November 23 and 24 in the first phase, examining all 403 seats.
The Samajwadi Party and the Congress have each constituted four-member panels to hold seat-sharing negotiations for the upcoming 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections, marking a formal and structured start to opposition coordination ahead of the polls.
The two parties will hold two-day talks in Delhi on November 23 and 24 in the first phase, examining all 403 seats on a constituency-by-constituency basis with a focus on local strength and electoral prospects.
Who all have been included in the panels
The SP panel is headed by national general secretary and Rajya Sabha MP Ram Gopal Yadav, the party said on X. The other members are Lok Sabha MPs Rajiv Rai and Iqra Chaudhary (also known as Iqra Hasan), and SP state president Shyam Lal Pal.
The Congress panel comprises the party’s UP in-charge Rajendra Pal Gautam, state president Aradhna Mishra, state working president Imran Masood and AICC general secretary (organisation) KC Venugopal.
SP chief Akhilesh Yadav has repeatedly emphasised that the seat-sharing formula will rest on winnability rather than any fixed number of seats. “We will sit and talk about who can win from where and then decide our candidates. Winnability will be the sole criterion, as only through this can we defeat the BJP,” he said earlier.
What Congress, SP have said on seat-sharing
The development comes over a week after Yadav said at the HT Leadership Summit that the Congress was seeking 181 seats in an alliance for the 403-member assembly.
The Congress has since clarified that it will not be rigid on numbers and is looking for a “respectable share.”
Speaking to the media in Mau on Sunday, SP panel member Rajiv Rai said, “We are going to hold discussions on all 403 seats. It will be a two-day meeting initially and we will see who is strong on which seat and ultimately decide.”
Congress UP in-charge Rajendra Pal Gautam said, “We will have a threadbare discussion one after the other (on) seats, sitting across the table in Delhi tomorrow.”
Responding to the formation of SP and Congress panels for seat-sharing talks, UP BJP spokesperson Anand Dubey said, “The Samajwadi Party and the Congress alliance for 2027 assembly polls will not have any impact on state’s political landscape. Voters are fully aware of the SP’s previous tenure in the state when lawlessness and crime was rampant. As the Congress has no base left in the state, the Samajwadi Party will only be at the receiving end by conceding seats to the Congress."
The negotiations reflect a pragmatic approach by both parties within the INDIA bloc framework. In the 2022 assembly elections, the BJP won a second successive term, securing a decisive majority with 255 seats, while the SP won 111 and the Congress managed only two.
By contrast, the two parties, contesting as allies, performed strongly in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections in Uttar Pradesh. The SP won 37 seats, the Congress six, and the BJP 33. With 202 seats needed for a majority in the 403-member assembly, leaders from both sides have signalled that a winnability-driven, seat-by-seat understanding is essential to mount a united challenge to the BJP. The Delhi talks are expected to set the tone for further alliance coordination in the months ahead.
The Samajwadi Party has been out of power in Uttar Pradesh since 2017 and the Congress since 1989.

The story so far: After 26 years of holding on to its measles elimination status, the United States lost this distinction. This is the highest annual total since 1989-91, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention(CDC). As per data put out by the Unicef, 96% of cases are in unvaccinated people or those with unknown vaccination status. Children under five account for 18% of cases and those aged 5-19 for 40%.

What to know about tear gas and reproductive health, as concerns are raised in France
French activists and lawmakers are demanding after recent protests that police stop using tear gas because of rising concerns about menstrual changes and reproductive health issues
PARIS -- French activists and lawmakers are demanding after recent street protests that authorities suspend the use of tear gas to disperse crowds over concerns it's caused menstrual changes and other reproductive health problems, though scientists have not confirmed a medical connection.
The demands come after police used tear gas during student protests and demonstrations over the cost of living, some marred by violence. Some women reported painful cramps, unexpected bleeding and disrupted menstrual cycles after exposure, and an advocacy group says it has collected more than 10,000 complaints. Opposition lawmakers are seeking a ban and independent research into possible health effects.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has rejected the calls, saying police use of tear gas is essential to crowd control as an alternative to using more dangerous weapons.
Here’s what is known — and what is not — about tear gas and reproductive health.
Tear gas grenades used by French police contain CS, a chemical irritant that affects the eyes, skin and respiratory tract. CS is a crystalline powder dispersed into the air as fine particles. Its effects depend upon how much is used and how long people are exposed to it.
Those exposed during the protests include peaceful demonstrators — including children, pregnant women and older people — and residents near the sites of protest marches.
Mélina Galland, 24, was working as an independent photographer during Oct. 17 protests in Paris that were marred by rioting and looting. She wore a double surgical mask along with a diving mask when tear gas grenades were fired.
“Heading back home, I felt intense belly pain which was unusual because I never experience pain that intense at that stage of my period,” she said.
Chloé Baroux, 25, also a photographer, first noticed pain and irregular periods after covering protests against a security bill in 2020 and 2021. She said her menstrual cycles eventually became more regular, and she didn't think of a potential link to tear gas until she covered the recent protests, noting, “over the past two months, it’s become irregular again.”
Eva-Luna Tholance, a former journalist who investigated the issue six years ago, decided to found the “Lacrymos de sang” ("Tears of blood") advocacy group during the protests to raise awareness about possible effects on menstrual cycles and pregnancies. The group asked people last month to complete a questionnaire describing their exposure and symptoms. Its collection of accounts doesn't establish how common symptoms are among those who say they were exposed to tear gas, and they were not reviewed by independent doctors.
Still, Tholance said, many women described pain or unexpected bleeding, and thousands are asking questions about what’s happening in their bodies.
“Some people experience mild cramps, but a huge number tell us about cramps that are far worse than what they normally experience during their periods,” she said, adding that bleeding reports range “from spotting to extremely heavy bleeding lasting several days. Some people bleed for weeks.”
Others reported bleeding despite being postmenopausal or taking hormonal contraception that normally prevents menstrual bleeding, Tholance said.
An Associated Press investigation during the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests in the U.S. found there had been limited study and oversight of tear gas, though it did raise concerns about tear gas exposure in confined spaces, excessive use and canisters fired directly at people.
A recent study collected accounts of symptoms reported after the BLM protests. It found a “potential relationship” between exposure and “adverse reproductive health outcomes” but did not prove cause and effect.
That’s in part because the study relied on self-reported information collected at one point in time — similar to the French group’s questionnaire — and because people who felt most impacted may have been more likely to respond.
“There’s a lot of theories. We don’t really 100% know,” said the study’s lead author, Asha Hassan of the University of Minnesota Medical School. The study calls for more research “urgently.”
Hassan said much early research on tear gas involved healthy young men in military settings, which could help explain why menstrual and other reproductive health effects have gone undocumented.
Alsetex and Nobel Sport, two leading suppliers of tear gas grenades to French law enforcement, did not respond to requests for comment.
The Interior Ministry says no published scientific studies show that CS causes menstrual changes or miscarriages. It said other effects of tear gas generally resolve within hours, although it acknowledged that some longer-lasting symptoms affecting the skin and eyes “cannot be ruled out.”
Some other possible effects in the body “have been suggested, but not demonstrated,” it said.
The ministry said it conducted several studies in 2021 and 2022 assessing individual exposure to tear gas, particularly among law enforcement personnel. It did not respond to an AP request for copies.
—-
AP journalist Teresa Suarez contributed to this story.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has proposed a set of safeguards against electronic payment frauds, including an account-wide ‘Stop Switch’ and a ‘Trusted Person Mechanism’ (TPM) for high-value transactions. The central bank has invited feedback on the draft directions by December 14, 2026, with the proposed rules set to come into effect from July 1, 2027. Under the Draft Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Responsible Business Conduct) Fifth Amendment Directions, 2026, banks will have to provide a ‘Stop Switch’ that allows customers to immediately disable all outgoing debits, new payment mandates and new UPI app registrations. The switch will not block incoming credits or existing standing instructions. Customers will be able to activate, modify or deactivate it through bank branches, ATMs, mobile apps, internet banking and interactive voice response (IVR) services. Banks will also have to ensure that re-enabling digital payment channels or deactivating the Stop Switch requires at least the same level of authentication as its activation. The RBI has also proposed a voluntary Trusted Person Mechanism (TPM) for high-value transfers. Under this facility, account holders can nominate an adult as an additional authentication layer for transactions above a specified threshold. The nominated person will have to approve such transactions within a one-hour window. However, the trusted person will not have any legal authority over the account or access to its details. Banks will be responsible for verifying the identity and eligibility of nominated individuals. Any activation or modification of the TPM will also be subject to a 24-hour cooling-off period. The RBI had first floated a similar proposal in June this year, suggesting an additional authentication layer for digital transactions above ₹10,000 made by citizens aged 70 and above. Beyond these measures, banks will have to offer customers granular controls over their digital payment channels. These will include options to enable or disable individual channels, set time windows for their deactivation and establish transaction limits per transfer, per beneficiary or through aggregate daily caps. The draft also proposes that all digital payment channels remain disabled by default during customer onboarding and be activated only with explicit consent. Further, newly issued physical and virtual cards will be restricted by default to domestic contact-based ATM and point-of-sale (POS) transactions. Newly enabled digital payment channels will also be subject to a transfer limit determined by the bank for the first 24 hours. Earlier this year, the central bank issued directions requiring banks to compensate eligible victims of digital payment frauds. The latest proposals take a more preventive approach, giving customers greater control over payment channels and adding authentication safeguards to help stop fraudulent transactions before they are completed.

The monthly medicines bill for the mother of one of us comes to approximately ₹2,900. This month, a chance visit to the Jan Aushadhi outlet near home came as a pleasant surprise. The bill for the same monthly list of medicines was ₹663, a near 23 per cent of the usual spend. It provokes a question: how does a bill fall by more than three-fourths?
The bill is not a fluke. It is the visible end of a long chain of efforts by the Government of India to make medicines affordable for the common people. The Jan Aushadhi scheme, launched in 2008 and revamped in 2015, has put low-cost medicines within the reach of people across the country. It banks on a manufacturing base that has made India the largest supplier of generic medicines in the world. What remains to be done is increasing health expenditure as a percentage of the GDP to ensure meaningful outreach.

WASHINGTON —The MAHA Institute, a nonprofit launched last year to support Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s health agenda in Washington, burned over $1 million in 2025, leaving it with little cash on hand to continue operating, tax documents obtained by STAT show.
The group started 2025, its first year in operation, with nearly $1.3 million in its coffers, but ended the year with just $171,000, per its latest IRS return, filed this week. That 86% drop was hardly offset by the group’s revenue, which was just shy of $67,000 for the year.
“To have lost over $1 million is pretty notable to me,” said Brian Mittendorf, a professor at Ohio State University who specializes in nonprofit accounting.

At least 13 people have died, and more than 300 have been hospitalised since November 18 after they consumed spurious liquor in Manipur's Chandel district, police said on Saturday (November 21, 2026).
The patients are mostly from Chakpikarong and surrounding areas and have been hospitalised across multiple healthcare facilities in Imphal, including JNIMS, RIMS, Shija and Babina Hospital.
"Thirteen people have been reported dead till 9 p.m. on Friday, while 346 patients have been admitted to hospitals due to suspected methanol poisoning, as they consumed spurious liquor," an official told PTI.
Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh visited Shija Hospital and Babina Hospital on Friday afternoon (November 20, 2026) to assess the situation and meet patients undergoing treatment.
In a social media post, Mr. Singh said, "Visited Shija Hospital at Lamphelpat, and Babina Hospital at Sajiwa, today [on Friday] to enquire about the health condition of the persons undergoing treatment after consuming spurious liquor from Chakpikarong area in Chandel District."
The Chandel district administration has intensified emergency response measures, and a team has been constituted for coordinated monitoring of the situation, an official notification said.
Four rapid response teams, equipped with adequate medicines and oxygen supplies, have been deployed in the district, the official said.
"Over 140 patients were admitted to Shija Hospital and over 41 patients at Babina Hospital. The death toll has touched 11 during the last 48 hours. The patients are undergoing medical evaluation and treatment under the close supervision of the doctors," he said.
"A medical team, led by a Specialist in General Medicine, along with essential medicines, has left for Chandel District to strengthen on-ground treatment and response", he said adding, "The government will conduct an enquiry and the culprits will be punished."
Joint managing director of Shija Hospitals, Chetan .K, told reporters that the patients admitted to the hospital reported symptoms of dizziness, stomach pain and other complications.
"Some patients are also undergoing hemodialysis", he added.
A JNIMS doctor said, "Many of the hospitalised include individuals who had consumed local liquor and had come to the hospital due to fear."
Shija Hospitals also informed that "over 312 patients [have been] attended [to] till now at Shija Hospitals due to methanol poisoning."
Preliminary reports suggest that the suspected contaminated alcohol was purchased from Sugnu in Kakching district.
Chandel constituency MLA S.S. Olish said arrangements are being made to bring more patients up to Imphal and has requested the chief minister to look into the situation.
She said, "I have spoken personally to CM Yumnam Khemchand, and requested him to look into the situation affecting Chandel. He agreed willingly and has visited the patients at Shija Hospitals and will visit Babina later."
"Moreover, party workers, especially in Chakpikarong, are working constantly, arranging vehicles to bring patients up to Imphal", she added.
Bishnupur, Senapati, Kakching and Thoubal district administrations have issued separate public advisories, requesting people "to refrain from consuming locally brewed liquor or alcoholic beverages of doubtful or unverified origin."
