The people of Iraq are in urgent need of better health care and their situation is deteriorating by the day. The UN has today appealed for at least $325 million in emergency funds to meet the immediate health, nutrition, water and sanitation needs of the most vulnerable populations. Out of this amount, the World Health Organization urgently appeals for $185 million.
This request is part of the wider United Nations humanitarian appeal for $2.1 billion to provide assistance to the people of Iraq over the next six months. This appeal is being launched jointly by all the UN humanitarian agencies in New York and Geneva.
WHO is already working in Iraq to provide badly needed medical assistance. The health status of the Iraqi people has been seriously affected by more than two decades of war and economic sanctions. Child death rates today are more than twice as high as they were in 1990: one in eight children dies before the age of five, one in three children is malnourished and one in four begins life as an underweight baby.
"Overall, the health of people in Iraq is poor and likely to get worse," said Dr Gro Harlem Brundtland, Director General of the World Health Organization. "This appeal is not an optional extra. It is the only way of stabilising the situation, and indeed improving it."
The three biggest child killers in Iraq are acute respiratory infection, diarrhoeal diseases and measles. Almost half of the country's 24.5 million people are children whose future depends on a massive and rapid improvement in the country's health and infrastructure.
Conflict is already adding to the strains on the health of the population and on the infrastructure on which they depend. For example, damage to the electricity and water supply in the southern city of Basra is expected to lead to additional health problems, particularly for children and other vulnerable groups. People elsewhere may soon face similar or worse emergencies.
A substantial investment is needed to provide essential care to people who are either injured in the conflict or whose health suffers as a result of damage to the infrastructure. In the months to come, more will be needed to begin rebuilding the most critical and most badly effected parts of the public health system.
That means building up the capacities of hospitals and health centres; it means providing some $60 million of medicines, medical supplies and equipment; it means repairing and rehabilitating vital hospitals and health centres.
There must be substantial investment in the ability to detect and respond to outbreaks of disease, in the training and equipment of health workers and in the health information which is vital to prioritise health work.
WHO today has more than 300 staff working hard in Iraq to support the health system and to bring badly needed medical assistance to people across the country. During the current conflict, WHO has successfully sent teams to help with an outbreak of diarrhoeal disease in northern Iraq and to assess the health needs of people who have left their homes. WHO is ready to do much more work across the whole country in support of the health system.
In the weeks and months to come, Iraq's health system will almost inevitably come under unprecedented pressure. Health is a crucial part of the economic and social system.

Pentagon sharply rebukes Canada over defense spending and the F-35 fighter jet review
The Pentagon has accused Canada of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke to its longtime ally over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets
TORONTO -- The Pentagon accused Canada on Monday of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke to its longtime ally over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets.
In an unusually blunt fact sheet, the Defense Department accused Ottawa of failing to make the tough decisions needed to modernize its military and meet NATO commitments.
“Canada’s defense shortfalls speak for themselves,” it said. “Canada must get serious and focused.”
The criticism follows a classified directive from U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds said largely restricts officials’ participation in Canadian think tank events and social engagements. Relations have been battered by President Donald Trump’s trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st state.
In May, Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby announced a pause in the Permanent Joint Board on Defense, a bilateral advisory body established in 1940, accusing Canada of failing to make credible progress on its defense commitments.
The rebuke also follows criticism of Washington at the Halifax International Security Forum, where its president, Peter Van Praagh, a former adviser in Conservative Prime Minister Stephen Harper’s government, warned Friday that the United States can no longer be counted on as a predictable leader of the democratic world.
The Pentagon accused Canada of leaving American taxpayers to shoulder the burden of continental defense. It said only 41.9% of Canada’s air force fleet was serviceable in the 2025-26 fiscal year and 53.9% of its naval fleet, while the army’s operational readiness stood at 48%.
“Underinvestment in defense has atrophied the Canadian Armed Forces and limited Canada’s ability to contribute to the defense of North America," the fact sheet said. "Secretary Hegseth is laser focused on incentivizing and enabling Canada’s military modernization after decades of American taxpayers footing the bill for its homeland defense.”
It also criticized Ottawa’s review of its planned purchase of 88 American-made F-35s, warning that a mixed fighter fleet could worsen personnel shortages. The Pentagon accused Canadian leaders of putting domestic economic interests ahead of military effectiveness, creating uncertainty for the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD, which the countries operate jointly.
Prime Minister Mark Carney put the F-35 purchase under review as Trump threatened Canadian sovereignty and imposed tariffs. Canada has examined Swedish-made Gripen fighters, which could bring manufacturing jobs.
Canada’s military did not immediately provide a substantive response to the Pentagon’s criticism.
Carney has acknowledged readiness problems, saying only one of Canada’s four submarines was seaworthy. Ottawa has since named Germany’s Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems as preferred supplier for up to 12 replacements, pending contract negotiations.
“We should no longer send three-quarters of our defense capital spending to America,” Carney said in June.
Canada reached NATO’s previous target of spending 2% of gross domestic product on defense and joined allies pledging to reach 5% by 2035, including related security investments. Its latest budget projects combined defense and security spending of 4.1% of GDP by the 2027-28 fiscal year, but core defense spending of only 2.6%. Canada’s parliamentary budget watchdog says the path to 5% remains unclear.
The Pentagon accused Ottawa of postponing the largest increases until after the 2029 federal election.
Other NATO allies also remain short of the new target. Yet Colby praised Germany’s military buildup Sunday as a “tectonic shift” and called Poland a “true model ally.” He also praised Romania’s plan to reach 5% by 2031.
Speaking Saturday at the Halifax International Security Forum, Rounds said the directive was not expected to affect joint military operations or intelligence sharing.
The Trump administration had already barred Pentagon officials from the Halifax forum under 2025 restrictions on think tank participation.

What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war
- Published
Anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.
The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi, co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?
The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.
Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes, has called it "a dangerous escalation".
It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.
Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.
Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks – what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" – have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.
The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.
And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.
It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".
Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.
Throughout this year the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has condemned all attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and today the global shipping community will be wondering whether this attack does indeed set a dangerous precedent.
If Ukraine can plan and execute such a bold attack on Russian ships in a nominally neutral harbour so far from home, where does this stop?
Impact elsewhere in Europe
As the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches, this war has already been spreading, notably in other parts of Europe.
On Friday, several Russian projectiles landed well inside Poland's borders, just 60 miles from an Anglo-French exercise of forces intended to be deployed following an eventual ceasefire in Ukraine.
This, said Poland's PM Donald Tusk, was "a deliberate provocation" by Moscow.
It's not the first time Russian munitions have landed inside Poland, and therefore inside Nato territory, but observers have pointed out that Russia's probing of Nato's borders is becoming ever more brazen and some are calling for a firmer response.
But Russia is already heavily sanctioned by the West, with Europe having reduced much – but not all – of its energy imports from Russia, so the options for retaliation are limited, short of military confrontation, which no one wants.
Both Romania and Moldova have found themselves frequently struck by overflying Russian drones targeting Ukraine's Black Sea ports, while Bulgaria and Romania have suffered maritime drone attacks on commercial shipping just offshore in the Black Sea.
In the case of Romania, a Nato member, fast jets have had to be scrambled to intercept incoming Russian drones and there is a profound suspicion that these incursions are not all accidental.
The three Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – all have borders with Russia and all consider themselves right on the front lines in this war.
There have been a number of anonymous attacks on military industrial facilities in these countries, blamed on agents acting on Moscow's behalf.
Russia, for its part, suspects Estonia of being complicit in Ukrainian drone attacks on the Baltic involving overflights through Estonian airspace.
Hybrid attacks
Hybrid warfare isn't new but it is on the rise.
It refers to the practice, by either side, of carrying out largely anonymous and unattributable operations using methods like cyber attacks, the burning down of warehouses supplying military equipment and the dispatching of drones, both for surveillance and loaded with explosives.
This autumn, Germany's Leipzig-Halle airport, which is used as a resupply hub by Ukraine's cargo aircraft, was targeted by three explosive drones that were discovered before anyone was hurt.
There have been other incidents involving explosive packages sent across Europe targeting Germany, Poland and the UK. Moscow denies any involvement.

A crude bomb was allegedly hurled by ABVP activists at a bookstall set up by the Students’ Federation of India (SFI) in College Street, Kolkata’s principal hub of bookshops and publishing houses, late on November 18.
Titled Sangrami Boipotro (Literature of Struggle), the stall was set up by the Calcutta University unit of the SFI to commemorate the November Revolution. ABVP activists allegedly attempted to vandalise the stall, accusing the Left student outfit of selling ‘anti-national’ books, resulting in day-long tension in the ‘boi para’.
The confrontation began around 11 am on Wednesday and continued late into the evening. Tensions escalated when ABVP activists allegedly hurled a firecracker, locally known as a ‘chocolate bomb’, into the SFI stall as activists, including women, were packing up the books before closing for the day. Video footage shows the firecracker exploding in a small burst of flames and smoke filling up the area.
The incident took place in the presence of a large contingent of Kolkata Police personnel. SFI activists alleged that the police attempted to shield the ABVP activists. The Right-wing student organisation, on the other hand, claimed SFI activists had assaulted its members and vandalised its bookstall.
Reacting to the allegations and counter allegations of violence, BJP state president Samik Bhattacharya said, “These are matters related to student politics. They are young. Political movements were never entirely peaceful here. These things happen.” He also said ABVP was not related to the BJP.
The SFI’s Version of Events
According to SFI activists and videos circulated on social media, the confrontation began around 11 am. The bookstall was scheduled to open at that time, with senior Left leader Biman Bose slated to inaugurate it.
However, as SFI activists were setting up the stall, a group of ABVP activists gathered outside the main gate of Calcutta University, which opens onto College Street, and attempted to prevent them.
To contain the situation, a contingent of Kolkata Police personnel formed a human barricade between the two groups. Videos show ABVP activists repeatedly raising slogans and displaying aggression. However, the police did not remove them from the spot.
Around 1 pm, tensions appeared to ease somewhat, with ABVP workers setting up a makeshift bookstall a few metres away from the SFI stall. The two stalls were positioned on either side of the university’s main gate, with the ABVP stall to its left and the SFI stall to its right. Police personnel placed metal barricades in front of the SFI stall to prevent a direct confrontation between the groups.
Around 2 pm, Left leaders Biman Bose and Sujan Chakraborty visited the stall.
However, as Bose was leaving, ABVP workers were heard raising slogans such as “Biman Bose Go Back” and “Slap Biman Bose across the face with shoes”.
The ABVP protest blocked a section of College Street. Its activists allegedly charged towards the SFI stall several times in the presence of police personnel. They also threw water and eggs at the stall, staining a National Flag at the venue and several books, the Left outfit alleged.
Around 7 pm, the situation escalated with the ABVP gathering allegedly hurling bricks, wooden sticks and water bottles towards the SFI enclosure, while police personnel continued to maintain a barricade between the two groups.
Videos also show plastic chairs being hurled form either side.
Around this time, SFI activists were packing up the stall for the day when a ‘chocolate bomb’ was seen flying towards it from the direction of the ABVP gathering.
The firecracker exploded inside the SFI enclosure, producing a flash and filling the area with smoke. The explosion further escalated tensions, with SFI activists seen rushing towards the ABVP gathering. Police personnel struggled to pull them back and prevent a direct confrontation.
Following the incident, the SFI decided to lodge an FIR at the nearby Jorasanko police station. Activists also organised a protest march from College Street to the police station.
According to SFI activists, police initially resisted registering a written complaint but eventually agreed following their sustained pressure.
SFI activists further alleged that after they had left for the police station, ABVP workers vandalised the stall site, damaging tables, benches and chairs.
The SFI is scheduled to reopen the bookstall at the same location on Thursday. It will remain open until November 20.
Trouble Erupted on November 17 as well
According to SFI sources, the organisation has been setting up the bookstall at the same location for the past four years. This year, too, its members informed the Joint Commissioner of Kolkata Police about the stall and its schedule through an email. They also paid the requisite fee to the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) for setting up the stall. However, on Monday, the police informed them that they would not be allowed to erect any permanent structure at the site.
On Tuesday morning, a contingent of Kolkata Police personnel arrived in front of Calcutta University and attempted to prevent SFI activists from setting up the bookstall.
Around 12:30 pm, SFI activists blockaded College Street and began selling books while sitting on the road.
This led to a scuffle with the police, following which 41 SFI activists, including the organisation’s West Bengal state secretary, Debanjan Dey, were detained and taken to Lalbazar, the headquarters of Kolkata Police.
In response, the SFI organised a mobilisation outside Lalbazar, demanding the release of those detained. Around 6 pm, all 41 activists were released.
According to SFI activists, the joint commissioner of police held lengthy discussions with them, following which it was agreed that they could set up the stall without erecting any permanent structure. They were also asked to ensure that the stall did not obstruct traffic on College Street.
The SFI activists attempted to set up the stall on Wednesday in accordance with these conditions. However, their efforts were disrupted by ABVP activists, who objected to the organisation’s programme.
The ABVP’s Response
ABVP further alleged that SFI activists had destroyed books on Swami Vivekananda, claiming that its own bookstall had been set up to encourage reading among students. It accused the SFI of sabotaging an initiative intended to promote education.
The Facebook page of ABVP Paschimbanga also shared a clipping from Bengali news channel TV9 Bangla, which purportedly showed Arunava Dutta, an ABVP national executive council member, being assaulted by SFI activists.
In a separate post, ABVP shared a video showing a stone being hurled from near the Left book stall.
In a separate Facebook post, ABVP Paschimbanga condemned what it described as attacks on its activists at Calcutta University, Calcutta Medical College and Presidency University. “The throwing of bombs inside university campuses and the targeted attacks on ABVP activists by SFI and Left organisations are deeply alarming and condemnable,” the organisation said.
In the video, ABVP national secretary Shravan B Raj said, “The SFI and Left extremist groups are unleashing violence on ABVP karyakartas.”
Vandalism at Calcutta Medical College
In another incident on the same day, intern doctors at Calcutta Medical College, located adjacent to Calcutta University and barely a 100-metre from the site of the book-stall clash, alleged that ABVP-backed miscreants entered the college campus and assaulted them.
The incident came amid a protest by students and junior doctors against show-cause notices issued to eight interns who had spoken out against alleged mismanagement at government hospitals following the stampede at a Durga Puja pandal which claimed 19 lives.
According to a Facebook post by the West Bengal Junior Doctors’ Front, the college principal and other senior officials had initially agreed to withdraw the notices after acknowledging a shortage of medicines. However, following a phone call from a “higher authority”, the principal reportedly refused to issue a written order confirming their withdrawal. This prompted students to stage a sit-in protest.
The post alleged that around 70–80 outsiders subsequently entered the campus, vandalised property and assaulted interns and medical students, leaving several injured. It further alleged that the principal left the campus under heavy police protection while the attackers continued their rampage in the presence of police personnel.

Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31
- Published
The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 bought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.
The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.
Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.
After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.
Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".
The world is preparing for life beyond 1.5C
This was the first COP since the UN warned that global temperatures are expected to exceed 1.5C degrees above pre-industrial levels. That is the threshold which countries agreed not to breach as part of the Paris Climate Agreement signed in 2015.
The draft agreement had acknowledged the uncomfortable reality that climate action to date has failed on its most crucial of targets.
Without agreement, that recognition has been lost.
Almost exactly a decade ago a group of the world's climate scientists - the official UN body the IPCC - warned what would happen if temperatures rose 1.5C vs 2C:
- Sea level rise would be 10cm higher - that would expose 10 million more people to flooding, external
- The ocean would become more acidic risking irreversible damage to some marine life
- Extreme heat - that's hot days and nights - in every inhabited part of the world
Throughout the talks and during the final day, many countries still acknowledged that the target remained their north star of climate action.
"This COP sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with even more urgency to reduce emissions," said UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh at the close of the talks.
The draft had called for that overshoot to be kept as small and short-lived as possible – it also suggested something called carbon dioxide removal (CDR).
This is a process which takes greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere and has not been explicitly mentioned in a COP final agreement before.
Carbon dioxide can be removed naturally by planting trees - although there are limits to the scale and permanence of that.
There are other technological solutions, but these are controversial, external and are not well advanced.
Countries divided over approach on fossil fuels
This year's negotiations have exposed a troubling problem - consensus does not last forever.
On the central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts – countries could not bridge the divide on including language on fossil fuels.
And yet the very same pledge had been made just three years ago at COP28 in Dubai.
Rich nations also failed to put a figure to how much more money could be given to developing countries to adapt to climate change.
This is despite there already being a commitment from last year to triple the figure by 2035 from $40bn (£30bn) - but the interpretation of that pledge remains contested.
If governments cannot even agree to reaffirm commitments they've already made, it raises troubling questions about their ability to work together as the climate crisis intensifies.
- Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed 
  - Published3 hours ago
Minister Chris Bowen from Australia, who was co-leading the negotiations, pointed out at the end of the talks that the world is a very different place from when these commitments were struck just a few years ago.
"The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory".
That was made apparent during the final meeting when pointed remarks were delivered. EU representative Darragh O'Brien said the talks had been "hijacked by some oil states".
Russian delegate Sergei Kononuchenko switched from Russian to English to directly address the EU delegation. He accused them of providing climate finance only in the form of loans to developing nations: "This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner".
It is a serious blow not just to climate action, but to multilateralism itself - the idea that countries can put aside their differences on other issues to tackle problems they can't solve alone.
COP31 had some good news
Much of the coverage of COP31 has focused on the failure to get the central political agreement passed.
But much of the work at these summits is putting into action agreements made at previous meetings.
On money that is going towards adaptation for example, countries need to agree how is it being distributed, is it making an impact and how can this be tracked, and which areas are particularly vulnerable.
In fact, there were 164 other items on this year's agenda that were being thrashed out in the negotiating rooms.
And some of those were agreed at the talks.
The funds raised from a global system of carbon credits – money given in exchange for releasing greenhouse gases – will go towards helping developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change.
They agreed to advance a just transition framework designed to protect workers and communities as global economies shift toward clean energy.
But there were many more that could not be agreed and some will now be picked up at COP32, including crucially the work programme responsible for driving forward action on cutting emissions.
Renewable energy growth remains unstoppable
What governments agree in the COP negotiating rooms is only part of what determines the speed of the energy transition.
The International Energy Agency's latest World Energy Outlook, external points to another powerful force: energy security.
It says the disruption to oil and gas supplies through the Strait of Hormuz has been the biggest energy supply shock in history. The longer the uncertainty continues, the stronger the incentive for countries to switch from imported fossil fuels to electricity generated at home.
The economics have been changing too.
Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles have become increasingly competitive.
As clean energy develops its own commercial momentum, formal negotiations may become less important in determining its direction and pace.
Against the headwinds of inflation new investment announcements emerged at COP as part of the "Action Agenda".
This is the part of the COP process that tries to mobilise action outside of formal talks from businesses, investors and cities – this year the focus was on electrification. Turning more of our energy from fossil fuels to electricity.
"We are not entering the age of electricity, we have arrived at the age of electricity," Fatih Birol, head of the IEA, told the BBC. He says energy security and climate policies are now "closely aligned".
That doesn't make COP irrelevant.
Governments still have a crucial role in facilitating the transition, according to Dr Jennie Dodson, a senior director at the World Business Council for Sustainable Development which includes among its members the likes of Amazon and Apple.
"A key message from business is we can go so far, a lot of it is cost competitive, but there are policy barriers both around infrastructure and permitting".
The COP process needs to change
COP31 has shown how the role of these annual UN climate conferences is changing.
For the first 30 COPs, the emphasis was on building the international framework for tackling global warming.
The great diplomatic breakthrough came in Paris in 2015, when almost every country agreed to keep global warming well below 2°C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.
Paris also established machinery designed to turn promises into progress. Every five years, governments assess collective progress in a global stocktake and submit new national climate plans, known as NDCs.
Then came further agreements: a fund for climate damage at COP27, a commitment to transition away from fossil fuels and triple renewable energy capacity at COP28, a new climate finance target at COP29 and increased support for adaptation at COP30.
The international architecture for tackling climate change has, in other words, largely been built.
Now comes the harder business of making it work. That's why this year's conference in Antalya, Turkey, had been billed as an "implementation COP".
The emphasis now is shifting towards delivering commitments already made. Camilla Born, who helped develop the UK's strategy for COP26 and now heads the campaign group Electrify Britain, told the BBC this is making COP more procedural - less about fundamental negotiations than ensuring the machinery actually works.
This could mean doing away with a cover text – the central political agreement that countries sign up to with new pledges.
It is not a requirement to have one, and for many years countries managed without. Australia chose to push one for this COP, and it is where they fell down.
On many of the procedural issues Camilla Bonn spoke of, they did agree things. That may be important. It isn't necessarily exciting.
And there is a fundamental limit to what this machinery can achieve. Under the Paris Agreement countries have no mechanism to force them to meet their emissions targets.
So, when critics berate the COP process for failing to tackle the problem fast enough, it isn't really the system that is at fault, says Alden Meyer, a veteran climate negotiator now at the climate think tank E3G.
The COP process, he suggests, is "like a mirror that we hold up to ourselves every year". If the reflection is disappointing, the problem is the governments, not the mirror.

The 2026 midterm elections were less than three weeks ago — and the new Democratic congressional majorities chosen by voters are still more than a month from taking office — but if the 2028 Democratic presidential primary isn’t fully underway, then at the very least, potential candidates are already starting to jockey for position.
Is Raphael Warnock running for president?
How one potential 2028 Dem is thinking about the future of his party.
Some of that maneuvering was on display earlier this month at the fittingly named “What’s Next” political conference in Denver. The conference drew Democratic operatives, strategists, and presidential hopefuls from around the country — and Vox’s America, Actually podcast, where host Astead Herndon asked attendees for their thoughts about Democratic Party’s future.
Herndon also sat down with one possible 2028 candidate: Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-GA). His background is especially relevant after the midterms: He’s the senior pastor at the historic Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta at a time when more Democratic candidates are embracing religious appeals; and he’s a student of the civil rights movement, the legacy of which could be seen in surging Black turnout across the South after the Supreme Court rolled back parts of the Voting Rights Act.
Warnock has kept the door open on a presidential bid; his colleague Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) is also frequently discussed as a potential candidate.
Herndon and Warnock discussed how Democrats can win in the South following election victories by Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom and others; why Warnock made the trip to Michigan to campaign for Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed; and the need for presidential leadership to resolve some of America’s toughest problems at home and abroad.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.
I feel like some of the reason the South hasn’t seen some of that investment is a presumption that white Southerners are unpersuadable.
And in your race, and I think what happened in Georgia, it wasn’t just turnout, but it was also persuasion. It was convincing people to move on from Republicans and embrace Democrats. How do you make that persuasion happen?
As a pastor, there’s something that I call the ministry of presence. Sometimes you can’t solve people’s problems because they’re complicated or complex. They may take time, or you may not be able to fix it immediately. But there’s something healing about having people show up for you.
And so when I was running in 2021, and then again had to turn around and run in 2022, I would show up in these little towns all across Georgia. The folks were surprised that I was there. And you might be thinking, “Well, of course they were surprised that a Democrat was there.” No, they were surprised that anybody running for the United States Senate was in their little town.
And as we sat down and talked about their hospital that had just closed, as we talked about the struggles that their farmers were having under the tariffs that Trump imposed in his first term, we realized that we had things in common, and we shared a faith. And I got enough of those voters to build the kind of moral, multiracial coalition to win.
Some of the playbook here, though, feels kind of intuitive. You know, show up, lean in to a kind of shared identity. Campaign everywhere.
Even when I’ve heard Southerners talk about building structures over a long period of time, part of me wonders: Why has it been such an effort to make that happen? Are we talking around racism here? Is it just because these are people who have been written off?
That’s a good point, and it’s an interesting thing. Here’s what Black Southerners and white Southerners have in common — particularly poor white Southerners in these rural districts: They’re written off. Like, that’s a shared identity. And if we’re ever to have a moment in this country that transforms it into something that Dr. King called the beloved community, we’ll somehow traverse those boundaries and recognize how much we have in common and how much our interests are connected.
I thought it was really interesting how you went to Michigan to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, who obviously was victorious in that race. You made a clear pitch to Black voters. I thought it was an interesting message. I want you to just describe it — why was that advocacy important to you?
First of all, I wanted us to win the majority. But also, as I looked at that debate as it was unfolding, I had to show up. I’m a child of the Black church. And when we say the Black church, let me hasten because people don’t know this history.
We’ve never meant anything racially exclusive about that. Black church is just a moniker for the anti-slavery church. Because almost all of American Christianity acquiesced — not just acquiesced, aided and provided a kind of moral covering, if you will, for slavery. So the Black church was literally born fighting for freedom. It was born fighting bigotry.
“We need somebody who doesn’t need the job; who really is driven by a deep sense of moral vocation and mission, and for whom the job is a set of tools.”
And when I saw the all-out assault on Brother Abdul on the basis of his religious identity — bigotry is bigotry, and religious bigotry is bigotry. The Black church was born fighting bigotry. And so you literally have people saying that he’s unfit because of where he prays and how he prays.
And if there was anybody that I felt should be the tip of the spear rejecting that idea, it was the Black church, and so I went, among other things, to remind my colleagues there of who we are.
It wasn’t just Republicans who used some of those Islamophobic attacks. There was the infamous scene of Haley Stevens, the Democratic congresswoman who lost that primary, going to the Black church [with Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers].
Here she is standing with somebody who is engaged in this kind of Islamophobic rhetoric, and she’s in a Black church doing this. It’s deeply insulting.
We had Abdul El-Sayed on our show, and he made the case for cutting off aid to Israel. In 2025, you and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff voted to block a measure from Bernie Sanders that would’ve stopped $8 billion in aid for Israel.
I recently saw a stat that 74 percent of Democrats oppose additional funding for Israel, per a poll from the New York Times and Siena. Was that vote a mistake?
We’ve had several [Joint Resolution of Disapproval] votes. You chose only to mention the one that I didn’t vote for. I have voted on multiple occasions to limit military aid to Israel.
My North Star where that issue is concerned is a region where Israeli mothers and Palestinian mothers can put their children to sleep at night, know that they’re safe, and have them awaken to a world that embraces their full humanity.
I support a two-state solution. Clearly, Netanyahu does not. He is a problem. and what we need in this moment is leadership. I don’t shirk that one bit. But I will tell you this, as someone who has voted for these [joint resolutions] on a few occasions in response to the moral atrocities that we’ve seen in Gaza, I can tell you that what I’ve learned is that there is no replacement for presidential leadership, and we haven’t had that on this issue in quite some time.
Would you include President Biden in that?
We have not had the kind of leadership that I would want to see on that issue in quite some time. The people are crying out for more.
I am just old enough to remember when an American president took two old men in a room at Camp David and he wouldn’t let them go until they worked something out.
Of course, Anwar Sadat paid a very high price for that. I remember that, too. I think I was in seventh grade. We need American presidential leadership in this moment for that and for a whole range of reasons.
You’ve mentioned presidential leadership. What’s one nonnegotiable for the next Democratic presidential nominee? What’s one thing you think they have to do?
We need somebody who doesn’t need the job; who really is driven by a deep sense of moral vocation and mission, and for whom the job is a set of tools. But the mission is what is central. I think when you have somebody who’s grounded in that kind of deep commitment, then we’re onto something.
I’ve seen you kind of dodge this question about whether you’re considering a run for president in 2028. Your go-to answer was, “Well, I’m focused on the midterms.” Now that we have results from the midterms, I’m going ask you again.
Are you thinking about running for president in 2028?
I remain very committed, and deeply honored to be in this fight for the people of Georgia.
You know, who gets to represent 11 million people? Stand up, get up, fight for them every day? And I remain prayerful about what’s the best use of my gifts in this moment.
I hope that at the end of my life, I will have poured it all out and gone ’till the wheels fall off. And that’s what I’m trying to do — give it all I have.
Give me a sense of how that decision calculus works. Very few people are ever in the position to think about such a thing. How do you go about making a decision about whether that’s true for you?
I have been praying this prayer since I was a kid. I ask God to order my steps. And so you just do the work, and I think you’ll know what you need to do when the time comes.

Sen. Chuck Schumer has led the Senate Democratic caucus for 10 years, and he’s now facing the most serious challenge to his post that he’s ever encountered.
The real reason Senate leaders keep becoming incredibly unpopular
Is Chuck Schumer the problem? Or is it the job itself?
Just as Democrats are about to take their largest majority since the beginning of Barack Obama’s presidency, Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen is challenging Schumer for the role of leading that new majority. Van Hollen has won the backing of several senators so far, as well as various outside progressive groups.
In one sense, the reasons Democrats might want to move on from Schumer are obvious. Schumer is 75 years old, and is not a particularly charismatic messenger or compelling speaker. His personal positions on issues like US support for Israel, and his longtime cultivation of Wall Street and corporate donors, put him out of step with the Democratic base. And polls regularly show that he is extremely unpopular.
At the same time, the job of Senate majority leader also isn’t really about winning a national popularity contest. It’s about leading the Senate — a challenging remit that involves a multitude of tasks, including but not limited to setting the legislative calendar, crafting legislative and big-picture policy strategy, dealing with outside interest groups, coordinating with the speaker of the House and president, and trying to hold the majority in the next election.
And there’s another underappreciated part of the job: volunteering to be the one political figure who’s most likely to be hated. Many of the leaders considered especially effective in their role — from Mitch McConnell to Nancy Pelosi — were consistently unpopular, often because the position requires taking constant slings from both outside and inside their party.
It’s this last component that’s perhaps discussed the least — and in conversations with legislative veterans from across the political spectrum, I’ve been surprised how often it’s come up as a critical part of the case for choosing either of them.
The Senate majority leader’s “heat shield” function
How would Van Hollen do the job differently? Publicly, he’s touched on a few points.
In first announcing his leadership bid last week, Van Hollen told MS NOW’s Jen Psaki that Democrats should end President Donald Trump’s “illegal and senseless” Iran war this year, by giving Trump a choice: end the war, or the government gets shut down.
He said at a conference in Denver that he opposed the Senate filibuster — the rule that requires 60 votes to advance nearly all legislation — and said he would have to “talk to the caucus” about it.
And asked by NPR’s Steve Inskeep to name a specific issue in which his approach would be different from Schumer’s, Van Hollen said he would hold a floor vote on the PRO Act, a labor rights bill.
All three positions seem intended to suggest that Van Hollen would try to lead what will be a 56-member Senate caucus in a more progressive direction.
But some experts were skeptical about how well that would work.
“A leader is like a middleman,” James Wallner, a former Republican Senate aide, told me. “They’ve got to negotiate with everybody. In the Senate we haven’t really seen leaders come from a wing of the party. They usually are going to be dispositionally moderate — and that puts them in a position to negotiate with their own colleagues.”
Indeed, current and former Senate leadership aides described the job rather differently — as less about pushing the caucus to do what you want, and more about channeling what senators already want to do, crafting a consensus among them, and serving their needs.
Justin Goodman, a former Schumer aide, told me a crucial part of the job was being a “heat shield for the members when difficult decisions need to be made, and they’re difficult decisions the caucus has support for.”
The premise here is that much, and perhaps most, of what the Democratic base wants can’t happen. Either because of Trump’s veto pen, the chamber’s rules, or simply because many Democratic senators don’t actually want it to happen — the idea is that many disappointments are inevitable, and that the leader will be the fall guy for them. (Another commonly used term? A “sin-eater.”)
Take, for instance, the PRO Act — which, in 2021 and 2022, the last time Democrats controlled Washington, Schumer did indeed refuse to bring to a floor vote. According to Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT), Schumer told him he wouldn’t do it unless Sanders could already line up the 60 supporters necessary to beat the filibuster.
The implication is that, if the bill was certain to fail anyway, Schumer did not want to make his vulnerable members take a vote that might be uncomfortable for them — which would expose them to either the base’s fury, or to general election attack ads.
Van Hollen’s professed desire to hold a PRO Act vote would signal a different approach — one that would make progressives happy, and force some moderates to take an uncomfortable vote.
It is not so clear that that approach would be more successful at getting progressive priorities actually signed into law. (And the last time Schumer was majority leader, he did in some instances put moderates on the spot — such as in his push to change Senate rules to pass a voting rights bill, which Sens. Joe Manchin and Kyrsten Sinema voted down.)
But Schumer’s most famous example of “sin eating” occurred in March 2025, when he helped orchestrate the passage of a government funding bill, despite progressives’ desire to threaten a shutdown in hopes of fighting back against what they viewed as the new Trump administration’s authoritarian abuses. “I believe so strongly I did the right thing,” Schumer said then.
“Nobody wants the government to shut down. But a lot of people don’t want to be the ones to vote ‘yes’ to keep it open,” Goodman told me. “So Sen. Schumer, as the leader, was often the one getting the job done and taking the heat for it.”
Schumer later endorsed a more confrontational strategy that resulted in a 43-day government shutdown that fall— but though Democrats were viewed as winning the politics of that fight, some of their members grew increasingly concerned about the pain caused by lapses in government benefits.
Eventually, some Democrats peeled off and voted with the GOP to reopen the government — and though Schumer officially opposed reopening this, he still got blamed for not doing enough to stop it.
Has Schumer lost too much credibility to sell these compromises to the base?
That said, just because Schumer took on the “sin eater” role in the past doesn’t mean he’s the only one who could do it in the future. It’s possible someone more in touch with the party’s base might be better at finding consensus.
Van Hollen is backed by several of the most progressive senators and senators-elect — including Sanders, Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota — but he and his supporters have also pushed back against attempts to frame this contest as purely one of progressives versus moderates.
Indeed, when I talked to Ezra Levin, co-founder of the progressive group Indivisible, he made a rather different case. Levin argued that, actually, Van Hollen would do a better job at selling the compromises that inevitably will have to be made to the base — including to progressives like him.
Levin said he entirely agrees that part of the next leader’s job will be to get the caucus to “do some things that are going to be greatly unpopular” — including funding the government, and raising the debt ceiling. “Senate Majority Leader Chris Van Hollen, if he does his job right, is going to piss off me and other folks a lot,” Levin said.
But, he continued, because of Schumer’s history and the longstanding lack of trust in him from the base, Schumer will simply have a harder time selling those compromises.
“If the Senate majority leader is a sponge for anger, you’ve got to change that sponge more than once a decade,” Levin said. “Or that sponge will stop being useful.”
Indeed, House Republicans have twice experienced a dynamic like this, where the base’s deep distrust of Speakers John Boehner and Kevin McCarthy resulted in Boehner’s resignation and McCarthy’s ouster. Then, their more conservative successors, Paul Ryan and Mike Johnson, advanced similar legislative compromises without facing serious revolts of their own. Getting a new face really can buy some goodwill and tamp down disquiet, for a time.
“If I’m a moderate in the Senate, I want somebody else to take the blame if we do have to push through something,” Levin said. “Who can absorb that blame? Who has credibility with the outside actors? With the grassroots groups blowing up my phone? With all the constituent parts of the Democratic Party?”

This exchange, following the FAA nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13, truly occurred Nov. 16 outside the White House. While some posts paraphrased the question and answer, Trump responded to the question about ensuring safe air travel, in part, "Well, they fly a little bit slower, but very safe."
In mid-November, a rumor spread that U.S. President Donald Trump answered a reporter's question about ensuring safe air travel by saying, "Well, they'll just have to fly a little slower."
The claim, purporting that Trump said he believed pilots would fly slower for safety reasons, circulated after the Federal Aviation Administration experienced an outage of the air traffic control system on Nov. 13 and ordered a nationwide ground stop — the longest such stoppage of air travel since the Sept. 11 attacks. The Trump administration said the outage was caused by the upgrading of new technology overloading older parts.
For example, some people shared the purported quote on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived), TikTok (archived) and X (archived).
(@liquidmagik via TikTok)
In sum, Trump truly said these words (though some posts paraphrased the exchange). Therefore, we've rated this quote as correctly attributed to him.
A search located the quote in a transcript on the Roll Call website. The exchange, between Trump and ABC News journalist Rachel Scott, occurred Nov. 16 outside the White House (emphasis ours):
SCOTT: Can you assure Americans that it's safe to fly, given that nationwide ground stop?
TRUMP: Very safe.
SCOTT: How can you assure them that this won't happen again?
TRUMP: Very safe, well they fly a little bit slower, but very safe. But we want to make it beyond safe. We want to have the best system in the world, and for that we need Congress.
SCOTT: Why didn't Republicans pass that when they had the majority for the last two years?
TRUMP: People have been trying, well we've been trying to get the money for two years to fix it, and [former Democratic Transportation Secretary Pete] Buttigieg ruined the system. He totally ruined it. The Democrats really, it's very old, but what they did really set back the system a long way.
SCOTT: But Republicans had the majority [inaudible].
[Trump walks away, waves arm at Scott.]
Scott's question appears at the 11:59 mark in an official White House video featuring the same media gaggle:
Snopes emailed the White House to ask if the Trump administration could respond to users sharing the quote and to explain what the president meant about planes flying slower. We will update this article if we receive additional information.
For further reading, we previously reported about Trump appearing to believe that grocery stores commonly keep apples in refrigerators, as well as Trump telling a story in which he kept changing the year man invented the paper clip.

The Union Health Ministry has proposed an amendment to the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019, to include ‘antimicrobials’ in the definition of ‘New Drug’ under Rule 2(1)(w)(v).
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global public health concern and the proposed amendment has been initiated in view of concerns regarding the grant of manufacturing licences for antimicrobial products without adequate regulatory scrutiny, including the requirement for studies such as bioavailability and bioequivalence and stability studies.
The proposed amendment seeks to bring antimicrobials within the regulatory framework applicable to new drugs under the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019. Accordingly, manufacturers would be required to obtain permission from the Central Licensing Authority before applying for a manufacturing licence from the concerned State Licensing Authority. This is expected to strengthen central regulatory oversight and help ensure the quality, safety and efficacy of antimicrobial products.
Meanwhile, the Ministry has also proposed amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945, to introduce a separate application form (Form 19-BC) and licence form (Form 20-BC) for the sale of bulk drugs (active or inactive bulk substances), distinct from the existing licensing provisions for formulations.
At present, a common licence covers the wholesale sale of both formulations and bulk drugs. The proposed amendment seeks to establish a dedicated licensing framework for bulk drugs, enabling more focused regulatory oversight of their wholesale sale and greater accountability in the pharmaceutical supply chain.
The proposal was agreed upon by the Drugs Consultative Committee (DCC) in its 67th meeting held on November 17, 2025, and by the Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB) in its 93rd meeting held on February 16, 2026.
Under the proposed framework, the licence will capture the categories of bulk drugs handled by wholesalers, including drugs covered under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985. The sale of bulk drugs will be carried out under the personal supervision of a competent person, thereby strengthening accountability in their distribution and handling.
“Upon implementation, the proposed amendment will: give better control over the sale of bulk drugs by way of wholesale, strengthen enforcement control in relation to antimicrobial resistance and the movement of NDPS drugs and require wholesalers of bulk drugs to obtain a separate license for sale.” Stakeholders and members of the public are invited to submit their objections and suggestions.

Arion Kurtaj, who pleaded guilty last week to hacking Grand Theft Auto VI developer Rockstar Games and other companies, including Uber and Revolut, was sentenced to seven years in prison but released on license, the BBC reports. After hacking Rockstar, Kurtaj leaked 90 videos of GTA VI in 2022, years before the game’s public release last week.
The hacker behind early GTA VI leaks has been sentenced — and released
Arion Kurtaj, who hacked Rockstar Games and leaked 90 videos of the game, was released after pleading guilty.
Prior to his sentencing, Kurtaj had already spent time in a hospital because of his autism and in prison.
“You are obviously a very talented young man,” the judge in the case said, according to Sky News. “Don’t waste those talents by spending the rest of your life in and out of prison.” Kurtaj cannot use platforms Telegram and Discord as part of a five-year Serious Crime Prevention Order, the BBC says.
Rockstar launched GTA VI last week to positive reviews. The studio said the game made $3.79 billion in its first day of sales.

FIFA has joined forces with the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in supporting the #BeActive campaign launched on the UN International Day of Sport for Development and Peace to encourage people to be #HealthyAtHome as the world comes together in the fight against COVID-19, today and every day.
WHO recommends all healthy adults do at least 30 minutes a day of physical activity and children at least 60 minutes per day. As part of this, #BeActive and remain #HealthyAtHome include the following suggestions along with any other form of recreation to stay healthy at home:
- Taking some online exercise classes,
- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,
- Jumping rope, and
- Practising muscle strength and balance training.
“We are delighted that football is strongly supporting the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by asking everyone to #BeActive and to remain healthy at home during this difficult time,” said António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations. “FIFA has asked the football community, from member associations and clubs, to players and fans, to show their support, to put their rivalries aside and to show a new solidarity so we can overcome the coronavirus. This is an important lesson not only for today, but for every day.”
“More than ever, especially now, one thing must be clear to everyone, health comes first,” said FIFA President Gianni Infantino. “FIFA is delighted to support both the United Nations and the World Health Organization in amplifying the #BeActive campaign today, and we are encouraged that the football community is also playing an active role in ensuring the message understood globally. For the first time ever, we are all on the same team and together, with team spirit and positive energy, we will win.”
“WHO is proud to collaborate as part of the UN family with FIFA and football lovers worldwide to promote the importance of being active for both physical and mental health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “The #BeActive campaign supports WHO’s drive to help people be healthy at home.”
The campaign kicks off with Real Madrid CF, FC Barcelona, Liverpool FC and Manchester United FC asking football fans to set aside their rivalries and to come together to #BeActive in order to defeat the coronavirus. Other clubs, including Club América, CD Guadalajara, Beijing Guoan FC, Shanghai Shenhua FC, Mohun Bagan AC, East Bengal FC, Melbourne City FC, Sydney FC, Auckland City FC, Team Wellington FC, CA River Plate, Olympique de Marseille, TP Mazembe, CR Flamengo and SE Palmeiras will also join the initiative in the coming days.
As part of the campaign, world-famous players share the following message: “At this time, even rivals need to stick together. We have to keep our distance, but we do not lose our focus. We can show solidarity by being active, and active means following the guidelines from the WHO.”
The video campaign will be published on various FIFA digital channels, with regular subsequent updates from clubs and players across the world during subsequent days. #BeActive is also being supported with graphics toolkits for the 211 FIFA member associations and various media agencies to facilitate additional localisation and to further amplify the message.
WHO, the UN’s specialized health agency, and FIFA, football’s world governing body, collaborate closely to promote healthy lifestyles through football globally and launched the “ Pass the message to kick out coronavirus” campaign last month to share advice effective measures to protect people from COVID-19.

Warning: this article contains discussion of eating disorders
"If you keep this up, you'll be in a wheelchair at 30."
That is what doctors told British long-distance runner Jake Smith four years ago.
From the outside looking in, his career was flying.
By the age of 23, he had signed a professional contract with Nike and represented Great Britain on the global stage.
But at the same time, his body was deteriorating - enduring a relentless pattern of race, illness, injury, repeat.
Balancing an intense training regime with disordered eating meant the 28-year-old returned from a running camp in Uganda weighing just eight stone (51kg) at 5ft 5in (1.7m). He had such brittle bones that he was told his career could be over.
After suffering two stress fractures in the space of four months, Smith sought professional help and was diagnosed with REDs – relative energy deficiency in sport.
It is a syndrome that can affect anyone and if left undiagnosed or untreated, can have an impact on performance and cause serious, long-lasting health problems.
The symptoms are slightly better documented in women - just last month, tennis player Emma Navarro revealed her diagnosis and subsequent decision to step away from competition until 2027.
But men are just as susceptible and due to stigma and lack of obvious warning signs, it can go undetected for longer and means many, like Smith, suffer in silence.
BBC Sport explains what the condition is, how it affects men and women and why, despite its prevalence and severity, REDs remains a relatively under-reported and overlooked area of sports science.
REDs can cause bone stress injuries, disrupted sleep, fatigue and low mood. Left untreated, the condition can lead to serious long-term health problems, including osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and fertility issues.
Dr Nicky Keay, an expert in hormone health, says many of these symptoms stem from hormonal disruption caused by insufficient energy intake.
"Hormones go to every single bit in your body. So, if your hormones are not working well for you, you're going to feel it in all sorts of different areas," she says.
"In order to have healthy hormones, they need to be fed regularly. If you're not doing that and there's an energy deficit, often some of those hormone systems will slow down or shut down completely."
Women have a monthly barometer of their hormone health with the menstrual cycle, described by Keay as a "free monthly medical check".
Put simply, she says, a woman suffering from REDs has her periods "switched off".
For men, it is more subtle – testosterone levels will drop, resulting in a reduced libido and fatigue.
The impact on a woman's period is why the condition was first referred to in the early 1990s as the "female athlete triad".
But it was renamed by the International Olympic Committee in 2014 to acknowledge the broader range of symptoms of energy deficiency and that it also harms male athletes.
"We realised we were ignoring the other half of the population," Keay says.
"It's a strange situation because normally it's women's health that is the one being ignored but, in this situation, it's the men who weren't being recognised or represented."
Twelve years later that decision appears to be vindicated, with recent research highlighting the prevalence in men.
Meta-analysis published in Australian journal Sports Medicine last year, following a study involving thousands of elite and amateur athletes around the world, indicated 44.2% of female athletes and 49.4% of male athletes had low energy availability.
So why is REDs so common?
One of the answers lies in the phrase 'lighter is faster'.
For decades, it had been an accepted wisdom in sports like endurance running, cycling, climbing, horse riding, dancing and aesthetic sports like diving and gymnastics.
And for athletes like Smith, it is how his problems started.
"I believed it for years. I thought that was the way forward," he says.
"I started thinking 'how do I improve my half marathon by 10 seconds? Is it a drop in weight?'. And that's when my head completely went."
Initially, the strategy can work.
When it comes to choosing energy to cover training demand or energy to stay healthy, the body has learned through evolution and threat of predators to always prioritise movement.
It means that athletes can drop weight and still train and exercise and achieve good results.
But eventually, the luck runs out.
Described by Keay as "fool's gold", the body will adjust to the energy deficit and cause a drop in performance and high risk of injuries.
Olympic and world champion Jonny Brownlee acknowledges under-fuelling mistakes he made in his triathlon career contributed to serious injuries.
"I didn't see the importance of it. Training came first and I think we weren't educated enough in how important fuelling was," he tells BBC Sport.
"You were seen, culturally, as a bit weak if you were fuelling on the bike. And the impact of that was definitely injuries - probably not recovering from my training quite as well as I should have done, stress responses, stress fractures. So there's that side of it and probably underperformance in races as well."
Brownlee, who recently announced his retirement, believes the culture of not fuelling on the bike has now changed but a stigma lingers around REDs and the perception that it is a "female issue".
"In females, there are more obvious signs but in males it can go under the radar a little bit and then it hits you by a really serious injury," he says.
"I think there's a stigma attached in there, or it's not looked at as the obvious answer to some of your problems, it's found later down the line. Men also don't like to talk about under-fuelling because it's just seen as 'you probably should feel better and you should be on top of that'."
It is those attitudes among male athletes that prompted Keay to conduct an experiment in 2019.
Assessing 50 male competitive cyclists, Keay found in her initial screenings that nearly half had poor bone health and 25% were suffering from REDs.
The cyclists were then split into two groups and across a six-month period, one half continued their training and fuelling habits as before while the others were tutored by Keay and offered nutrition and training advice.
"The group that I left to their own devices unfortunately went on the default and they lost even more bone mineral density, similar to an astronaut in space… And they performed OK, but relative to their functional threshold power, they didn't get the race results that you would have expected.
"For the group I took under my wing, there was an improvement in their bone health and really good race results.
"So, I had evidence that REDs definitely does exist quite extensively in my group of the male cyclists and you're going to underperform if you don't fuel sufficiently. The good news is that REDs is reversible. But if you don't take action, it's a decline."
As the syndrome and its symptoms are still not commonly known, it is often difficult to know where to find help.
After former GB runner Pippa Woolven's struggles with the condition, she set up a website called Project REDs which offers information and practical resources for athletes, coaches, parents and healthcare professionals.
Keay also helps people competing at all levels to recover from REDs. Most of her patients are women, but she is starting to see more men reach out for help who, she says, are often in "bad shape".
"I think the men are maybe more reluctant than the women, or maybe they don't realise they've got it. Sometimes they might use a different word for it, they say burnout," Keay says.
"I don't mind that though because there is definitely a psychological aspect to REDs. Why are you doing this? Why are you not eating the carbohydrates?"
Sometimes, it's hard to answer those questions because the under-fuelling is unintentional, either from not understanding or underestimating energy requirements or failing to match an increase in the intensity or duration of exercise with higher calorie or carbohydrate intake.
For others, former British cycling champion Brian Smith among them, the answer comes from intention.
Competing in the road race for Great Britain at the 1996 Olympics should have been the highlight of his career but, behind the scenes of the success, Smith was suffering with an eating disorder and serious mental health condition called bulimia – something he believes he developed from his sport's obsession with weight.
"I always felt like I was overweight. Everybody was under pressure regarding weight, but nobody really spoke about it," he says.
"I'm just under six foot and I've got large glutes and thigh muscles. As a road cyclist, I used to race at 68kg and for my height and build, that's quite skinny. I even got down to about 66kg and when I got down to that, I felt underpowered, I felt bad."
Smith, now 59, only discovered he had been suffering from REDs during his career when he started running eight years ago and developed three severe stress fractures, including one in his femur.
Such has been the toll on his body that Smith says he would now never encourage anyone to pursue a career as a professional cyclist.
"It really is not healthy," he says. "If you want to go to the highest levels of the sport, you will suffer later on in life. You're destroying your body.
"Sporting teams don't care - all they're worried about is performance. So they will nurture a rider, they will feed a rider, they'll get a rider to be a certain weight. They don't care about what happens to them later in life.
"I'm suffering now and I've so many regrets. I just wish I'd known more about this."
While Smith believes his sport has a long way to go in changing attitudes, British Cycling says a lot of progress has been made through education that starts at academy level and annual physical and psychological screenings.
"One of the big things we've done in the past 10 years is try and turn this into a performance-related conversation," Dr Nigel Jones, British Cycling chief medical officer, tells BBC Sport.
"Now, we couch the conversation with an athlete around 'if you under-fuel, you will not be able to perform at your best', whereas previously, conversations in power-to-weight ratio sports might have been 'you need to be lighter'.
"I think it would be naive to say REDs is never going to be an issue. But I would like to believe that its prevalence will reduce with the work that we're doing," he adds.
British Cycling is not alone in this approach, with World Climbing taking things a step further two years ago with the introduction of mandatory health checks on athletes.
Using a combination of pre-season questionnaires and 'random and targeted' screenings at competitions - similar to the way doping tests are enforced – climbers at World Championship or World Cup-level competitions are monitored for any indicators of low energy availability or REDs and could be prevented from competing if they are not deemed to be healthy.
The policy was drawn up by expert Professor Naama Constantini, who says she is "proud" of the move by World Climbing and believes other federations should follow suit.
"We are trying to educate and prevent. I'm not a policeman and we're not looking for cheaters. I'm a medical doctor and we want to make sure our athletes are healthy," she says.
"Prevention is the best medicine you can give. We want athletes and coaches to understand that it's not about weight. It's about strength, it's about performance and fuelling the body and you pay a price if you lose weight in an unhealthy way."
With more awareness and education, it is hoped the tide can be turned on REDs.
But many still suffer in ignorance, as well as silence. That is what motivates Jake Smith to keep sharing his recovery on social media, with hundreds of men and women messaging him for advice and support.
Smith has managed to reverse his condition and is now racing better than ever, recently completing the Berlin marathon in a personal-best time of two hours, nine minutes and 24 seconds.
The big goal is the 2028 Olympics, but he is adamant that the priority is making sure he stands on every start line as healthy as possible.
"I'd never want to see an athlete go through the years I've had. I'm 10-15 kilos heavier than I've ever been and the biggest thing I can say is I've never been so happy. You need a healthy body to do everything else.
"I'm heavier, I'm faster, I'm happier."

Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.
The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.
The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.
The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.
The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.
Otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, said: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.”
Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, said she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted quickly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them.
“As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their new leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she said.
The rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres.
Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them.
“A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” said Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.”
Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit.
The trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.”
Baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants.
The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” said Venter.
A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping company allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.

Owono did not deserve 12-match ban - Pique
- Published
FC Andorra owner Gerard Pique says goalkeeper Jesus Owono did not deserve the 12-match suspension he received following his challenge which resulted in the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.
Owono, 25, was sent off after colliding with De Miguel late on in the second-tier match between Andorra and Tenerife on 2 November.
De Miguel died the following day, aged 30, and a disciplinary committee from the Spanish football federation confirmed Owono's ban last week.
In a video posted on social media, Pique said players past and present, plus coaches and other goalkeepers, felt the incident was "an accident".
The former Spain and Barcelona defender added: "I truly believe that imposing the maximum sanction on Jesus for this action puts him in a situation he does not deserve, because he is not to blame for all of this having happened."
- Tenerife striker De Miguel dies after on-field collision 
  - Published3 November
- Goalkeeper involved in fatal collision gets 12-game ban 
  - Published3 days ago
The 12-match suspension was the maximum punishment Owono, 25, could have received, as the disciplinary committee could only consider the offence on the pitch and not "the tragic outcome of the incident".
Following the decision, Tenerife manager Alvaro Cervera said he accepted the regulations do not specifically account for what happened, but acknowledged the ban "might feel light".
Pique also highlighted a recent on-field incident in Spain, when Albacete winger Jose Corpas accidentally kicked Sabadell midfielder Quadri Liameed in the head during a Spanish second division match.
Nigerian Liameed was knocked unconscious but was later discharged from hospital following medical checks, while Spaniard Corpas was shown a straight red card and handed a three-match ban.
"Fortunately Quadri is fine, the consequences in this case were not fatal, and the committee decided to sanction Corpas with three matches," Pique said.
"With all this, my reflection is: what is being sanctioned, the action or the consequences?"
Owono has withdrawn from Equatorial Guinea's squad for Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers against Zimbabwe this month, and Pique said it was unlikely he would return to action as soon as his suspension is served.
He added: "Jesus is going to need far more than 12 matches before he is available and able to compete.
"No sanction is going to bring [De Miguel] back to us."
