Taiwan warns Canada faces the China risks Carney has cautioned against
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has tried to deepen trade ties with China.
HALIFAX, Nova Scotia -- Taiwan’s deputy foreign minister warned on Saturday that Prime Minister Mark Carney risks exposing Canada to the very economic coercion he has cautioned against by deepening trade ties with China, saying that Taiwan has learned the hard way that dependence on Beijing comes with consequences.
“We worry. We worry,” Chen Ming-chi told The Associated Press in an interview at the Halifax International Security Forum when asked about Carney’s efforts to improve relations with China.
Carney has warned that major powers are using economic integration as a weapon, citing U.S. tariffs and China’s restrictions on critical minerals. He has urged middle powers to diversify their trade relationships to avoid economic coercion.
Chen praised Carney’s speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, but questioned whether Canada should deepen ties with countries that don’t share its democratic values.
“Who do you want to choose as your partners?” he asked.
“You have your own history. You have two Michaels,” Chen said, referring to former Canadian diplomat Michael Kovrig and businessman Michael Spavor, whose ne arly three-year detention in China prompted accusations of hostage diplomacy.
The two were arrested in 2018 shortly after Canada detained Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou on a U.S. extradition request. They were released in September 2021, the same day Meng returned to China. Beijing denied their detention was politically motivated.
Chen’s warning came days after Carney met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen and agreed to additional tariff reductions as Canada seeks to diversify trade during U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war.
Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if negotiations with Washington fail to preserve a viable Canadian auto industry. Trump has threatened 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles and auto parts beginning on Jan. 1.
Chen warned that Chinese electric vehicles could threaten Canadian manufacturers and pose surveillance risks because of their connected technology, even if manufactured in Canada.
Carney has argued that Canada’s trade relationship with China differs from Washington’s more complicated ties with Beijing. Canada primarily exports agricultural products, energy and other commodities rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
Chen said that Taiwan had dramatically reduced its economic dependence on China after experiencing Beijing’s use of trade restrictions to exert political pressure.
“They are very good at weaponizing interdependence,” he said. “They are very good at leveraging our dependence to reach political goals.”
Taiwan reduced the share of its outbound investment going to China from more than 80% in 2010 to 3.8% last year, Chen said. Its exports to China and Hong Kong fell from nearly 44% of total exports in 2020 to about 27% last year, according to Taiwanese government figures.
Chen also accused Beijing of exploiting a striking photograph from this week’s summit in Shenzhen showing Xi seated prominently between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin to project China as the world’s leading power.
“The main idea is to prove not only to his domestic audience that he is the world leader,” Chen said. “They are so good at propaganda."
He described the summit as “more symbolic than substantial.”
Chen said China was intensifying military operations around Taiwan, despite the potentially enormous costs of an invasion. He warned that Chinese vessels could be rehearsing for a maritime quarantine of the self-governing island.
Despite his concerns about Beijing, Chen praised Carney’s international leadership and welcomed his commitment to sign a long-delayed trade cooperation arrangement with Taiwan.
“We have a high respect of Prime Minister Carney’s vision. And we want to be part of this vision,” he said.

Your Mileage May Vary is an advice column offering you a unique framework for thinking through your moral dilemmas. It’s based on value pluralism — the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other. To submit a question, fill out this anonymous form. Here’s this week’s question from a reader, condensed and edited for clarity:
You’re anxious about AI. Can religion help — even if you don’t believe in God?
Religion was made for moments like this.
My husband and I are not religious. He’s from an Episcopalian family and grew up in the Unitarian Universalist church, and I grew up attending an interdenominational church, but we don’t attend services now. Lately, though, he’s become so anxious about AI safety and the possibility of human extinction that he’s been having trouble sleeping. In the wake of all this existential uncertainty, he’s expressed a renewed interest in attending church. And he’s not interested in the UU church (with its believe-what-you-want attitude); he said he needs “the strong stuff.”
It’s all a bit mystifying to me because he does not believe in God. But I want him to feel better, and I don’t know what I or anyone can say about AI that will help him manage his anxiety. If religion is what he needs to find solace in the face of radical uncertainty, I want to support him. That said, I have misgivings about attending church myself and about us attending with our kids. I feel a bit self-conscious about being interlopers, and I also feel weird about him going alone every single weekend. More significantly, I wish I understood what the allure is for him. He says he’s hoping it will help him make peace with the end. I’m hoping there is something short of becoming churchgoers we can do that will help him find solace.
Dear Secular and Scared,
There are a couple of premises I would challenge your husband on, but the idea that religion can be supremely useful in a time like this is not one of them.
In fact, I think this is exactly what religion was made for — and not just because several religions actually grew out of apocalyptic movements (I’m looking at you, Christianity).
Is AI changing your relationship with faith? Tell us about it.
Are you turning to faith to navigate your worries about AI? Or are you a religious leader talking with your community about AI? Vox wants to hear from you. Share your experience here.
Faith has always focused on tackling the biggest moral and spiritual questions of the day. And in our day, lots of those questions center on technology. AI companies are striving to build a machine god, promising it’ll govern our world more intelligently, rationally, and morally than we ever could. Should we welcome that or cling to our own agency? Which kinds of labor should we outsource to AI, and which should we keep because they’re essential to human dignity? Where does human dignity come from, anyway?
These kinds of questions are the bread and butter of religion. And over the millennia, wisdom traditions of all kinds have had the chance to articulate answers, test and fine-tune them, and develop powerful stories around them that can move people to action. Whether you believe in God or not, I don’t think you need to feel weird about tapping into these wellsprings of wisdom. I think it’s a waste not to.
But there are two points on which I would gently challenge your husband. First, he said he doesn’t want to go to UU because he needs “the strong stuff.” I totally get this impulse — I also find UU services too “anything goes” for my taste — but don’t assume that the stricter a tradition is, the better an answer it has on AI.
Most people would consider Catholicism more hardcore than UU. And Pope Leo has strong opinions about AI, many of them great. Yet I actually think he’s fallen into a common “pro-human” trap: trying to argue that there are certain fixed traits that make humans unique, and locating value only in humans as they currently exist. He writes in his encyclical Magnifica Humanitas that “ours is the pressing duty to remain profoundly human.” But that feels insufficient as a guide to the future, because “human” has never been a static category — and it definitely won’t stay one. Instead, religious leaders should be offering us an answer to the question of what we want humanity to become in a tech-augmented world.
Second, your husband seems to be assuming that “the strong stuff” would be church services that help him “make peace with the end.” Services that look the grim reaper straight in the eye and accept that his scythe is coming for all of us, and fast. But it’s not a foregone conclusion that we’ll get an AI takeover resulting in human extinction!
Yes, AI companies are building this technology at a blistering pace. They are gambling with all of our futures as they race toward recursive self-improvement — AIs that can build the next, even smarter AIs themselves. Fear is an appropriate reaction to that.
This month, AI alignment pioneer Paul Christiano said he now believes there’s “a high risk of an AI takeover within the next three years,” meaning that AIs end up calling the shots on Earth. He believes that if we keep building the tech in the fastest, easiest way possible, “we’d be looking at something like a coin flip” — a 50 percent chance of takeover. Others have an even starker view: AI researcher and arch-doomer Eliezer Yudkowsky puts the odds of AI-driven human extinction at 99.5 percent.
But as plenty of experts have pointed out, it’s not clear that AIs will soon be able to outcompete and overpower humans across the board. For starters, AI research can suffer from diminishing returns: The easy discoveries get made first, and then everything you throw at it — more computing power, more experiments, more AI copies — moves things ahead less and less. What’s more, even though AI capabilities improve very fast on well-specified tasks in verifiable domains like math, the real world is messy. So it’s unclear how much their capabilities will generalize to other skills.
And when I investigated the case Yudkowsky makes, I found a lot of assumptions stacked on top of each other: that intelligence is a unitary property you can evenly maximize; that maximizing it in a machine means that machine has so much power it’s tantamount to magic; and that humans will just roll over and let AI grab all the power even as the risks become more glaring.
Should we acknowledge that there’s a chance of human extinction here and be appropriately scared of that? Yes. But when faced with a tower of assumptions, of “maybes” and “probablys” that compound, we should not treat extinction as a sure thing.
Instead, we should treat it as a possible thing, while treating other AI risks as extremely probable. I think it’s all too likely that AI could mess up our civilization not by staging an abrupt takeover but by gradually disempowering us and weakening the resilience of critical systems. Just imagine: Deepfakes and misinformation pollute our information ecosystem, so we’re barely capable of rational public discourse. Mass surveillance has a chilling effect on dissent, so democracy falters. Unemployment and wealth inequality skyrocket, so social unrest morphs into mobs and riots. Throw in some large-scale cyberattacks and blackouts, and you’ve got a recipe for global dysfunction.
If this is the default outcome we’re currently heading toward, then the implication isn’t that we should “make peace with the end.” It’s that we should fight tooth and nail to increase the resilience of each part of a functioning civilization!
And here’s where religion can really help. Religious traditions are packed with stories about people who fought to save the world, or who refused to give in to despair even when facing a high probability of disaster.
To illustrate, let me tell you a story from my own tradition, Judaism. It comes from the Talmud, and it’s about a child who out-argues the despair of all the adults.
When the Israelites are enslaved in Egypt, Pharaoh orders that every one of their baby boys be thrown into the Nile and killed. An Israelite leader named Amram leaves his wife, reasoning that there’s no point having children only to see them killed. Other men follow his lead. But then his young daughter, Miriam, confronts him: Dad, your verdict is even harsher than Pharaoh’s! His only targets boys; yours targets girls too. Plus, Pharaoh is wicked, so his decree may or may not come to pass, but you’re righteous, so yours certainly will.
Miriam’s probabilistic argument wins. Amram gets back together with his wife and, nine months later, Moses is born. Miriam doesn’t just passively wait for the Egyptians to kill the baby. She watches over him as he floats on the Nile in a little ark. When Pharaoh’s own daughter sees the baby and pities him, Miriam makes it possible for her to adopt him by casually mentioning that she knows a woman who can be his wet nurse (it happens to be her own mother). And so Moses survives, and grows up to lead his people out of slavery.
If I were a religious leader giving a sermon this weekend, this is the story I’d tell. It reminds us that even if you’re looking at a 50 percent chance of doom, the right move is not to just give up, which raises the odds to 100 percent. It’s to act bravely — and to use every shred of agency you’ve got to increase your community’s resilience and make your desired outcome more likely.
Of course, religion doesn’t have a monopoly on stories of moral courage. As the historian Ada Palmer recently pointed out, we’ve saved the world many times before: during the Cuban Missile Crisis, when we fixed the ozone layer, and so on. If it feels most natural to you to find inspiration in examples like these, go for it.
But religion does have a few comparative advantages. For one, its stories have incredible memetic power: They’ve spread across the globe and carry a huge amount of emotional and moral weight. That’s partly because these stories have been retold for centuries. But I think the causation also runs the other way. These stories have survived so long precisely because they encode something true and hard-won. And notice who their heroes tend to be. Not diplomats (like in the Cuban Missile Crisis) or atmospheric chemists (like in the ozone layer crisis), but a little girl arguing with her dad. Those are characters anyone can imagine becoming.
Crucially, religion also insists that something can always come along and deliver an outcome we didn’t predict. Typically, it calls that something “God.” But even if you don’t use that language, you can benefit from these nudges to remember that, however confident the forecast, the future is never fully knowable — and that’s a reason to act, not surrender.
So if your husband can find a congregation that reminds him of that, feeding his sense of agency instead of letting him acquiesce to despair, I say encourage him. And, unless you have an alternative wellspring that offers you the same benefits, maybe even consider joining him.
Bonus: What I’m reading
- For the New Yorker, Sam Kriss takes a trip to the Monastic Academy for the Preservation of Life on Earth, or MAPLE — a Vermont community that believes “that A.I. is a religious problem that also has a religious solution.”
- Ruxandra Teslo writes about how even Silicon Valley’s “positive” visions for an AI-filled future are actually terrible: “One common and ostensibly optimistic vision is known as ‘handover’: humanity cedes control of its future to a godlike AI and we become the comfortably maintained inhabitants of a civilisation whose direction is no longer ours to decide.”
- Writing for Harper’s, Sam Kestenbaum takes us inside a community of chatbot devotees — people who genuinely believe they’re receiving revelations from AI systems. “They have revived a tradition of a sort,” he writes. “It is another variety of religious experience: the heralding of AI slop as transcendence, revelation, the work of spirits.”

In Ukraine, the fight to keep winter outside begins with a broken window
As the winter cold sets in, Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities face a growing shortage of window installers as Russian attacks leave homes shattered and families exposed to the cold
KYIV, Ukraine -- For weeks after a missile exploded in front of her apartment block, Oleksandra Horban found pieces of glass in her small apartment.
She threw out her 2-year-old son’s plush toys which were covered with glass shards. Outside her ground-floor home, mangled window frames were piled onto a mountain of debris awaiting removal. Pieces of glass were mixed with autumn leaves on the muddy ground.
“Even now we still find glass,” Horban said. “If we vacuum three times, wash the floor and clean up, we’ll still find those microscopic pieces somewhere, in the bed or in the toys.”
As winter sets in, Ukraine is facing a severe shortage of replacement windows with Russian missile and drone attacks continuing to damage buildings, leaving residents exposed to the cold. Temperatures in Kyiv fell to minus 20 degrees Celsius (minus 4 degrees Fahrenheit) last winter.
Government assistance can take months, skilled installers are in short supply and replacement costs have soared, hitting low-income districts near industrial zones hardest.
Horban lives in a Soviet-era “groundscraper” - an enormous horizontal apartment block in the Ukrainian capital. A missile blast in October damaged a vertical section of apartments and shattered hundreds of facade windows.
Most shattered windows have been temporarily covered with fiberboard or tarps. Some boards have small openings fitted with Plexiglas to let daylight into apartments.
New windows in Horban’s apartment would cost about $1,700, more than three times the country’s average salary. Government compensation can take three to four months.
Many cannot afford to wait. Without proper windows, apartments are exposed to cold, damp and mold, particularly during power outages.
Housing damage is among the largest costs of the war. An estimated 3 million housing units were destroyed or badly damaged by the end of last year, adding $90 billion to Ukraine’s reconstruction needs, according to the World Bank.
Ukraine’s window manufacturers can meet demand for replacement windows. The bottleneck is the shortage of skilled installers.
Mykhailo Orlenko, executive director of the Association of Ukrainian Manufacturers of Transparent Structures, said businesses were unable to exempt their employees from military service, including many installers.
“The market lost a large number of these specialists,” he said.
Factories can manufacture windows in about 10 working days, but installation can be delayed for a lot longer as customers wait for a crew to become available. High demand means installation bills have at least doubled over the past year.
Oleksandr, a 42-year-old installer who has worked in the industry for 25 years, said power outages add to the challenges. His team relies on battery-powered tools and normally has to carry heavy materials up stairs with elevators out of service.
On one recent job, his team replaced balcony doors and windows in a fourth-floor apartment, carrying the materials up by hand.
“That was 18 trips up and down the stairs, carrying heavy loads. It would have been easier with a working elevator, but we didn’t wait for the power to come back on — we got straight to work,” he said.
Oleksandr asked to be identified only by his first name, citing security concerns following Russian attacks on private businesses.
To address the shortage, the industry is investing in training. A vocational college in Kyiv opened a European Union-funded facility in March, where 26 10th graders have started a three-year program to become window, door and facade installers.
Teenagers in new overalls practice around mock window openings built from brick, cinder block, wood and synthetic materials. Their classes are frequently disrupted by missile and drone alerts.
The program was established after professional associations lobbied the government to formally recognize window installation as a profession, allowing the industry to access grants and create structured training courses.
Graduates can expect starting salaries of around $900, on par with law graduates due to Ukraine’s acute skill drain, Orlenko said.
Instructor Volodymyr Tserbii hopes the apprentices will help rebuild the country, their training offering students a path into a profession needed for reconstruction.
The massive task of repairing Ukraine’s damaged homes, schools, roads, power plants and other infrastructure will take at least a decade, according to government planners.
For Horban, the wait for new windows is added to a long list of her household’s problems.
Her apartment has no gas, forcing the family to cook on a portable cylinder. They heat their son’s room when electricity is available. A leaking kitchen roof has added to the damage.
The blast also left her toddler son, Viacheslav, frightened. The sounds of war have become part of his vocabulary.
Pressing his nose against a windowpane that survived the attack, he waves to passersby and asks his mother whether more bombing is coming, using the words “bam bam” to describe the explosions.
“Bam bam?” he asks.
“No bam bam,” she answers.
“This is not life, this is surviving,” Horban said. "This is dragging out an existence, not a life.”

Vasilisa Stepanenko, Evgeniy Maloletka and Susie Blann in Kyiv contributed.

India’s Gukesh Dommaraju is making his first defense of the world chess championship against fast-rising Uzbek star Javokhir Sindarov over the next three weeks in the affluent Geneva suburb of Cologny. Both players are 20 years old, making it the youngest matchup in the 140-year history of the sport’s most coveted title. But is that all you need to know? What about the format, how much they’re getting paid and why the world’s No 1-ranked player is watching from the sidelines? Read on for all the answers … When and where is the World Chess Championship? The best-of-14-games contest is set to take place from 24 November to 12 December at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, the picturesque enclave overlooking Lake Geneva. The opening ceremony is scheduled for 22 November, with games played once daily from 24 November except for designated rest days on 27 November and 1, 5 and 9 December. It’s the first time a world title match has been held in Switzerland since 2004, when Vladimir Kramnik retained his title by drawing 7-7 with Peter Leko in Brissago, two years before the sport’s rival championships were reunified. Who is Gukesh Dommaraju? Gukesh Dommaraju, commonly known as Gukesh D, was only 18 when he became the 18th and youngest ever undisputed world chess champion by defeating China’s Ding Liren in 2024. An aggressive player known for creating sharp, tactically complex positions aimed at unsettling opponents, the Chennai native rose to international prominence when he became the second-youngest grandmaster in history at the time, aged 12 years and seven months. Five years later he stunned the chess establishment by winning the eight-man Candidates tournament at 17 to secure a world title shot. He went on to win and shatter the age record held by Garry Kasparov, who was 22 when he dethroned Anatoly Karpov in their 1985 rematch in Moscow. His victory made him a national hero in India, where he was mobbed by supporters on his return and feted by prime minister Narendra Modi. But the 20-year-old has struggled badly for form since then, plummeting to No 26 in the world from a career-high ranking of No 3 after an extended string of underwhelming performances. Gukesh Dommaraju receives a hero’s welcome at Chennai airport after becoming the youngest undisputed world chess champion in December 2024. “Clearly so far I’ve not been able to handle it in the best possible way,” Gukesh admitted in a recent interview. “There have been major setbacks ... Obviously there is something with a lot of expectations, a lot of pressure that I’m dealing with and I’ve not found the right way to maybe handle it.” From Bobby Fischer to Magnus Carlsen: 22 of the most famous world chess championship games Read more Who is Javokhir Sindarov? Javokhir Sindarov is an Uzbek prodigy, roughly six months older than Gukesh. Known for his cool-headed precision and ability to mine advantages from seemingly quiet positions, the Tashkent-born grandmaster earned his crack at the world championship with an imperious performance at this year’s Candidates in Cyprus, finishing unbeaten with six wins and eight draws to turn back a stacked field that included longtime stars Fabiano Caruana, Hikaru Nakamura and Anish Giri. The first player from Uzbekistan to challenge for the title, Sindarov has climbed into the world’s top five after a breakthrough 12-month stretch that included winning the Fide World Cup last November in Goa. He enters the biggest match of his life on a tailwind of confidence, having won a four-player rapid tournament in St Louis three weeks ago over Nakamura, Caruana and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, capped by a brilliancy against the world No 2 that showcased his tactical brio. His ascent has added fuel to a remarkable chess boom in Uzbekistan, where he belongs to a golden generation of grandmasters, along with Nodirbek Abdusattorov, Shamsiddin Vokhidov and Nodirbek Yakubboev, who have transformed the central Asian nation into a global powerhouse with two golds and a bronze at the past three Chess Olympiads. Javokhir Sindarov explains his brilliant victory over Hikaru Nakamura to grandmaster Maurice Ashley after their game in St Louis. “This tournament will be the hardest tournament in my life,” Sindarov said in August of his showdown with Gukesh. “I don’t know if I will get a second chance [at the world championship]. It’s hard to play 14 games against the same person in three weeks.” Tale of the tape Where do they rank internationally? Sindarov, ranked 25th in the world a year ago, has climbed to a career-best No 4 with a Fide classical rating of 2782, while Gukesh has slipped to No 26 with a rating of 2710. That makes Gukesh the lowest-ranked reigning world champion of the Elo era, which dates back to 1971, eclipsing the previous low of No 23 set by Ding in 2024. The 22-place gap between them is the widest of any world championship matchup since the title was reunified in 2006. Who is the current world No 1 in chess? Magnus Carlsen holds the top position in Fide’s world rankings with a classical rating of 2823. The 35-year-old Norwegian has been at No 1 for more than 16 years uninterrupted, though that extraordinary reign is suddenly under threat after a disastrous 10-game winless streak last week in Budapest reduced his once-comfortable lead over his nearest rivals to single figures. He was considered the best player on the planet even before removing all doubt against India’s Viswanathan Anand in their 2013 world title clash. If you can name only one chess player active today, chances are it’s him. The youngest undisputed men’s classical world chess champions Carlsen bolstered his claim as the greatest player of any era in 2021 when he crushed Russia’s Ian Nepomniachtchi in his fourth defense by a margin of four wins and no defeats, the most lopsided result in a world championship match since José Raúl Capablanca’s dismantling of Emanuel Lasker exactly 100 years prior. But he decided against defending it for a fifth time before the 2023 cycle, citing a lack of motivation to endure the months-long slog of preparation that world title matches demand. The abdication marked only the second time in history that a holder voluntarily declined to defend his title after Bobby Fischer controversially forfeited the crown ahead of his scheduled 1975 match with Karpov in Manila. Instead, Ding outlasted Nepomniachtchi in a thrilling, sometimes messy scrap for the vacant title, even if critics including Kasparov branded it an “amputated” event without the world’s best player involved. Ding’s reign lasted only 593 days before Gukesh unseated him in Singapore in 2024, taking the decisive 14th game on a catastrophic blunder to claim a 7½–6½ victory and become the first teenager to win the sport’s biggest prize. Carlsen remains active at the highest level, though he’s increasingly shifted his focus away from classical chess toward alternative formats. In February, he defeated Caruana 2½–1½ in Germany to win the Fide freestyle world championship, his eye-watering 21st world title across classical, rapid, blitz and freestyle disciplines. Also known as Fischer Random or Chess960, the variation randomizes the starting positions of the pieces on the back rank, placing a premium on creativity over rote opening preparation. (He’s also gotten married, become a father and is by all accounts pretty good at fantasy football, too.) How do Gukesh and Sindarov match up? Despite being contemporaries, they have played only three times in classical games. Sindarov holds a 2½-½ advantage with two wins and one draw in their lifetime head-to-head, which dates back to their first encounter as tweens at the Moscow Open in 2018. Their most recent meeting happened in January at the prestigious Tata Steel tournament in Wijk aan Zee, where a tense positional struggle gave way to a wild, time-scrambled endgame before the pair settled for a draw after 78 moves. Sindarov also holds a 2-1 edge in their three rapid and blitz contests this year. Allow content provided by a third party? This article includes content hosted on lichess.org. Allow and continue Gukesh’s form has largely gone off the rails since reaching the summit 23 months ago in Singapore. After making it to No 3 in the world with a peak rating of 2794, the Indian suffered a prolonged run of disappointing results, including a joint-last finish at March’s Prague Chess Festival and last-place showings at Norway Chess and the Chennai Grand Masters. He subsequently withdrew from the classical portion of the Grand Chess Tour and had tumbled to No 32 in the rankings by September, when his live rating briefly dipped below the 2700 barrier for the first time in four years, although his performances improved at that month’s Chess Olympiad. Many of the world’s top players have expressed deep pessimism about Gukesh’s chances in Geneva due to his lengthy slump and Sindarov’s sustained upward tick. So too have the bookmakers, who have installed the Uzbek as a clear frontrunner at roughly 1-3 odds despite Gukesh being the champion. Carlsen has described Sindarov as “a pretty significant favorite”, citing the Indian’s tendency to take excessive risks. “His evaluations are way too optimistic,” the world No 1 said recently. “That makes him take way more chances than he should. I think especially now his confidence hasn’t been too high, he just tries to do a little bit too much.” Yet one factor in Gukesh’s favor is his firsthand experience in the cauldron of a world championship match, where the intense psychological and physical rigors of facing the same opponent for weeks on end can be as punishing as the chess itself. Caruana, the world No 3 and former world title challenger who pushed Carlsen to the brink in 2018, has cautioned against writing off the champion despite his struggles. “The kind of ability he had – or has, whatever you want to say – it doesn’t disappear overnight,” Caruana said in September. “So, in my opinion, it can reverse at any moment.” Who are their seconds? Neither Gukesh nor Sindarov has publicly disclosed his full team of seconds, the trusted cadre of advisers who help prepare openings and analyze the opponent. That’s not unusual: players tend to keep the identities of their seconds closely guarded before and during a match to avoid revealing clues about the direction of their preparations. But we do know a little bit. Gukesh will again work with Polish grandmaster Grzegorz Gajewski, who led a formidable backroom team during his 2024 title-winning campaign that included five other GMs and analysts from Poland, India and Germany, with additional support from Anand (acting as more of a mentor than a practical second). According to reporting from ChessBase, Sindarov is expected to be working with Ukrainian coach Roman Vidonyak, while the 22-year-old Abdusattorov, the former world rapid champion and current world No 5, revealed on a podcast that he will be in Geneva to help his compatriot prepare. Another Uzbek grandmaster, Mukhiddin Madaminov, has also been mentioned as a member of Sindarov’s team. Photograph: Europe Echecs What’s the prize money for winning the World Chess Championship? The overall prize fund is $2.5m (£1.9m), unchanged from 2024. Each player will receive $200,000 for each game won, including games won by forfeit. What’s left will be split equally between them. If the winner is decided on tiebreakers, the champion receives $1.3m with the runner-up taking home $1.2m. The same split applies if the match finishes 7½–6½ with 13 decisive games or 8–6 with 14 decisive games. Gukesh’s world ranking Each player received a $200,000 advance on their winnings one month before the first game, deducted from the prize fund. The remaining balance will be remitted to the players within 30 working days after the completion of the match. The stakes are particularly high in a sport where even the biggest stars rarely earn seven figures in annual prize money. According to a new ranking published by World Chess, no player has crossed the $1m mark in tournament winnings in 2026, with India’s Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu leading the way on $666,229. Sindarov ranks third with $589,061, while Gukesh sits 48th with just $41,500. The world championship alone will assure its winner at least $1.25m, enough to vault either player to the top of the annual earnings list. What is the schedule and how does the match work? Gukesh and Sindarov will play up to 14 classical games with each player awarded one point for a win and a half-point for a draw. Whoever reaches seven and a half points first will be declared the champion (and no dead rubbers will be played). The time control for each game is 120 minutes per side for the first 40 moves, then 30 minutes for the remainder of the game, with a 30-second increment per move starting with move 41. That means games can stretch beyond seven hours, testing both players’ concentration and endurance. Players are not permitted to agree to a draw before black’s 40th move, a rule designed to discourage short, uneventful games. A draw claim before then is only allowed in the case of threefold repetition or stalemate, subject to approval by the chief arbiter or deputy arbiter. If the score is level after 14 games, a series of tiebreaks will be played on 12 December, starting with four rapid games at 15 minutes per player plus 10 seconds per move. If still tied, the players will contest two games at 10 minutes plus five seconds, followed if necessary by two blitz games at three minutes plus two seconds. Further single blitz games will be played until a winner emerges. Three of the past five world championship matches have been deadlocked after the classical portion and required tiebreaks: 2016, 2018 and 2023. The complete official regulations can be found here. Fans can also watch every game live on Fide’s official YouTube and Twitch channels. All games start at 3pm local time, 2pm GMT, 9am on the US east coast and 7.30pm in India. What else should I know? The World Chess Championship is typically held every two years, though this schedule has varied over time. Robert Sapolsky, a biologist and neuroscientist at Stanford University, says an elite chess player can burn up to 6,000 calories a day while playing in a tournament, three times what an average person consumes daily. Karpov infamously lost 22lbs (10kg) during his grueling world title encounter with Kasparov in 1984 before it was called off controversially after five months and 48 games due to concerns over player health. Chess has enjoyed a sustained pop-cultural resurgence since the pandemic, a boom that reached Broadway with last year’s reimagining of … Chess, the cult-classic Cold War musical featuring songs by Abba’s Benny Andersson and Björn Ulvaeus. Starring Lea Michele, Aaron Tveit and Nicholas Christopher, the revival centered on a love triangle involving American and Soviet grandmasters loosely inspired by Fischer and Boris Spassky’s epochal 1972 encounter in Reykjavík (with secondary nods to Karpov and Viktor Korchnoi). Critics were less enthusiastic – the Guardian’s two-star review called it a “messy Broadway revival” that wasted its catchy songs – but the Grammy-nominated cast recording that came out in April goes dumby hard and Michele’s snub for a Tony nod was the worst blunder since Ding’s 55 Rf2?? in Singapore. That Sindarov is even playing for the world title is a historic achievement. His victory came two years after Gukesh became the youngest Candidates winner at 17, then the youngest undisputed world champion at 18. Together, they represent the youngest pairing ever to play for the world title by some distance. Sindarov will celebrate his 21st birthday on 8 December, the scheduled date of Game 12. Sindarov’s emergence is part of an extraordinary period of success for Uzbek chess. He helped the country win its first Chess Olympiad gold medal in Chennai in 2022, when Uzbekistan went unbeaten against a field of 186 teams. They followed it with a bronze in 2024 before another gold on home soil in Samarkand last year, cementing the nation’s place among the sport’s leading powers. And yes, that was him among the Uzbek fans supporting the White Wolves as they made their Fifa World Cup debut last summer in the US. The matchup also reflects the shifting geography at the top of the sport. Gukesh’s victory over Ding made him India’s second world champion after Anand and marked the first time in the competition’s 138-year history that two players from Asia had competed for the crown. Now it will happen for a second world title match in a row. The Fondation Martin Bodmer is a library and museum founded by a Swiss bibliophile who built his collection around what he considered the five pillars of world literature: the Bible, Homer, Dante, Shakespeare and Goethe. (Sounds about white.) Its 160,000 treasures include a Gutenberg Bible, Shakespeare’s First Folio and a copy of Isaac Newton’s Principia Mathematica once owned by his great rival Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. Not the worst backdrop for another battle of intellects. A former British champion who once beat Fischer in blitz, the 97-year-old has chronicled the sport’s comings and goings across parts of eight decades, from Mikhail Botvinnik’s Soviet supremacy and Fischer’s Cold War apotheosis to Kasparov’s long-running dominance and the emergence of Gukesh and Sindarov. Suspected Chinese intelligence operatives are using fake companies and job offers on platforms such as LinkedIn to target current and former US government officials, seeking access to sensitive information. Hundreds of suspicious websites identified, according to a report published in the CNN.
The network has expanded as thousands of federal employees left government jobs during President 
Donald Trump
's first year back in office, leaving many without adequate guidance on how to identify and avoid such approaches.
The suspected operation relies on fake consultancy firms that advertise lucrative research and consulting assignments. Former government officials and private consultants are approached through professional networking platforms and asked to prepare reports on issues related to China and other areas of interest. In some cases, those taking up the assignments do not know who the actual client is.
How Trump's mass layoffs created larger pool of potential targets
Hundreds of thousands of workers left the federal government through firings, resignations and other means during Trump's first year back in the White House. 
The departures created a larger pool of unemployed people in the Washington, DC, area, including former officials who held security clearances and had access to sensitive government information.
Foreign powers, including China and Russia, responded by stepping up efforts to recruit Americans working in national security, particularly those who had been fired or feared losing their jobs, CNN reported.
“We created a vulnerability that was not necessary,” a former senior US intelligence official said, as quoted by CNN, referring to the mass layoffs. “We created access and opportunity to tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands, of people without the tools needed to deal with the Communist Party of China.”
How suspected Chinese spy network operates
The fake companies typically use artificial intelligence and stolen identities to create professional-looking corporate websites, according to court documents. They then post vague but well-paying consulting jobs on platforms such as LinkedIn, often seeking people with expertise in China-related issues.
Applicants may be asked to prepare research reports for the companies without knowing who is commissioning the work. While an individual report based on publicly available information may reveal little, intelligence officials say a large collection of such reports could help build a detailed picture of US national security policy and its vulnerabilities.
The FBI seized 13 websites in June that officials said were linked to fake consulting firms. However, an analysis by CNN and Max Lesser, a senior analyst at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, found several more suspicious websites with links to the seized domains.
Lesser has identified more than 100 other web domains that share characteristics with the websites taken down by the FBI. Many remained online months after he publicly revealed them in November 2025, although several have since gone offline.
“Those 13 domains are just the tip of the iceberg,” Lesser told CNN. Seizing them is “necessary but not sufficient,” he added, calling for faster action when suspicious domains are reported.
The FBI said it was continuing to investigate the activity and take authorised steps to address the threat. China has denied the allegations. A spokesperson for its embassy in Washington said: “I am not familiar with what you mentioned. China opposes vilifying China by peddling the so-called ‘Chinese spy’ narrative.”
Former Pentagon official approached with paid assignment
One of the people approached was Wes Bryant, a former Air Force master sergeant who worked in a Pentagon office focused on reducing civilian harm during military operations. He said he was forced to resign in spring 2025 after criticising cuts to his office.
In January 2025, Bryant received an email from someone claiming to represent a Malaysian think tank called MRDA. The sender expressed interest in his military experience and proposed collaboration on regional security issues.
After leaving the Pentagon, Bryant decided to test the offer while checking the organisation with former colleagues. He prepared a report on how the Trump administration might approach a security pact with Australia and the UK, using only publicly available information.
The purported representative, identified as Lily, paid him $1,200. She later said the unnamed client believed there was “room for improvement” in the report. Bryant suspected this was an attempt to draw out more sensitive information. Former colleagues subsequently told him that MRDA did not exist and that Lily had contacted other Pentagon employees.
The Foundation for Defense of Democracies found that MRDA's website used a Chinese-language font and that images posted by one of its representatives carried watermarks from the Chinese social media platform RedNote. Researchers at the University of Toronto's Citizen Lab described the organisation as “likely China-related”, but said they had not found conclusive digital evidence linking it to the Chinese government.
Another target, global affairs consultant Andres Loretdemola, said he was contacted on LinkedIn in 2025 by a woman offering up to $1,000 for reports on Russian affairs and geopolitics. He became suspicious after she appeared more interested in his connections with Washington think tanks.
Loretdemola shared a recording of their conversation with the FBI. The bureau said the messages he provided were consistent with the pattern of activity described in the warrant used to seize the websites.
The use of fake consultancies to approach US officials is not new. In 2018, Singaporean Dickson Yeo set up a fake company and advertised jobs, according to the US Justice Department. Ninety per cent of the resumes he received were from US military and government personnel with security clearances. Yeo was later sentenced to 14 months in prison after pleading guilty to acting as an agent of Chinese intelligence.
US officials said the growth of artificial intelligence and the popularity of professional networking platforms have made such operations more effective.
A LinkedIn spokesperson said creating fake accounts or misrepresenting one's identity violates the platform's terms of service. “We remain focused on detecting state-sponsored abuse and will continue to enforce our policies against fake accounts,” the spokesperson said as quoted by CNN.
The US and its Five Eyes intelligence partners, Australia, Canada, New Zealand and the UK, warned in June that information acquired through such schemes could put frontline military personnel at risk, weaken economic prosperity and enable interference in democratic processes.

A version of this article first appeared on the Substack of “Why Should I Trust You?”
On Tuesday, after the United States lost its measles elimination status, health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. posted on X that he wanted to stop measles from spreading in America. “We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend [measles, mumps, and rubella] vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.”
Well, Secretary Kennedy, do I have an idea for you …
It involves mobilizing a movement you helped build, a movement that has successfully organized millions of Americans around issues related to their health. I’m talking about MAHA.
Right now, the discourse is playing out like this: Medical societies are expressing alarm over the loss of measles elimination status, while many politicians blame Kennedy and the Trump administration for failing to adequately respond.
Kennedy’s defenders clap back by reminding us that other countries have lost elimination status in recent years, too, that these are all efforts to undermine Kennedy and that his administration is doing what it can.
I understand on some level that, as a society, we need to litigate what went wrong. But candidly, I’m much more interested in something else: Who might be best positioned to reach the Americans that public health officials are struggling to persuade to get the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine?
What I learned from listening
I’ll start by saying that I believe in the measles vaccine. I was vaccinated as a child. I’ve vaccinated my two kids. I don’t identify as particularly vaccine skeptical. I’ve sometimes wondered why we have so many vaccine recommendations in this country compared with others, but I generally trust my doctors and haven’t (yet) experienced any major adverse reactions that might have led me to question that trust.
Over the last two years of making the podcast “Why Should I Trust You?,” my co-hosts and I have had the privilege of speaking with many people who feel quite differently than I do about vaccines, public health, and the medical system, and what they see as blind faith in expertise.
I’ve learned a tremendous amount. These conversations have made me question my own assumptions and better understand why I trust institutions, while sometimes realizing that I, too, harbor mistrust. While some of these conversations have been with people who are unwaveringly anti-vaccine, most have been with people who have taken some vaccines and harbor doubts about others.
They’ve also given me a front-row seat to something else: the MAHA grassroots movement’s astonishing ability to organize.
I’ve watched as MAHA supporters rally around pesticides, toxic pollutants in our air and water, microplastics, and PFAS (aka “forever”) chemicals. I’ve been to conferences and meetings, and been included in many group chats and Zoom meetings, where you can practically feel the energy around you: people exchanging ideas, meeting with lawmakers to draft legislation, and mobilizing others to organize local action. I constantly hear two questions: “What do you need? How can I help?”
That energy doesn’t seem to have disappeared after the midterms. But it’s definitely looking for places to go.
MAHA is politically weak right now. Candidates backed by the movement suffered significant electoral defeats, and there’s anger at the Trump administration over what seem like broken promises on pesticides, corporate influence, and environmental health. Yet the grassroots supporters haven’t given up. They’ve already been regrouping around issues like data centers and their effects on communities, while continuing to fight toxic pollutants and corporate influence. They don’t want to wait for the government or medical establishment to fix problems for them.
Measles presents a different kind of challenge. Public health officials need to reach parents who hesitate before vaccinating their children, including families in communities that view government institutions with suspicion.
I’ve heard from public health officials that many local health departments are so underfunded, they struggle to reach these families — and even when they have the resources, they may lack the cultural fluency or trusted relationships to connect with them.
But what if some of the people who could help actually share those families’ skepticism about pharmaceutical companies, admire Kennedy, or prefer alternative medicine — yet believe the MMR vaccine is worth getting?
Spoiler: Most MAHA parents trust the MMR vaccine
MAHA is not a fringe movement. According to KFF’s analysis of the 2026 midterm election, roughly 3 in 10 voters said they support MAHA, including 21% who strongly support it.
And, perhaps surprisingly, most MAHA-supporting parents vaccinate their kids. A separate KFF/Washington Post survey found that 86% of MAHA-supporting parents believe it’s important for children in their communities to be vaccinated against measles. Nearly 8 in 10 expressed confidence in the safety of the MMR vaccine. And about 75% reported that their children were up to date on routine childhood vaccinations, excluding Covid and flu.
Truthfully, very few MAHA supporters I’ve met haven’t taken MMR or vaccinated their children against polio, even if on a delayed schedule. I’ve met plenty who feel differently about Covid, flu, or the hep B birth dose, and certainly there are those who reject MMR. But among rank-and-file supporters, I’ve encountered far fewer MMR skeptics than you might expect from listening to some of the movement’s most prominent influencers. Which is important for the challenge at hand: You can believe deeply in MAHA’s core concerns about food, pesticides, water, chronic disease, and even have mistrust in flu and Covid shots — but still have confidence in the value of the measles vaccine.
We don’t acknowledge this enough. Some of MAHA’s most prominent vaccine skeptics may not speak for the broader movement when it comes to MMR.
The science on MMR is clear: Two doses are approximately 97% effective at preventing measles. But knowing the facts and trusting the person delivering them are two very different things. A fact like that can land differently when it comes from someone who has wrestled with the same doubts you have.
Roberta’s story: a Kennedy supporter who trusts MMR
I think about Roberta Devers, a mother and midwife practicing in Lancaster County, Pa., whom my colleagues and I met working on an episode about the measles outbreak there.
Roberta was vaccine skeptical, a Kennedy supporter, and chose not to vaccinate her son when he was a baby. But after seeing what measles was doing to people in Lancaster County, she changed her mind. She believes MMR is effective against measles and encourages Amish families in outbreak areas to get vaccinated, too. She tells me she now gets one or two calls a week from families who want to get vaccinated.
What’s particularly interesting to me, though, is what hasn’t changed.
Roberta still admires Kennedy. She hasn’t suddenly decided the medical establishment deserves her trust. If anything, she tells me the measles outbreaks are a reflection of a lack of trust communities continue to have for health systems. One of her ongoing campaigns is to fight for home-birth midwives to receive the same recognition as those working in hospitals. She talks about holistic living, alternative medicine, eating whole foods, even using brown paper toilet paper because she believes in living close to the earth. She hasn’t changed her values or worldview. She’s simply reconsidered what she believes about measles vaccination.
Imagine a vaccine-hesitant parent hearing from someone like Roberta, who shares many of their concerns but has seen measles up close and reached a different conclusion. Roberta doesn’t need to defend pharmaceutical companies or persuade anyone that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is always right. Just telling her story could lead to a conversation that perhaps a public health official would have a harder time brokering.
I’m not suggesting this movement will suddenly lead the charge on getting Americans vaccinated for measles. Some of MAHA’s most influential voices have spent years not just questioning, but actively sowing distrust in vaccines, including MMR, using claims not rooted in scientific fact. And I expect for many, encouraging vaccination, even during an outbreak, would be a bridge too far for them, a betrayal of their principles.
And organizing a rally isn’t the same as running a public health response.
But shouldn’t we at least try to make an active effort to reach MAHA supporters who believe in MMR? Because the polling shows it looks like there are a lot of them.
In his statement, Kennedy said his department is working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust. He also promised to collaborate with trusted health care providers and community leaders.
He could start by elevating voices who support MMR. People like Devers, who can speak to vaccine-hesitant families with credibility and trust that public health institutions often lack. Find more people like her.
Then encourage those MAHA supporters who trust the measles vaccine to organize conversations about measles prevention. Bring in trusted physicians or other clinicians to answer questions. But also listen to families’ fears and doubts — because chances are, many MAHA supporters have wrestled with those same questions themselves. Help families find vaccines. Connect them with parents who share their values but have decided to vaccinate their children.
Would everyone in MAHA welcome that effort? Almost certainly not. Would Kennedy face backlash from the anti-vaccine wing of his movement? Very likely.
But for the past two years, MAHA supporters have pushed back against being characterized as anti-vaccine. Instead, they say, they are concerned about mandates, informed consent, conflicts of interest, and what they see as an unwillingness to acknowledge questions about safety.
Well, guys, here’s an opportunity to demonstrate what that distinction means in practice.
If you’re not anti-vaccine, helping people make informed decisions about a vaccine that the overwhelming majority of your own supporters trust shouldn’t betray your principles. It should express them.
The public health establishment has a responsibility here, too. If people within MAHA are willing to help, officials should work with them. That doesn’t mean overlooking misinformation or compromising on evidence. But it does mean recognizing common ground.
I know some readers will think I’m naive. Doesn’t she get that parts of MAHA have contributed to the distrust that makes measles prevention so difficult? I do. But even if parts of MAHA contributed to the problem, isn’t it worth asking whether some of its supporters might be particularly well positioned to contribute to the solution?
At a moment when MAHA is regrouping after an election rout, the movement now has an opportunity to demonstrate that it truly offers a big tent. Not by abandoning its core priorities, but by directing some of its powerful grassroots energy toward a disease affecting American children and their parents — the very people MAHA claims to put at the center of its mission.
Brinda Adhikari is a journalist and co-host of the “Why Should I Trust You?” podcast.

A video showing two women pleading with folded hands to stop the demolition of their house as a bulldozer demolishes tin-roofed houses is going viral on social media (here, here, and here), with the claim that it shows minority homes being demolished in Tripura and Assam. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows minority homes being demolished by a bulldozer in Tripura and Assam.
Fact: The video shows an anti-encroachment drive in the Kalshi area of Mirpur, Dhaka, Bangladesh, on 20 May 2026, during which authorities demolished illegal constructions. The demolition reportedly triggered clashes between authorities and residents, leaving several people injured. The video is unrelated to Tripura or Assam. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple Bangladeshi media reports (here, here, and here) featuring the same visuals. According to these reports, the video is from the Kalshi area of Mirpur in Dhaka, Bangladesh, where the administration conducted an anti-encroachment drive to remove illegal constructions on 20 May 2026. The demolition drive reportedly triggered clashes between authorities and residents, leaving several people injured.
To sum up, a video of an anti-encroachment drive in Dhaka is falsely shared, linking it to India.

The Earthly Education organization posted the video on Facebook and Instagram in November with overlaid text reading, "Reminder: this is what it will sound like 24/7 if a data center is built in your neighborhood." The post's caption accurately noted that the audio — which was captured separately from the video — was recorded in Dowagiac, Michigan, from a home located across the street from a Hyperscale Data data center.
In mid-November, the Earthly Education organization posted a video intended to raise awareness about data centers' environmental impact, as well as to urge people to act on a piece of legislation making its way through the U.S. Congress.
Earthly's website describes its purpose as aiming to "drive systemic change on the climate and ecological crisis through building awareness and mobilising communities into tangible action."
The video, posted on Facebook (archived) and Instagram (archived), displayed a picturesque view of two moose crossing a stream. According to the captions, the audio featured authentic audio — recorded separately from the visuals — of data center noise in Dowagiac, Michigan.
The video was overlaid with text reading, "Reminder: this is what it will sound like 24/7 if a data center is built in your neighborhood."
The caption began, "This sound is recorded from a homeowner's porch, beside the 30-megawatt data center in Dowagiac, Michigan. Residents have already sued over the sound emissions, and yet Hyperscale Data Inc. wants to build an expansion to the current facility." The post also urged people to fight back against a bill that would reportedly accelerate the buildout of data centers.
In sum, the video's captions accurately described the authentic audio. Therefore, we rated the claim true.
Aya Miller, an independent journalist formerly with the Michigan-based MLive.com, confirmed via email that she recorded the audio on June 4 as part of video footage she posted it to TikTok days later.
Miller previously wrote about plans for Hyperscale Data to expand the 30-megawatt bitcoin mining data center into a 340-megawatt artificial intelligence computing facility. The company reportedly ceased bitcoin mining operations in early September, leading to a temporary reprieve from the constant sound from cooling fans, and planned to begin AI computing sometime in November — purportedly with less noise.
A class-action lawsuit, which Detroit attorney Laura Sheets filed in May on behalf of some homeowners, accused Alliance Cloud Services — a subsidiary of Hyperscale Data — of emitting "unreasonable and excessive noise" and "causing property damage through nuisance and negligence."
Snopes emailed a representative for Alliance Cloud Services. Additionally, we reached out to Sheets to ask what she knows about the current status of the data center site, as well as whether she wished to share a statement about the lawsuit. We will update this article if we receive further information.
Researching the rumor
A search for videos of the Dowagiac data center located reposts of a video on Facebook, Instagram and Reddit that matched the audio, including booming noises at the beginning and wind chime sounds several seconds in.
That original video displayed the hand of a person sitting on a front porch and holding a sound level meter reading about 60 decibels, with the camera tilting up to show the data center across the street. The text overlay read, "This is the sound emitted 24/7 from a 30 megawatt data center in Dowagiac, MI measured from a homeowner's porch."
One of the search results showed MLive.com posted the video on June 15. That post credited Miller, who had shared the video three days earlier on TikTok.
Miller's video shows the view from a resident's front porch on Louise Avenue in Dowagiac. Google Street View hosts 360-degree images of the same house and view.
Other videos shared online also demonstrated the noise from the same facility.
For further reading, we previously investigated whether a Meta data center introduced a rare bacterium in a Wyoming city's water.

Tilak Varma (100, 149b, 7x4, 1x6) put up a stiff resistance but failed to propel India-A to a win against Pakistan-A in the Rising Stars Asia Cup 2026 in Doha on Sunday.
Chasing 314 on a sluggish wicket, Tilak ran out of partners as India-A folded on 265, handing its arch-rival a 48-run win.
Abhishek Sharma’s 40-ball 72 provided some impetus at the top, but the rest of the batting order could not emulate the southpaw and India-A fell behind the asking rate.
From the other end, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi and Ayush Badoni fell cheaply in the PowerPlay, while none of Kumar Kushagra, Rinku Singh, and Suryansh Shedge could accompany Tilak after Abhishek’s dismissal.
At 129 for six, Tilak and Shahbaz Ahmed added 112 runs for the sixth wicket. But Ali Raza (3/56) got rid of the latter just in time to secure a win for his side. Hasan Nawaz was the pick among the bowlers with his three for 45.
In the first innings, after Pakistan-A won the toss and opted to bat, Maaz Sadaqat, Nawaz, and Farhan Yousuf notched up fifties to ensure their side had a par score on board.
Pakistan got off to a front-foot start, as Shamyl Hussain and Maaz raced past 50 in next to no time. Ayush Badoni and Harshit Rana brought a halt to their endeavour, accounting for Shamyl and Rohail Nazir respectively in quick succession, bring Hasan to the crease.
He stitched partnerships with Maaz and captain Abdul Samad to keep the scoreboard moving. Both Maaz and Hasan fell shy of three figures, but the role of adding the finishing touches was taken up by Farhan.
The youngster showed flair and ambition in his brisk knock that took Pakistan A to 313, though its innings ended four balls shy of 50 overs.
Those runs would prove crucial hours later, as the added cushion of crossing 300 meant that Pakistan-A could just hold on against Tilak’s rearguard effort.

The craze for fairness is more than skin-deep, and the trade-off can be costly. Inferior cosmetic products can end up harming your vital organs.
A 17-year-old girl in Keralam’s Malappuram developed a serious kidney ailment allegedly after using a fairness cream purchased online following its promotion by social media influencers, according to the doctors treating her.
The incident came to light after the authorities at the hospital that treated the teenager, who was diagnosed with membranous nephropathy, held a press conference on Friday. Lab tests had confirmed 1.25% mercury in the cosmetic product, according to the hospital sources.
Medical experts say that the use of fairness creams containing heavy metals such as mercury to lighten the skin is emerging as a major health hazard that can lead to serious conditions such as kidney failure if not diagnosed early.
Lack of awareness
Warning against following social media beauty trends and using topical creams seen online or bought over the counter without a prescription, M.M. Faizal, former president of the Indian Association of Dermatologists, Venereologists and Leprologists, says people lack awareness of how topical applications can enter the bloodstream.
“People are obsessed with fair skin. We have observed a rise in the number of people buying steroid creams that are easily available over the counter and applying them to their faces. Such steroid-based applications and creams containing heavy metals such as mercury can damage your kidneys easily. The government needs to bring in some mechanisms to control this,” he says.
Vulnerable group
A rise in the number of teenagers relying on spurious beauty products has forced the Keralam Drugs Control department to launch awareness campaigns targeting students in Classes XI and XII, an age group particularly vulnerable to online campaigns. Frequent inspections are carried out in marketplaces to confiscate spurious cosmetics.
State Drugs Controller K. Sujith Kumar says raising awareness about such spurious cosmetic products is the only way forward.
“We have seized cosmetics that have high mercury levels from offline markets. But there is no way to track or regulate online marketplaces,” he says.
Prolonged use of such creams can lead to kidney damage, says former secretary of the Nephrology Association of Kerala, Jayant Thomas Mathew, who has come across a few cases of kidney disorders among users. The condition could be detected early because the patients were aware of the symptoms.
“The patients had used fairness creams and noticed symptoms related to kidney disorders. They probably had membranous nephropathy, and since they sought medical help at a very early stage, treatment was possible,” says Dr. Mathew.
The symptoms
Swelling in the legs and face and frothing in the urine are some of the signs people need to be wary about, the doctor adds.
Much has changed in the beauty industry, with social media driving trends, says Liji Coleenz, a make-up artist and salon owner in Kochi with 20 years of experience.
“Even teenagers fall prey to the beauty aspirations set on social media. Our fixation with fairness is troublesome. We can never aspire to have Korean skin and need to be comfortable in our skin,” she maintains.

The biggest downsides to using Apple's Magic Mouse
Apple switched the Magic Mouse to USB-C but left its most questionable design decision untouched, and that isn’t the only thing users dislike.
There are a handful of things that Apple's Magic Mouse does that would make regular mice envious. The shimmery Multi-Touch surface lets you scroll sideways on a spreadsheet and move across macOS even without that conventional scroll wheel. But then, it is also brilliantly designed to be unusable when the charging cable is plugged in. That's not a small trade-off, especially for a device whose very purpose is to make computer use a breeze.
And it isn't the only reason even committed Mac users are calling it quits on the official Apple mouse. The weirdly slender body looks gorgeous but offers barely any palm space, while the aluminum sides aren't universally loved either. For those who've used a traditional mouse for years, the controls on the Magic Mouse can also feel severely limiting.
Even after ditching the Lightning port with the 2024 refresh alongside the much faster M4 iMac, Apple decided to leave most of those pain points untouched. Now, in all honesty, the Magic Mouse has a pretty strong fan base, especially among users who love its touch gestures and that classic Apple minimalist design. But if you're spending hours using it, the things it cuts out can matter a lot more than the cool tricks it has.
The Magic Mouse is awkward to charge and to hold
Apple unveiled the rechargeable Magic Mouse 2 back in October 2015 with its Lightning port at the bottom. A seemingly controversial design choice even back then, it somehow survived the switch to USB-C almost a decade later. So, every time your Magic Mouse is out of juice, you need to flip it over and leave it be until there's enough power to start using the mouse again.
The saving grace here is that the mouse's battery is good for around a month or more between charges, so flipping your Magic Mouse on its back isn't a daily ordeal. But that doesn't make it any less weird, especially since Apple allows its Magic Keyboard and Magic Trackpad to be used while they're plugged in. There's also no clarity from Apple on how many years the rechargeable battery in the Magic Mouse is expected to last.
Now, let's talk about that shape which puts this slim mouse at just 0.85 inches tall. There's also barely any palm support, and depending on how you're holding it, those aluminum edges can press uncomfortably against your fingers. If you use a fingertip grip, this might be less of a problem, but if you're more of a "resting your entire hand on a mouse" type of person, adjusting your grip is something you'll have to get used to.
The Magic Mouse has plenty of gestures but too few buttons
Since Apple is asking $79 for the Magic Mouse in white and $99 for the black version, you'd expect the basic functions. While Apple's mouse supports right-clicking with its touch-sensitive surface, there's no middle-click or a programmable thumb button. Using CAD software is where you miss those buttons the most, since holding the middle mouse button is how you usually pan around drawings. Sure, third-party utilities can add some of the missing functionality, but having to install extra software to bring conventional features to a premium mouse is frustrating to say the least.
You've got to give some credit to the Multi-Touch surface, especially for making scrolling without the usual wheel still feel natural. But do expect accidental swipes like you would on a phone screen since there are no physical controls. Some owners have even faced issues like stuttering and inconsistent tracking. Those could very well be isolated incidents though, and in one case, the lag started right after a macOS update.
The good part is that Apple doesn't force the Magic Mouse down your throat just because you own a Mac. You can use one of the best wireless mice from other brands on macOS, although you would be missing out on gestures that make the Magic Mouse so special. Logitech's Signature M650, for instance, packs a typical scroll wheel and comes equipped with physical side buttons. Costing about half as much as the Magic Mouse at $39.99, the M650 comes with a contoured grip in place of the Magic Mouse's glossy finish.

South Korea’s education minister resigned on Sunday after an AI-assisted cheating scandal that erupted in the lead-up to the country’s key university entrance exams.
The country has been gripped by fears of AI-assisted exam cheating since last Sunday, when the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score, just four days before the crucial university entrance exam known as the suneung.
The confession sent officials scrambling to roll out a slew of preventive measures for the entrance exams last week, including blocking public wifi in testing areas.
But the education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, struggled to reassure the public, and teachers’ unions criticised the government response as belated.
The annual eight-hour suneung determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.
“The exam concluded without any major incidents … However, as the minister in charge, I do not believe I am immune from public criticism that we failed to prepare adequately in advance,” Choi wrote on X.
“Now that the exam is over, I take full responsibility and hereby offer my resignation,” he added.
President Lee Jae Myung accepted his resignation, the presidential office said.
Asked during a parliamentary hearing on Monday whether he was confident that authorities could catch would-be cheaters on exam day, the 72-year-old Choi replied: “Due to my age, I am not confident I could.” His response quickly drew public backlash.
Choi did not appear at press conferences in the days leading up to Thursday’s exam, where a vice minister instead announced the preventive measures.
South Korea goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft take-offs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended. The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre.
In the aftermath of the cheating scandal earlier this month, the government announced that smart devices would have to be turned off and handed in for the suneung, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials would also inspect all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars, sleeves and buttons for concealed cameras.
The government also sent emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sounded at full volume and could not be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who has not handed in their device.
Officials said 111 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices were identified during Thursday’s exam, nearly half of which were detected through the emergency alerts.

According to a survey by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), severe anaemia was observed in less than 2% of people in the majority of age groups. The Survey for Assessment of Markers of Population Health, Activity, Diet and Anthropometry (SAMPADA) 2023-2025 was released on Monday (November 23, 2026).
It showed that children aged 12-59 months had 42% anaemia prevalence, adolescent girls aged 10-19 years had anaemia prevalence of 46%, adolescent boys aged 10-19 years and men aged 20–59 years had 22-23% anaemia prevalence, whereas women of reproductive age had 56% prevalence.
The survey also found that mild anaemia constitutes a substantial proportion of the overall anaemia burden.
“SAMPADA provides nationally representative estimates of anaemia across children, adolescents, adults, pregnant and lactating women and older adults, together with detailed information on micronutrient deficiencies to evaluate potential causes of anaemia. It is encouraging that prevalence of anaemia is lower in SAMPADA compared to previous national surveys. The comprehensive anaemia profiling in the SAMPADA survey provides an evidence base to strengthen the ongoing national efforts towards Anaemia Mukt Bharat,” said Rajiv Bahl, secretary, Department of Health Research.
The report noted that about half of anaemic women, including pregnant and lactating women, adolescent girls, and children, have mild anaemia, indicating considerably lower risk of serious health consequences than moderate or severe anaemia. Anaemia prevalence is much lower among adolescent boys, adult and older men, and even among those affected, three-fourths have only mild anaemia, said the release issued by the Union Health Ministry.
SAMPADA represents one of the largest and most comprehensive nutrition surveys undertaken globally. The survey covered more than 2 lakh individuals from over 81,000 households across 183 districts in 35 States and Union Territories. More than 1.7 lakh blood samples were analysed for haemoglobin estimation across different age, sex, and physiological groups.
“A major strength of SAMPADA is the use of gold standard method of venous blood sampling and automated analysers for haemoglobin estimation, providing greater accuracy and reproducibility. In a sub-sample, the survey also assessed iron status, folate, vitamin B12, together with inflammatory biomarkers C-reactive protein (CRP) and alpha-1-acid glycoprotein (AGP) to obtain national level prevalence estimates,” the release said.
Iron deficiency accounts for about half of the anaemia cases in women, adolescent girls, and children, said the report.
The micronutrient assessment showed that although iron deficiency is the predominant contributor to anaemia in vulnerable population groups, it accounts for about half of the overall anaemia burden, highlighting the need to simultaneously address multiple nutritional and non-nutritional causes of anaemia, including infections, hemoglobinopathies, and inflammation related to chronic disease.
However, the prevalence of vitamin B12 and folate deficiency was similar in both anaemic and non-anaemic individuals across population groups, indicating a limited contribution of these micronutrient deficiencies to anaemia in India.
Iron deficiency is concentrated in specific life-stages and in moderate and severe cases of anaemia. SAMPADA findings show that iron deficiency is largely restricted to population groups including under-five children, adolescent girls, and women of reproductive age, while adolescent boys, men, and the elderly have a low prevalence of iron deficiency. Importantly, people with moderate and severe anaemia have a high prevalence of iron deficiency and need to be identified by testing for appropriate treatment and tracking till resolution as envisaged in AMB 2.0.
“These findings support more targeted, population-specific and life-course approaches to anaemia prevention and management. The evidence can contribute, while also identifying areas where further research and improved surveillance are required,” said Bharati Kulkarni, director, ICMR-NIN.
